title: Accountants and auditors
claude_rationale: Accounting work is predominantly digital and cognitive, involving data analysis, financial reporting, and compliance checking - all areas where AI tools are already making significant impact by automating routine tasks like data entry, basic calculations, and standard report generation. However, the profession requires regulatory compliance, client interaction, strategic advisory work, and professional judgment that AI cannot fully replace. Demand elasticity is moderate because while cheaper accounting services could expand access for small businesses and enable more frequent financial analysis, growth is constrained by regulatory requirements, business formation rates, and the fact that most entities already have mandatory accounting needs. The occupation will survive but require substantial skill shifts toward advisory, analytical, and strategic roles as routine tasks become automated.
opus_rationale: Core accounting and auditing work — examining financial records, computing taxes, analyzing data, identifying risks, preparing reports — is overwhelmingly digital and cognitive, putting it directly in AI's path; routine tasks like data entry, reconciliation, and document review are already being automated by AI and RPA tools. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster financial analysis unlocks some latent demand (more small businesses get proper advisory services, more granular analysis, more frequent auditing), but core demand is structurally capped by regulatory requirements, the fixed number of entities needing audits, and the fact that compliance needs don't multiply with lower cost. The combination of very high disruption with moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but shifts decisively toward advisory, judgment, and client-facing roles while routine preparation work shrinks, requiring workers to substantially upskill — the hallmark of restructuring rather than wholesale replacement.
opus5_rationale: Accounting and auditing work is almost entirely digital and document-based: reconciling records, preparing tax returns, testing controls, drafting reports — all tasks squarely in AI's path, and already being automated via RPA, cloud platforms, and LLM-based document review. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper compliance means more small businesses and individuals get proper books, more continuous/full-population auditing replaces sampling, and advisory services expand, but statutory audit and filing requirements are fixed in volume and licensure plus regulatory sign-off caps unlimited growth. The result is a profession that persists but shifts sharply from preparation and verification toward exception handling, judgment, advisory, and AI oversight — with junior preparer roles thinning while credentialed advisors gain leverage. That combination of very high disruption with moderate demand expansion fits restructure rather than outright replacement.
openai_rationale: AI is already impacting accountants and auditors by automating routine tasks such as data entry and basic financial analysis, allowing professionals to focus more on advisory and analytical roles. This results in a high disruption score as AI tools become more integrated into their workflows. However, the demand elasticity is moderate because while AI can enhance productivity, the need for human judgment in complex decision-making and compliance with evolving regulations remains significant. Thus, the occupation will likely restructure, with a shift towards more strategic and consultative roles, requiring adaptation by the workforce.
gpt55_rationale: Accounting and auditing are heavily digital, rules-based, document-centered, and analytical, making many tasks such as transaction coding, reconciliations, tax preparation, audit sampling, anomaly detection, and report drafting highly exposed to AI and automation. However, the occupation still requires professional judgment, regulatory accountability, client communication, audit signoff, and interpretation of ambiguous business situations, so AI is more likely to transform workflows than eliminate the role outright. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper accounting can unlock more advisory services, better controls, and higher-quality analysis for small businesses and individuals, but many core needs such as annual audits, tax filings, and compliance cycles are structurally limited. This fits a restructure outcome: routine production work shrinks while accountants who can supervise AI, validate outputs, manage risk, and provide strategic advice remain valuable.
gpt56sol_rationale: Accounting is predominantly digital and rules-based, allowing AI to automate transaction classification, reconciliation, tax preparation, document review, anomaly detection, and portions of audit testing. Demand should expand moderately as lower costs make sophisticated accounting, compliance, risk analysis, and advisory services accessible to more small businesses, but statutory requirements and the finite number of entities limit expansion. The occupation will therefore restructure: fewer workers will perform routine preparation and testing, while greater emphasis shifts toward judgment, validation, client communication, regulatory accountability, and strategic advice.
fable5_rationale: Accounting work is predominantly digital and rule-based — examining financial records, computing taxes, preparing reports — placing core tasks squarely in AI's path, with tools already automating reconciliation, tax prep, and audit sampling; however, judgment-intensive work like forensic investigation, advisory, and CPA sign-off responsibilities temper the score. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper accounting unlocks latent demand from small businesses and individuals who currently forgo proper accounting and advisory services, but statutory requirements (audits, tax filings) represent largely fixed demand that won't multiply with lower cost. The occupation will survive but shift substantially from compliance and record-keeping toward advisory, analysis, and AI oversight, displacing workers who don't move up the value chain — a classic restructure profile.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on examining financial records, tax computation, risk analysis, report writing, and advisory recommendations—predominantly digital, cognitive, and language-based work where AI and RPA already automate routine bookkeeping and data processing while assisting higher-level analysis. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs can unlock more professional services for small businesses and individuals, yet regulatory mandates (audits, tax filings, SEC requirements) and structural caps keep overall volume from expanding dramatically. This combination produces restructure: the occupation persists but shifts heavily toward judgment, client advisory, and AI oversight, so non-adapters face displacement while adaptable workers thrive.

title: Actors
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts acting through deepfakes, digital doubles, voice synthesis, and virtual performers that can handle certain roles, especially background work, commercials, and some lead roles in digital media. However, the core human elements of live performance, authentic emotional expression, and audience connection remain largely irreplaceable. Demand elasticity is moderate - while cheaper digital actors could expand content creation in some areas (like personalized content, indie films, or interactive media), traditional entertainment demand is somewhat constrained by audience attention and cultural factors, though new formats may emerge.
opus_rationale: Acting's core involves physical, embodied performance and the human appeal of recognizable performers, which AI cannot fully replicate, but AI is encroaching on voiceover, background/extra work, digital doubles, and synthetic media — pushing disruption to a moderate level. Demand for content is somewhat elastic as cheaper production unlocks more video and media, but the value of human celebrity and live performance caps how much AI productivity translates into more human acting work. Because the disruption score sits at or below 6 and the human-presence core remains intact, the occupation is best categorized as resilient, with AI eroding certain subfields (extras, voiceover) rather than reshaping the central craft.
opus5_rationale: The core of acting is embodied, in-person performance — auditions, rehearsals, live stage work, theme-park shows, on-set camera work under a director — which AI does not perform for the worker; AI instead threatens substitution in specific digital-output subfields (voiceover, narration, background extras, digital doubles and likeness replication), which is significant but not the majority of the occupation's work. That mix of largely physical/presence-based tasks with a meaningful digitally-replicable slice puts disruption at the top of the moderate band rather than high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper production budgets do expand total content and live entertainment output, but much of the AI-driven cost reduction bypasses human performers entirely, and live venue capacity and audience attention cap growth. With disruption at 6, the occupation classifies as resilient — the theatrical, live, and star-driven core persists, though voice and background-performer niches will contract and workers will increasingly negotiate over likeness and performance-capture rights.
openai_rationale: AI can potentially disrupt the acting profession by generating digital characters or enhancing visual effects, but the core of acting involves human creativity, emotional expression, and physical presence, which are difficult for AI to fully replicate. Thus, the disruption is moderate. Demand elasticity is moderate as well; while AI could make production cheaper and faster, the unique appeal of human actors and the limited capacity for audiences to consume more content restricts massive demand expansion. Overall, the occupation is resilient, as AI will augment rather than replace the human element in acting.
gpt55_rationale: Acting has an embodied, interpersonal, and live-performance component that AI cannot fully replicate, especially in theater, theme parks, and high-status screen roles. However, a large share of recorded-media work—voiceover, dubbing, extras, commercials, background performances, synthetic avatars, and some low-budget screen acting—is directly exposed to generative audio and video tools, making disruption high. Demand could expand as cheaper production enables more ads, games, training videos, localization, and niche entertainment, but audience attention, celebrity economics, union rules, and preference for human performers limit how much of that expansion becomes employment for actors. The occupation is therefore likely to be substantially restructured, with more value placed on distinctive human performance, likeness rights, live work, and hybrid AI-production skills.
gpt56sol_rationale: Generative video, synthetic voices, digital likenesses, and automated dubbing directly threaten voiceover work, extras, and some screen roles while also changing auditions and production workflows. Live theater, interactive performances, celebrity appeal, and roles requiring authentic ensemble interaction remain comparatively resistant, keeping disruption below the highest levels. Cheaper production could generate more localized, personalized, and niche entertainment, but limited audience attention and production budgets constrain how much of that expansion will employ human actors. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around distinctive human performance, live work, and likeness management rather than disappear altogether.
fable5_rationale: Much of acting output is delivered as digital media — film, TV, voiceover, commercials, and background/extra work — all of which generative AI video and voice synthesis can increasingly produce without human performers; BLS itself flags AI replacement in subfields. Live theater and theme park performance retains an irreplaceable human-presence premium, but that covers only a minority of roles, keeping disruption at the high end. Elasticity for human actors is low: while cheaper production will expand total content volume, that expanded content will disproportionately use synthetic performers rather than hiring more humans, and audience demand for named, authentic human stars is concentrated among a small elite rather than the broad workforce. High disruption plus limited demand absorption for human performers points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.
grok45_rationale: Actors’ core daily work requires physical presence, live or on-camera embodiment of characters, emotional authenticity, memorization under performance conditions, and real-time collaboration with directors and cast—tasks that remain predominantly non-digital and presence-dependent; AI currently assists only peripheral elements such as script analysis, digital extras, or voice synthesis and is not yet close to replacing high-quality human performance across theater, film, and live venues. Demand elasticity is high because entertainment output is strongly cost-constrained: dramatically cheaper production would expand the volume of films, series, ads, games, and experiential content, creating more total roles even after some substitution. With only moderate disruption to core tasks, the occupation remains resilient overall—AI alters industry economics and certain subfields without reshaping the fundamental human performance work.

title: Actuaries
claude_rationale: Actuaries work primarily with data analysis, statistical modeling, and risk assessment - all core AI capabilities that are rapidly advancing. AI can already perform sophisticated statistical analysis, pattern recognition in large datasets, and predictive modeling that forms the foundation of actuarial work. However, demand for actuarial services is relatively inelastic because insurance needs are largely fixed by regulatory requirements, population demographics, and existing business structures - companies don't suddenly need 10x more risk assessments just because they become cheaper to produce. The combination of high AI disruption potential with constrained demand expansion suggests significant headcount reduction as AI tools enable fewer actuaries to handle the same workload.
opus_rationale: Actuarial work is predominantly digital and cognitive—statistical modeling, data analysis, forecasting, and report generation—which are squarely in AI's path, driving a high disruption score. However, demand elasticity is low because the volume of insurance products, regulatory filings, and risk assessments is structurally and regulatorily constrained; cheaper actuarial output does not unlock dramatically more demand, and certification requirements gate the role rather than expand its scope. While BLS projects strong nominal growth, AI productivity gains are likely to compress per-task headcount needs, so the combination of high disruption and limited demand expansion fits the replace category, though strong projected growth and the heavy communication/judgment component may soften the contraction toward restructuring.
opus5_rationale: Actuarial work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — compiling and cleaning data, building statistical and stochastic models, running reserve and pricing calculations, coding in R/Python/SQL, and writing explanatory reports — all of which sit directly in the path of current AI and ML tooling. Predictive modeling is increasingly performed by data science pipelines and automated model-governance tools, and LLMs already accelerate the documentation, memo-writing, and exam-level technical reasoning that consume much of a junior actuary's time; the residual human core is professional judgment, regulatory sign-off, and stakeholder communication. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: the number of insurance products, reserve filings, pension plans, and rate submissions is structurally bounded by the number of insurers, regulators, and statutory reporting cycles, so 10x cheaper modeling mostly means more granular analysis per filing rather than 10x more filings. High disruption combined with capped, regulation-bound demand points to headcount contraction relative to output — particularly at the trainee/data-compilation tier — even though credentialing requirements will slow the adjustment and keep senior signing actuaries valuable.
openai_rationale: Actuaries primarily engage in knowledge work involving statistical analysis, risk assessment, and financial modeling, which AI can assist with but not fully automate due to the complexity and need for human judgment. AI tools can enhance efficiency in data analysis and modeling, but the core tasks still require human oversight and decision-making. Demand elasticity is low because the need for actuarial services is driven by regulatory and industry-specific requirements, which do not expand proportionally with cost reductions. Thus, while AI will augment actuaries' capabilities, it is unlikely to significantly reduce headcount, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: Actuarial work is highly digital and analytical: compiling data, building statistical models, pricing products, calculating reserves, writing reports, and explaining results are all tasks that AI can substantially accelerate. Human actuaries will still be needed for regulatory accountability, professional judgment, assumptions governance, and communication with executives and regulators, but much of the junior and mid-level modeling, coding, documentation, and scenario analysis is directly exposed. Demand for actuarial analysis may expand somewhat as firms model more risks, personalize insurance products, and use enterprise risk management more broadly, but insurance regulation, required sign-offs, and the limited number of pricing/reserving decisions constrain expansion. Because disruption is high and elasticity is relatively low, productivity gains are likely to reduce the number of actuaries needed for many routine analytical functions, even if senior credentialed roles remain important.
gpt56sol_rationale: Actuarial work is predominantly digital and analytical, including data preparation, statistical modeling, forecasting, policy testing, and report production—all tasks increasingly accelerated by AI. Demand may expand as new risks, data sources, and insurance products emerge, but regulation, certification requirements, market size, and the limited need for repeated formal risk assessments constrain how much additional output will be consumed. Human judgment, communication, model validation, and professional accountability remain important, but substantial productivity gains are likely to reduce staffing needs per portfolio, making replace the best fit.
fable5_rationale: Actuarial work is almost entirely digital and cognitive—compiling data, statistical modeling, pricing risk, and writing reports—all squarely in AI's path, with modern ML already outperforming traditional actuarial models in many pricing and reserving tasks. Demand elasticity is low: the volume of insurance policies, pensions, and regulatory filings requiring actuarial analysis is driven by market size and regulation, not by the cost of actuarial labor, so 10x cheaper analysis mostly means fewer analysts per book of business rather than 10x more risk assessment (though some expansion in enterprise risk management and new insurance products exists). Professional certification requirements and regulatory sign-off obligations will slow displacement and preserve a senior credentialed core, but junior analytical headcount is vulnerable. High disruption combined with low-to-moderate elasticity places this in the replace category, despite BLS's optimistic projection which predates full accounting of generative AI capabilities.
grok45_rationale: Actuaries' core work—compiling data, statistical modeling of risk probabilities and costs, designing policies, calculating reserves, and generating reports—is almost entirely digital, quantitative, and language-based, placing it squarely in AI's path; modern ML and generative tools already accelerate forecasting, scenario testing, and documentation. Demand elasticity is low because the volume of insurance products, regulatory filings, and enterprise risk assessments is constrained by market size, regulation, and fixed institutional needs rather than analysis cost; cheaper actuarial output does not unlock 10x more policies or risk studies. High disruption combined with limited demand expansion therefore implies significant headcount contraction as AI absorbs routine modeling and junior analytical tasks.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
claude_rationale: Administrative services and facilities managers have moderate disruption potential as AI can assist with data analysis, scheduling, compliance monitoring, and some administrative tasks, but the core work requires physical oversight of facilities, staff management, and real-world problem-solving that demands human presence and judgment. Demand elasticity is low because organizations have relatively fixed needs for facility management and administrative oversight - making these services 10x cheaper wouldn't cause companies to dramatically expand their office space or administrative infrastructure. Since disruption is at the boundary (6) but doesn't reach the high threshold of 7+, this occupation falls into the resilient category where AI enhances some tasks but doesn't fundamentally reshape the role.
opus_rationale: The role mixes significant knowledge work (records management, procurement analysis, scheduling, compliance documentation) that AI can streamline with substantial physical-presence and human-coordination duties — supervising maintenance staff, monitoring buildings, handling on-call emergencies, and managing renovation projects. AI will automate the administrative and recordkeeping portions but cannot replace the oversight of physical facilities and people management, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is structurally tied to the number of buildings and organizations needing management rather than to cost suppression, so productivity gains mostly reduce per-manager workload rather than unlocking large latent demand, yielding low elasticity. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes peripheral tasks but not the core supervisory and facilities-oversight work.
opus5_rationale: The role mixes substantial knowledge work — scheduling, vendor contracts, procurement, records and information management, compliance documentation, energy/space analytics — much of which AI and smart-building software can automate or accelerate, pushing disruption toward the high end. But the core of the job is physical-world oversight: walking facilities, supervising maintenance and janitorial staff, handling emergencies on call, negotiating with contractors, and answering to regulators, all of which requires human presence and accountability. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate: the amount of building space, staff, and records an organization has is fixed by its physical footprint, so cheaper administration does not create dramatically more facilities to manage, though span-of-control could widen. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands in the resilient band — AI reshapes the administrative and records-heavy periphery (and may thin out clerical support beneath these managers) without displacing the supervisory, on-site core.
openai_rationale: Administrative services and facilities managers engage in a mix of tasks, including supervision, compliance, and maintenance oversight, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist with data management and operational efficiency, the core tasks require human judgment and presence. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could enhance efficiency, the need for human oversight in compliance and facility management limits dramatic demand expansion. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing core functions.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially change the administrative, records, compliance, procurement, scheduling, reporting, and energy-analysis portions of this occupation, and AI-enabled building systems can support predictive maintenance and monitoring. However, much of facilities management still requires onsite judgment, vendor coordination, staff supervision, emergency response, inspections, and accountability for safety and regulatory compliance in physical spaces. Demand elasticity is limited because organizations do not need dramatically more facilities management simply because it becomes cheaper; demand is tied to the number, size, and complexity of buildings and organizations. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to fully reshape the physical and managerial core of the job, the occupation fits the resilient category.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially improve records management, compliance tracking, procurement, scheduling, energy analysis, reporting, and preventive-maintenance planning. However, supervising staff, inspecting facilities, coordinating contractors, handling emergencies, and bearing responsibility for safety and regulatory compliance still require substantial human judgment and real-world presence. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations will not need proportionally more facilities or administrative oversight when management becomes cheaper, but the occupation remains resilient because disruption does not fully reach its physical and interpersonal core.
fable5_rationale: The knowledge-work portions—recordkeeping, scheduling, compliance documentation, procurement tracking, and records/information management—are squarely in AI's path and already being automated, but core duties like supervising staff, physically monitoring building safety, overseeing maintenance crews, and responding on-call to facility emergencies require human presence and judgment on the ground. Elasticity is low because organizations need a roughly fixed amount of facilities oversight tied to their physical footprint; making administration 10x cheaper doesn't mean companies consume 10x more facilities management, and productivity gains likely mean fewer administrative managers per organization. With moderate disruption concentrated in the admin/records side and demand largely tied to building stock rather than cost, the occupation is resilient overall, though records and information managers specifically face restructuring pressure.
grok45_rationale: Core duties blend knowledge work (policy recommendations, energy analysis, records management, compliance planning) that AI already assists via predictive tools and automation with irreducible physical presence for facility inspections, staff supervision, on-site maintenance oversight, and emergency response, producing only moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster management could unlock some latent demand for better energy efficiency, security, and records practices across more organizations, yet overall headcount remains constrained by the relatively fixed stock of buildings and firms. The combination keeps the occupation resilient: AI changes tools and peripheral efficiency but does not displace the human-centered core.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts the knowledge-work portions of teaching through personalized learning platforms, automated assessment, and adaptive curriculum delivery, but core human elements like cultural sensitivity, motivation, and one-on-one support remain essential. Demand elasticity is high because adult education is currently constrained by cost and accessibility - AI-powered tools could dramatically expand access to basic education, ESL instruction, and GED preparation for underserved populations globally. While AI will transform how these teachers work, the massive latent demand for affordable adult education means employment could grow despite productivity gains.
opus_rationale: The core work involves in-person instruction, motivating adult learners, cultural sensitivity, and adapting to diverse abilities — tasks requiring human presence and interpersonal judgment that AI cannot fully replace, though AI tutoring tools materially assist lesson planning, language practice, and individualized instruction, placing disruption at the moderate-to-high boundary. Demand has some latent elasticity since cheaper personalized language and literacy instruction could expand access, but structural factors like declining enrollment, government funding constraints, and the social/motivational nature of these classroom programs cap that growth at moderate. Because the disruption score lands at 6 — AI augments planning and practice but does not reshape the human-centered core of teaching adult learners — this occupation fits the resilient category rather than restructure.
opus5_rationale: The instructional core here — teaching reading, writing, math, and conversational English, generating leveled lesson plans, assessing progress, and drilling practical vocabulary — is exactly the language- and cognitive-work that LLMs and AI tutoring apps already do competently and at near-zero marginal cost, so disruption is high even though some in-person motivation, cultural mediation, and case-management work remains human. Elasticity is low because demand for these programs is not price-suppressed in the usual sense: enrollment is set by government funding formulas, declining numbers of adults lacking a high school credential, and learners' willingness to attend scheduled classes, and any latent demand for cheap language learning is likely captured by self-serve AI apps rather than by hiring more teachers. With high task exposure and structurally capped, funding-dependent, already-shrinking demand (BLS projects -14%), productivity gains convert into fewer instructor positions per program rather than expanded service. That combination — disruption >= 7 with elasticity <= 4 — places it in the replace category.
openai_rationale: AI can assist adult education and ESL teachers by providing tools for personalized learning, language translation, and progress tracking, which moderately disrupts the occupation. However, the core tasks of teaching, adapting to individual student needs, and cultural sensitivity require human interaction and judgment, limiting AI's impact. Demand elasticity is low because the number of adults seeking basic education or ESL services is not significantly suppressed by cost, and societal factors like high school graduation rates and government funding heavily influence demand. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing teachers.
gpt55_rationale: Much of this occupation is language-based and cognitive: lesson planning, explaining concepts, grading, progress monitoring, individualized practice, and ESL conversation support are all areas where AI tutors and adaptive learning tools are already useful. However, teachers still provide motivation, classroom management, cultural sensitivity, assessment of nonacademic barriers, and connections to community resources, which keeps disruption below the most automatable digital occupations. Demand could expand because cheaper personalized instruction would help adults who cannot attend scheduled classes or afford tutoring, especially ESL learners, but growth is limited by public funding, student time constraints, credentialing needs, and declining adult education enrollment. The result is a substantial shift in the teacher role toward facilitation, coaching, assessment, and support rather than straightforward replacement, so the net effect is restructure.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can already generate lessons, translate explanations, assess proficiency, provide conversational practice, and personalize exercises, materially changing much of teachers’ instructional and administrative work. Human teachers remain important for motivation, cultural sensitivity, classroom management, disability recognition, and connecting vulnerable learners with community resources. Demand is highly elastic because inexpensive, individualized instruction could reach many adults currently excluded by cost, scheduling, geography, or limited program capacity, so expanded access should absorb substantial productivity gains and make augmentation more likely than replacement.
fable5_rationale: The core work — language instruction, lesson planning, assessment, and personalized practice — is precisely what AI tutoring systems now do well, and ESL/literacy instruction is among the most directly substitutable teaching domains since apps already deliver adaptive language learning at near-zero cost. While latent demand for language learning and basic skills is enormous, that demand is increasingly captured by AI tutors and apps directly rather than by hiring more human teachers, and the occupation depends on shrinking public funding and declining enrollment (BLS already projects -14%). The classroom presence and community-connection elements provide some resilience, but they don't anchor enough of the job to offset substitution. High disruption combined with demand that flows to software rather than headcount makes this a replace scenario.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks such as lesson planning, content creation, assessment, progress monitoring, and adaptive instruction are predominantly cognitive and language-based, already materially assisted by AI tools and adaptive platforms for basic skills and ESL, placing the occupation in the high-disruption range even though real-time classroom facilitation, cultural sensitivity, and student motivation still require human presence. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs and greater personalization can unlock additional participation among immigrants, low-literacy adults, and workforce-development programs, yet expansion is constrained by declining GED need from higher high-school graduation rates, public funding limits, and a finite population requiring these credentials. The combination produces restructuring: the role shifts toward AI-orchestrated facilitation, high-touch coaching, and resource navigation, so adaptable teachers remain valuable while pure content-delivery headcount contracts.

title: Advertising sales agents
claude_rationale: Advertising sales involves predominantly cognitive tasks like client research, proposal creation, presentation development, and relationship management that AI can increasingly automate or significantly enhance. AI tools already assist with lead generation, personalized outreach, proposal writing, and market analysis. The elasticity is low because advertising budgets are typically fixed or constrained by business revenue - companies don't dramatically increase advertising spend just because sales processes become more efficient. The existing 6% projected decline in employment reflects structural shifts toward automated digital ad placement, confirming that productivity gains won't translate to expanded demand for human sales agents.
opus_rationale: The work is predominantly digital and language-based — prospecting, drafting proposals, preparing reports, analyzing sales statistics, and ad placement — much of which is already being automated by programmatic ad-buying platforms and AI-assisted CRM/outreach tools, driving high disruption. Demand elasticity is low: advertising budgets are constrained by client revenue and marketing spend, and the shift to automated programmatic ad placement directly removes the human intermediary rather than expanding the need for agents, as reflected in the BLS -6% projection. Productivity gains accrue to platforms and tools rather than unlocking dramatically more human-sold ad inventory. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 4, headcount contraction is the expected outcome, fitting the replace category.
opus5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — prospecting, gathering client background, drafting proposals and media kits, preparing cost estimates and contracts, analyzing sales statistics, follow-up correspondence — are digital and language-based, and AI plus programmatic self-serve ad platforms already automate much of the workflow, so disruption is very high even though relationship selling retains a human element. Elasticity is low because total ad spend is bounded by advertisers' marketing budgets rather than by the cost of a salesperson; when ad buying gets cheaper and easier, spend migrates to automated auction platforms that require no agent at all rather than expanding the number of agents. The structural shift from print to programmatic digital is already driving BLS-projected declines, and AI accelerates the disintermediation. High disruption with inelastic, already-shrinking demand puts this squarely in the replace category.
openai_rationale: Advertising sales agents face high disruption as AI and digital tools increasingly automate tasks like client targeting, ad placement, and performance analysis. The shift towards digital advertising reduces the need for traditional sales roles. Elasticity is low because while digital advertising is growing, it doesn't require a proportional increase in sales agents due to automation efficiencies. Thus, the net effect is 'replace' as AI absorbs core tasks and demand does not expand sufficiently to maintain headcount.
gpt55_rationale: Advertising sales agents perform highly language- and information-based work: prospecting, writing outreach, preparing pitches, generating proposals, recommending ad formats, maintaining CRM records, and analyzing account performance. AI and automated ad platforms can already handle much of lead generation, campaign recommendation, proposal drafting, reporting, and self-service ad placement, although human relationship-building and complex negotiations remain important for larger accounts. Demand for advertising is not fixed, but it is constrained by client budgets, available attention, and measurable ROI; cheaper sales support may help small advertisers somewhat but will not create proportionate demand for human agents. Because disruption is high and elasticity is relatively low, AI is likely to reduce headcount while leaving a smaller group focused on strategic relationship management and complex accounts.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can automate prospect research, lead scoring, outreach, proposal generation, pricing, reporting, account administration, and much of digital ad placement. Human persuasion, negotiation, and relationship management remain important for complex or high-value accounts, but a large share of routine sales activity is directly exposed. Demand expansion is limited by advertisers’ budgets, finite consumer attention, and the growing use of self-service advertising platforms, so cheaper sales work will not produce a proportional increase in agents. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to replacement and significant headcount contraction.
fable5_rationale: The core workflow — prospecting, drafting proposals and contracts, preparing sales presentations, pricing estimates, and account correspondence — is digital and language-based, squarely in AI's path; moreover, programmatic ad platforms already automate ad placement itself, disintermediating the human sales role for a growing share of the market. Elasticity is low because total ad spending is set by client marketing budgets, not by the cost of the sales intermediary; making agents 10x more productive doesn't cause businesses to buy meaningfully more advertising, it just means fewer agents (or self-serve platforms) handle the same spend. BLS already projects a 6% decline before accounting for accelerating AI capabilities. High disruption combined with inelastic demand points clearly to replacement, with residual human roles concentrated in complex, high-value relationship accounts.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks such as client research, proposal and media-kit preparation, sales analytics, contract drafting, and personalized outreach are predominantly digital/cognitive and already materially assisted by AI tools, while relationship-building and closing remain human but are heavily augmented; this places the role in the high-disruption band. Demand for advertising sales labor is largely inelastic because total ad budgets and the shift to programmatic/self-serve platforms constrain volume; 10x productivity gains therefore translate into fewer agents rather than proportionally more advertising sold. The combination of high disruption and low elasticity produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the already-projected decline.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
claude_rationale: Marketing and advertising managers face high disruption as AI transforms core tasks like market research, campaign optimization, content creation, and data analysis - areas that are predominantly digital and cognitive. AI tools already materially assist with audience targeting, A/B testing, creative generation, and performance analytics. However, demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster, and more precise marketing capabilities unlock significant latent demand - small businesses can access sophisticated marketing previously available only to large corporations, and the explosion of digital channels creates more opportunities for targeted campaigns. The net effect is augmentation as productivity gains enable each manager to handle more campaigns and clients rather than reducing headcount.
opus_rationale: Marketing management is predominantly knowledge work—campaign planning, content strategy, market analysis, copy generation, ad placement, and audience segmentation are all directly in AI's path, with generative AI and automated ad platforms already materially changing daily workflows. However, marketing demand is highly elastic: cheaper and faster content production, personalization, and analytics unlock vastly more campaigns, channels, micro-segments, and continuous optimization that were previously cost-prohibitive. Because productivity gains expand the total volume of marketing output rather than simply reducing headcount, demand absorbs the disruption, and the managerial layer (strategy, judgment, client relationships, brand stewardship) remains essential to direct AI tools. This fits 'augment'—each manager produces far more output while overall employment stays stable or grows.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language/analysis-based — campaign planning, copy and creative direction, media buying optimization, market research synthesis, pricing analysis, and performance reporting are all squarely in AI's path, and generative AI plus automated ad platforms already reshape day-to-day workflow. Elasticity is high because marketing output is highly cost-suppressed: cheaper creative and analytics unlock far more personalized campaigns, more variants, more channels, more segments, and marketing for smaller firms that previously could not afford it, while competitive dynamics mean rivals must match spending. Headcount for the managerial/strategic layer should hold or grow even as the supporting production and ad-placement roles compress, though pure advertising and promotions managers tied to legacy print/media buying face contraction. Net effect is augment: each manager orchestrates dramatically more output, with the skill mix shifting toward AI-tool fluency, data interpretation, and brand judgment.

gpt56sol_rationale: Most core tasks involve physical labor, dexterity, machinery operation, and work with crops or animals in variable outdoor environments, placing them beyond the direct reach of current generative AI. AI-enabled precision agriculture, autonomous equipment, robotic harvesting, and livestock monitoring will automate selected tasks, but deployment costs and difficult real-world conditions will limit occupation-wide disruption over the next decade. Demand is highly inelastic because food consumption will not rise proportionally if agricultural labor becomes much cheaper, while land, water, and biological constraints further limit output expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient under the scoring framework, although conventional labor roles may gradually shift toward operating and servicing automated equipment.
fable5_rationale: Agricultural work is overwhelmingly physical — planting, harvesting, herding, lifting, and machine operation in unpredictable outdoor environments — where language-model AI has little direct reach; the relevant threat is robotics and mechanization, which proceeds slowly and mainly shifts labor toward equipment operation rather than AI-driven task replacement. Demand for food is fundamentally inelastic — cheaper farm labor does not make people consume dramatically more agricultural output, so productivity gains from automation translate into fewer field workers, as BLS's projected decline reflects. AI may assist peripherally with crop monitoring, breeding records, and precision agriculture planning, but the core hands-on labor is untouched. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient to AI specifically, even though long-run mechanization pressures headcount.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical, manual, and outdoors—planting, harvesting, herding, cleaning pens, and operating machinery in unstructured environments—so AI and robotics assist mainly via precision tools, sensors, or autonomous equipment rather than replacing daily labor. Demand for agricultural output is highly inelastic; cheaper or faster production does not lead society to consume dramatically more food or livestock products, so productivity gains historically and prospectively shrink headcount. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate, the occupation stays resilient even as some tasks become more automated.

title: Air traffic controllers
claude_rationale: Air traffic control involves significant cognitive work (monitoring radar, making quick decisions, coordinating multiple aircraft) that AI could potentially assist with, but the core responsibility requires real-time human judgment for safety-critical decisions in unpredictable situations with human lives at stake. The work is heavily regulated and requires immediate physical presence in control towers and facilities. Demand for air traffic control is essentially fixed by the number of flights and airports - even if AI made controllers 10x more efficient, we wouldn't suddenly have 10x more air traffic, and safety regulations would likely maintain minimum staffing requirements regardless of technological capabilities.
opus_rationale: Air traffic control is heavily cognitive and data-driven, and AI/automation systems like NextGen already increase per-controller capacity, suggesting meaningful disruption to workflow. However, the core work involves real-time, life-safety decision-making under strict regulatory accountability where full automation is socially and legally constrained, keeping humans firmly in the loop and capping disruption at moderate. Demand is highly inelastic — the number of flights to coordinate is fixed by air traffic volume, not by the cost or speed of control services, so productivity gains translate into modestly more traffic handled per controller rather than expanded demand. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the role's safety-critical human-in-the-loop nature is durable, this occupation is resilient.
opus5_rationale: The core work is cognitive and screen-mediated — monitoring radar, sequencing aircraft, computing separations — which is nominally in AI's path, and decision-support automation (conflict detection, NextGen trajectory-based routing, digital tower/remote tower systems) is already increasing per-controller throughput. But the safety-critical, real-time, legally mandated human-in-the-loop nature of the job, plus FAA certification rules, union structures, and extreme verification burden for any autonomous system, means the core task of holding responsibility for live traffic will not transfer to AI within a decade; AI shifts controllers toward supervisory and exception-handling roles rather than replacing them. Elasticity is low because demand is a direct function of flight volume and airspace/airport capacity, not the cost of controller labor — cheaper control does not induce many more flights, and staffing is set by regulatory minimums per sector and facility. With disruption at 5 the occupation lands in the resilient category: AI reshapes the tooling and raises per-controller capacity (capping growth, as BLS already notes), but does not reshape the fundamental job.
openai_rationale: Air traffic control involves a mix of digital and cognitive tasks, such as monitoring radar screens and communicating with pilots, which AI can assist with but not fully automate due to the need for real-time decision-making and human judgment in unpredictable situations. AI can enhance efficiency by aiding in data analysis and traffic prediction, but human oversight remains crucial for safety. Demand elasticity is low because the number of flights is not highly sensitive to the cost of air traffic control; thus, productivity gains from AI are unlikely to significantly increase the number of controllers needed. Overall, while AI may augment certain tasks, the core responsibilities and demand for human controllers remain stable, making the occupation resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: Air traffic control is highly cognitive, real-time, and screen/radio-mediated, with core tasks such as monitoring aircraft, detecting conflicts, sequencing traffic, and issuing clearances all in the path of advanced automation and AI decision-support systems. However, safety certification, liability, and the need for human oversight in abnormal situations will slow full substitution, so the disruption score is high but not maximal. Demand elasticity is low because the number of controllers needed is tied mainly to flight volumes, airport capacity, and regulation; cheaper controller labor would not cause society to fly several times more. Given high disruption and low elasticity, AI-enabled productivity would mostly reduce staffing needs over time rather than unlock enough new demand to offset displacement.
gpt56sol_rationale: The work is predominantly digital, cognitive, and communications-based, making conflict detection, routing, clearances, monitoring, and handoffs increasingly amenable to AI-assisted automation. Safety-critical edge cases, regulatory requirements, and the need for accountable human judgment will slow full autonomy, but controllers may supervise substantially more traffic with automated support. Demand for controllers is tied mainly to flight volume rather than the cost of control services, so cheaper processing would generate little additional demand. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to replacement pressure and gradual headcount contraction, even if humans remain in the loop.
fable5_rationale: Air traffic control is fully cognitive and digital in nature, which puts it theoretically in AI's path, but extreme safety-criticality, FAA certification requirements, legal accountability for human decision-making, and the decades-long timeline of aviation system upgrades (as seen with NextGen) mean AI will function as decision-support rather than replacing the human-in-the-loop within 10 years. Demand elasticity is very low: the number of controllers needed is driven by air traffic volume and airspace structure, not the cost of controller labor, so productivity gains (like NextGen already demonstrates) simply let each controller handle more traffic rather than expanding total demand. BLS projections of just 1% growth despite rising air traffic confirm that efficiency gains suppress headcount rather than expand output. With moderate disruption capped by regulation and safety culture, the occupation is resilient over the 10-year horizon, though longer-term automation pressure is real.
grok45_rationale: Core ATC work mixes digital monitoring, cognitive decision-making, and radio communication with an absolute requirement for real-time human presence, judgment under uncertainty, and regulatory accountability; AI already supplies decision-support tools (conflict prediction, trajectory optimization, NextGen) that raise productivity but leave final clearances and emergency handling with controllers, placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand for controllers is tightly coupled to flight volume, which expands only gradually and is constrained by airport capacity, airspace rules, and safety certification; productivity gains therefore translate mainly into higher traffic handled per controller rather than large headcount growth. Because disruption remains at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes tools and throughput but does not displace the core human role.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
claude_rationale: This occupation scores low on disruption because the core work is predominantly hands-on physical maintenance, repair, and inspection of aircraft components that requires direct manipulation of mechanical systems, working in uncomfortable positions, and real-world problem-solving with safety-critical equipment. While AI might assist with some diagnostic data interpretation or maintenance scheduling, the fundamental tasks of physically repairing engines, replacing parts, and conducting safety inspections cannot be automated. Elasticity is low because aircraft maintenance demand is largely fixed by regulatory requirements, fleet size, and flight hours - even if AI made diagnostics faster, the same number of aircraft still need the same physical maintenance cycles. The net effect is resilient because AI touches only peripheral aspects like documentation or diagnostic assistance while leaving the core mechanical work unchanged.
opus_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, inspection, and maintenance of aircraft requiring dexterity, physical strength, and in-person presence in hangars and on airfields — tasks largely outside AI's direct reach. AI may assist with diagnostics, predictive maintenance scheduling, and interpreting test data, but these are peripheral aids that don't replace the manual labor or FAA-regulated certification requirements. Demand is structurally tied to fleet size and flight hours and is heavily constrained by safety regulation, so productivity gains wouldn't dramatically expand the volume of physical maintenance needed. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery while the regulated, physical core remains intact.
opus5_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, inspection, and component replacement in hangars and on airfields, requiring dexterity, physical presence, and FAA-certified human accountability. AI can improve predictive maintenance analytics, diagnostic support, documentation/recordkeeping, and manual/technical-reference lookup, but these are peripheral to turning wrenches and signing off airworthiness. Demand is driven by fleet size, flight hours, and regulation-mandated maintenance schedules, so cheaper diagnostics only modestly expands work (some latent deferred maintenance, growing space sector), not 10x. With low disruption to core tasks and heavy regulatory anchoring, the occupation is resilient.
openai_rationale: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians perform tasks that are predominantly physical and hands-on, such as repairing and inspecting aircraft components, which limits the impact of AI on their core tasks. While AI can assist with diagnostics and maintenance scheduling, the physical nature of the work and strict regulatory requirements mean disruption is low. Demand elasticity is also low because the need for maintenance is driven by the number of aircraft and regulatory requirements, not cost. Thus, even if AI increases productivity, it won't significantly expand demand. The occupation remains resilient due to the essential and regulated nature of the work.
gpt55_rationale: AI can materially assist the diagnostic and documentation portions of this occupation, including troubleshooting avionics faults, interpreting maintenance manuals, analyzing sensor data, and generating records. However, the core work remains hands-on, safety-critical, site-specific repair, inspection, installation, and testing of physical aircraft systems under FAA certification requirements, so AI is unlikely to absorb most daily tasks within 10 years. Demand is only modestly elastic because maintenance is tied to fleet size, flight activity, and regulatory schedules rather than discretionary consumption, though cheaper diagnostics and reduced downtime could support some additional aviation activity. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and the physical, regulated core persists, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will improve fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, interpretation of technical manuals and flight data, parts identification, and recordkeeping. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will enhance technicians' productivity without replacing most hands-on duties.
fable5_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — replacing parts, soldering, torquing bolts, inspecting airframes — which AI cannot perform; AI mainly assists with diagnostics, predictive maintenance scheduling, and documentation lookup, so disruption is low. grok45_rationale: Core work is predominantly physical and hands-on—diagnosing then repairing/replacing aircraft components with tools, climbing, inspecting in hangars or on airfields under strict FAA rules—so AI assists only knowledge portions like predictive diagnostics, data interpretation, manuals, and records rather than reshaping the occupation. claude_rationale: While AI assists with flight planning, weather analysis, and navigation systems, the core piloting tasks remain fundamentally physical and require real-time human judgment for safety-critical decisions, emergency response, and aircraft control. Current autopilot technology handles routine flight phases but pilots must actively monitor systems and take control during takeoffs, landings, and emergencies. Demand elasticity is low because air travel is largely driven by economic factors and route capacity rather than pilot costs, and regulatory requirements mandate human pilots for passenger safety. The occupation remains resilient as AI enhances existing systems rather than replacing the essential human oversight role.
opus_rationale: While modern aircraft are heavily automated and AI can enhance flight planning, autopilot, and systems monitoring, the core work of piloting requires physical presence in the cockpit, real-time judgment in emergencies, and—critically—deep regulatory and safety/liability constraints that mandate certified human pilots for the next decade and beyond. Passenger trust and FAA certification requirements make full autonomy implausible within 10 years, so AI touches only the periphery (planning, monitoring, copilot assistance). Demand for air travel is moderately elastic—cheaper operations could expand routes and frequency—but pilot headcount per flight is regulated and unlikely to compress significantly. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI augments tools but does not reshape the fundamental human-in-the-loop nature of flying.
opus5_rationale: Flying is already heavily automated in cruise, but the core job — physical presence in the cockpit, hands-on takeoff/landing, preflight inspection, real-time judgment in emergencies, and legal command responsibility — is protected by deep FAA certification requirements and public/regulatory resistance to reduced-crew or autonomous passenger flight. AI over the next decade will mainly improve flight planning, weather routing, fuel optimization, and cockpit decision support rather than replace pilots, though single-pilot cargo operations are a plausible edge case late in the window. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper flight operations could expand regional, charter, and cargo air service somewhat, but demand is bounded by aircraft fleets, airport slots, and travel demand rather than by pilot labor cost alone. With disruption well below the threshold and strong regulatory insulation, this occupation is resilient over the next 10 years.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of airline and commercial pilots involve significant physical presence and real-time decision-making, such as navigating aircraft and responding to changing conditions, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist with flight planning and monitoring, the critical role of pilots in ensuring safety and managing emergencies limits disruption to peripheral tasks. Demand elasticity is low because the number of flights is primarily driven by passenger and cargo demand, which is not highly sensitive to reductions in pilot costs. Thus, AI's impact on this occupation is limited, making it resilient.
gpt55_rationale: Piloting already relies heavily on automation, and AI can further improve flight planning, weather/routing decisions, system monitoring, communications support, and simulator training. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to remove the human-centered core over the next decade, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI and advanced automation can improve flight planning, monitoring, communications, and routine aircraft control, potentially reducing some cockpit workload. fable5_rationale: Flight decks are already highly automated, and AI will further assist with flight planning, weather analysis, fuel optimization, and monitoring — but FAA regulations, certification regimes, and public safety expectations firmly anchor human pilots in the cockpit for at least the next decade, keeping core disruption moderate. grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on real-time physical control of aircraft, takeoffs/landings, emergency response, and cockpit presence under unpredictable conditions, so AI mainly augments peripheral cognitive elements like flight planning, system monitoring, weather analysis, and decision support rather than displacing the human pilot. Demand is moderately elastic, growing with pet ownership and willingness to spend, but it is constrained by the physical nature of the service rather than cost or speed of cognition. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.
opus5_rationale: The core work — feeding, bathing, grooming, exercising, restraining, and training live animals — is intensely physical, tactile, and unpredictable, making it essentially outside AI's reach; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, record-keeping, behavior-monitoring apps, and customer communication. Demand elasticity is fairly high in principle because pet-care spending is discretionary and cheaper/more convenient services (mobile grooming, sitting, training) would expand consumption, and BLS already projects 11% growth driven by pet humanization. However, since disruption is low, productivity gains from AI cannot substitute for the hands-on labor, so headcount tracks pet ownership rather than AI capability. This makes it clearly resilient: AI may modestly improve scheduling and health monitoring but does not reshape the core job.
openai_rationale: Animal care and service work is predominantly physical and hands-on, involving tasks such as feeding, grooming, and exercising animals, which are not easily automated by AI. The disruption score is low because AI's role is limited to peripheral tasks like scheduling or record-keeping. gpt55_rationale: The core work is hands-on, physical, and location-specific: feeding, cleaning, grooming, exercising, observing, restraining, and training live animals in unpredictable real-world settings. gpt56sol_rationale: Core duties such as feeding, grooming, exercising, restraining, cleaning up after, and training animals require hands-on presence in unpredictable physical settings. fable5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — feeding, grooming, exercising, training, and physically handling live animals — require hands-on presence with unpredictable creatures, placing this work almost entirely outside AI's reach; AI touches only peripheral scheduling, record-keeping, and customer communication. grok45_rationale: Core tasks—feeding, cleaning enclosures, grooming, exercising, restraining, and hands-on training—are almost entirely physical and require unpredictable real-world presence with live animals, so AI is limited to peripheral aids such as camera-based monitoring, digital record-keeping, or scheduling. gpt55_rationale: A large share of broadcast announcing and radio DJ work is language-, audio-, and software-based: writing scripts, reading copy, selecting music, producing segments, doing promos, and engaging audiences online, all of which AI voice, generative writing, recommendation, and automation tools can already affect. Live event DJs and emcees are more resilient because they require physical presence, crowd reading, client interaction, and real-time social performance, but even there playlists, mixing, planning, and announcements can be partially automated. gpt56sol_rationale: AI can already generate scripts, research summaries, playlists, advertisements, voiceovers, and synthetic radio personalities, putting much of broadcast announcing directly in its path. gpt56sol_rationale: AI will substantially accelerate literature review, interview transcription and coding, GIS and remote-sensing analysis, artifact classification, data management, and report drafting. title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators
