opus5_rationale: Baking is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: measuring, kneading, shaping, monitoring ovens, decorating, and cleaning equipment. AI touches only peripheral functions like inventory forecasting, recipe scaling, ordering, and demand prediction for shop owners; automation in commercial baking is driven by mechanical equipment rather than AI, and that trend long predates current AI tools. Demand for baked goods is moderately expandable with lower cost, but it is fundamentally capped by food consumption and requires physical production capacity. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — BLS projects 6% growth and the core craft remains human.
openai_rationale: Baking is predominantly a physical and manual occupation, involving tasks like kneading dough, shaping pastries, and monitoring baking processes, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist in recipe management or inventory tracking, it does not significantly alter the core tasks of bakers. Demand elasticity is moderate; while cheaper production could increase demand for baked goods, the physical nature of baking limits how much productivity gains can be scaled. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption, with core tasks remaining largely unchanged.
gpt55_rationale: Baking is primarily hands-on physical work: measuring and handling ingredients, shaping dough, loading ovens, monitoring product quality, cleaning equipment, and working safely around heat and machinery. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as inventory, production planning, recipe scaling, scheduling, quality monitoring, and demand forecasting, and some commercial bakeries will continue automating production lines, but the core occupation still requires real-world manipulation and sensory judgment. Demand for baked goods would expand somewhat if production became cheaper, especially for specialty, customized, or fresher products, but food consumption is limited by population, diet, retail space, and price sensitivity rather than unlimited latent demand. Because disruption to the core daily work remains low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Baking is predominantly hands-on work involving ingredient handling, dough shaping, oven operation, cleaning, and real-time quality inspection in a physical environment. AI may improve recipe planning, production forecasting, equipment monitoring, and administrative tasks, while advanced automation will have more impact in large commercial facilities than in retail or specialty bakeries. Demand is relatively inelastic because consumers are unlikely to eat dramatically more baked goods even if production becomes much cheaper, although lower costs could support greater variety and customization. Because AI does not substantially reshape the occupation's physical core, bakers remain resilient despite some automation-related pressure.
fable5_rationale: Baking is overwhelmingly physical, hands-on work — mixing, kneading, shaping, monitoring ovens — where AI language and analysis tools are largely irrelevant to core tasks; the main automation risk comes from industrial machinery in commercial facilities, not AI, and that automation is already mature. AI may assist peripherally with recipe scaling, inventory ordering, and demand forecasting for bakery owners. Demand for baked goods is fairly stable and tied to food consumption, so even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatic new demand, though artisanal and specialty segments have some room to grow. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI touches admin edges but does not reshape the craft.
grok45_rationale: Core baker duties—measuring and mixing ingredients, kneading and shaping dough, loading ovens, and monitoring physical baking—are overwhelmingly manual and require real-world presence around hot equipment and perishable materials; AI can only touch peripheral elements such as recipe scaling, demand forecasting, or vision-based quality checks. Demand for breads and pastries is largely fixed by population, dietary habits, and stomach capacity, so even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically higher total consumption. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient: AI may improve efficiency at the margins without reshaping the essential hands-on work.

title: Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
claude_rationale: This occupation scores low on disruption because the core work is fundamentally hands-on and physical - cutting, styling, coloring hair requires manual dexterity, spatial awareness, and real-time adaptation to each client's unique hair texture and face shape. While AI might assist with peripheral tasks like scheduling or trend analysis, the tactile nature of hair manipulation and the need for immediate physical presence makes this work largely immune to AI disruption. Elasticity is moderate-low because while cheaper services might increase frequency of visits somewhat, demand for haircuts and styling is relatively stable and tied to personal grooming needs rather than being heavily price-constrained. The resilient category fits because AI cannot meaningfully change the core manual work of this occupation.
opus_rationale: The core work is entirely physical and hands-on—cutting, coloring, and styling hair require manual dexterity, in-person presence, and tactile judgment that AI cannot perform. AI is irrelevant to the actual service and touches only peripheral tasks like appointment scheduling or inventory management. Demand is largely fixed by biological hair growth and personal grooming habits, so even if AI made back-office tasks cheaper, people don't need dramatically more haircuts. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.
opus5_rationale: The core work is entirely manual, tactile, and interpersonal — cutting, coloring, and styling hair on a live client in an unpredictable physical setting that robotics is nowhere near replicating. AI touches only peripheral tasks: booking and scheduling apps, marketing, inventory, client records, and virtual style previews/consultation tools. Demand is bounded by hair growth rates and personal grooming budgets, so cheaper back-office automation would not multiply appointments, though slight expansion is possible via better marketing and add-on services. Very low disruption places this firmly in the resilient category regardless of elasticity.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are predominantly physical and hands-on, involving direct interaction with clients and manual manipulation of hair and other personal care services. AI has limited impact on these tasks, as they require a human touch and creativity that AI cannot replicate. Thus, the disruption score is low. Demand elasticity is also low because while AI could potentially streamline booking or inventory management, the core service is not significantly constrained by cost or speed. Therefore, productivity gains from AI do not translate into a substantial increase in demand for these services. Consequently, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: The core work is hands-on, physical, and performed in close proximity to clients: cutting, coloring, styling, shaving, sanitation, and real-time adjustment to hair texture and client preferences. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as appointment scheduling, marketing, customer records, product recommendations, and virtual hairstyle visualization, but it is unlikely to replace the dexterous, trust-based service interaction at scale over the next decade. Demand would expand somewhat if services became cheaper or faster, especially for coloring, styling, and premium treatments, but basic haircut demand is constrained by hair growth, time, and in-person service capacity. Because disruption to the core occupation is low, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core services require close physical presence, fine motor control, visual judgment, and safe manipulation of highly variable hair, skin, chemicals, and tools. AI can improve appointment scheduling, marketing, recordkeeping, style visualization, and client recommendations, but practical robotic substitution is unlikely to become broadly economical within 10 years. Cheaper and faster services could encourage somewhat more frequent visits and advanced treatments, although hair growth, client time, and customary grooming schedules limit demand expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI primarily improves peripheral business and consultation tasks rather than replacing hands-on service delivery.
fable5_rationale: The core work—cutting, coloring, and styling hair—is entirely hands-on, physical, and performed on a human body in person, placing it far outside AI's reach; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, marketing, and style visualization consultations. Elasticity is low because demand for haircuts is bounded by how often people need or want them, not by cost of the knowledge-work components, so AI-driven productivity gains barely change service throughput. With disruption near the minimum, the occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS projections of faster-than-average growth driven by demographic and grooming demand rather than technology.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—cutting, coloring, styling, shampooing, and client consultation—are almost entirely physical, manual, and require real-time human presence and dexterity with tools, so AI only touches peripheral elements such as style-recommendation apps, booking, payments, and inventory. Demand is constrained by hair-growth cycles, population size, and preference for in-person service; even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically higher volume of haircuts or treatments. With disruption well below the threshold for structural change, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Bartenders
claude_rationale: Bartending scores low on disruption because the core work is fundamentally physical and interpersonal - mixing drinks by hand, engaging with customers face-to-face, monitoring intoxication levels, and managing the physical bar environment. While AI might help with inventory management or payment processing, it cannot replicate the manual dexterity, real-time customer interaction, and physical presence required. Elasticity is low because demand for bartending services is relatively fixed - people don't dramatically increase their bar visits or drink consumption just because service becomes more efficient. The occupation remains resilient as AI cannot meaningfully transform the core human-centered, physical aspects of bartending work.
opus_rationale: Bartending is overwhelmingly physical and interpersonal — mixing drinks, serving, monitoring intoxication, checking IDs, and engaging customers all require human presence and dexterity, so AI touches only peripheral functions like inventory management or POS systems. The core social and hospitality experience that draws people to bars cannot be automated meaningfully. Demand is somewhat tied to discretionary income and the social atmosphere customers seek, which limits how much cheaper service would expand consumption. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is clearly resilient: AI may streamline ordering or stocking, but the hands-on, face-to-face nature of the work remains intact.
opus5_rationale: Bartending is almost entirely physical and interpersonal: mixing and pouring drinks, checking IDs, judging intoxication, conversing with patrons, and hauling kegs. AI touches only peripheral elements like POS systems, inventory forecasting, and scheduling; automated drink dispensers are robotics rather than AI and remain niche in a business where hospitality and social atmosphere are the product. Demand for bars and restaurants could expand moderately with income growth and lower operating costs, but people don't consume unlimited drinks and the experience itself is the constraint. With disruption near the floor, the occupation is clearly resilient.
openai_rationale: Bartending is primarily a physical and social occupation, involving tasks like mixing drinks, serving customers, and monitoring intoxication levels, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI may assist with inventory management or payment processing, the core tasks require human interaction and presence, resulting in low disruption. Demand elasticity is low because the service is not significantly suppressed by cost; people do not consume more alcohol simply because it is cheaper or faster to serve. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: Bartending is primarily in-person, physical, and social work: mixing and serving drinks, checking IDs, monitoring intoxication, handling cash or tabs, cleaning, restocking, and managing customer interactions in a real-world setting. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as inventory forecasting, scheduling, menu recommendations, POS automation, and training, and some robotic drink systems may appear in high-volume or novelty venues, but the core hospitality and responsibility functions remain human-centered. Demand would expand only modestly if labor became cheaper because alcohol consumption and bar visits are limited by time, regulation, venue capacity, health concerns, and the fact that customers often pay for atmosphere and service rather than just drink production. Because disruption is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite some automation at the margins.
gpt56sol_rationale: Bartending is predominantly physical, customer-facing work requiring real-time drink preparation, cleaning, stocking, social interaction, and judgment about age and intoxication. AI can improve ordering, payments, inventory management, scheduling, and recipe guidance, while automated dispensers may handle standardized drinks, but these tools affect only part of the role. Cheaper and faster service could modestly increase consumption or venue capacity, but demand is constrained by alcohol preferences, regulation, and the number of hospitality occasions, so low disruption makes the occupation resilient.
fable5_rationale: Bartending is overwhelmingly physical and social work — mixing and pouring drinks, engaging customers, monitoring intoxication, and managing the physical bar space — none of which AI software touches meaningfully; automated cocktail machines exist but the social hospitality role is the core value proposition, especially in tipped venues. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper drink service wouldn't dramatically expand alcohol consumption, though the experiential nature of bars keeps human bartenders in demand. With disruption at 2, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI may help with inventory management and POS peripherals, but the core work is untouched, consistent with BLS projecting faster-than-average growth.
grok45_rationale: Core bartender tasks—physically mixing and pouring drinks, checking IDs, monitoring intoxication, cleaning, restocking, and real-time customer engagement—are overwhelmingly physical, sensory, and presence-based; AI currently assists only peripheral elements such as recipe lookup or inventory tracking and is not close to replacing the hands-on service loop. Demand elasticity is low because alcohol service and bar experiences face structural caps from social norms, health concerns, licensing rules, and limited leisure hours; even large productivity gains would not unlock dramatically higher total consumption. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient: AI may trim admin edges but leaves the essential work and headcount trajectory largely intact.

title: Bill and account collectors
claude_rationale: Bill and account collectors face very high disruption as their core tasks—contacting debtors, negotiating payment plans, tracking accounts, and maintaining records—are predominantly digital and language-based activities that AI can increasingly handle through automated calling systems, chatbots, and intelligent debt management software. The BLS already notes that enhanced software and automated systems are increasing productivity and allowing fewer employees to handle more accounts. Demand elasticity is very low because the volume of debt collection is fundamentally constrained by the amount of overdue debt in the economy, not by the cost or speed of collection services—making debt collection 10x cheaper doesn't create 10x more debt to collect. The combination of high AI disruption and inelastic demand points to significant workforce contraction, which aligns with the BLS projection of -10% employment decline through 2034.
opus_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language-based — phone negotiations, skip tracing via databases, record updating, and applying scripted legal disclosures — all squarely in the path of AI voice agents, automated dialers, and NLP-driven negotiation tools. Demand is highly inelastic: the volume of overdue debt is fixed by the economy and lending activity, not suppressed by collection cost, so making collection cheaper simply lets fewer workers handle the same accounts rather than expanding total work. The BLS already projects a 10% decline driven by automation. High disruption combined with low elasticity yields clear headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely phone- and screen-based: skip tracing via databases, scripted disclosures, negotiation of standardized payment plans, and record-keeping — all directly in the path of AI voice agents, automated dialers, and LLM-driven negotiation and compliance workflows. Debt collection volume is bounded by the amount of delinquent debt outstanding, not by the cost of collection, so cheaper collection does not create meaningfully more debt to collect; regulatory constraints (FDCPA, state rules, contact frequency caps) further limit expansion. Productivity gains therefore flow to headcount reduction, consistent with BLS's projected -10% decline. High disruption plus inelastic demand places this squarely in the replace category.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of bill and account collectors, such as contacting debtors, negotiating payment plans, and updating records, are highly susceptible to automation through AI and enhanced software. AI can efficiently handle many aspects of communication and data management, reducing the need for human intervention. The demand elasticity is low because the need for debt collection is not significantly suppressed by cost or speed; rather, it is driven by the volume of outstanding debt, which does not increase proportionally with reduced collection costs. Therefore, AI advancements are likely to lead to a reduction in headcount as productivity gains do not translate into increased demand for collectors.
gpt55_rationale: Bill and account collection is heavily phone-, text-, database-, and script-based work, with core tasks such as skip tracing, debtor outreach, recordkeeping, compliance scripting, and repayment-plan negotiation directly addressable by AI voice agents and workflow automation. AI can already prioritize accounts, generate compliant messages, summarize calls, update systems, and increasingly conduct routine negotiations with human escalation only for difficult cases. Demand elasticity is low because the stock of delinquent accounts is finite, collection contacts are legally constrained, and cheaper collection does not create much new socially or commercially desired activity beyond pursuing smaller balances. Because disruption is very high and demand expansion is limited, productivity gains are likely to translate mainly into fewer collectors rather than much more employment.
gpt56sol_rationale: The occupation is dominated by digital and language-based tasks—locating debtors, making calls, explaining obligations, negotiating standardized payment plans, and documenting interactions—that AI voice agents and automated collection systems can increasingly perform. Humans will remain valuable for complex disputes, emotionally sensitive negotiations, compliance oversight, and escalated cases, but these represent a shrinking share of accounts. Cheaper collection may make pursuing some low-balance debts economical, yet total demand is constrained by the number of delinquent accounts, consumer-protection rules, and creditor policies. Very high disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to replacement and substantial headcount contraction.
fable5_rationale: Nearly every core task—skip tracing via databases, scripted phone outreach, negotiation of repayment plans, record-keeping, and compliance disclosures—is digital and language-based, squarely in the path of AI voice agents and automated workflows that already exist in collections today. Demand is fundamentally capped by the stock of delinquent debt, which does not grow because collection becomes cheaper; at best, marginally smaller debts become economical to pursue, but regulation (FDCPA contact limits) and social pressure constrain expanded collection activity. Productivity gains therefore translate directly into fewer human collectors handling more accounts, consistent with BLS's projected 10% decline. High disruption with inelastic demand makes this a clear replace case.
grok45_rationale: Core work is almost entirely digital and language-based—skip tracing via databases, outbound calling, scripted negotiation, record updates, and compliance checks—all of which AI voice agents, LLMs, and automated dialers already perform or assist at scale, with rapid further gains expected. Demand for collection services is largely fixed by the stock of overdue debt rather than suppressed by cost; making collection 10x cheaper mainly lets firms process the same accounts with far fewer people, with only modest expansion into marginal small-balance debts. This combination of high task substitutability and low demand elasticity produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS’s projected 10% decline.

title: Biochemists and biophysicists
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts biochemistry and biophysics through automated data analysis, protein structure prediction, molecular modeling, and literature review - core knowledge work activities that comprise much of the daily work. However, physical laboratory experimentation, complex hypothesis generation, and interdisciplinary collaboration still require human expertise. Demand elasticity is high because AI-accelerated research dramatically reduces the cost and time for drug discovery, genetic analysis, and biotechnology development, unlocking massive latent demand from pharmaceutical companies, biotech firms, and research institutions seeking faster innovation cycles. The combination of high disruption with high elasticity suggests workers will become dramatically more productive rather than displaced.
opus_rationale: Much of the analytical, computational modeling, literature review, data mining, and report-writing work is directly in AI's path, and AI tools like protein-structure prediction (e.g., AlphaFold) already materially transform parts of this field. However, the core requires substantial hands-on wet-lab experimentation, physical manipulation of biological samples, and team-based research presence that AI cannot replace, keeping disruption moderate at 6. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster discovery accelerates drug development, diagnostics, and biotech research where latent demand is enormous and currently bottlenecked by cost and time. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient — AI dramatically augments the knowledge-work portions but does not reshape the physically grounded experimental core.
opus5_rationale: Roughly half of the work is wet-lab and instrument-based, but the intellectual core — literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, protein structure and function prediction, omics data analysis, molecular design, grant and paper writing — is squarely in AI's path, and tools like AlphaFold, generative protein design, and LLM-based literature mining are already reshaping daily practice, justifying a high-but-not-maximal disruption score. Demand elasticity is high because the space of unexplored targets, diseases, enzymes, crops, and biomaterials is effectively unbounded and currently rate-limited by the cost and slowness of experimentation; cheaper, faster discovery cycles pull forward far more programs rather than simply reducing scientist headcount, though grant funding caps and lab capital costs keep it below the top tier. With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 7, the occupation lands in augment: each scientist orchestrates far more computational and automated experimentation, with skill demands shifting toward computational and AI-fluent experimental design rather than headcount contraction.
openai_rationale: Biochemists and biophysicists engage in complex research tasks that involve significant cognitive and analytical skills, which AI can assist but not fully replace. AI tools can enhance data analysis, modeling, and simulation, but the core experimental and hypothesis-driven nature of the work requires human oversight and creativity. The demand for biochemists and biophysicists is likely to expand as AI reduces costs and increases the speed of research, unlocking new opportunities in drug development, biotechnology, and environmental sciences. Thus, while AI will significantly augment their work, the demand elasticity suggests that the occupation will grow rather than shrink.
gpt55_rationale: AI is already materially changing biochemistry and biophysics through protein-structure prediction, molecular design, literature synthesis, image analysis, omics analysis, experiment planning, and automated report or grant drafting. The disruption score is tempered by the fact that core work still depends on wet-lab experimentation, physical instrumentation, safety protocols, biological validation, and interdisciplinary judgment. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster biological research would unlock more drug discovery, diagnostics, synthetic biology, agricultural biotech, and environmental applications, although clinical trials, regulation, lab capacity, and funding constraints limit unlimited expansion. Because disruption is high but expanded research output is likely to absorb much of the productivity gain, the occupation is best categorized as augment.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI is increasingly central to literature synthesis, molecular modeling, protein and drug design, data analysis, experimental planning, and scientific writing, substantially changing the occupation’s cognitive tasks. However, laboratory execution, validation, safety oversight, interdisciplinary judgment, and research leadership still require skilled scientists and real-world experimentation. Cheaper and faster discovery should unlock substantial additional research in medicine, agriculture, energy, and environmental protection, although laboratory capacity, funding, regulation, and clinical trials limit expansion. High disruption combined with high latent demand therefore makes augmentation more likely than broad replacement.
fable5_rationale: A significant share of the work — literature review, grant writing, data analysis, and especially molecular structure prediction (e.g., AlphaFold-style tools) — is squarely in AI's path and already being transformed, but core wet-lab experimentation, protein synthesis, and hands-on validation still require physical presence and are only partially addressed by lab automation. Elasticity is high because drug discovery, biotech, and agricultural research have deep latent demand: cheaper, faster hypothesis generation and computational screening means more candidate molecules get investigated and more research programs become fundable. Because disruption sits at the moderate-high boundary with the hands-on experimental core intact, the occupation lands as resilient — AI dramatically accelerates the computational portions while human researchers remain essential for experimental design, bench work, and validation. Scientists who integrate AI tools will be far more productive, but headcount is likely to hold or grow given expanding biotech demand.
grok45_rationale: Core work mixes wet-lab experiments with heavy cognitive tasks (literature synthesis, experimental design, data analysis, molecular modeling, grant/paper writing); AI already materially transforms the latter via tools like AlphaFold, automated bioinformatics, and generative writing, placing the occupation in the high-disruption range even though physical lab presence remains. Demand is highly elastic because R&D cost and speed currently suppress output in drug discovery, agriculture, biofuels, and environmental applications; 10x cheaper/faster research would unlock far more projects and products as aging populations and biotech markets expand. High disruption plus high elasticity therefore yields augmentation: each scientist produces dramatically more discoveries while total headcount holds or grows.

title: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers
claude_rationale: Biomedical engineers face high disruption as AI increasingly transforms their core tasks including device design, statistical modeling, simulation development, and research analysis - areas where AI tools are already proving highly capable. However, demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster biomedical engineering could dramatically expand access to medical devices, personalized treatments, and healthcare innovations globally, particularly in underserved markets where cost has been a major barrier. The net effect is augmentation as the healthcare sector's massive unmet needs and regulatory approval processes will absorb productivity gains through expanded innovation rather than workforce reduction.
opus_rationale: Much of the design, simulation, statistical modeling, and technical reporting work is digital and directly aided by AI, but core tasks like installing/maintaining biomedical equipment, hands-on device testing in hospitals, clinician training, and physical prototyping require real-world presence, keeping disruption moderate at 6. Demand is genuinely elastic — cheaper and faster R&D would unlock more medical devices, drug therapies, and personalized solutions, since healthcare needs vastly exceed current supply. Because disruption is at or below 6, the occupation lands in 'resilient': AI substantially augments the knowledge-work portions but does not reshape the physical, regulated, and collaborative core of the work.
opus5_rationale: Much of the work — simulation, statistical modeling, software for instruments, design iteration, regulatory documentation, technical reports, and literature synthesis — is digital and squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven protein/molecule design and generative CAD already materially change R&D workflows; however, a substantial share involves physical prototyping, lab experimentation, clinical validation in hospitals, and hands-on device support, capping disruption at the lower end of 'high'. Demand elasticity is high because biomedical innovation is strongly cost- and cycle-time-constrained: cheaper, faster design and testing unlocks more device programs, more personalized implants, more drug-delivery and diagnostic products, and broader access in underserved markets, so productivity gains largely convert into more projects rather than fewer engineers. Regulatory approval timelines (FDA) and clinical trial requirements do throttle expansion somewhat, keeping elasticity from reaching 9-10. Net effect is augment: each engineer will supervise AI-driven design and simulation pipelines while total demand for biomedical devices and therapies expands enough to sustain or grow headcount.
openai_rationale: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers engage in tasks that are predominantly knowledge-based, such as designing equipment, developing simulations, and conducting research. AI can significantly aid in these areas by enhancing design processes, optimizing simulations, and analyzing complex biological data. However, the need for human oversight in the development and implementation of medical devices and systems remains crucial. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can make development faster and cheaper, the demand for biomedical solutions is somewhat constrained by regulatory and safety considerations. Thus, while AI will disrupt the field, the demand for skilled engineers who can integrate AI into biomedical contexts will persist, leading to a restructuring of the occupation.
gpt55_rationale: Biomedical engineering includes substantial AI-exposed knowledge work: literature review, statistical modeling, simulation, software development, design optimization, documentation, and analysis of biological or device data. However, the occupation also requires hands-on experimentation, prototyping, validation, clinical interaction, manufacturing coordination, and regulatory judgment, which limits full automation. Demand for biomedical devices, diagnostics, prosthetics, implants, and personalized medical technologies would expand if design and analysis became cheaper, but growth is constrained by clinical testing, regulation, reimbursement, manufacturing, and adoption cycles. Because disruption is high but demand elasticity is only moderate, AI is likely to substantially restructure the work rather than simply eliminate or broadly expand headcount.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will substantially accelerate modeling, simulation, literature review, software development, statistical analysis, design optimization, and technical documentation. However, physical prototyping, laboratory experiments, clinical validation, regulatory compliance, equipment support, and collaboration with clinicians and manufacturers remain human-intensive. Lower development costs should enable more biomedical research and product exploration, but regulation, trials, manufacturing, and healthcare budgets limit how fully productivity gains translate into additional demand. The occupation will therefore persist with substantially changed workflows and greater emphasis on experimental judgment, systems integration, validation, and AI-enabled design.
fable5_rationale: A substantial share of the work — statistical modeling, simulation, software design, technical writing, and data analysis — is squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven protein folding and generative design tools are already accelerating biomedical R&D. However, the core work remains anchored in physical prototyping, wet-lab experimentation, clinical validation in hospitals, regulatory testing, and hands-on equipment support, which caps disruption at the boundary of the high category. Elasticity is high because demand for medical devices, implants, and biological therapies is heavily suppressed by R&D cost and time — cheaper development would expand the pipeline of devices and treatments dramatically. With disruption at 6, this lands as resilient (bordering augment): AI supercharges the analytical portions while the physical and regulatory core keeps humans essential, and expanding demand supports stable-to-growing headcount.
grok45_rationale: Core work centers on cognitive tasks—device/software design, statistical modeling and simulation, data analysis, technical writing, and research synthesis—all of which AI already accelerates via generative design, automated simulation, literature review, and report drafting, even while physical prototyping, lab experiments, installation, and clinician collaboration retain human presence. Demand is highly elastic because development cost and speed currently suppress the volume of medical devices, implants, diagnostics, and biotech solutions; dramatically cheaper and faster engineering unlocks large latent markets driven by aging populations, personalized medicine, and underserved needs. High disruption paired with high elasticity therefore yields augmentation: each engineer produces far more output while total employment holds or grows with expanded innovation pipelines.

title: Biological technicians
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts the data analysis, documentation, and experimental design aspects of biological technician work, which comprise a substantial portion of their duties, but the core laboratory work remains hands-on and requires physical manipulation of samples and equipment. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster biological analysis could unlock significant research that is currently constrained by cost and time - more drug discovery, environmental monitoring, and biotechnology applications would become feasible if analysis costs dropped dramatically. The combination of meaningful disruption with high demand expansion suggests workers will become more productive while total employment remains stable or grows.
opus_rationale: The work blends significant physical lab tasks (setting up equipment, preparing biological samples, conducting bench experiments, fieldwork) with cognitive tasks (data analysis, reporting) that AI can accelerate. AI tools can materially assist the documentation, data interpretation, and modeling portions, but the hands-on wet-lab work requires physical presence and cannot be automated by current AI, capping disruption at moderate. Demand has moderate elasticity since cheaper, faster research could expand biotech and synthetic biology projects, but growth is constrained by funding, regulatory, and physical-lab capacity limits. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the analytical periphery while the core physical and observational lab work remains human-dependent.
opus5_rationale: Core work is substantially physical and hands-on — pipetting, culturing, staining, maintaining instruments, collecting field samples — which AI alone cannot perform; disruption comes from the knowledge-work slice (data analysis, modeling, report writing, protocol documentation) plus growing AI-driven lab automation platforms that could compress routine bench tasks over the decade. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper and faster experimentation genuinely unlocks more biotech, synthetic biology, and screening work, but research volume is gated by grant funding, capital equipment, regulatory validation, and physical lab capacity rather than purely by labor cost. With disruption at 5, the occupation lands in the resilient band — AI reshapes the analytical and documentation periphery and raises expectations for computational literacy, but the wet-lab core remains human. Technicians who add data/automation skills will be advantaged, yet aggregate headcount should hold roughly stable.
openai_rationale: Biological technicians perform a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, such as setting up lab equipment and analyzing data. AI can assist with data analysis and documentation, but the hands-on nature of lab work and sample preparation limits full automation. Thus, disruption is moderate. Demand elasticity is moderate because while AI can enhance productivity, the demand for biological research is not highly suppressed by cost; it is driven by scientific and medical needs. Therefore, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing the core tasks.
gpt55_rationale: Biological technicians do a mix of hands-on wet-lab work, sample preparation, equipment maintenance, observation, documentation, and data analysis, so AI will materially affect the digital and analytical parts but not eliminate the need for physical laboratory presence. AI tools and lab automation can improve experimental design, image analysis, recordkeeping, anomaly detection, and interpretation, but many tasks still require manual sample handling, compliance with protocols, and troubleshooting real instruments and biological materials. Demand elasticity is fairly high because cheaper, faster experimentation would likely increase the volume of biotech, pharmaceutical, environmental, agricultural, and synthetic biology research. Because disruption is meaningful but still capped by the occupation’s hands-on laboratory core, the net effect is resilient rather than replace, restructure, or augment.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will substantially assist experimental design, data analysis, anomaly detection, documentation, and report writing, while laboratory automation will increasingly handle standardized assays and sample processing. However, technicians still must prepare biological materials, operate and troubleshoot specialized equipment, monitor experiments, maintain contamination controls, and sometimes collect field samples, limiting end-to-end automation. Demand is relatively elastic because cheaper, faster experimentation should enable more biotechnology, pharmaceutical, synthetic-biology, and environmental research, although funding and regulatory constraints prevent unlimited expansion. With disruption remaining moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, but its work will shift toward instrument oversight, quality control, and handling nonstandard experiments.
fable5_rationale: The core work is hands-on: setting up and maintaining lab equipment, preparing physical biological samples, running wet-lab experiments, and fieldwork — tasks requiring physical presence that AI cannot perform directly. AI meaningfully assists the knowledge portions (data analysis, report writing, experiment documentation) and lab automation is advancing, but robotic replacement of general-purpose bench work remains limited within a 10-year horizon. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper and faster analysis would expand research throughput (biotech, synthetic biology, drug discovery have deep latent demand), though headcount is capped by physical lab capacity and research funding. With disruption at 4, this occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the analytical periphery while the wet-lab core persists.
grok45_rationale: Core duties center on hands-on lab work—sample preparation, equipment setup/maintenance, and conducting physical experiments—which require real-world presence and manual precision that AI cannot fully replace, though AI already assists data analysis, modeling, documentation, and report writing. This mixed profile yields moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster technician output would expand biotech R&D, synthetic biology, and testing volumes in pharma and environmental applications, yet funding, lab infrastructure, and regulatory constraints limit unlimited growth. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation remains resilient overall as AI augments rather than reshapes the physical core.

title: Boilermakers
claude_rationale: Boilermakers perform highly physical, hands-on work in challenging environments that requires manual dexterity, physical presence, and real-world problem-solving in confined spaces and at heights. While they read blueprints and may use some automated welding equipment, the core work involves manual assembly, installation, maintenance, and repair of large industrial equipment that cannot be done remotely or digitally. Demand for boilermaker services is relatively inelastic because it's tied to fixed infrastructure needs - existing boilers require maintenance regardless of cost, and new installations are driven by industrial capacity rather than price sensitivity. The projected 2% employment decline reflects structural shifts away from coal power rather than AI displacement.
opus_rationale: Boilermaking is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on work performed in cramped, dangerous, real-world environments—welding, riveting, aligning heavy plates, inspecting confined spaces—none of which AI can perform; only peripheral tasks like blueprint reading have any digital component, yielding a very low disruption score. Demand is structurally constrained by the slow installation/maintenance cycle of long-lived boilers and the secular shift away from coal-fired generation, so even dramatically cheaper analysis would not expand headcount needs. Because disruption is far below the threshold for any AI-driven category, this occupation is resilient; its modest projected decline stems from energy-market trends rather than automation.
opus5_rationale: Boilermaking is overwhelmingly physical: welding, rigging, cutting, and crawling into confined vessels at height in unpredictable field conditions. AI touches only peripheral elements such as blueprint interpretation, inspection analytics, predictive maintenance scheduling, and drone/robotic inspection assistance, none of which displace the hands-on assembly and repair core. Demand is driven by the installed base of boilers and pressure vessels and the energy transition away from coal, not by the cost of cognitive labor, so productivity gains from AI would not unlock much new demand. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient; its projected decline stems from energy-sector shifts rather than AI.
openai_rationale: Boilermakers perform tasks that are predominantly physical and hands-on, such as assembling, installing, and maintaining boilers and large vessels. These tasks require manual dexterity, physical strength, and the ability to work in confined spaces, which are not easily automated by AI. Therefore, the disruption score is low. The demand elasticity is also low because the need for boilermakers is driven by specific construction and maintenance requirements that do not expand significantly with reduced costs or increased speed. As a result, the net effect is 'resilient,' as AI will not significantly alter the core tasks or demand for boilermakers.
gpt55_rationale: Boilermakers perform mostly physical, site-specific work involving installation, welding, alignment, inspection, cleaning, and repair in hazardous, cramped, and variable environments. AI may help with blueprint interpretation, scheduling, predictive maintenance, robotic welding, and inspection tools, but it does not replace the core hands-on field work over the next decade. Demand is relatively inelastic because the need is tied to the installed base of boilers, tanks, pressure vessels, and industrial facilities, and cheaper labor would not cause customers to build or maintain vastly more of them. Because disruption is low-to-moderate, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite weak demand growth.
gpt56sol_rationale: Boilermaking is dominated by physical, site-specific work in hazardous and confined environments, including fitting, welding, cleaning, inspection, and repair. AI can assist with blueprint interpretation, predictive maintenance, defect detection, safety monitoring, and robotic welding, but unstructured worksites and large custom equipment limit substitution for skilled workers. title: Budget analysts
claude_rationale: Budget analysts perform predominantly knowledge work involving data analysis, financial modeling, report writing, and numerical computation - all areas where AI tools are already materially useful and rapidly improving. AI can automate much of the data processing, variance analysis, and report generation that forms the core of budget analysis work. However, demand elasticity is low because organizations have relatively fixed budgeting needs regardless of cost - they don't suddenly need 10x more budget analyses just because AI makes them cheaper or faster. The combination of high AI disruption potential with inelastic demand suggests significant headcount contraction as AI absorbs much of the analytical workload without proportional demand expansion.
opus_rationale: Budget analysis is almost entirely digital, cognitive, and language-based work—data analysis, cost-benefit modeling, report writing, and spending monitoring all sit directly in AI's path, and current AI tools already automate much of the data processing and report generation. High disruption plus structurally capped demand yields net headcount contraction.
openai_rationale: Budget analysts primarily engage in knowledge work involving data analysis, financial forecasting, and report preparation, which AI can significantly assist with. gpt55_rationale: Budget analysts perform largely digital, cognitive work: consolidating spreadsheets, reviewing proposals for completeness and compliance, forecasting needs, analyzing tradeoffs, monitoring variances, and drafting reports. gpt56sol_rationale: Budget analysis is predominantly digital and structured, making consolidation, compliance checks, forecasting, variance analysis, scenario modeling, and report drafting highly amenable to AI. claude_rationale: Bus driving scores low on disruption because it remains fundamentally a physical, real-world occupation requiring human presence, safety judgment, and passenger interaction - while autonomous vehicles exist in testing, full deployment for passenger transport faces significant regulatory, safety, and infrastructure barriers that will take decades to resolve. Elasticity is low because demand for bus transportation is relatively fixed by population, school enrollment, and existing transit routes - making buses 10x more efficient wouldn't dramatically increase ridership as people's transportation needs are fairly inelastic. opus_rationale: Bus driving is overwhelmingly physical and presence-based: operating a vehicle in unpredictable real-world conditions, managing passenger safety, assisting riders with disabilities, and handling unruly passengers. Demand is structurally constrained by fixed routes, school enrollment trends, and public transit budgets, so even cheaper operation would not dramatically expand ridership. The low disruption score places this firmly in the resilient category regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: Core work is physical driving plus in-person passenger management — supervising children, assisting riders with disabilities, handling unruly passengers, and safety judgment — none of which language-model AI touches. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper transit operation could expand service frequency and rural/paratransit coverage where demand is currently cost-suppressed, but ridership is structurally bounded by school enrollment and municipal budgets. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient over the next decade, with the caveat that autonomy could shift the picture sharply in the following decade.
openai_rationale: Bus driving is predominantly a physical task requiring human presence, such as navigating traffic and assisting passengers, which limits AI's ability to disrupt core tasks. Elasticity is moderate: aging demographics and cheaper screening could expand cardiac testing volumes somewhat, but procedures are capped by physician availability, capital equipment, reimbursement rules, and clinical indication rather than by analysis cost. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the reporting and quality-check periphery while the physical, procedural core remains human.
