The occupation therefore faces substantial skill and role changes, with remaining programmers moving toward architecture, requirements interpretation, system integration, validation, and oversight of AI-generated code.
fable5_rationale: The core tasks — writing, testing, and debugging code from specifications provided by others — are fully digital and squarely in AI's strongest current capability zone; coding assistants already automate exactly this translation-of-design-into-code work. While demand for software overall is highly elastic, that expanded demand flows to software developers and engineers who own design and architecture, not to pure implementers; when AI handles implementation directly from a developer's specification, the intermediary programmer role is bypassed rather than multiplied. BLS already projects a 6% decline, and AI accelerates the trend of higher-skilled tasks shifting to developers while routine coding is automated. High disruption (9) combined with low role-specific elasticity (4) places this occupation in the replace category, even though adjacent occupations like software developer face a very different, augmentation-oriented outlook.
grok45_rationale: Writing, modifying, testing, and debugging code is almost entirely digital/cognitive work already being materially accelerated by AI coding assistants, with rapid further trajectory toward automation of core tasks. Cheaper/faster programming unlocks meaningful latent demand for more software, features, and custom applications, yet expansion is only moderate because many tasks shift upward to software developers or get fully automated, constraining pure programmer headcount. High disruption plus mid-range elasticity therefore produces restructure: the occupation persists but requires substantial adaptation to AI-augmented workflows.

title: Computer support specialists
claude_rationale: Computer support work is predominantly digital and cognitive, involving troubleshooting, documentation, and user guidance - tasks that AI chatbots, automated diagnostic tools, and self-service systems are already handling effectively. The BLS projects a 3% decline specifically citing automation through chatbots replacing user support functions. Demand elasticity is low because organizations have relatively fixed IT support needs regardless of cost - they don't suddenly need 10x more help desk tickets resolved just because it becomes cheaper, and many are actively seeking to reduce support volume through better systems and automation.
opus_rationale: The core work — diagnosing problems, guiding users through troubleshooting steps via chat/phone/email, documenting issues — is highly language- and knowledge-based and directly in the path of AI chatbots and automated diagnostic tools, which BLS already cites as driving employment decline. Demand elasticity is low because IT support demand is largely fixed by the existing installed base of users and devices; cheaper support doesn't meaningfully cause organizations to consume dramatically more troubleshooting, and routine tier-1 tickets are precisely what automation absorbs. With disruption high (8) and elasticity low (4), productivity gains translate into fewer headcount rather than expanded output, consistent with BLS's projected decline; the hands-on hardware setup and complex network troubleshooting portions provide only partial insulation.
opus5_rationale: Help-desk and user support work is overwhelmingly language-based troubleshooting — reading ticket descriptions, diagnosing from symptoms, walking users through steps, documenting resolutions — which is squarely in the path of current LLM chatbots and agentic IT automation; self-healing endpoint tools and AI knowledge bases already resolve a large share of tier-1 tickets. Some hands-on hardware setup, physical repair, and onsite network maintenance keeps disruption below the maximum. Elasticity is low: support demand is derived from an installed base of users and devices, and organizations treat IT support as a cost center to minimize rather than a service to consume more of — cheaper support does not make firms want 10x more tickets. High disruption plus inelastic, cost-center demand yields headcount contraction, consistent with BLS's projected decline, though the residual complex-escalation and onsite tier-2/3 roles will remain and command higher skill.
openai_rationale: Computer support specialists are experiencing high disruption due to AI advancements, particularly in automated troubleshooting and support tools like chatbots. These technologies can handle routine inquiries and problems, reducing the need for human intervention in many cases. However, the demand elasticity is low because the need for support services is not significantly suppressed by cost; rather, it is driven by the complexity and frequency of IT issues, which do not increase proportionally with reduced service costs. As a result, the occupation will likely restructure, with specialists focusing more on complex issues and less on routine tasks, requiring an adaptation of skills.
gpt55_rationale: Computer support work is heavily digital, language-based, and procedural: diagnosing user problems, documenting tickets, guiding users step-by-step, and escalating cases are all tasks that AI chatbots, copilots, and automated remediation tools can already handle for many common issues. Demand is only weakly elastic because the volume of support is largely tied to the number of users, devices, and incidents rather than a desire to consume much more support when it becomes cheaper. gpt56sol_rationale: Most user-support work consists of digital diagnosis, documentation, and step-by-step guidance that AI agents can already automate, although onsite hardware work and complex network troubleshooting remain less exposed. Because disruption is high while demand expansion is limited, AI is likely to reduce overall headcount and concentrate remaining workers in complex, security-sensitive, and hands-on cases.
fable5_rationale: The core work — diagnosing problems via chat/phone/email, walking users through fixes, documenting tickets — is language-based, procedural knowledge work squarely in AI's path; chatbots and AI agents already resolve a large share of tier-1 tickets, and BLS itself cites automation as the driver of projected decline. Elasticity is low because support demand is derived from problems occurring, not suppressed by cost: cheaper support doesn't make users consume 10x more troubleshooting, and AI simultaneously reduces incident volume through self-healing systems and embedded AI assistants that solve issues before a ticket is filed. Physical hardware setup and on-site network work preserve a residual human role, but that's a minority of the 880k jobs. grok45_rationale: Core tasks of diagnosing user-described problems, guiding step-by-step fixes, documenting tickets, and routine network monitoring are almost entirely digital/language-based and already being handled by AI chatbots and automated tools, with BLS explicitly citing this automation as a driver of decline; physical setup/repair is a minority of the work. Demand for support services expands only modestly with cheaper delivery (more small firms or devices covered) but is fundamentally capped by the volume of actual problems and systems rather than unlocking near-unlimited new consumption. High disruption plus low elasticity therefore produces net headcount contraction as AI absorbs the bulk of routine tickets without commensurate growth in total work.

title: Computer systems analysts
claude_rationale: Computer systems analysts face high disruption as AI can automate much of their core work including system analysis, requirements gathering, cost-benefit analysis, and even some system design and testing tasks. opus_rationale: Disruption is very high because the core work—analyzing systems, data modeling, programming, writing documentation, testing, and designing improvements—is almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing it squarely in AI's direct path; coding assistants and analytical AI tools already materially accelerate these tasks. The combination of high disruption and high elasticity, reinforced by the BLS projection of 9% growth, means productivity gains are largely absorbed by expanded output rather than headcount reduction, so each analyst produces more while overall employment stays stable or grows—fitting the augment category.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language-based: requirements gathering, data modeling, cost-benefit analysis, system configuration, testing, documentation, and some programming — all directly in AI's path, and AI tools already draft specs, diagrams, test plans, and integration code. Elasticity is high because organizational demand for system modernization, integration, and AI-enabled workflow redesign is currently gated by scarce analyst capacity and project cost; cheaper analysis means far more systems get evaluated, upgraded, and customized, including at smaller firms previously priced out. The stakeholder-liaison and domain-knowledge component also resists full automation, keeping humans central while their throughput multiplies. Hence augment: substantial task transformation with demand expansion absorbing the productivity gains, though the mix shifts toward business judgment and AI orchestration over hands-on documentation and coding.
openai_rationale: The role of computer systems analysts involves significant knowledge work, including analyzing and designing IT systems, which AI can increasingly assist with. AI tools can streamline tasks like data modeling, cost-benefit analysis, and system testing, leading to high disruption. However, the demand for IT systems and improvements is likely to expand as AI reduces costs and increases efficiency, making IT solutions more accessible to a broader range of organizations. This high elasticity suggests that productivity gains from AI will be absorbed by increased demand, leading to stable or growing headcount.
gpt55_rationale: Computer systems analysts perform predominantly digital, cognitive work: requirements analysis, system design, cost-benefit analysis, testing, documentation, and some programming, all of which AI tools can materially accelerate. However, the role also depends on organizational context, stakeholder communication, change management, and translating business needs into workable systems, which limits full automation. Demand elasticity is high because many organizations have large backlogs of modernization, integration, cybersecurity, cloud, data, and AI-adoption projects that become more feasible if analysis and implementation planning get cheaper. Because disruption is high but cheaper work is likely to unlock substantial additional IT transformation demand, the occupation is best classified as augment.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most systems-analysis tasks are digital and cognitive, including requirements analysis, technology research, system design, documentation, testing, and some programming, making them highly amenable to AI assistance. Cheaper and faster analysis should unlock substantial demand from modernization backlogs, system integration, cybersecurity needs, and adoption of AI itself, although organizational capacity will constrain expansion. High disruption combined with high demand elasticity therefore points to augmentation, with analysts producing more and shifting toward architecture, governance, and stakeholder management.
fable5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — requirements analysis, cost-benefit studies, system design, data modeling, documentation, testing, and light programming — are digital and language-based work squarely in AI's current path; AI tools can already draft specifications, generate diagrams, and write manuals. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper systems analysis unlocks demand as more organizations (especially small firms) can afford custom IT integration and AI adoption itself creates new systems work, but demand is capped by organizational change-management capacity rather than pure analysis throughput. The stakeholder-liaison and organizational-context portions remain human, but analysts who don't shift toward AI orchestration, architecture judgment, and business translation will be displaced. High disruption with moderate elasticity fits restructure.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—requirements analysis, systems design, cost-benefit modeling, data modeling, documentation, testing, and light programming—are almost entirely digital/cognitive and already materially accelerated by AI coding assistants, architecture generators, and analytics tools, producing very high disruption. Elasticity is high because cheaper, faster systems work unlocks latent demand: more frequent upgrades, deeper customization, continuous optimization, and AI-system integration projects that smaller firms previously deferred. The result is an augment dynamic in which each analyst produces far more value and overall employment holds or expands as organizations consume more systems-improvement work.

title: Concierges

However, the core human elements of greeting guests, building relationships, and handling complex personal requests still require physical presence and emotional intelligence. Demand elasticity is low (3) because concierge services are typically bundled into existing facilities rather than purchased separately - hotels, apartments, and offices won't dramatically expand concierge headcount even if AI makes individual concierges more productive. The combination of moderate-high disruption with low elasticity suggests restructuring, where successful concierges will need to adapt by focusing more on high-touch personal service while AI handles routine information and booking tasks.
opus_rationale: Much of the informational and booking work (reservations, recommendations, travel arrangements) is digital and increasingly handled by apps and AI assistants, but the core value lies in in-person greeting, physical presence at a front desk, errand-running, package handling, and personalized human hospitality that AI cannot replace. The BLS itself notes hotel concierge roles being automated while residential and senior-living demand grows, which caps but doesn't eliminate the occupation. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because these services are tied to physical buildings and resident counts rather than scalable with cheaper output. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient — AI reshapes the informational periphery but the physical, interpersonal core endures.
opus5_rationale: Much of a concierge's informational work — recommendations, reservations, travel arrangements, message-taking — is language-based and already being absorbed by apps and AI assistants, which BLS explicitly cites as reducing hotel concierge roles. However, the core value proposition is in-person hospitality: greeting people, physical package handling, running errands, responding to resident needs, and creating a human welcome that is itself the product being sold, so disruption stays moderate. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper concierge-style service does expand into residential and senior-living settings where amenity competition drives demand, but the physical staffing at a desk is roughly fixed per building rather than scaling with output. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI hollows out the information-lookup periphery while the in-person presence remains the job.
openai_rationale: The role of a concierge involves a mix of digital and physical tasks, such as making reservations and providing personalized service, which AI can assist with but not fully replace. AI can streamline some tasks like booking and information provision, but the human touch in customer service remains crucial. Demand elasticity is low because the need for personalized, human interaction is not significantly suppressed by cost. While AI can enhance efficiency, it is unlikely to lead to a substantial increase in demand for concierge services. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: AI chatbots, voice agents, booking tools, recommendation systems, and building-management software can automate many concierge tasks such as answering routine questions, making reservations, arranging transportation, handling emails, and routing maintenance requests. However, the occupation still relies heavily on in-person hospitality, greeting residents or guests, handling packages, resolving ambiguous interpersonal issues, and providing a reassuring physical presence, especially in residential and senior-living settings. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper concierge-like services could expand to more buildings and lower-end hotels, but on-site staffing is constrained by the number of properties and the premium placed on human service. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to eliminate the physical and interpersonal core, the occupation fits the resilient category.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI assistants and apps can automate many information-heavy duties, including recommendations, reservations, travel planning, messaging, and routing service requests. Demand is constrained by the number of hotels, residences, and offices rather than by the cost of producing concierge advice, so cheaper service is unlikely to generate proportionally more jobs. Because AI will substantially alter but not fully overtake the occupation's on-site core, the occupation is resilient at the upper boundary of moderate disruption.
fable5_rationale: A significant share of concierge tasks — recommendations, reservations, travel arrangements, answering inquiries — are language-based and already being absorbed by apps and AI assistants, but the core value in residential and senior-living settings is physical presence, package handling, greeting, and high-touch personal service that AI cannot replicate. Elasticity is low: cheaper concierge-style information doesn't lead buildings or hotels to hire more concierges; instead, informational functions get automated or consolidated into front-desk roles, and demand is tied to building counts rather than service cost. The occupation persists because its in-person hospitality core remains human, even as the knowledge portion erodes (already visible in declining hotel concierge employment). With disruption at a moderate 5, the occupation is resilient, though tilted toward the residential/senior-care segments where human presence is the product.
grok45_rationale: Disruption is moderate because roughly half the duties (recommendations, reservations, tickets, info, emails) are language/cognitive and already assisted by AI apps and chatbots, while the other half (greeting, packages, errands, in-person problem-solving, relationship-building) requires physical presence and unpredictable real-world interaction that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low because demand is largely tied to the fixed stock of hotels, apartments, and offices that choose to staff a desk; cheaper service unlocks some additional residential/senior facilities but does not create dramatically higher volume of human concierge work. The combination keeps the occupation in the resilient category: AI trims peripheral tasks and accelerates hotel automation already noted by BLS, yet core human-facing work remains intact.

title: Conservation scientists and foresters
claude_rationale: Conservation scientists and foresters have moderate disruption as AI assists with data analysis, GIS mapping, and forest monitoring through satellite imagery and drones, but the core work remains heavily field-based requiring physical presence for site assessment, fire suppression, and hands-on land management. Elasticity is moderate because while AI-enhanced monitoring and analysis could make conservation work more efficient and potentially expand coverage of protected lands, demand is constrained by government budgets, regulatory frameworks, and the finite nature of land resources. Since disruption is moderate (4), this occupation falls into the resilient category where AI enhances but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core work.
opus_rationale: Disruption is moderate because while AI strongly enhances the analytical portions—GIS mapping, satellite/drone imagery analysis, modeling of fire spread, timber inventory and growth estimation—the core work requires substantial physical field presence: site preparation, controlled burns, fire suppression, walking remote terrain, and in-person negotiation with landowners. Elasticity is moderate as cheaper, faster environmental analysis could unlock more monitoring and conservation planning, but demand is largely driven by public budgets, regulatory mandates, and land area rather than by cost barriers, capping expansion. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI augments the data-heavy peripheral tasks but cannot replace the hands-on, judgment-driven, physically demanding core work.
opus5_rationale: A meaningful share of the work is analytical and digital — GIS mapping, remote sensing, drone and satellite imagery analysis, growth modeling, plan writing, and regulatory compliance documentation — all of which AI can substantially accelerate. But the core of the job remains field-based: site inspection, controlled burns, fire suppression, physical timber measurement, supervising crews, and negotiating with landowners in person, which caps disruption at moderate. Demand is largely set by government budgets, public land acreage, and regulatory mandates rather than by the cost of analysis, so cheaper monitoring expands coverage somewhat (more parcels assessed, more private landowners advised) but does not multiply headcount. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the mapping and reporting periphery while the field-management core, and the wildfire-driven demand growth BLS projects, remain intact.
openai_rationale: The role of conservation scientists and foresters involves a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, such as managing land quality, overseeing conservation activities, and using GIS technology. While AI can assist with data analysis and GIS tasks, the core work requires human judgment and physical presence, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate as increased efficiency could lead to more comprehensive environmental management and monitoring, but the overall demand is constrained by regulatory and environmental factors. Thus, the net effect is resilient, as AI will augment but not fundamentally alter the occupation.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially affect the analytical and office-based parts of this occupation, including GIS mapping, remote-sensing interpretation, forest inventory estimation, fire-risk modeling, compliance documentation, and management-plan drafting. However, much of the core work still requires field judgment, travel to remote sites, stakeholder negotiation, supervision of crews, regulatory accountability, and participation in activities such as fire suppression or habitat restoration. Demand could expand moderately because cheaper monitoring and planning would allow more landowners and agencies to assess forests, rangelands, wildfire risk, water quality, and habitat conditions, but total demand is constrained by public budgets, land area, permitting, and implementation capacity. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to replace the field-based and supervisory core, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially improve satellite and drone-image analysis, GIS mapping, wildfire modeling, inventory estimation, regulatory documentation, and management-plan development. Lower costs could enable more frequent monitoring and management of currently underserved forests and rangelands, although government budgets, regulation, and the finite land base limit demand expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI enhances a sizable knowledge-work component without replacing its field-based core.
fable5_rationale: Core work involves substantial fieldwork — site visits, fire suppression, walking rugged terrain, physically assessing timber and land conditions — which AI cannot perform, though AI meaningfully accelerates the analytical portions like GIS mapping, remote sensing analysis, management plan drafting, and regulatory compliance documentation. grok45_rationale: Core work mixes substantial outdoor physical tasks (site preparation with equipment, fire suppression, on-site tree measurement with clinometers and tapes, long-distance terrain walking) with knowledge work (GIS/satellite analysis, management planning, compliance, landowner negotiation), so AI will strongly assist data modeling, remote sensing interpretation, and plan optimization but cannot replace required real-world presence. Demand is constrained by finite public and private land acreage, government budgets, and regulatory structures; cheaper analysis may modestly expand private-landowner advisory work or wildfire mitigation intensity but will not unlock large latent volume. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient—AI reshapes analytical tools without displacing the hands-on core.

title: Construction and building inspectors
claude_rationale: Construction and building inspectors face moderate disruption as AI can assist with report writing, code compliance checking, and data analysis, but the core work requires physical presence at construction sites, hands-on equipment use, and real-world judgment about structural safety. Demand elasticity is low because inspection requirements are largely fixed by regulations and safety standards - making inspections faster or cheaper doesn't create demand for more inspections of the same buildings. The physical, regulatory, and liability-driven nature of this work keeps it in the resilient category despite some digital augmentation potential.
opus_rationale: Disruption is moderate: while plan review, code compliance checks, report writing, and documentation are increasingly AI-assisted (and remote inspection technology is already cited by BLS as reducing headcount), the core work still requires physical presence to climb, crawl, and use testing equipment at worksites that involve unpredictable real-world conditions. Elasticity is low because demand for inspections is structurally fixed by regulation and the construction cycle—buildings get inspected a set number of times regardless of cost, so cheaper/faster inspection unlocks little latent demand. Because disruption falls at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes the documentation and remote-monitoring periphery and may trim some headcount, but the hands-on, code-enforcement core of the job remains human-dependent.
opus5_rationale: Core work requires physical site presence — climbing ladders, crawling in attics, using moisture meters and electrical testers — which AI cannot replace, though plans examination, code lookup, report writing, and photo/video-based remote inspection are genuinely in AI's path and already reducing site visits (BLS explicitly cites remote inspection as a headcount drag). That puts disruption in the moderate band: a meaningful slice of the job (plan review, documentation, code interpretation) is digitizable while the field verification remains hands-on. Elasticity is low because inspection volume is set by construction activity and mandated code checkpoints, not by inspection cost — nobody orders extra inspections because they got cheaper, and regulatory frameworks fix the number of required checks. Since disruption is at 5, the occupation lands in 'resilient': AI reshapes the paperwork and enables some remote consolidation, causing slow erosion rather than a structural transformation of the core role.
openai_rationale: Construction and building inspectors perform tasks that are predominantly physical and require on-site presence, such as inspecting construction sites and using testing devices. While AI and remote inspection technologies may assist with documentation and some aspects of compliance checking, the core tasks still require human judgment and physical presence, leading to a low disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because the need for inspections is driven by regulatory requirements rather than cost or speed. Even if AI makes inspections faster, the number of inspections required is unlikely to increase significantly. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: AI can materially assist the office and cognitive parts of inspection work, including code lookup, plan review, report drafting, photo analysis, scheduling, and remote inspection workflows. However, the core job still depends heavily on physical site presence, practical construction knowledge, use of testing equipment, judgment in ambiguous field conditions, and legally accountable enforcement decisions. Demand elasticity is low because inspection volume is largely tied to construction activity, permitting rules, real estate transactions, and safety regulations rather than the price of inspection labor. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to streamline and partially reshape the role than replace the occupation at scale.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can automate plan review, code lookup, report drafting, image analysis, scheduling, and parts of remote inspection, materially changing the office-based portion of the job. However, core duties still require accountable onsite observation, testing equipment, access to difficult spaces, and judgment about varied real-world conditions. Demand is tied mainly to construction activity and legally required inspection cycles, so cheaper inspections would generate only limited additional volume. With moderate disruption rather than wholesale automation, the occupation is resilient, although inspectors will increasingly use AI, drones, and remote-inspection tools.
fable5_rationale: Core work requires physical presence at construction sites—climbing ladders, crawling through attics, using testing equipment on plumbing and electrical systems—which AI cannot replicate, though AI meaningfully assists with plans examination, code compliance checking, report writing, and remote inspection via drones and computer vision. Elasticity is low because inspection volume is driven by construction activity and regulatory mandates, not by inspection cost; making inspections 10x cheaper does not cause society to demand 10x more inspections, and BLS already projects slight decline partly from remote inspection tools. grok45_rationale: Core work mixes on-site physical inspection (climbing, crawling, using meters/testers, verifying systems and structures in unpredictable real-world conditions) with knowledge tasks like plan review, code checking, and report writing; AI already assists the latter via blueprint analysis, image processing, report generation, and remote/drone inspections, but human presence and judgment remain essential for most site work, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is largely fixed by construction volume, permitting rules, and safety regulations rather than price or speed, so cheaper/faster inspections unlock only limited extra volume (e.g., more home checks) and do not expand total need enough to offset productivity gains. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold, the occupation is resilient overall even as tools restructure peripheral tasks.

title: Construction equipment operators
claude_rationale: Construction equipment operation is fundamentally physical work requiring real-time coordination with heavy machinery in unpredictable outdoor environments, making it largely resistant to AI disruption. While some modern equipment incorporates GPS and computerized controls that AI could enhance, the core tasks of maneuvering bulldozers, excavators, and other heavy machinery require human presence, spatial awareness, and physical dexterity. Demand for construction equipment operators is relatively inelastic as infrastructure projects have fixed scope requirements - making roads 10x faster doesn't create 10x more road projects. The occupation remains resilient due to low disruption potential despite inelastic demand.
opus_rationale: The core work is operating heavy machinery in unpredictable outdoor environments requiring hand-eye-foot coordination, physical presence, equipment maintenance, and real-time crew coordination — tasks that are physical and manual, placing them outside AI's direct path. While GPS guidance and semi-autonomous machinery may augment certain repetitive grading or paving tasks, full autonomy in dynamic construction sites remains distant, so AI touches only the periphery. Demand is tied to infrastructure spending and physical project volume rather than cost-of-cognitive-work, so even efficiency gains wouldn't dramatically expand headcount needs. Because disruption is well below the 6 threshold, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: The work is overwhelmingly physical and site-based: maneuvering heavy machinery in unpredictable outdoor terrain, coordinating with crews via hand signals, and performing hands-on maintenance. GPS/machine-control and semi-autonomous grading systems are real and growing, and mining sites already run autonomous haulage, but general construction sites are too variable, cluttered, and liability-sensitive for broad autonomy within a decade, so AI mainly assists with grade guidance, telematics, and maintenance prediction. Demand is moderately elastic — cheaper earthmoving would unlock some deferred infrastructure and site work — but is capped by permitting, funding cycles, and land availability rather than operator cost. With disruption well under the threshold, the occupation is resilient; the main change is operators supervising increasingly automated machines rather than being replaced by them.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of construction equipment operators are predominantly physical and hands-on, involving the operation and maintenance of heavy machinery, which limits the potential for AI disruption. While some advancements in automation and AI may assist with equipment diagnostics or coordination, the unpredictable and physical nature of construction sites keeps disruption low. Demand elasticity is low because the need for construction equipment operators is closely tied to infrastructure projects and not significantly suppressed by cost. Even with increased efficiency, the demand for operators is unlikely to expand dramatically, as the work is constrained by the pace of construction projects and regulatory factors.
gpt55_rationale: Construction equipment operation is primarily physical, site-specific work involving heavy machinery, coordination with crews, safety judgment, maintenance, and adaptation to changing terrain and weather. AI, GPS grade control, sensors, teleoperation, and semi-autonomous equipment will improve productivity and may automate some repetitive grading, hauling, paving, or mining tasks, but widespread full autonomy on varied construction sites remains difficult over the next decade. Demand would expand only modestly if operation became cheaper because construction is constrained by infrastructure budgets, permitting, materials, land, and project timelines rather than operator labor alone. Because AI affects important tools but does not fully reshape the hands-on core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI-enabled machine guidance, autonomous grading and excavation, collision avoidance, and predictive maintenance will materially change equipment operation, especially on repetitive, well-mapped sites. Cheaper operation may enable somewhat more infrastructure and construction, but demand is constrained by project budgets, permitting, land, materials, and broader construction activity, so it will not expand proportionally. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, although operators will increasingly supervise automated equipment and use digital control systems.
fable5_rationale: Operating heavy machinery is fundamentally physical work in unpredictable outdoor environments, though autonomous and semi-autonomous equipment (GPS-guided grading, remote-operated dozers) is beginning to emerge in controlled settings like mining, warranting a low-but-not-minimal disruption score over the next decade. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper earthmoving could enable more infrastructure and construction projects, but demand is largely driven by public spending, land development cycles, and permitting rather than operator labor costs. grok45_rationale: Core tasks are almost entirely physical and site-based—maneuvering heavy machinery via levers/pedals, coordinating with crews via signals, and performing basic maintenance in unpredictable outdoor environments—so AI currently affects only peripherals like GPS precision aids, predictive maintenance, or training simulators, keeping disruption low. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster equipment operation would unlock some additional infrastructure and building projects currently delayed by cost, yet demand remains constrained by materials, capital budgets, regulations, and physical site limits rather than expanding unboundedly. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient as AI does not reshape the essential human presence and control required on construction sites.

AI is largely irrelevant to daily tasks, with only peripheral effects from prefabrication and robotics that the BLS notes may slightly reduce demand for some helper categories. Elasticity is moderate since construction demand responds to infrastructure investment and cost, but it is capped by physical labor requirements, capital, and permitting rather than AI productivity. With disruption far below 6, this occupation is clearly resilient—AI touches only the edges while the physical core remains firmly human.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely physical: hauling materials, digging, cleaning sites, erecting scaffolding, and operating handheld power tools in unpredictable outdoor environments. Because disruption is low despite meaningful latent demand, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core duties involve strenuous physical work, tool use, material handling, and adaptation to varied, hazardous jobsites, all of which remain difficult for AI and robotics to automate. gpt55_rationale: AI will materially improve construction managers' digital and cognitive tasks, including cost estimation, scheduling, contract review, progress reporting, procurement analysis, BIM coordination, and risk forecasting. Elasticity is moderate — cheaper management could enable more and smaller projects to get professional oversight, but total construction volume is constrained by land, capital, materials, and labor rather than management costs. With disruption capped at moderate levels by the irreducibly physical, relational nature of site supervision, the occupation is resilient; AI will make managers more productive on the paperwork side without displacing the role.
grok45_rationale: Core duties center on onsite supervision, real-time response to delays/emergencies, subcontractor coordination, and physical-site decision-making that require human presence and judgment, so AI mainly accelerates peripheral knowledge tasks such as cost estimating, scheduling, contract review, and progress reporting rather than replacing the occupation’s essence. Demand for construction management is driven by population growth, infrastructure needs, and building complexity rather than management cost alone; even large productivity gains are unlikely to unlock dramatically more projects because capital, materials, land, and trade labor remain the binding constraints. With only moderate disruption, the occupation fits the resilient category: AI tools will raise individual productivity but leave the fundamental role and headcount trajectory largely intact.

title: Cooks
claude_rationale: Cooking involves predominantly physical, hands-on tasks requiring real-time sensory judgment, manual dexterity, and unpredictable problem-solving that AI cannot replicate. While AI might assist with peripheral tasks like inventory management or recipe suggestions, the core work of food preparation, cooking techniques, taste adjustment, and kitchen coordination remains fundamentally human. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper food preparation could expand dining out and food delivery markets, but growth is constrained by physical kitchen capacity, food safety regulations, and consumer dining patterns. The low disruption score places this firmly in the resilient category despite moderate demand elasticity.
opus_rationale: Cooking is overwhelmingly physical and manual—preparing, handling, plating food, and operating kitchen equipment in real-world, unpredictable environments where AI software has minimal direct application. Disruption is driven only by peripheral automation in highly standardized fast-food settings (where some headcount decline is projected) and digital ordering systems, leaving the core hands-on work largely untouched. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper, faster food service does expand dining-out and delivery consumption, which is why restaurant cook employment is projected to grow 15 percent. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches only the edges while the manual core endures.
opus5_rationale: Cooking is overwhelmingly physical and sensory — knife work, heat management, plating, taste and smell — performed in crowded, fast-paced kitchens that resist automation; AI touches only peripheral functions like menu planning, inventory forecasting, and order routing. Robotic fry stations and automated assembly do threaten the fast food and short order segments (BLS already projects -13% and -6%), but these are robotics rather than AI cognition, and the larger restaurant cook category is projected to grow 15%. Demand for prepared food expands with income and convenience, so cheaper kitchen operations plausibly mean more outlets and more meals served rather than fewer cooks overall. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the back-office and some highly standardized stations but not the core craft.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of cooks are predominantly physical and hands-on, involving food preparation, cooking, and kitchen management, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist with inventory management and recipe suggestions, the disruption to core tasks remains low. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make some processes more efficient, the overall demand for cooks is driven by consumer preferences for dining experiences, which are not easily scalable. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption, with stable demand expected.
gpt55_rationale: Cooking is primarily hands-on work involving food handling, heat, timing, dexterity, cleaning, safety, and real-time coordination in a physical kitchen, so current AI affects mostly peripheral tasks such as recipe planning, inventory, scheduling, and order routing. Robotics and automated cooking systems are more relevant in standardized fast food, cafeteria, and short-order settings, but they are less capable in varied restaurant kitchens that require adaptation, sensory judgment, and human presence. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper prepared food could increase takeout, delivery, institutional meals, and customized meal services, but total food consumption is naturally limited and restaurants also sell service, convenience, and experience. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate for the occupation as a whole, the net effect is resilient despite some automation pressure in fast food and highly standardized kitchens.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core cooking tasks require physical dexterity, sensory judgment, sanitation, and real-time coordination in crowded kitchens, placing most of the work outside the direct reach of current AI. AI can assist with recipes, inventory, scheduling, order sequencing, and quality monitoring, while specialized kitchen robotics may reduce staffing in standardized fast-food and short-order settings. Demand could expand somewhat if preparation became cheaper, but food consumption is bounded and labor is only one component of meal prices, limiting the headcount benefit. Because disruption remains low for the occupation overall, cooks are resilient despite greater automation risk in highly standardized segments.
fable5_rationale: Cooking is fundamentally physical, hands-on work requiring dexterity, taste, smell, and real-time coordination in a chaotic kitchen environment — tasks far outside AI's language and analysis capabilities, though kitchen robotics and automation pose a modest longer-term threat in standardized fast-food settings. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper prepared food would expand dining-out demand somewhat, but food consumption is bounded and much of the cost structure is ingredients and real estate, not labor productivity. With disruption clearly low, the occupation is resilient; AI may assist with inventory, ordering, and menu planning at the periphery, while automation risk is concentrated in the fast-food segment (already projected to decline) rather than in skilled restaurant cooking.
grok45_rationale: Core duties such as weighing ingredients, grilling/frying/boiling, plating, and maintaining sanitation are almost entirely physical, manual, and sensory, requiring on-site presence and dexterity that current and near-term AI cannot replace; AI only assists peripheral tasks like inventory forecasting or recipe suggestions. Demand elasticity is moderate because substantially cheaper/faster food preparation would expand restaurant openings, takeout/delivery volume, institutional catering, and personal-chef services as price barriers fall, though biological limits on consumption and kitchen capacity prevent unbounded growth. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation stays resilient: AI touches the edges without reshaping the hands-on core.

title: Correctional officers and bailiffs
claude_rationale: This occupation involves predominantly physical presence, human judgment in unpredictable situations, and direct supervision of people - core tasks that AI cannot meaningfully assist with. While some administrative tasks like report writing might benefit from AI tools, the essential work of maintaining security, conducting searches, and managing human interactions remains fundamentally unchanged. Demand for correctional services is relatively fixed by crime rates, court decisions, and incarceration policies rather than cost considerations, so productivity gains would not expand the need for these services. The low disruption score keeps this firmly in the resilient category despite very low demand elasticity.
opus_rationale: The core work—guarding inmates, maintaining physical security, restraining individuals, escorting people, and maintaining courtroom order—is inherently physical, requires real-time human presence, and demands judgment in unpredictable, often dangerous situations that AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like report writing, surveillance monitoring, and logging, leaving the central duties essentially unchanged. Demand is inelastic and driven by incarceration rates and criminal justice policy rather than cost or speed of service, and the occupation is actually projected to decline due to sentencing reform and budget constraints unrelated to AI. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient to AI-driven transformation of its core work.
opus5_rationale: Core work is physical presence, supervision, restraint, and de-escalation inside secure facilities — tasks AI cannot perform. AI touches only the periphery: surveillance analytics, contraband detection, automated headcounts, and report/log generation, which may modestly reduce paperwork and per-officer staffing ratios but not replace the post. Elasticity is very low because demand is set by incarceration policy and court schedules, not by the cost of guarding; cheaper monitoring does not create more prisoners. Projected decline stems from sentencing reform and budgets rather than AI, so the occupation is resilient to AI disruption even as headcount shrinks for unrelated reasons.
openai_rationale: Correctional officers and bailiffs perform tasks that are predominantly physical and require human presence, such as maintaining order, enforcing rules, and escorting individuals. These tasks are not easily automated by AI, leading to a low disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because the need for these roles is driven by legal and institutional requirements rather than cost or speed of service. Even with increased efficiency, the number of officers needed is unlikely to expand significantly. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: Correctional officers and bailiffs perform work that is heavily tied to physical presence, legal authority, supervision, searches, escorts, restraint, and rapid response to unpredictable human behavior. AI can improve surveillance, incident detection, contraband screening, report writing, scheduling, and risk assessment, but these tools mostly support rather than replace the core custody and courtroom-security functions. Demand is highly inelastic because staffing needs are driven by inmate counts, court activity, law, safety rules, and government budgets; making the work cheaper would not cause society to consume many more jail or courtroom security services. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite low elasticity, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core duties require continuous physical presence, situational judgment, interpersonal authority, and the ability to respond to disturbances or restrain and escort people. AI can improve surveillance, threat detection, facility inspections, scheduling, and report writing, but legal accountability and unpredictable confrontations limit substitution over the next decade. Demand is tied primarily to incarcerated populations, courtroom activity, security requirements, and government budgets, so cheaper monitoring would not generate substantially more correctional or bailiff services. The occupation is therefore resilient to AI-driven task replacement, although technology may reduce staffing needs at the margin and alter monitoring and administrative work.
fable5_rationale: The core work — physically supervising people in custody, restraining individuals, conducting searches, escorting prisoners, and maintaining courtroom order — requires human presence in unpredictable, often dangerous physical situations that AI cannot perform. AI may assist with peripheral tasks like report writing, surveillance monitoring, and contraband detection, but these are secondary to the hands-on security role. Elasticity is low because demand is driven by incarceration rates and criminal justice policy, not cost — cheaper supervision would not lead society to incarcerate more people, and policy trends actually favor decarceration. With minimal disruption to core tasks, this occupation is resilient to AI, though it faces headcount decline from policy shifts unrelated to technology.
grok45_rationale: Core duties—physical supervision, cell searches, restraint, escorting inmates, and maintaining order in volatile environments—require real-world human presence, strength, and split-second judgment that AI cannot perform; AI only assists peripheral tasks such as camera analytics, automated logs, and risk scoring. Demand for correctional capacity is set by crime rates, sentencing laws, and budgets rather than labor cost or speed, so cheaper AI-augmented monitoring does not expand the number of prisoners or courtrooms and may even reduce staffing needs. Because disruption remains low, the occupation stays resilient even as technology improves surveillance efficiency.

title: Cost estimators
claude_rationale: Cost estimation is predominantly analytical work involving data processing, calculations, and pattern recognition from historical projects - core capabilities where AI excels and is already making significant inroads through specialized software. The work involves reading technical documents, analyzing databases, performing calculations, and generating reports, all of which are highly susceptible to AI automation. Demand elasticity is low because cost estimation is typically a fixed input per project - businesses don't suddenly need 10x more estimates just because they're cheaper to produce, and the BLS already projects -4% employment decline due to productivity improvements from estimation software.
opus_rationale: Cost estimation is predominantly cognitive, data-driven knowledge work—reading documents, analyzing materials/labor costs, running calculations, and preparing reports—all directly in AI's path, with estimation software already boosting productivity per BLS. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of construction and manufacturing projects requiring estimates is driven by underlying economic activity rather than the cost of estimation itself; cheaper estimating doesn't meaningfully increase how many buildings get built. With disruption at 7 and elasticity around 4, productivity gains translate into fewer estimators needed rather than expanded output, consistent with the BLS-projected employment decline.
opus5_rationale: Cost estimating is almost entirely digital analytical work: reading blueprints and specs, quantity takeoffs, database lookups of material and labor costs, calculation, and report writing — all directly in the path of AI plus BIM/estimating software automation, with multimodal models increasingly able to parse drawings and generate itemized estimates. Demand is largely derived from the volume of construction and manufacturing projects, which is capped by capital, permitting, and physical building capacity rather than by the cost of producing estimates; cheaper estimating might unlock somewhat more bid coverage and more frequent re-estimation on smaller jobs, but not proportionally more work. Site visits, client negotiation, and accountability for costly errors preserve some human role, but they are a minority of the task mix. High disruption combined with low elasticity implies headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS -4% projection, so 'replace' fits.
openai_rationale: The role of cost estimators involves significant data analysis, calculation, and the use of specialized software, making it susceptible to AI-driven automation. AI tools can enhance productivity by quickly processing large datasets and simulating various cost scenarios, which are core tasks of this occupation. However, the demand elasticity is low because the need for cost estimation is relatively fixed; businesses require accurate estimates, but making the process faster or cheaper does not significantly increase the volume of projects requiring estimation. As a result, increased productivity from AI is likely to lead to a reduction in headcount, fitting the 'replace' category.
gpt55_rationale: Cost estimating is heavily digital and analytical: reading plans, extracting quantities, comparing databases, calculating labor/material costs, preparing bids, and writing reports are all tasks that AI-enabled estimating, BIM, CAD, and document-analysis tools can increasingly automate. Human judgment, site visits, contractor coordination, and handling unusual project conditions still matter, but much of the daily workflow is in AI's direct path. Demand elasticity is low because the number of construction, manufacturing, and repair projects does not expand proportionally just because estimates become cheaper, though firms may run more scenarios or serve smaller bids. With high disruption and limited demand expansion, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount rather than be fully absorbed by new demand.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most estimating tasks—reading digital plans, extracting quantities, comparing cost databases, modeling scenarios, and drafting bids—are directly amenable to AI integrated with BIM and CAD software. Human judgment, site visits, stakeholder coordination, and responsibility for unusual project risks remain important, preventing full automation. Demand is linked primarily to the number of construction and manufacturing projects, so cheaper estimates may generate more bid scenarios but will not produce a proportional increase in projects. High disruption combined with limited demand expansion points to fewer estimators handling more work, making replace the best fit.
fable5_rationale: Cost estimation is almost entirely digital knowledge work — reading blueprints, extracting quantities, pricing labor and materials, and producing reports — all tasks squarely in AI's path, and takeoff/estimation software integrated with BIM is already automating much of it (BLS itself cites software productivity as driving projected decline). Demand for estimates is tied to the underlying volume of construction and manufacturing projects, which doesn't expand just because estimating gets cheaper; contractors may bid on somewhat more jobs, but total project volume caps demand. With high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains translate directly into fewer estimators needed, consistent with the projected -4% employment decline, making 'replace' the fitting category.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—reading blueprints and technical documents, querying cost databases, calculating material/labor/time estimates, running simulations, and producing bids/reports—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already being accelerated by estimation software and highly amenable to multimodal AI and predictive models. Demand for estimates is tightly coupled to the volume of construction and manufacturing projects, which is set by broader economic activity rather than estimation cost; cheaper/faster estimates enable more iterations or slightly better coverage but do not unlock large latent project volume. High disruption plus low elasticity therefore points to net headcount contraction as productivity gains are not absorbed by expanded output.

title: Court reporters and simultaneous captioners
claude_rationale: AI speech-to-text technology has advanced dramatically and can now transcribe spoken dialogue with high accuracy in real-time, directly targeting the core function of court reporters and captioners. Modern AI systems can handle multiple speakers, legal terminology, and produce formatted transcripts - capabilities that were the exclusive domain of human stenographers just years ago. Demand elasticity is low because legal proceedings require a fixed number of transcripts regardless of cost, and accessibility requirements for captioning are largely regulatory-driven rather than price-sensitive. The combination of high AI disruption to core transcription tasks and inelastic demand for these services positions this occupation for significant headcount reduction as AI tools become more reliable and widely adopted.
opus_rationale: The core work—converting speech to accurate text in real time—is squarely in the path of speech-recognition and transcription AI, which has improved dramatically and already handles captioning and much transcription. Demand is largely inelastic: the number of legal proceedings, broadcasts, and CART needs is fixed by court schedules, regulation, and population, so cheaper transcription doesn't meaningfully multiply the volume of proceedings. Some latent demand exists (more captioning of online content, aging population), but courts and regulatory requirements cap growth and AI productivity gains translate primarily into fewer human reporters per output. High disruption with low elasticity yields headcount contraction, fitting replace, even though residual roles for review, certification, and legal-record verification will persist.
opus5_rationale: The core task — converting spoken language into accurate verbatim text in real time — is precisely what modern automatic speech recognition and diarization systems now do at near-human accuracy and a tiny fraction of the cost; the remaining human work (speaker identification, certification, editing, exhibit handling) is peripheral to the transcription itself, so disruption is very high even though courtroom presence and state certification rules slow adoption. Demand is highly inelastic: the number of depositions, hearings, and broadcast hours is set by litigation volume and captioning mandates, not by transcription price, so cheaper transcription does not generate proportionally more proceedings. Some latent demand exists for captioning more meetings, classes, and live events, but that expansion is being served almost entirely by automated captioning rather than by hiring more human captioners. High disruption plus inelastic demand points to headcount contraction, with surviving roles shifting toward reviewing and certifying machine-generated records.
openai_rationale: AI can assist in transcription tasks, making the process faster and more accurate, but human oversight is still crucial for ensuring the accuracy and context of legal records. This results in moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is low because the need for verbatim legal records and captioning is driven by regulatory and legal requirements, not cost or speed. Thus, even with productivity gains, the demand for court reporters and captioners is unlikely to expand significantly. The occupation is resilient as AI aids but does not replace the core tasks, and demand remains stable due to legal necessities.
gpt55_rationale: The core work is converting speech into accurate text, speaker labels, timestamps, and searchable transcripts, which is almost entirely language-based and already directly affected by automatic speech recognition, diarization, and AI editing tools. Human workers will still be needed in high-stakes legal settings to certify, monitor, correct, and handle unclear audio, objections, gestures, and procedural context, but much of the capture and first-draft transcription work can be automated. Demand is only modestly elastic: cheaper transcription may increase captioning for meetings, online video, classes, and accessibility use cases, but court and deposition volumes are relatively fixed and many new uses will be served by self-service AI rather than occupational headcount. Because disruption is very high and demand expansion for human reporters/captioners is limited, the likely net effect is replacement with a smaller group of workers focused on verification, certification, and exception handling.
gpt56sol_rationale: Speech recognition, speaker diarization, punctuation, and transcript editing are almost entirely digital tasks already handled increasingly well by AI, placing the occupation directly in its path. Human expertise will remain important for certifying legal records, resolving inaudible or ambiguous speech, identifying speakers, and documenting gestures and exhibits, but these functions can shift toward supervising automated transcription. Demand for legal records is tied largely to the number of proceedings, while cheaper captioning may unlock some additional accessibility use but probably not enough to offset large productivity gains. Consequently, fewer professionals are likely to oversee more proceedings and captioning sessions, making replacement the most likely net effect.
fable5_rationale: The core task — converting speech to accurate text in real time — is precisely what modern AI speech recognition does well and continues to improve at rapidly, making this occupation almost entirely digital and directly in AI's path; only edge cases like accuracy certification, speaker attribution in chaotic settings, and legal admissibility slow full automation. Demand is largely inelastic: the number of trials, depositions, and broadcast hours does not multiply because transcription gets cheaper, and while captioning coverage would expand (more content captioned), that expanded demand would be served by AI itself rather than by more human stenographers. Regulatory requirements for certified human reporters in courts provide a temporary buffer, but this is a legacy protection rather than genuine demand growth. High disruption combined with fixed underlying demand puts this squarely in the replace category, with existing pipeline shortages likely masking the contraction in official projections.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on real-time speech-to-text transcription, speaker identification, and producing verbatim legal or accessibility records—almost entirely language and digital work already being transformed by AI tools like advanced ASR systems that generate drafts for human review. Physical presence is declining with remote options, and accuracy/legal certification barriers are eroding as models improve on multi-speaker, technical, and noisy audio. Demand for official court transcripts is tightly constrained by the volume of legal proceedings, judicial budgets, and regulatory requirements rather than price, so cheaper output does not generate proportionally more cases or depositions; captioning sees only modest expansion from accessibility rules and demographics, most of which AI auto-captions already absorb. High disruption plus low elasticity therefore points to replace, with headcount contraction as AI handles the bulk of capture and humans shrink to residual editing/oversight roles.

title: Craft and fine artists
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts many core artistic tasks - digital artists already use AI tools extensively, illustrators can leverage AI for concept generation and refinement, and even traditional artists increasingly use AI for portfolio development and marketing. However, the creative conceptualization, personal artistic vision, and physical craftsmanship remain distinctly human. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster art production unlocks massive latent demand - businesses need more visual content, personalized art becomes accessible to broader markets, and the explosion of digital platforms creates endless opportunities for visual content. While AI transforms how art is made, the democratization of art creation and the insatiable appetite for visual content means total demand for artistic output will likely expand faster than productivity gains reduce the need for human artists.
opus_rationale: This occupation is split between digital illustrators/cartoonists/digital artists whose core work (creating images) is directly in AI's path via generative image tools, and physical craft artists (ceramics, glassblowing, sculpture, jewelry, tattoo, furniture) whose hands-on, material-based work AI cannot perform. The digital subset faces high disruption while the physical and gallery/reputation-driven fine-art market values human authorship and originality, which AI cannot replicate and which buyers specifically pay a premium for. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper commercial illustration could expand some volume, but the fine-art and craft market is driven by scarcity, provenance, and human meaning rather than cost or speed, capping expansion. Because overall disruption to the blended occupation sits at the moderate level (much of the core work remains physical or rooted in human authenticity), the resilient category fits—AI reshapes the commercial-illustration periphery without overturning the core craft and fine-art work.
opus5_rationale: The occupation is sharply bifurcated: digital and commercial subsegments (illustrators, cartoonists, concept and digital artists, some medical/scientific illustration) are squarely in the path of generative image models and are already seeing commissioned work absorbed, while the majority of the field — ceramics, glass, fiber, furniture, jewelry, sculpture, tattooing, public installations — is hands-on material work where AI at most assists with ideation, marketing, and online sales. That mix places overall disruption at the top of the moderate band rather than the high band. Elasticity is low because the value of fine and craft art rests on scarcity, provenance, and human authorship rather than on production cost; making images 10x cheaper does not make collectors buy 10x more paintings, and cheap machine-made lookalikes historically suppress rather than expand demand for handmade goods. Net effect is resilient overall (core physical and reputational work persists, BLS projects flat employment), though the commercial illustration niche within it faces genuine replacement pressure and those workers will need to shift toward physical media, direct-to-audience brands, or AI-augmented art direction.
openai_rationale: Craft and fine artists engage in highly creative and manual tasks such as painting, sculpting, and crafting, which are not easily replicated by AI. While digital tools can assist in certain aspects like digital art creation or marketing, the core artistic process remains largely human-driven. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could lower costs in digital art production, the demand for unique, handcrafted art is not significantly suppressed by current costs. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption, with traditional skills remaining essential.
gpt55_rationale: AI image generators and design tools can materially affect ideation, sketching, illustration, portfolio development, marketing copy, grant applications, and some digital-art workflows. However, much of this occupation still involves hands-on manipulation of physical materials, studio practice, client/gallery relationships, and the market value of human authorship, provenance, and reputation. Demand could expand for cheaper visual concepts, decorative images, and customized designs, but demand for original fine art and handmade craft is constrained by income, taste, scarcity, and physical production. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough across the broad occupation to replace the physical and reputation-based core, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can substantially accelerate ideation, sketching, digital illustration, portfolio creation, marketing, and grant writing, placing commercial illustrators and digital artists under particular pressure. However, much of the occupation involves physically manipulating materials, operating specialized equipment, and producing handmade objects whose provenance and human authorship are part of their value. Lower production costs could expand demand for customized imagery and art products, but discretionary spending, limited buyer attention, and the scarcity value of original work constrain that expansion. Because disruption is significant but does not broadly replace the occupation's hands-on core, the aggregate occupation is resilient, with substantial restructuring in its digital specialties.
fable5_rationale: This occupation splits sharply: illustrators, cartoonists, and digital artists face severe disruption from generative image AI, while ceramicists, glassblowers, sculptors, furniture makers, and other craft artists do fundamentally physical, hands-on work where AI is peripheral — averaging to moderate disruption. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because the value of fine and craft art derives from human authorship, scarcity, and provenance; making image generation 10x cheaper floods the market with commodity visuals but doesn't expand demand for original human-made works, and may actually depress commercial illustration income. The physical, authenticity-driven core of the occupation keeps it resilient overall, though the illustration segment specifically faces replacement-level pressure and workers there will need to reposition around distinctive personal style and physical media.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks for most craft and fine artists center on physical manipulation of materials (pottery, glassblowing, painting, sculpting, fiber work, jewelry) that require dexterity, real-world presence, and unpredictable material handling; AI assists ideation, digital sketching, portfolios, and marketing but leaves the hands-on creation largely intact, placing disruption in the moderate mixed range. Demand for original handmade or fine art is only modestly elastic—cheaper production unlocks some commercial illustration and decorative use but is constrained by collector preferences for authenticity, limited display space, and competition from machine-made substitutes, so productivity gains do not expand total headcount much. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation remains resilient overall, with AI touching periphery rather than reshaping the core craft.

title: Credit counselors
claude_rationale: Credit counseling involves substantial knowledge work - analyzing financial data, creating debt management plans, explaining complex financial concepts, and negotiating with creditors - tasks that AI can increasingly assist with or automate. AI tools can already help with financial analysis, document preparation, and basic client communications. However, the work still requires significant human judgment for complex situations and interpersonal skills for building client rapport. Demand elasticity is moderate because while cheaper credit counseling could expand access (especially for underserved populations), growth is constrained by regulatory requirements, the personal nature of financial distress, and the fact that people generally seek these services only when in financial trouble rather than proactively.
opus_rationale: The core work — gathering financial information, assessing income/debt, calculating repayment plans, budgeting, and preparing written recommendations — is heavily cognitive and language-based, all squarely in AI's path; the BLS itself notes automation software is already making these workers more efficient. The empathetic, rapport-building counseling and creditor negotiation components require human presence, keeping disruption high but not maximal. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster debt counseling could reach more underserved consumers and expand access, but growth is structurally constrained by the size of the debt-burdened population and existing institutional channels (colleges, credit agencies). With disruption at 7 and elasticity at 5, the occupation survives but shifts toward higher-touch counseling and oversight of AI-driven analysis, displacing those who only perform routine calculations.
opus5_rationale: Core tasks — gathering financial information, assessing income/debt/expenses, calculating repayment capacity, generating debt management plans, and drafting client documents — are cognitive, numeric, and language-based, and current AI tools plus automation software already handle much of the analysis and document generation; the BLS itself notes automation may temper growth. Disruption is capped below 8 because trust-building, emotional counseling for distressed borrowers, live negotiation with creditors, and referral to community resources still favor a human intermediary. Elasticity is moderate: there is large latent demand for personal financial guidance that cost has suppressed, but most jobs sit in institutionally budgeted settings (colleges, hospitals, nonprofit agencies) whose headcount is funded by fixed budgets and enrollment rather than client willingness to pay, and much unlocked demand will be met by self-serve AI tools rather than more counselors. That combination — high task exposure with only partial demand absorption — fits restructure: the role shifts toward high-touch case management, complex negotiation, and oversight of AI-generated plans, with fewer routine-intake positions.
openai_rationale: Credit counselors perform a mix of cognitive and interpersonal tasks, such as assessing financial situations and advising clients, which can be partially supported by AI tools. However, the core of their work involves personalized advice and negotiation, which still requires human judgment and empathy. Thus, disruption is moderate. Demand elasticity is moderate as well; while AI can enhance productivity, the need for personalized financial advice and negotiation is not likely to expand dramatically. Therefore, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing the core human elements of the job.
gpt55_rationale: Credit counseling is largely language- and analysis-based: gathering financial information, assessing debts and budgets, explaining options, drafting plans, and communicating with creditors are all tasks AI can substantially assist or partially automate. Human judgment, trust-building, empathy with distressed clients, and some negotiation or referral work still matter, so the occupation is not fully automatable. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper counseling could reach many people who currently do not receive personalized debt, student loan, or budgeting help, but the total need is still bounded by debt distress, institutional programs, and clients' willingness or ability to engage. Because disruption is high while demand expansion is meaningful but not enough to fully absorb productivity gains, the occupation is likely to restructure rather than simply grow or disappear.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most core tasks—collecting financial data, assessing budgets and debts, generating repayment plans, explaining options, and drafting communications—are digital and increasingly automatable with AI. Human counselors remain important for trust, empathy, complex negotiations, regulatory accountability, and clients in financial distress. Lower costs could extend counseling to many underserved borrowers, but demand is constrained by clients’ ability to pay, institutional budgets, and the finite number of debt problems requiring intervention. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around oversight, relationship management, and difficult cases rather than disappear.
fable5_rationale: The core tasks — gathering financial data, assessing income and debt, calculating budgets, drafting repayment plans, and explaining options — are language-based knowledge work squarely in AI's current path; chatbots and financial planning tools can already perform much of this analysis and client education. Demand elasticity is low: while latent demand for financial guidance exists among people who can't afford advice, AI will largely serve that demand directly through consumer-facing apps rather than through more counselors, and much of current employment is tied to fixed institutional needs like college financial aid offices whose demand tracks enrollment, not counseling cost. The empathetic, trust-building element in debt crises preserves some human roles, but not enough to offset automation of the analytical core. High disruption with capped demand expansion points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.
