Elasticity is moderate: cheaper fundraising lets more small nonprofits professionalize their development efforts, but the total pool of philanthropic dollars is finite, so productivity gains can't be absorbed indefinitely by more giving. The occupation will survive but shift toward relationship management and strategy, with AI handling research, writing, and campaign mechanics — a classic restructure profile.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks such as donor research, crafting appeals, digital campaign optimization, record-keeping, and success evaluation are predominantly cognitive, language-based, and already materially assisted by AI tools for personalization, predictive analytics, and content generation, though high-touch relationship building for major gifts and in-person event execution still require human presence. Demand is highly elastic because professional fundraising capacity has long been cost-constrained for smaller nonprofits and under-resourced causes; dramatically cheaper and faster outreach unlocks far more campaigns, personalized solicitations, and total dollars raised across the sector. High disruption combined with high elasticity means AI multiplies each fundraiser’s output while expanding the overall market enough to keep headcount stable or growing for those who adapt to AI-augmented strategy and relationship roles.

title: Funeral service workers
claude_rationale: Funeral service work involves substantial physical presence, emotional counseling, and hands-on preparation of remains - core tasks that require human empathy, cultural sensitivity, and physical manipulation that AI cannot replicate. While AI might assist with administrative tasks like filing death certificates or scheduling, the essential work of comforting grieving families, preparing bodies, and managing funeral logistics requires human presence and emotional intelligence. Demand for funeral services is highly inelastic as it's driven by death rates rather than cost considerations - people don't consume more funeral services when they become cheaper, and the number of deaths in a population is relatively fixed. The low disruption and inelastic demand clearly place this occupation in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: Core tasks are deeply physical and interpersonal — preparing remains, embalming, arranging logistics, transporting bodies, and providing in-person grief counseling and compassionate face-to-face service to families. AI can help with peripheral administrative work (death certificates, insurance claims, obituary drafting, scheduling) but cannot touch the human-presence-dependent, emotionally sensitive core. Demand is inherently inelastic since it is tied to the death rate, not price or speed; cheaper processing won't make people consume more funerals. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient — AI augments paperwork at the edges while the essential work remains firmly human.
opus5_rationale: Core work is physical and deeply interpersonal: body removal and preparation, embalming, staging services, transporting remains, and in-person grief counseling with families in a compressed 24-72 hour window. AI can meaningfully help with the administrative periphery — death certificate filings, insurance and VA/SSA paperwork, obituary drafting, scheduling, prearrangement sales and funeral home marketing — but that is a minority of the job and does not displace the licensed, present human. Elasticity is very low because demand is set by the death rate, not by price or speed; cheaper administration will not produce more funerals, and the industry's cost trend (cremation) is already shrinking service intensity. With low disruption and inelastic demand, headcount tracks demographics rather than AI, making this occupation resilient.
openai_rationale: Funeral service workers perform tasks that are largely physical and require human presence, such as preparing bodies and providing emotional support to grieving families. AI may assist with administrative tasks like filing documents, but the core tasks remain human-centric, leading to a low disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because the need for funeral services is not significantly suppressed by cost; people do not opt for more funerals if they become cheaper. The occupation is resilient as AI will not fundamentally alter the core human elements of the work.
gpt55_rationale: AI can meaningfully assist with administrative and language-heavy tasks such as drafting obituaries, preparing forms, scheduling services, explaining options, marketing, and handling benefits or insurance paperwork. However, the occupation’s core still depends on in-person grief support, culturally sensitive judgment, licensed handling and preparation of remains, transportation, service coordination, and trust-based family interaction. Demand is highly tied to mortality and family customs, so making planning cheaper or faster would not create many more funerals, though it may increase preplanning and personalization somewhat. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite low demand elasticity, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can substantially streamline paperwork, scheduling, obituary drafting, benefits applications, marketing, and routine client communications. However, preparing and transporting remains, coordinating ceremonies, managing facilities, and compassionately guiding grieving families require hands-on presence, judgment, and trust. Demand is largely fixed by mortality and demographic trends, so cheaper services would not generate many more funerals, although preplanning could expand modestly. Because AI changes administrative portions rather than the occupation’s physical and interpersonal core, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: The core work — comforting grieving families in person, preparing and transporting bodies, embalming, and coordinating physical ceremonies — is hands-on, emotionally sensitive, and requires physical presence, so AI touches only peripheral tasks like paperwork, obituary drafting, scheduling, and insurance filings. Demand elasticity is very low because funeral demand is fixed by the death rate; making services cheaper or faster does not cause society to consume more funerals, and trends like cremation already compress spending. With disruption at 3, the occupation is resilient: AI streamlines administrative overhead but the human, ceremonial, and physical core remains intact.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on physical handling and preparation of remains, in-person removal and site coordination, and high-empathy counseling of grieving families—all of which require unpredictable real-world presence and human interpersonal skills that AI cannot perform. AI can only assist peripheral digital work such as document filing, scheduling, option menus, and obituary drafting. Demand is almost entirely inelastic because the volume of funerals is fixed by mortality rates; making planning or administration 10x cheaper does not cause more deaths or unlock large latent volume, so productivity gains would not expand headcount. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Gambling services workers
claude_rationale: Gambling services work is predominantly physical and interpersonal, requiring real-time human presence for customer interaction, game operation, and security monitoring in casino environments. While AI might assist with some administrative tasks or basic customer queries, the core functions of dealing cards, managing tables, enforcing rules, and providing personalized customer service remain fundamentally human-centered activities. Demand for gambling services is relatively inelastic as it's driven by entertainment preferences and regulatory constraints rather than cost efficiency - making gambling 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically increase the number of people gambling or the frequency of their visits. The low disruption score combined with inelastic demand places this occupation firmly in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: The core work is physical and customer-facing: dealing cards, managing tables, monitoring floors, and providing in-person hospitality experiences that AI cannot replace. While online gambling automation and sports book digitization threaten the writer/runner subgroup, the bulk of these jobs (dealers, supervisors) depend on physical presence and social interaction that are largely outside AI's path. Demand is also relatively inelastic—gambling capacity is constrained by regulation, physical floor space, and licensing rather than cost or speed of human labor. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient; AI touches peripheral betting-processing tasks but does not reshape the core dealer/supervisor roles.
opus5_rationale: Core work is physically and socially embodied: dealing cards, managing dice and chips, monitoring players in person, and providing the entertainment experience customers pay for. AI touches only the periphery — surveillance analytics, player-tracking, scheduling, and automated sports-book wagering (which mainly pressures the small writers/runners category). Elasticity is low-to-moderate because gambling demand is capped by regulation, licensing, and the fixed number of physical venues, and the shift to online betting substitutes automated platforms rather than expanding in-person dealer headcount. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient in structure, though flat overall employment reflects channel shift rather than AI displacement.
openai_rationale: Gambling services workers perform a mix of tasks, some of which are susceptible to AI disruption, such as handling bets and payouts, which can be automated, especially with the rise of online gambling. However, the core tasks involving customer interaction, supervision, and ensuring compliance with rules require human presence and judgment, limiting AI's impact. Demand elasticity is low because the number of gambling establishments is not expected to increase significantly, and online gambling does not require the same workforce. Thus, while AI may change some aspects of the job, the overall demand for human workers in physical establishments remains relatively stable, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: Most gambling services work is in-person, customer-facing, and operational: dealing cards, monitoring tables, explaining rules, handling disputes, and maintaining the casino experience. AI and automation can affect parts of the job, especially sportsbook ticketing, fraud detection, surveillance, scheduling, customer service, and online gambling interfaces, but the core casino-floor role still depends heavily on human presence and hospitality. Demand elasticity is low because gambling demand is constrained by regulation, location, licensing, consumer budgets, and social limits; cheaper labor does not lead people to gamble 10 times more. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient, even though some subroles such as sportsbook writers and runners may face more automation pressure.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most workers, especially dealers and floor supervisors, perform in-person tasks involving physical game operation, customer interaction, rule enforcement, and real-time judgment, limiting direct AI substitution. AI and automation can still streamline bet processing, payouts, surveillance, scheduling, and administrative work, while online gambling particularly reduces demand for sportsbook writers and runners. Overall gambling demand is constrained by regulation, consumer spending, and market saturation, so cheaper operations are unlikely to produce enough additional play to offset automation fully. Because disruption remains moderate for the occupation's large in-person workforce, the aggregate occupation is resilient despite contraction in its more transactional roles.
fable5_rationale: The core work of dealing cards, running table games, and managing casino floors is fundamentally in-person hospitality and entertainment — customers at physical casinos are paying for human interaction and atmosphere, which AI does not replace. The real threat is online gambling substitution (a channel shift, not AI performing the dealer's tasks), and AI touches only peripheral areas like surveillance, scheduling, and player analytics. Elasticity is low because demand for in-person gambling is driven by regulation, licensing, and consumer entertainment preferences rather than the cost of dealer labor; making dealers more productive would not meaningfully expand table game demand. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient to AI even as it faces structural pressure from online betting platforms.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks for the bulk of workers (dealers, floor supervisors, runners) center on physical presence at tables or windows, manual handling of cards/chips/tickets, real-time customer interaction, and monitoring unpredictable human behavior—areas where AI remains peripheral (e.g., enhanced surveillance analytics or back-office scheduling). Managers involve more cognitive work but still require on-floor leadership. Demand elasticity is low because gambling volume is constrained by regulation, physical floor space, and social limits on consumption; cheaper or faster operations may enable modest expansion of tables or online products but will not generate proportional headcount growth, as already reflected in BLS projections of flat employment amid online automation.

title: General maintenance and repair workers
claude_rationale: General maintenance and repair work is predominantly physical and hands-on, involving tasks like fixing plumbing, electrical work, painting, and machinery repair that require real-world presence and manual dexterity. While AI might assist with some peripheral tasks like work order management or diagnostic guidance, the core work of physically repairing and maintaining equipment and buildings remains largely unchanged. Demand for maintenance services is relatively inelastic - buildings and equipment need a fixed amount of maintenance regardless of cost, and making repairs faster/cheaper doesn't typically generate significantly more maintenance work. The low disruption score combined with inelastic demand places this occupation firmly in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on—fixing plumbing, electrical, flooring, painting, and machinery across varied and unpredictable real-world locations, which AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like diagnostics, ordering supplies, and record-keeping. Demand is somewhat tied to the existing building stock and maintenance needs rather than suppressed by cost, so elasticity is modest. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient; physical presence and dexterity keep humans firmly in the loop.
opus5_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair across varied, unpredictable environments — plumbing, electrical, painting, machinery — requiring dexterity, ladders, cramped spaces, and on-site presence that AI and robotics cannot replicate in the next decade. AI touches only peripheral aspects: diagnostic assistance, predictive maintenance scheduling from sensor data, parts ordering, work-order documentation, and AR-guided troubleshooting that may modestly broaden what a generalist can handle. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper diagnosis could shift some work from licensed specialists to generalists and enable more preventive maintenance, but building stock and equipment volume ultimately cap demand. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is clearly resilient — headcount is driven by physical building and equipment needs, not by information-processing productivity.
openai_rationale: General maintenance and repair work is predominantly physical and hands-on, involving tasks like fixing machines, repairing buildings, and performing routine maintenance, which are not easily automated by AI. Thus, the disruption score is low. While AI could assist with diagnostics or administrative tasks, the core work requires human presence and dexterity. The demand elasticity is low because the need for maintenance is relatively fixed and not significantly suppressed by cost or speed. Even with increased efficiency, the demand for these services is unlikely to expand dramatically, as the work is driven by the physical state of buildings and equipment rather than by cost factors. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: General maintenance and repair work is dominated by hands-on physical tasks in varied real-world settings: inspecting equipment, using tools, replacing parts, painting, repairing flooring, and working around buildings and machinery. AI can help with troubleshooting guides, work-order triage, predictive maintenance alerts, supply ordering, estimating, documentation, and training, but it does not perform the core manual repair work without capable general-purpose robotics. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper, faster maintenance would unlock some deferred repairs and more preventive upkeep, especially in aging buildings, but the need is still bounded by the stock of buildings and equipment. Because disruption to the core occupation remains low-to-moderate, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most core tasks require physical presence, dexterity, tool use, and adaptation to varied buildings and machinery, keeping direct AI disruption low. AI can improve diagnostics, preventive-maintenance scheduling, parts ordering, estimates, recordkeeping, and access to repair instructions, but workers must still perform the repairs. Lower costs may unlock some deferred maintenance and more preventive work, although demand remains constrained by the installed stock of buildings and equipment. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI primarily improving worker productivity rather than replacing the hands-on role.
fable5_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — fixing plumbing, electrical, HVAC, machinery, and building components in unpredictable real-world environments that AI and robotics cannot handle in the next decade. AI touches only the periphery: diagnostic assistance, work-order management, parts ordering, and predictive maintenance scheduling. Elasticity is moderate since cheaper diagnostics and better preventive maintenance could expand demand somewhat, but total maintenance need is largely driven by building stock, not price. With disruption at 2, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on hands-on physical repair of buildings, machines, plumbing, electrical systems, and equipment using tools in unpredictable real-world settings, so AI only assists peripheral elements like diagnostics from sensors/images, blueprint analysis, cost estimates, supply ordering, and record-keeping. Demand elasticity is low because the stock of buildings and equipment sets a relatively fixed need for upkeep; cheaper or faster work may unlock some deferred maintenance or more frequent preventive service but will not produce dramatically higher total volume. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient as AI does not reshape the essential on-site presence and manual work.

title: General office clerks
claude_rationale: General office clerks perform highly routine, digital tasks like data entry, document processing, filing, and phone answering that AI and automation can already handle effectively. Most core duties involve structured information processing with minimal human judgment required. Demand for clerical work is relatively fixed - organizations need a certain amount of administrative support regardless of cost, and making it cheaper doesn't create substantially more need for filing, data entry, or basic customer service. The BLS already projects 7% employment decline, reflecting ongoing automation of these routine tasks.
opus_rationale: Core tasks—typing, filing, data entry, scheduling, answering phones, processing routine documents—are almost entirely digital and language-based, putting them squarely in AI's direct path; automation already handles much of this work today. Demand is highly inelastic: organizations need a fixed amount of clerical throughput and cheaper processing doesn't create more administrative documents to file, it just reduces the headcount required. With disruption very high and elasticity near zero, productivity gains translate directly into fewer positions, consistent with the BLS-projected decline.
opus5_rationale: Core tasks — typing and formatting documents, data entry, filing, routing calls and mail, processing bills, answering routine questions — are almost entirely digital, routine, and language-based, placing them directly in AI's path; automated phone systems, electronic records, and document generation tools already erode this work today. The residual physical elements (moving paper, greeting visitors, operating copiers) are minor and increasingly obsolete. Demand is highly inelastic: organizations do not want more memos filed or more calls transferred as clerical throughput gets cheaper, and the work is a fixed overhead cost absorbed by other staff via self-service software. High disruption plus near-zero latent demand expansion means productivity gains flow straight to headcount reduction, consistent with BLS's projected -7% decline.
openai_rationale: General office clerks perform tasks that are increasingly susceptible to automation, such as data entry, document preparation, and scheduling, which are well within the capabilities of current AI and software tools. This results in a high disruption score as AI can significantly change how these tasks are performed. However, the demand for general office clerks is relatively inelastic; making these tasks faster and cheaper does not lead to a proportional increase in demand for clerical work. Instead, it results in fewer clerks being needed, as evidenced by the projected decline in employment. Thus, the net effect is 'replace' due to high disruption and low elasticity.
gpt55_rationale: General office clerks perform many routine digital and language-based tasks—answering calls, scheduling, typing and formatting documents, filing records, processing forms, and entering data—that are directly targeted by AI, workflow software, automated phone systems, and document management tools. Some duties still involve physical office presence, mail handling, visitors, and local coordination, but these are a minority of the core task bundle in many settings. Demand elasticity is low because organizations do not need dramatically more filing, data entry, scheduling, or routine document processing simply because it becomes cheaper; productivity gains mostly reduce the number of clerks needed. Therefore the occupation fits the replace category: disruption is high and demand expansion is too limited to offset automation-driven headcount pressure.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most core duties—data entry, document preparation, scheduling, record management, billing, and routine communications—are directly automatable with current AI and workflow software. In-person reception and handling physical mail provide some residual need, preventing a maximum disruption score. Demand for clerical processing is largely tied to a fixed volume of organizational transactions, so lower costs are unlikely to generate enough additional work to offset productivity gains, making significant headcount replacement likely.
fable5_rationale: The core tasks — typing and formatting documents, data entry, filing, preparing bills, answering routine phone inquiries, scheduling — are precisely the routine digital and language-based work that current AI tools already handle well; only minor physical tasks like sorting mail or greeting visitors resist automation. Demand for clerical support is derived from the fixed administrative overhead of organizations, and making it 10x cheaper doesn't lead offices to consume 10x more filing or phone answering — productivity gains flow directly to headcount reduction, as BLS's projected -7% decline (predating full generative AI absorption) already suggests. With high disruption and inelastic demand, this occupation faces significant contraction as AI and self-service tools absorb the work. The 'replace' category clearly fits.
grok45_rationale: Core duties—data entry, document typing/editing, scheduling, phone handling, filing, and bill processing—are predominantly routine digital and language-based tasks already being automated by AI chatbots, document tools, electronic filing systems, and scheduling software, placing the occupation firmly in AI’s path. Demand for general clerical support is largely fixed by organizational size and operational volume rather than price; making the work dramatically cheaper does not unlock proportional new demand for more phone answering or record-keeping. This combination of high disruption and inelastic demand produces net headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS projection of a 7% decline.

title: Genetic counselors
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts genetic counseling by automating risk assessment calculations, pattern recognition in genetic data, and generating initial interpretations of test results, but the core human elements of empathetic counseling, complex family dynamics navigation, and personalized decision support remain essential. Demand elasticity is high because genetic counseling is currently severely supply-constrained with only 4,000 practitioners nationwide - AI tools that make counselors more efficient could dramatically expand access to genetic services for the millions who currently lack it, especially as genetic testing becomes more common and affordable. The combination of meaningful AI assistance with substantial unmet demand positions this as an augmentation scenario where productivity gains enable serving many more patients rather than reducing headcount.
opus_rationale: The analytical portions of genetic counseling — interpreting test results, researching hereditary disorders, evaluating risk, and documenting sessions — are highly amenable to AI assistance, but the core of the role hinges on compassionate, in-person psychological support and nuanced communication with distressed families, which AI cannot replace; this keeps disruption at a moderate 6. Demand is highly elastic because genetic testing is expanding rapidly, costs are dropping, and counseling capacity is currently a bottleneck — cheaper, AI-augmented workflows would let counselors serve far more clients as genomic medicine becomes mainstream. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI reshapes the data-analysis periphery but the empathetic, interpersonal counseling core remains human-centered, and expanding demand supports continued employment growth.
opus5_rationale: Much of the work is information-intensive cognitive labor — collecting pedigrees, interpreting variant data against literature, calculating risk, drafting documentation and letters to referring physicians — all directly in AI's path, and clinical decision-support tools already automate variant curation and risk modeling. The counter-weight is the irreducible human element: delivering emotionally charged results, psychosocial support, and shared decision-making with distressed families, plus state licensure gatekeeping, which keeps disruption at high-but-not-extreme. Elasticity is high because with only ~4,000 counselors nationally, genetic counseling is severely supply-constrained while genomic and pharmacogenomic testing volume is exploding; population screening, oncology, and prenatal care all have large latent unmet demand that cheaper, faster counseling would unlock. Since disruption is high and demand expansion should more than absorb productivity gains, the occupation is augmented — each counselor supervises AI-generated interpretations and handles far more cases, with headcount stable or growing.
openai_rationale: Genetic counseling involves a mix of cognitive tasks, such as evaluating genetic information and providing counseling, which AI can assist with, particularly in data analysis and risk assessment. However, the interpersonal and empathetic aspects of the job, such as providing emotional support and discussing sensitive information, require human presence and judgment, limiting AI's full disruption. Demand elasticity is high because as genetic testing becomes cheaper and more accessible, more people will seek genetic counseling to understand their results and implications, expanding the market. Thus, while AI will augment the work, the demand for genetic counselors is likely to grow, absorbing productivity gains.
gpt55_rationale: Genetic counseling is heavily cognitive and language-based: collecting histories, interpreting genetic test results, explaining risks, documenting sessions, and researching new findings are all areas where AI can substantially assist. However, the role also involves licensed clinical judgment, informed consent, coordination with physicians, and emotionally sensitive counseling, which limits full automation. Demand is fairly elastic because genetic testing and genomic medicine are expanding, and access to counseling is currently constrained by cost, availability, and specialist shortages. Because AI is likely to let counselors handle more cases and support broader use of genetic testing rather than simply eliminate the human role, the net effect is augment.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can substantially automate pedigree analysis, variant interpretation support, risk calculations, literature review, patient education, and clinical documentation. However, communicating uncertain or distressing results, supporting consequential decisions, and assuming clinical responsibility still require licensed professionals with empathy and contextual judgment. Cheaper delivery should unlock meaningful demand as genetic testing expands, but testing volumes, reimbursement, regulation, and the episodic nature of counseling limit expansion. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity therefore points to restructuring around AI-assisted analysis and more complex, human-centered counseling.
fable5_rationale: The core work — collecting family histories, evaluating genetic data for risk, documenting sessions, and explaining test results — is largely cognitive and language-based, and AI variant-interpretation tools and LLM-generated patient education materials are already directly in its path; only the empathetic counseling of distressed clients resists automation, yielding high disruption. Elasticity is high because genetic testing volume is exploding while only ~4,000 counselors exist nationally — access to counseling is severely rationed by workforce scarcity and cost, so cheaper, faster risk interpretation would unlock enormous latent demand as genomic medicine expands into cancer, pharmacogenomics, and routine care. With AI handling interpretation and documentation, each counselor can serve far more patients in a market that is demand-constrained, making augment the right fit.
grok45_rationale: Disruption is high because core work is predominantly cognitive and language-based—interpreting genetic data, risk assessment, educating clients on complex results, and documentation—areas where AI tools already assist with variant analysis, pedigree generation, literature synthesis, and report drafting, even as empathetic counseling and nuanced decision support still require human presence. Elasticity is high because demand is currently constrained by a severe shortage (only ~4,000 counselors) and cost/access barriers amid exploding genetic testing and precision medicine; making counseling 10x faster/cheaper would unlock far more sessions across prenatal, cancer, and population screening. This combination fits augment: productivity gains expand total output and access enough to keep headcount stable or growing rather than contracting.

title: Geographers
claude_rationale: Geographers' core work involves data analysis, GIS programming, mapping, and research synthesis - predominantly digital knowledge work that AI can increasingly automate, including satellite image analysis, pattern recognition in geographic data, and report generation. Demand elasticity is low because geographic analysis needs are largely driven by fixed government planning requirements, regulatory compliance, and infrastructure projects rather than cost considerations - making 10x cheaper analysis unlikely to generate proportionally more demand. The combination of high AI disruption potential in data-intensive analytical work and constrained demand growth suggests significant headcount contraction is likely.
opus_rationale: Geographers' core work — GIS analysis, data collection, mapping, spatial modeling, report writing, and data visualization — is overwhelmingly digital and cognitive, placing it directly in AI's path; modern AI and automated GIS tools already perform much of the analysis and visualization that previously required manual effort. Demand is structurally constrained: 68% of these workers are in federal government with employment tied to fixed budget allocations, and society does not consume dramatically more geographic analysis simply because it becomes cheaper, keeping elasticity low. With high disruption (8) and low elasticity (3), plus a BLS-projected employment decline, productivity gains translate into fewer needed workers rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category.
opus5_rationale: Geographers' core work — GIS analysis, remote sensing interpretation, spatial statistics, map production, and report writing — is almost entirely digital and squarely in AI's path; foundation models for satellite imagery segmentation, automated geospatial pipelines, and LLM-assisted report generation already displace substantial portions of routine analysis and cartographic production. Some fieldwork and stakeholder-facing advisory work resists automation, but it is a minority of tasks. Elasticity is low because 68% of employment is federal government positions whose headcount is set by appropriations rather than by demand for spatial analysis; cheaper geospatial insight tends to be absorbed by existing staff and by GIS-enabled workers in other occupations (planners, geoscientists, analysts) rather than by hiring more geographers. With very high task exposure, a tiny 1,500-person budget-constrained occupation, and an already-declining BLS projection, contraction is the likely outcome.
openai_rationale: Geographers' work involves a mix of digital and field tasks, with a significant portion relying on GIS and data analysis, which AI can assist with. However, the need for field observations and human judgment in interpreting geographic data limits full AI disruption. Demand elasticity is low because the occupation is largely driven by government funding and specific project needs, which are not significantly expanded by cost reductions. Thus, while AI can enhance productivity, it is unlikely to lead to a substantial increase in demand, making the occupation resilient to AI-driven changes.
gpt55_rationale: Geographers perform a large share of digital and analytical work: GIS analysis, remote sensing interpretation, map production, data linkage, visualization, and report writing are all areas where AI and automated geospatial tools are already becoming materially useful. Some tasks still require human fieldwork, interviews, project framing, and interdisciplinary judgment, which keeps disruption below the most exposed fully digital occupations. Demand for geographic analysis may grow somewhat with climate risk, infrastructure planning, disaster response, and location intelligence, but employment is small and heavily tied to government funding and fixed planning budgets, limiting expansion. With high disruption and relatively low elasticity, AI is likely to reduce the number of workers needed for routine mapping, analysis, and reporting even as remaining geographers shift toward higher-level interpretation and advisory roles.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most geographic analysis is digital and data-intensive, including GIS processing, remote-sensing interpretation, mapping, statistical analysis, visualization, and report writing, all of which AI can substantially accelerate. Field observations, interviews, methodological judgment, and stakeholder communication remain important human tasks, preventing near-total automation. Cheaper geographic analysis could expand its use in planning, climate adaptation, logistics, and risk assessment, but government budgets and the finite number of major planning decisions limit demand growth. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with greater emphasis on problem framing, validation, domain expertise, and oversight of AI-enabled geospatial workflows.
fable5_rationale: The core work — GIS analysis, satellite imagery interpretation, spatial data modeling, map creation, and report writing — is almost entirely digital and squarely in AI's path, with AI-powered remote sensing analysis and automated cartography already advancing rapidly; only fieldwork and stakeholder engagement resist automation. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper geospatial analysis has genuine latent demand in business, climate adaptation, and infrastructure planning, but 68% of geographers work for the federal government where headcount is budget-driven rather than demand-driven, capping expansion. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation restructures — geographers who shift toward directing AI-driven geospatial pipelines, validating outputs, and framing policy-relevant questions will thrive, while those doing routine GIS production and data compilation face displacement.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on GIS analysis, satellite/remote-sensing interpretation, spatial data modeling, map creation, and report writing—predominantly digital/cognitive work already being accelerated by geospatial AI, computer vision, and generative tools—while fieldwork and interviews form a minority of duties for most practitioners. Demand is heavily constrained by federal and state budgets (nearly 80% of employment) plus structural limits on specialized research volume, so 10x productivity gains translate mainly into fewer positions rather than dramatically more studies. This combination of high disruption and low elasticity produces net replacement pressure and headcount contraction.

title: Geological and hydrologic technicians
claude_rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while AI can assist with data analysis, report writing, and pattern recognition in geological samples, the core work requires significant fieldwork including sample collection, equipment installation and maintenance, and physical presence in remote locations. The elasticity is low because demand for geological and hydrologic services is largely driven by regulatory requirements, infrastructure needs, and natural resource extraction - areas where cheaper analysis doesn't dramatically expand total demand. Since disruption is moderate (5) rather than high (7+), this occupation falls into the resilient category where AI enhances some analytical tasks but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core work.
opus_rationale: The work splits between physical fieldwork (collecting samples, installing/maintaining equipment, traveling to remote sites) and cognitive office work (data analysis, modeling, report and map generation). AI strongly augments the data-intensive and reporting portions, but the field sampling and hands-on equipment work require physical presence that AI cannot replace, keeping disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate: extraction and water monitoring demand is driven by commodity markets, regulatory requirements, and federal funding rather than the cost of technician labor, so cheaper analysis would not dramatically expand consumption. With disruption at 5, the occupation falls into resilient—AI reshapes the analytical periphery but the physical, field-based core remains essential.
opus5_rationale: Roughly half of this work is physical and site-based — installing and maintaining field instruments, collecting mud/water samples in remote locations, lab sample prep — which AI cannot perform, though drones and automated sensors substitute for some manual data collection. The data-analysis, mapping, and report-writing half is squarely in AI's path, so the office-based portion of the role will be substantially automated or accelerated. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper monitoring could expand water-quality and mineral exploration coverage (more sensors, more sites analyzed), but demand is anchored to commodity cycles and federal budgets, which cap growth. Because the core hands-on field and lab component remains human-dependent, disruption stays at or below 6 and the occupation is best classified as resilient, with a gradual shift toward sensor/drone operation and data interpretation skills.
openai_rationale: Geological and hydrologic technicians perform a mix of fieldwork and laboratory analysis, with tasks such as data collection, sample analysis, and report preparation. AI can assist in data analysis and report generation, but the physical and unpredictable nature of fieldwork limits disruption. Demand elasticity is low because the need for geological and hydrologic data is driven by specific projects and regulatory requirements, not easily expanded by cost reductions. Thus, while AI may enhance productivity, it is unlikely to significantly alter headcount, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: This occupation has a substantial AI-exposed component: organizing sensor and lab data, GIS mapping, report drafting, database compilation, and interpreting routine geological or hydrologic measurements can be accelerated by AI, drones, remote sensing, and automated analytics. However, many core tasks still require physical presence in the field or lab, including collecting samples, installing and maintaining equipment, handling instruments, and working in remote or variable conditions. Demand could expand moderately if monitoring, mapping, and analysis become cheaper, especially for water management, environmental compliance, and resource exploration, but it is constrained by project funding, regulation, commodity cycles, and the need for physical sampling. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire occupation, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can substantially assist with data cleaning, sample interpretation, GIS mapping, modeling, and report preparation, especially for office-based technicians. However, collecting physical samples, installing and maintaining instruments, conducting laboratory procedures, and operating in remote or unpredictable environments still require substantial human presence. Lower costs could support denser environmental monitoring and more resource analysis, but demand remains constrained by project activity, regulation, commodity markets, and government funding. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI reshapes its analytical components without displacing most of its field and laboratory core.
fable5_rationale: Core work is a mix of physical fieldwork — installing equipment, collecting mud and water samples in remote locations — and lab/office analysis; AI and automated sensors can meaningfully speed up the data compilation, mapping, and report-writing portions, and drones already threaten some exploration tasks, but the hands-on sampling and equipment maintenance remain human work. Demand is tied to resource extraction budgets, federal funding, and regulatory monitoring requirements rather than the cost of technician labor, so cheaper analysis would not dramatically expand the volume of sites monitored or samples collected. With moderate disruption confined to the desk-based half of the job and structurally constrained demand, the occupation is resilient — though flat headcount and sensor automation mean modest attrition on the margins.
grok45_rationale: Core duties center on physical fieldwork (sample collection with tools/shovels/gauges in remote outdoor sites), equipment installation/maintenance, and hands-on lab testing, which AI cannot perform; AI only assists secondary digital tasks like data compilation, report writing, GIS mapping, and analysis. Demand elasticity is low because resource exploration, water monitoring, and extraction volumes are constrained by geology, energy markets, regulations, and government funding rather than technician cost or speed—productivity gains from AI or drones (already noted by BLS) mostly reduce headcount needs rather than unlock large new volumes of work. With disruption only moderate, the occupation remains resilient as AI reshapes peripheral analysis without displacing the human presence required for core tasks.

title: Geoscientists
claude_rationale: Geoscientists face moderate disruption as AI can assist with data analysis, pattern recognition in geological data, and report writing, but the core work requires extensive fieldwork, physical sample collection, and real-world presence that AI cannot replace. The occupation involves substantial physical components like hiking to remote locations, drilling, and hands-on laboratory work. Demand elasticity is low because geological surveys and resource assessments are typically driven by specific project needs rather than cost considerations - making geological work 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically increase the number of oil wells drilled or environmental assessments conducted. The combination of moderate disruption and low elasticity places this in the resilient category, where AI enhances certain analytical tasks but doesn't fundamentally reshape the occupation.
opus_rationale: Geoscientists split their work between fieldwork (collecting samples, surveys, remote locations) and knowledge work (data analysis, modeling, GIS, report writing). AI strongly augments the analytical portions—interpreting seismic data, processing remote sensing imagery, and modeling—but the core requires substantial physical field presence and human judgment, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is structurally tied to energy exploration, environmental compliance, and resource management, with moderate potential to expand as cheaper analysis unlocks more exploration and monitoring, but constrained by capital costs of extraction and regulatory cycles. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the desk-bound analytical tasks but does not displace the field-dependent, judgment-heavy core.
opus5_rationale: A substantial share of geoscientists' work is data-heavy and digital — seismic interpretation, remote sensing analysis, GIS modeling, report writing — all areas where AI already materially accelerates output, pushing disruption toward the high end. But the occupation retains an irreducible physical core: field surveys in remote locations, sample collection, laboratory testing, and licensed professional judgment on regulatory and engineering projects, which caps disruption at moderate-high. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper subsurface analysis could unlock more exploration, hazard mapping, and environmental assessment work (especially for critical minerals and geothermal), but demand is ultimately tethered to capital-intensive drilling, mining, and construction projects and to government budgets rather than to analysis cost. With disruption at 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes the interpretation and reporting workflow but does not displace the fieldwork, licensure, and stakeholder-facing core.
openai_rationale: Geoscientists engage in a mix of fieldwork, laboratory analysis, and data interpretation. While AI can assist with data analysis and modeling, the physical and unpredictable nature of fieldwork limits AI's disruption. The demand for geoscientists is moderately elastic; while AI can enhance productivity, the need for human expertise in interpreting complex geological data and conducting field studies remains. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing core tasks.
gpt55_rationale: Geoscientists do substantial digital and cognitive work—GIS analysis, remote sensing interpretation, modeling, lab-data analysis, mapping, reporting, and presentations—that AI can materially accelerate. However, the occupation also depends heavily on fieldwork, sample collection, site-specific observation, laboratory procedures, professional judgment, and often licensure, which limits full automation of the core role. Demand could expand moderately as cheaper analysis enables more environmental monitoring, hazard assessment, resource evaluation, and renewable-energy siting, but it remains constrained by physical projects, regulation, budgets, and field access. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially accelerate remote-sensing interpretation, GIS analysis, geological modeling, deposit estimation, mapping, and report preparation. However, field surveys, sample collection, laboratory work, site-specific judgment, client coordination, and licensed professional accountability still require substantial human involvement. Lower analysis costs could expand environmental assessments, hazard mapping, and resource exploration, but demand remains constrained by fieldwork, regulation, and the number of viable development projects. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI substantially enhances its analytical components without fully reshaping its mixed field-and-office core.
fable5_rationale: Geoscientists split time between fieldwork (sample collection, surveys, remote-site travel), laboratory testing, and office analysis; AI meaningfully accelerates the analytical portions — interpreting seismic and remote sensing data, building geologic models, drafting maps and reports — but the field and lab components require physical presence and cannot be automated. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis could expand demand for resource exploration, hazard assessment, and environmental monitoring, but total demand is tied to energy markets, regulation, and government budgets rather than analysis costs. Because core work remains anchored in physical data collection and site-specific judgment, disruption stays at moderate levels, making 'resilient' the fitting category even as the office-based skill set shifts toward AI-augmented interpretation.
grok45_rationale: AI already materially accelerates core cognitive tasks such as seismic/remote-sensing interpretation, geologic modeling, GIS mapping, sample data analysis, and report writing, which occupy a large share of office and lab time, yet essential fieldwork—sample collection, on-site surveys, and remote expeditions—remains irreducibly physical and presence-dependent, producing high-but-not-maximal disruption. Cheaper, faster geoscience output would unlock additional exploration, environmental-assessment, and hazard-mapping projects, yet demand remains bounded by commodity markets, capital-intensive drilling/permitting, and regulatory budgets, so elasticity is only moderate. Because disruption sits at the upper edge of the moderate range, the occupation is classified resilient: AI reshapes tools and productivity without eliminating the need for human geoscientists.

title: Glaziers
claude_rationale: Glaziers perform predominantly physical, hands-on work requiring precise measurement, cutting, lifting, and installation of glass in real-world construction environments. While AI might assist with peripheral tasks like reading blueprints or project planning, the core work of handling heavy glass, working at heights, and performing precise physical installations cannot be automated. Demand elasticity is low because glass installation needs are tied to construction projects and building maintenance, which don't dramatically expand even if installation became cheaper - buildings need a fixed amount of windows and glass fixtures regardless of labor costs.
opus_rationale: Glaziers perform almost entirely physical, hands-on work: measuring, cutting, lifting, and installing glass at jobsites and heights, with only peripheral tasks like blueprint reading that AI could touch. The core work requires unpredictable real-world presence and physical strength, making AI largely irrelevant to the daily tasks. Demand is tied to construction cycles and physical building needs, so it cannot expand dramatically even if some planning tasks become cheaper. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: Glazing is almost entirely physical: measuring, cutting, lifting, and securing heavy glass at heights in variable jobsite conditions, none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like estimating, blueprint interpretation, and scheduling, leaving the core work unchanged. Demand is tied to construction cycles and building stock rather than the cost of cognitive labor, so productivity gains from AI would barely shift total volume. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of glaziers are predominantly physical and hands-on, involving the installation and fitting of glass, which requires human presence and manual dexterity. AI has minimal impact on these tasks, as they are not digital or cognitive in nature. Therefore, the disruption score is low. On the elasticity dimension, while there might be some increase in demand due to cost reductions in glass production or installation efficiency, the overall demand for glaziers is relatively inelastic. The need for glass installation is driven by construction and replacement cycles, which are not significantly influenced by cost alone. Thus, the net effect is 'resilient' as AI does not significantly alter the core work or demand dynamics for glaziers.
gpt55_rationale: Glaziers’ core work is physical, site-specific installation: measuring openings, lifting and positioning heavy glass, fastening frames, sealing joints, and working safely at heights or in variable construction environments. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as blueprint interpretation, estimating, scheduling, digital measurement, fabrication planning, and quality checks, but it does not directly replace the manual jobsite execution. Demand is somewhat price-sensitive because cheaper installation could encourage more window replacement, energy-efficiency retrofits, and architectural glass use, but it remains constrained by construction cycles, material costs, building codes, and the pace of renovation. Because disruption is low and the core occupation remains hands-on, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Glaziers perform predominantly physical, site-specific work involving heavy and fragile materials, precise fitting, work at heights, and adaptation to variable building conditions. AI may assist with blueprint interpretation, measurements, estimating, scheduling, and safety planning, but current robotics cannot economically handle most field installation tasks. Cheaper and faster installation could stimulate some additional renovation and architectural-glass demand, although construction volumes, material costs, and replacement cycles limit expansion. The low disruption score therefore makes the occupation resilient over the next decade.
fable5_rationale: Glazier work is almost entirely physical and hands-on — lifting, cutting, fitting, and securing heavy glass at varied jobsites, often at height, in unpredictable real-world conditions where AI has no direct role. AI may marginally assist with peripheral tasks like estimating, scheduling, or reading digital blueprints, but the core installation work is untouched for the foreseeable horizon. Elasticity is low-moderate since demand is driven by construction cycles and building stock rather than the cost of glazier labor itself. With minimal disruption to core tasks, this occupation is clearly resilient.
grok45_rationale: Glaziers' core work is almost entirely physical—measuring, cutting, lifting, and fastening heavy glass on-site, often at heights and outdoors—which AI cannot perform and will not meaningfully automate within 10 years; any AI role is limited to peripheral blueprint interpretation or design optimization. Demand for glass installation is driven by construction and repair cycles with only modest expansion potential if costs fall, constrained by overall building activity rather than latent unmet need. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient to AI-driven change.

title: Graphic designers
claude_rationale: Graphic design scores high on disruption because AI tools like DALL-E, Midjourney, and Canva's AI features already materially change how visual content is created, from generating initial concepts to automating layout decisions and producing finished designs. The work is predominantly digital and cognitive, making it directly in AI's path. Elasticity is moderate because while cheaper design could unlock demand from small businesses and individuals who previously couldn't afford professional design services, the market faces structural constraints from established brand relationships, regulatory requirements for certain designs, and the finite attention span for visual content consumption. This combination suggests the occupation will survive but require substantial skill adaptation toward creative direction, client strategy, and AI tool mastery rather than manual design execution.
opus_rationale: Graphic design is almost entirely digital, cognitive, and visual work — exactly the domain where generative AI image tools, layout assistants, and automated design platforms already produce usable output, making disruption very high. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster visual content unlocks meaningful new demand as more businesses, products, and digital channels need visuals, but the market is partly saturated and much routine work (logos, social graphics) becomes commoditized rather than expanded proportionally. The combination of very high disruption (9) and moderate elasticity (6) fits restructure — the occupation persists but shifts toward art direction, brand strategy, AI-tool orchestration, and high-end creative work, displacing those who only execute routine production tasks.
opus5_rationale: Graphic design is almost entirely digital creative production — layouts, logos, illustration, photo editing, iteration on client feedback — and generative image and layout tools already produce usable output for much of the commodity end of this market. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper visuals do expand total demand (every small business, social channel, and product variant can now be designed, and volume of visual content is exploding), but much of that expanded demand is absorbed by non-designers using AI tools directly rather than by hiring designers, and brand-level work is capped by budgets and the number of clients. The net result is a substantial skill shift — toward art direction, brand strategy, prompt/AI-pipeline curation, and client-facing judgment — with the routine production tier, especially freelance commodity work, contracting. BLS's own 2 percent projection with an explicit AI caveat is consistent with restructuring rather than outright collapse or growth.
openai_rationale: Graphic design is predominantly digital and involves tasks such as creating visual concepts and using design software, which are directly in AI's path. AI tools are already capable of generating design elements and layouts, significantly impacting the workflow of graphic designers. However, the demand for graphic design is likely to expand as AI makes it cheaper and faster to produce high-quality designs, unlocking new markets and applications. This high elasticity suggests that while AI will change how graphic designers work, it will also increase the demand for their services, leading to an 'augment' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: Graphic design is almost entirely digital creative work involving layout, image generation, typography, editing, and client revisions, all of which are directly affected by generative AI and automated design tools. AI can already produce drafts, variations, logos, ads, social media graphics, and production-ready assets, shifting designers toward art direction, brand strategy, taste-making, prompt workflows, and client interpretation. Demand will expand somewhat because cheaper design enables more small businesses, creators, and marketing teams to produce more visual content, but much routine work will also be self-served by non-designers. Because disruption is very high but elasticity is only moderate, the occupation is best classified as restructure rather than full augmentation or replacement.
gpt56sol_rationale: Graphic design is predominantly digital, and generative AI can already produce concepts, illustrations, layouts, variations, and routine revisions, placing nearly all production tasks in AI’s direct path. Cheaper design will increase visual-content demand, especially among small businesses and for personalized digital marketing, but self-service tools and finite branding budgets limit how much of that expansion becomes demand for professional designers. Human value will shift toward art direction, brand strategy, client interpretation, quality control, and distinctive creative judgment. High disruption combined with moderate demand elasticity therefore points to restructuring rather than broad replacement or assured employment growth.
fable5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — layout, illustration, logo creation, photo editing, iterating on client feedback — are fully digital and squarely in the path of generative image and design AI, which already produces production-quality output for routine work; only client relationship management and high-level creative direction resist automation. Demand for visual content is genuinely elastic (cheaper design means more brands, campaigns, and content get professionally designed), but much of that expanded demand will be captured by non-designers self-serving with AI tools rather than flowing back to designers, and BLS already flags AI reducing freelance contracting. This caps elasticity at moderate: some segments (brand strategy, complex multi-channel campaigns) expand, while commodity design work evaporates. High disruption with moderate elasticity fits restructure — the occupation survives, but shifts toward creative direction, brand strategy, and AI-tool orchestration, displacing designers who compete on routine production work.
grok45_rationale: Graphic design is almost entirely digital knowledge work centered on software-driven creation of layouts, logos, illustrations, and visual concepts, tasks already materially accelerated by generative AI tools like image models and automated design platforms, matching the very-high disruption examples. Demand elasticity is high because dramatically cheaper and faster design unlocks substantial latent demand from small businesses, marketers, content platforms, and product teams that previously skipped professional work or relied on templates, expanding total visual output rather than merely shrinking headcount. The combination of disruption >=7 and elasticity >=7 produces an augment outcome in which AI multiplies each designer's productivity while overall volume of design work grows enough to stabilize or increase employment for those who adapt.

title: Grounds maintenance workers
claude_rationale: Grounds maintenance work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on, requiring real-world presence for tasks like mowing, planting, pruning, and equipment operation in unpredictable outdoor environments. While AI might assist with peripheral tasks like scheduling or plant identification, the core work of physical landscape maintenance remains largely untouched by current AI capabilities. Demand shows moderate elasticity as cheaper maintenance services could unlock more frequent care for existing properties and enable maintenance of previously neglected spaces, but the low disruption score keeps this occupation in the resilient category where AI touches only the periphery of the work.
opus_rationale: Disruption is minimal because grounds maintenance is almost entirely physical and outdoor work—mowing, trimming, planting, climbing trees, applying chemicals, and operating heavy equipment in unpredictable real-world environments that AI cannot perform. While robotic mowers and autonomous equipment exist, they handle only narrow tasks and the core work requires human dexterity, mobility, and judgment across varied terrain. Elasticity is low-to-moderate since landscaping demand is tied to physical property and seasonal need rather than suppressed by cost or speed, with steady but bounded growth. Because disruption is well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI may slightly augment equipment efficiency but does not reshape the fundamentally hands-on nature of the work.
opus5_rationale: Core work is almost entirely physical outdoor labor in unstructured environments — mowing, pruning, planting, climbing trees, applying chemicals — with essentially no digital or language-based task content for AI to absorb. Robotic mowers and autonomous equipment represent a mechanization trend rather than an AI one, and they address only a slice of duties on the most uniform terrain; scheduling, routing, and estimating are peripheral admin tasks. Demand for lawn and landscape services is moderately price-sensitive (households substitute their own labor when costs rise), so cheaper service could expand the market somewhat, but the total addressable amount of grounds needing upkeep is physically bounded. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.
openai_rationale: Grounds maintenance work is predominantly physical and hands-on, involving tasks like mowing, trimming, and planting, which are not easily automated by AI. The disruption score is low because AI has minimal impact on these core tasks. Demand elasticity is low because while there might be some increase in demand for landscaping services if costs decrease, it is limited by the physical nature of the work and the fact that these services are not typically suppressed by cost. The net effect is 'resilient' as AI will not significantly alter the core work or demand for grounds maintenance workers.
gpt55_rationale: Grounds maintenance is overwhelmingly hands-on, outdoor, and site-specific work involving mowing, planting, trimming, lifting, chemical application, tree work, and equipment operation in variable physical environments. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as scheduling, routing, customer communication, plant-health diagnostics, drone inspection, and some robotic mowing, but most core tasks still require human dexterity, judgment, and physical presence. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper service could lead homeowners, campuses, municipalities, and commercial properties to buy more frequent or higher-quality landscaping, but total land area, seasonality, and maintenance needs limit expansion. Because disruption to the core occupation remains low, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core tasks are physical, site-specific, and performed in variable outdoor environments using tools and heavy equipment, putting most of the occupation beyond near-term AI capabilities. AI can improve scheduling, plant-health diagnosis, landscape planning, and routing, while autonomous mowers and sprayers may automate some standardized work, but planting, pruning, cleanup, repairs, and tree work still require human dexterity and judgment. Lower costs could moderately expand demand for professional lawn care, landscaping, and urban green-space maintenance, although available land and customers' desired maintenance frequency impose limits. Because disruption remains low despite some equipment automation, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: Grounds maintenance is almost entirely physical, outdoor work — mowing, pruning, planting, applying chemicals — performed in unstructured, variable environments where AI language and analysis tools are largely irrelevant; robotic mowers may automate some routine mowing but cannot handle the diverse manual tasks that define the job. Elasticity is modest: cheaper landscaping would unlock some additional demand from homeowners and municipalities, but demand is fundamentally tied to physical land area and property budgets rather than being cost-suppressed at scale. With disruption at 1, this occupation is clearly resilient — AI touches only peripheral scheduling, routing, and plant-diagnosis tasks while the core work remains human hands and equipment outdoors.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—mowing, planting, pruning, pesticide application, and equipment operation—are almost entirely physical, outdoor, and require real-world presence and manual dexterity, so AI remains peripheral (scheduling apps, plant-ID tools, or early robotic mowers) and does not reshape daily work. Demand for grounds care has some price sensitivity—cheaper service could shift more homeowners from DIY and support expanded green spaces—but is structurally capped by finite land area, weather seasons, and institutional budgets, limiting large-scale expansion. Because disruption stays low, the occupation is resilient: AI may trim admin edges or enable modest productivity gains without displacing the bulk of hands-on labor.

title: Hand laborers and material movers
claude_rationale: This occupation scores low on disruption because the core work is almost entirely physical - manually moving materials, lifting heavy objects, packing by hand, and cleaning vehicles. While some workers use handheld scanners for tracking, the fundamental tasks require human presence and physical manipulation in unpredictable real-world environments. Elasticity is low-moderate because demand is somewhat constrained by structural factors - the amount of freight to move, garbage to collect, and vehicles to clean is largely determined by economic activity levels and population, though e-commerce growth does create some additional demand for stockers and order fillers. The resilient category fits because AI cannot meaningfully change the core physical nature of this work.
opus_rationale: The core work is physical and manual—lifting, moving, packing, cleaning, and bending in unpredictable real-world positions—which AI software cannot perform; disruption comes from physical robotics and warehouse automation rather than AI itself, and even that affects only peripheral and repetitive tasks. Demand is structurally tied to physical volumes of goods, trash, and store traffic, so cheaper handling does not unlock dramatic new latent demand, capping elasticity. Because the disruption score is well below 7, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery (routing, inventory tracking, sorting systems) but does not reshape the hands-on core, and BLS projects modest 4% growth overall.
opus5_rationale: Core tasks are almost entirely physical: lifting, carrying, packing, bagging, cleaning, and collecting refuse in unstructured environments. AI's language and cognitive capabilities touch only the peripheral record-keeping and scanning elements; the real threat is warehouse robotics and mechanization, which is capital-intensive, incremental, and largely separate from the current AI wave — dexterous picking in cluttered settings remains unsolved at scale. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper logistics does expand e-commerce volume and order-filling demand (as BLS projects for stockers), but total goods movement is bounded by physical consumption. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient over the next decade, though pockets like machine feeders and hand packagers will continue to erode from automation rather than AI.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of hand laborers and material movers are predominantly physical, involving manual movement of materials, packing, and cleaning, which limits AI's ability to disrupt these roles significantly. While some automation is occurring in warehouses, the majority of tasks still require human presence. The elasticity is low because the demand for these roles is not heavily suppressed by cost or speed; rather, it is driven by the physical need to move materials. Even with increased efficiency, the demand for laborers is unlikely to expand significantly, as the tasks are not easily scalable. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical: lifting, carrying, packing, stocking shelves, cleaning vehicles, feeding machines, and collecting refuse in varied real-world environments. AI-enabled warehouse robots, routing software, vision systems, conveyors, and automated sorting will reduce some picking, packing, and machine-feeding tasks, but broad replacement is limited by low wages, messy environments, and the need for flexible human handling. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because cheaper material handling can support more e-commerce and faster fulfillment, but the underlying quantity of goods, trash, vehicles, and store inventory is not likely to expand dramatically just because labor is cheaper. Because disruption remains below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with automation pressure concentrated in specific subgroups rather than a wholesale AI reshaping of the occupation.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core tasks involve physically lifting, sorting, packing, cleaning, and moving varied objects in real-world environments, so current AI mainly improves routing, inventory tracking, scheduling, and instructions. Robotics enhanced by AI will automate some structured warehouse, feeding, and packaging tasks, but deployment costs and difficulty handling irregular environments limit occupation-wide disruption over the next decade. Cheaper material handling may support more e-commerce and logistics activity, but demand remains tied to the volume of physical goods, waste, and vehicles rather than expanding proportionally with productivity. Therefore, AI will change workflows and reduce some specialized roles, but the broad occupation remains resilient.

opus_rationale: The core work is highly physical and hands-on—disassembling engines, lifting heavy parts, working in awkward positions on-site—which AI cannot perform. AI assists primarily with computerized diagnostics, which already exist as tools, but the actual repair, recalibration, and reassembly require human dexterity and presence, keeping disruption low. Demand is tied to the physical stock of heavy equipment and is relatively fixed by industry activity rather than suppressed by repair cost, so elasticity is modest. With disruption well below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches diagnostics at the periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally manual core.
opus5_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair — disassembling engines, replacing hydraulic pumps, lifting heavy parts, working in awkward positions and at remote worksites — none of which AI can perform. AI's contribution is confined to the diagnostic and documentation periphery: smarter fault-code interpretation, predictive maintenance telemetry, AI-assisted access to manuals and repair procedures, which may modestly shift time from troubleshooting to wrench time. Elasticity is moderate: equipment fleets grow with construction and agriculture and predictive maintenance could increase scheduled service events, but total demand is capped by the physical stock of machines, and better diagnostics could equally reduce some repair volume. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient — AI becomes another tool in the technician's kit rather than a replacement for the labor itself.
openai_rationale: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians perform tasks that are predominantly physical and hands-on, such as inspecting, maintaining, and repairing heavy machinery. While AI and computerized diagnostic tools assist in identifying malfunctions, the core work remains largely manual and requires human intervention. Thus, the disruption score is low. Demand elasticity is also low because the need for these services is driven by the existing stock of heavy equipment and machinery, which does not expand significantly with reduced service costs. Consequently, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption, as the core tasks remain largely unchanged and demand is not highly elastic.
gpt55_rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on inspection, disassembly, repair, replacement, welding, lifting, field travel, and work in unpredictable physical environments, which current AI cannot directly perform. AI will meaningfully assist with diagnostic software, service manuals, predictive maintenance alerts, parts identification, and guided troubleshooting, but these are complements to the technician’s physical and mechanical work rather than substitutes for the core job. Demand is relatively inelastic because the amount of repair work is mainly tied to the stock and utilization of heavy equipment, construction activity, farming, rail fleets, and maintenance cycles; cheaper diagnostics may increase preventive maintenance somewhat but will not create many times more equipment needing service. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the core work remains embodied and site-specific, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on inspection, disassembly, repair, welding, parts replacement, and fieldwork on large machines in varied physical environments. AI will improve fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, manual lookup, calibration guidance, and recordkeeping, but technicians must still manipulate heavy components and respond to unpredictable equipment conditions. Cheaper, faster service could encourage more preventive maintenance and reduce equipment downtime, although demand remains constrained by the installed fleet and actual wear rates. Because AI primarily assists troubleshooting rather than replacing physical repair work, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: The core work is intensely physical and hands-on — disassembling engines, replacing hydraulic pumps, welding, and lifting heavy parts in shops and at remote field sites — placing it far outside AI's direct path. AI assists at the periphery through smarter computerized diagnostics, predictive maintenance alerts, and AI-guided troubleshooting of increasingly software-driven equipment, but the repair itself still requires a skilled human with tools. Elasticity is moderate: predictive maintenance could shift some demand from breakdown repair to scheduled service, while a growing equipment stock and increasingly complex machinery sustain steady need for technicians.
