However, the human element in understanding organizational culture and interpersonal communication remains crucial. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can make consulting services more efficient and potentially cheaper, the demand is not infinitely expandable due to the bespoke nature of consulting projects and organizational capacity to implement changes. Therefore, the occupation will likely restructure, with AI augmenting the analytical tasks but requiring analysts to adapt to new tools and focus more on strategic and interpersonal aspects.
gpt55_rationale: Management analysts perform heavily cognitive, language- and data-based work: gathering documents, analyzing financial and operational data, drafting recommendations, building presentations, and writing reports, all of which AI can materially accelerate. Human judgment, client trust, interviews, onsite observation, organizational politics, and change management still matter, but much of the junior analytical and document-production workflow is in AI's direct path. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper consulting could let smaller firms, agencies, and internal teams buy or perform more operational analysis, but implementation capacity, budgets, and the need for trusted advisors limit unlimited expansion. The occupation is therefore likely to be restructured, with fewer routine analyst tasks and greater emphasis on domain expertise, client management, problem framing, and execution.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI directly affects most analytical tasks, including gathering information, analyzing financial and operational data, developing alternatives, and drafting reports, proposals, and presentations. Human analysts remain important for diagnosing ambiguous organizational problems, interviewing stakeholders, exercising industry judgment, building trust, and managing implementation. Cheaper consulting could unlock substantial demand among smaller organizations and enable more frequent analysis, but adoption is limited by management attention, implementation capacity, and the value clients place on accountable human advice. The occupation therefore will persist, but its skill mix and staffing model will shift substantially toward AI-enabled analysis, stakeholder management, and change execution.
fable5_rationale: The core tasks — gathering and analyzing data, synthesizing findings, writing reports, and building recommendations — are almost entirely digital and language-based, squarely in AI's current path; LLMs already draft strategy decks, analyze financials, and benchmark processes. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis unlocks latent demand from small and mid-size firms that couldn't afford consulting, and AI adoption itself generates new advisory work, but demand is capped by trust dynamics — clients pay for accountability, relationships, and change management, not just analysis, and some clients will use AI to bypass consultants entirely. The occupation persists but shifts sharply toward client relationship management, judgment, implementation oversight, and AI-augmented delivery, while junior analysts doing pure research and slide production face displacement. This high-disruption, moderate-elasticity profile fits restructure.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on data gathering, financial and operational analysis, solution design, report writing, and presentations—predominantly cognitive and language-based work where AI tools already accelerate research, synthesis, modeling, and drafting. Onsite interviews, client relationship management, and change implementation still require human presence, keeping disruption high rather than near-total. Demand is highly elastic because consulting spend is currently constrained by high cost and limited capacity; dramatically cheaper and faster analysis unlocks continuous optimization for smaller firms, governments, and more frequent engagements across industries. Productivity gains therefore expand total output and headcount rather than pure substitution, fitting the augment category.

title: Manicurists and pedicurists
claude_rationale: Manicurists and pedicurists perform predominantly hands-on, physical work requiring manual dexterity, direct client interaction, and precise manipulation of tools on human nails and skin - tasks that AI cannot perform. While AI might assist with peripheral business functions like scheduling or inventory management, the core work of cleaning, shaping, polishing nails and providing personal care services remains entirely human-dependent. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because nail services are already relatively affordable luxury services, and while some expansion is possible through mobile services or new demographics, the market is not heavily constrained by cost barriers that AI productivity gains could meaningfully address. The low disruption score places this occupation firmly in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: The core work is entirely physical and hands-on—cleaning, shaping, polishing nails and massaging hands and feet—requiring fine dexterity, real-world presence, and direct client interaction that AI cannot perform. AI is irrelevant to the core service and touches only peripheral tasks like salon scheduling, inventory, or booking. Demand is somewhat constrained but already grows steadily as a low-cost luxury, and AI productivity gains don't apply since the bottleneck is human manual labor, not cognitive cost. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: The core work is entirely manual, tactile, and delivered in physical proximity to a client's hands and feet — nail shaping, callus removal, massage, and intricate hand-painted design require fine dexterity and human presence that AI cannot substitute for. AI touches only peripheral elements: appointment booking, inventory and accounting for salon owners, and design inspiration or AR previews of nail art. Demand is moderately elastic in principle (a low-cost luxury service that grows with disposable income), but productivity per technician is capped by the physical time a service takes, so no AI-driven cost collapse is available to unlock latent demand. With disruption far below the threshold, this occupation is clearly resilient; BLS-projected 7 percent growth reflects demographic and lifestyle trends rather than technology.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of manicurists and pedicurists are highly physical and hands-on, involving direct interaction with clients and manual dexterity, which limits the potential for AI disruption. AI may assist in peripheral tasks like scheduling or inventory management, but the core service remains unchanged. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make some aspects of the business more efficient, the personal nature of the service means demand is not heavily suppressed by cost. The occupation is expected to grow, driven by lifestyle trends and increased demand for grooming services, making it resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: The core work of manicurists and pedicurists is hands-on, in-person grooming that requires fine motor control, sanitation judgment, client interaction, and adaptation to individual hands, feet, nails, and skin. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as appointment scheduling, design inspiration, marketing, inventory, and perhaps limited robotic polish application, but it does not substantially replace the full service experience. Demand would expand somewhat if services became much faster or cheaper, especially through quick manicures, mobile services, and broader use by price-sensitive customers, but grooming frequency and the desire for human service limit elasticity. Because disruption to the core occupation is low, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core services require precise physical manipulation of each client’s hands and feet, safe use of sharp tools and chemicals, sanitation, creativity, and in-person customer interaction. AI can assist with scheduling, marketing, inventory, design visualization, and business administration, but robotics is unlikely to handle the full treatment safely and economically within the next decade. If services became much faster and cheaper, customers could purchase them more frequently and broader income groups could participate, although grooming cycles and the need for in-person appointments limit expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI primarily improves peripheral tasks rather than reshaping its hands-on core.
fable5_rationale: Nail care is almost entirely hands-on physical work requiring fine motor dexterity, direct skin contact, and in-person presence — AI has essentially no path into the core tasks of cleaning, trimming, polishing, and applying nail art. AI might marginally help with scheduling, marketing, or design suggestions, but these are peripheral. Elasticity is moot since AI cannot deliver the productivity gains; demand is driven by disposable income and grooming trends rather than technology costs. With disruption near zero, this occupation is clearly resilient, consistent with BLS's above-average growth projection.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—trimming, filing, massaging, applying polish or artificial nails, and disinfecting tools—are almost entirely physical, dexterous, and client-present, so AI has negligible impact beyond peripheral admin, booking, or design-suggestion tools. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower cost and faster service would unlock more frequent visits, mini-sessions, and uptake among men or lower-income clients, yet total consumption remains bounded by personal time and preference rather than exploding. With disruption well below the threshold that reshapes the occupation, the net effect is resilient: AI touches the edges while the hands-on service model and employment trajectory stay intact.

title: Marine engineers and naval architects
claude_rationale: Marine engineering and naval architecture involves substantial digital design work including CAD, system layouts, detailed drawings, performance modeling, and technical documentation - all areas where AI tools are already proving valuable for design optimization, simulation, and documentation. However, the work requires deep understanding of complex physical systems, regulatory compliance, safety standards, and often involves hands-on testing and field work. Demand elasticity is moderate because while AI could make ship design faster and cheaper, the market is constrained by the limited number of shipbuilding projects, regulatory approval processes, and the fact that most vessels are large capital investments with long lifecycles rather than mass-market products.
opus_rationale: A substantial portion of the work—design, CAD drafting, simulation, structural analysis, cost estimation, technical reporting—is digital and increasingly aided by AI design and modeling tools, pushing disruption toward the high end. However, the core work involves significant physical presence (shop floors, sea trials, offshore rigs, prototype testing), regulatory coordination, and PE-licensed accountability that AI cannot replace, capping disruption at 6. Demand has moderate latent upside from emissions-driven ship redesign and offshore wind expansion, but the field is small and constrained by heavy capital costs and regulation, so cheaper design doesn't dramatically multiply vessels built. Because AI changes many core design and analysis tasks but demand expansion is only partial, the occupation is best categorized as restructure.

Lower design costs should support more design iterations and some additional vessel, offshore-energy, and coastal-infrastructure projects, but demand is constrained by high construction costs, long project cycles, and limited shipbuilding volume. fable5_rationale: A substantial share of the work — hull design, system schematics, performance simulations, cost estimates, and technical reports — is digital knowledge work where AI-assisted CAD, generative design, and simulation tools are already advancing, but the core also includes overseeing prototype construction, physical testing, shipyard presence, offshore work, and regulatory sign-off requiring PE licensure and human accountability. Elasticity is limited: ship and offshore platform demand is driven by capital-intensive procurement cycles, defense budgets, and trade volumes rather than engineering labor costs, so 10x cheaper design would only modestly expand the number of vessels built. With disruption at the boundary but held to 6 by the significant physical, safety-critical, and on-site components, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes the design workflow while the role itself persists.
grok45_rationale: Core work is predominantly knowledge-based—CAD layouts, hull/superstructure design, fluid/performance analysis, cost estimates, and technical reports—which AI already accelerates via generative design, simulation, and automated drafting, though physical prototype testing, shipyard oversight, and regulatory coordination keep it from higher scores. Demand elasticity is only moderate because the number of vessels, offshore platforms, and coastal structures is constrained by capital costs, global trade/military needs, and shipyard capacity rather than design labor; cheaper design unlocks more emissions-compliant redesigns and wind projects but not order-of-magnitude volume growth. claude_rationale: Market research analysts face high disruption as their core tasks—data collection, statistical analysis, trend forecasting, and report generation—are predominantly digital and cognitive work that AI tools can already meaningfully assist with or automate. AI excels at processing large datasets, identifying patterns, generating insights, and creating visualizations. However, demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster market research unlocks significant latent demand—more businesses can afford comprehensive market analysis, more products can be tested, and more granular consumer insights become accessible to smaller companies that previously couldn't afford such services. The net effect is augmentation rather than replacement because the expanded market for research services absorbs the productivity gains.
opus_rationale: The core work—gathering data, analyzing with statistical software, forecasting trends, and producing reports, charts, and presentations—is almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing it directly in AI's path; modern LLMs and analytics tools already automate much of the data synthesis, visualization, and report-writing. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster analysis enables more businesses (especially smaller ones) to access market research and supports the growing use of big data across industries, but core demand is partly capped by the number of products, campaigns, and strategic decisions needing analysis. With disruption high (8) and elasticity in the moderate range (6), the occupation survives but the skill set shifts toward overseeing AI tools, interpreting outputs, and strategic judgment rather than manual data crunching—classic restructure territory.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and language/data based: gathering competitor and consumer information, running statistical analyses, building charts, and writing up reports and presentations. All of these are squarely in the path of current LLM and AI analytics tools, which can already draft survey instruments, code and interpret analyses, synthesize open-ended responses and social listening data, and generate polished decks. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper research means many small and mid-sized firms that never bought market research will start consuming it continuously rather than episodically, and analysis can be run on far more segments and geographies — but a large share of the demand is tied to fixed corporate marketing budgets and to the value of the human relationship in interpreting and defending findings to executives. Net effect is restructure: headcount likely holds roughly flat while the job shifts from data collection and report production toward framing questions, validating AI output, and translating insight into business strategy.
openai_rationale: Market research analysts primarily engage in digital and cognitive tasks such as data analysis, forecasting, and report generation, which are highly susceptible to AI-driven automation. However, the demand for market insights is likely to expand significantly as AI reduces costs and increases the speed of analysis, unlocking new opportunities for businesses to leverage data-driven strategies. This high elasticity suggests that while AI will transform the role, it will also expand the market, leading to an 'augment' net effect where demand for skilled analysts remains robust.
gpt55_rationale: Market research analysts perform highly digital and cognitive work: designing surveys, gathering online and competitive data, analyzing datasets, forecasting trends, and producing reports and presentations. Generative AI and analytics tools can already automate or accelerate survey drafting, sentiment analysis, segmentation, dashboarding, visualization, and first-draft insight generation, though human judgment remains important for research design, client context, and strategic interpretation. Demand should expand because cheaper research enables more firms, products, campaigns, and customer segments to be analyzed, but it is limited by marketing budgets, managerial decision capacity, and the fact that not every business question needs extensive research. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is best classified as restructure: fewer workers will be needed for routine analysis and reporting, while demand rises for analysts who can frame problems, validate AI outputs, and translate findings into business strategy.
gpt56sol_rationale: Nearly all core tasks—data gathering, statistical analysis, trend forecasting, visualization, report writing, and competitive research—are digital and increasingly automatable with AI. Cheaper analysis will enable more frequent studies, finer customer segmentation, and greater adoption by smaller businesses, but demand remains constrained by marketing budgets, available data, and the finite number of consequential business decisions. The occupation will therefore restructure around research design, validation, domain judgment, stakeholder communication, and translating automated findings into strategy, while fewer workers may be needed for routine analysis and reporting.
fable5_rationale: Nearly every core task — survey design, data gathering, statistical analysis, report writing, chart creation, and trend forecasting — is digital and language-based, placing this occupation squarely in AI's direct path; current LLMs and analytics tools can already draft surveys, synthesize consumer sentiment from big data, and generate polished reports. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper research would let small businesses and product teams consume far more market insight than today, but much demand is bundled into fixed corporate marketing budgets and decision-making bandwidth, so consumption won't scale 10x with cost reductions. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the field survives but shifts toward strategic interpretation, research design, and stakeholder advising while AI handles data collection and synthesis — a classic restructure where non-adapting analysts are displaced.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—statistical analysis of consumer and competitor data, forecasting trends, generating charts/reports, and synthesizing insights—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, already being materially accelerated by LLMs, automated analytics platforms, and generative tools for survey design and visualization. Physical or in-person elements (focus groups, client presentations) are secondary and shrinking as secondary data and digital methods dominate. Demand is highly elastic because thorough market research has historically been cost-prohibitive for many firms and product iterations; 10x cheaper/faster output unlocks continuous monitoring, more A/B testing, deeper segmentation, and research by smaller businesses that previously skipped it. Productivity gains therefore expand total volume of research rather than simply shrinking headcount, allowing skilled analysts who leverage AI to produce far more value.

title: Marriage and family therapists
claude_rationale: Marriage and family therapy involves deep human connection, emotional intelligence, and real-time interpersonal dynamics that AI cannot replicate, though AI may assist with administrative tasks, treatment planning, and resource recommendations. The demand for mental health services is highly elastic - there is massive unmet need due to cost and access barriers, and cheaper/more accessible therapy would dramatically expand utilization across all demographics. However, since the core therapeutic relationship and emotional processing work remains fundamentally human-centered with only moderate AI disruption, this occupation falls into the resilient category despite high demand elasticity.
opus_rationale: The core work of marriage and family therapy depends on human empathy, building rapport, reading emotional cues, and navigating complex relational dynamics in real time—tasks AI cannot meaningfully replicate. AI touches only peripheral functions like documentation, scheduling, insurance billing, and possibly some preliminary screening, keeping disruption moderate-to-low. Demand for mental health services is heavily suppressed by cost, stigma, and access, so cheaper supporting tools could expand reach, but the human therapeutic relationship remains irreplaceable. Because disruption is well below the threshold (4), the occupation is resilient: AI augments administrative tasks but does not reshape the core relational work.
opus5_rationale: The core work is language-based conversation, which superficially sits in AI's path, but the therapeutic value derives from human empathy, trust, licensure, and real-time relational dynamics among multiple family members — things AI chatbots supplement rather than substitute. AI will materially affect the periphery: documentation, notes, treatment-plan drafting, insurance billing, client intake/triage, and between-session support tools, plus AI companions may absorb some low-acuity demand. Elasticity is high because mental health care is heavily cost- and access-constrained, with large unmet demand; cheaper administrative overhead lets therapists see more clients and expand reach. Because disruption stays at or below 6 — the relational core is not reshaped — this occupation is resilient, with BLS projecting strong growth.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of marriage and family therapists involve significant interpersonal interaction, empathy, and nuanced understanding of human emotions, which are challenging for AI to replicate. While AI can assist with administrative tasks and potentially offer supplementary tools for therapy, the core therapeutic process remains human-centric, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make therapy more accessible and affordable, the personal nature of therapy limits how much demand can expand. Overall, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing human therapists.
gpt55_rationale: Marriage and family therapy is largely language-based cognitive work: assessment, guided conversation, treatment planning, documentation, and follow-up are all areas where AI can materially assist or partially automate. However, the occupation still depends heavily on trust, rapport, clinical judgment, crisis recognition, ethics, and licensure, so AI is more likely to reshape delivery than fully replace therapists. Demand elasticity is high because mental health and relationship counseling have substantial unmet demand due to cost, provider shortages, scheduling barriers, and stigma, and cheaper AI-enabled services would likely bring many more people into care. Because disruption is high but latent demand is also high, AI is likely to augment therapists through blended care, documentation automation, triage, and between-session support rather than cause broad headcount contraction.
gpt56sol_rationale: Therapy is predominantly conversational and cognitive, placing assessment, treatment planning, documentation, and routine client support directly in AI’s path. AI-enabled productivity should therefore expand access and caseload capacity while substantially changing therapists’ workflows, making augment the best fit.
fable5_rationale: Therapy is language-based on the surface, but its core value lies in human rapport, trust, and navigating live emotional dynamics between multiple people in a room — something clients specifically seek from a human, and licensure/liability rules reinforce this. grok45_rationale: Core duties revolve around real-time interpersonal assessment, building therapeutic rapport, and guiding emotional processing in couples/families—tasks that demand human empathy, non-verbal attunement, and adaptive presence that AI cannot fully replace, even as tools already assist with notes, treatment-plan drafting, and admin. Demand is highly elastic because access to relationship and family therapy is currently constrained by cost, waitlists, and shortages; cheaper/faster delivery would unlock substantial latent need across underserved populations. title: Masonry workers
claude_rationale: Masonry work is almost entirely physical and hands-on, involving lifting heavy materials, precise manual placement of bricks/stones, and working with mortar in unpredictable outdoor environments. AI has minimal relevance to the core tasks of cutting, laying, and finishing masonry materials. While AI might assist with peripheral tasks like reading blueprints or calculating materials, the fundamental work requires human dexterity, physical strength, and real-world problem-solving. Demand elasticity is low because construction needs are largely driven by population growth, infrastructure requirements, and building codes rather than cost - making masonry 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically increase the number of buildings constructed.
opus_rationale: Masonry work is almost entirely physical and hands-on—laying brick, mixing mortar, cutting stone, finishing concrete—requiring dexterity, strength, and unpredictable real-world job-site presence that AI cannot perform. AI is irrelevant to the core craft and touches only peripheral tasks like blueprint interpretation or material estimation, so disruption is minimal. Demand is tied to overall construction activity and is structurally constrained (slow 2% projected growth, with prefab panels and substitute materials actually reducing some demand), so elasticity is low. With disruption far below the threshold, the occupation is clearly resilient—AI may slightly assist planning but will not reshape the manual labor at its center.
opus5_rationale: Masonry is almost entirely physical craft work performed in variable outdoor jobsite conditions, requiring dexterity, strength, and hand-eye coordination that AI cannot replicate; only peripheral tasks like blueprint reading, material estimating, and bidding are touched by AI tools. openai_rationale: Masonry work is predominantly physical and hands-on, involving tasks such as laying bricks, mixing mortar, and constructing walls, which are not easily automated by AI. gpt55_rationale: Masonry is overwhelmingly physical, site-specific work involving lifting, cutting, placing, aligning, finishing, and repairing heavy materials in variable outdoor and construction-site conditions. grok45_rationale: Core masonry tasks—cutting and laying brick/block/stone, mixing and spreading mortar, aligning structures with levels, and finishing surfaces—are almost entirely physical, manual, and site-based, requiring strength, dexterity, and real-world presence that AI cannot perform. opus5_rationale: Massage therapy is almost entirely physical, hands-on work requiring human touch, dexterity, and in-person presence; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, marketing, client notes, and billing for the 42% who are self-employed. openai_rationale: Massage therapy is a highly physical and hands-on occupation, with core tasks centered around manipulating clients' soft tissues and joints. On the elasticity side, while there is some potential for increased demand due to lower costs and increased awareness of massage benefits, the demand is not highly elastic. gpt55_rationale: Massage therapy is overwhelmingly hands-on, physical, and presence-based, with core tasks requiring tactile assessment, manual dexterity, client comfort, and real-time adjustment to the body. gpt56sol_rationale: The occupation’s core work is hands-on manipulation requiring physical strength, tactile feedback, real-time adaptation, trust, and in-person interaction, all of which remain difficult for AI or robotics to reproduce economically. fable5_rationale: Massage therapy is almost entirely hands-on physical work requiring skilled manipulation of soft tissue, real-time tactile feedback, and human presence — AI cannot perform any of the core tasks, and only peripheral activities like scheduling, marketing, and client documentation are touched. grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on hands-on physical manipulation of soft tissues, joint mobilization, and real-time tactile evaluation, all requiring human presence, strength, and dexterity that current or near-term AI cannot perform. openai_rationale: Material moving machine operators perform tasks that are largely physical and require real-world presence, such as operating machinery to transport materials. Demand elasticity is also low because the need for material movement is not significantly suppressed by cost; rather, it is driven by broader economic activity and logistics needs. Therefore, even with increased efficiency, the demand for operators does not expand significantly. The net effect is 'resilient' as AI impacts peripheral tasks but does not fundamentally alter the occupation.
gpt55_rationale: The work is primarily physical and site-based, involving safe operation of forklifts, cranes, conveyors, hoists, and dredging equipment around people, loads, and changing real-world conditions. gpt56sol_rationale: Autonomous forklifts, robotic material-handling systems, machine vision, and AI-based routing can increasingly perform the repetitive movement and monitoring tasks common in structured warehouses and factories. Demand for inventory tracking is structurally fixed: businesses need accurate records regardless of cost, and cheaper/faster recordkeeping does not cause companies to track dramatically more inventory, so productivity gains convert directly to fewer workers (low elasticity). Demand is highly inelastic: businesses need each shipment recorded exactly once, and cheaper recordkeeping does not create more goods to track, so productivity gains flow straight to reduced headcount. BLS already projects -6% employment on the strength of automated storage and retrieval and RFID adoption, a trend AI accelerates. High disruption plus near-fixed demand puts this squarely in the replace category, though the physical warehouse tasks mean contraction is gradual rather than abrupt.
openai_rationale: Material recording clerks perform tasks that are increasingly being automated through technologies like RFID and collaborative robots. The demand elasticity is low because the tasks performed by clerks are not significantly suppressed by cost; rather, they are dictated by the volume of goods handled, which does not expand proportionally with productivity gains. gpt55_rationale: Material recording clerks perform many routine, structured tasks—inventory records, shipment verification, scheduling updates, reports, invoices, and exception tracking—that are directly automatable with AI-enabled warehouse management systems, RFID, computer vision, and automated storage tools. AI systems are increasingly capable of processing medical images and performing complex dose calculations with high precision. However, demand elasticity is very low because the number of cancer patients requiring radiation therapy is relatively fixed and determined by disease incidence rather than cost or speed of dosimetry services. Making dose calculations 10x faster wouldn't meaningfully increase the total number of radiation treatments needed, as this is constrained by patient population and medical necessity rather than dosimetrist availability.
opus_rationale: Disruption is high because the core work—calculating radiation doses, designing treatment plans from CT/MRI scans, and performing QA on equipment—is heavily computational and image-based, exactly the kind of optimization and pattern-recognition task where AI/treatment-planning algorithms are already making rapid inroads. Elasticity is low because demand for radiation oncology is driven by cancer incidence and physician prescriptions, not by the cost or speed of dose planning; cheaper planning won't cause patients to receive dramatically more treatment, and the field is tightly regulated and physician-gated. With disruption >=7 and elasticity <=4, productivity gains from AI are likely to be absorbed by fewer dosimetrists per clinic rather than by expanded volume, fitting the replace category—though the small workforce and physician oversight/safety requirements may slow headcount contraction.
opus5_rationale: Core work is computer-based: reviewing CT/MRI images, contouring, and optimizing radiation dose distributions in treatment planning software — exactly the domain where AI auto-segmentation and knowledge-based/automated planning tools are already commercially deployed and validated, often producing plans in minutes that took hours. Only a small share of the job (immobilization devices, occasional patient positioning, QA on physical equipment) requires hands-on presence, so disruption is very high. Demand is driven by cancer incidence and physician-prescribed treatment courses, not by planning cost or speed; patients will not receive 10x more radiotherapy because plans are cheaper, so elasticity is low with only modest expansion from aging demographics and better access in underserved clinics. High disruption plus inelastic demand in a small (4,800-person) occupation means productivity gains concentrate into fewer dosimetrists per center, shifting the surviving role toward plan review, QA, and physicist-adjacent oversight.
openai_rationale: Medical dosimetrists perform tasks that are predominantly cognitive and technical, involving calculations and treatment planning that can be assisted by AI. However, the core tasks require significant human oversight and collaboration with a medical team, limiting AI's ability to fully automate the role. The disruption score reflects the potential for AI to assist but not replace the nuanced decision-making required. Demand elasticity is low because the demand for radiation therapy is driven by patient needs rather than cost, and AI improvements in speed or cost are unlikely to significantly increase the number of treatments. Thus, the net effect is 'resilient' as AI will augment but not fundamentally change the occupation.
gpt55_rationale: Medical dosimetry is highly computer-based and centered on image review, dose calculation, treatment-plan optimization, documentation, and quality checks, all areas where AI-assisted contouring, auto-planning, and verification tools are already advancing. Human expertise will remain important because the work is safety-critical, regulated, and integrated with physicians, physicists, and radiation therapists, but the core technical planning workflow is directly in AI’s path. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of radiation treatment plans is driven mainly by cancer incidence, physician prescriptions, equipment capacity, and clinical protocols rather than the cost or speed of dosimetry alone. Since AI can substantially reduce planning labor while cheaper planning is unlikely to generate enough additional treatment volume, the occupation fits the replace category.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most treatment planning, image review, dose calculation, optimization, and documentation are digital tasks that AI and automated planning systems can substantially accelerate. Human dosimetrists will remain important for unusual cases, quality assurance, regulatory accountability, equipment checks, and coordination with the oncology team, but these functions may require fewer labor hours per patient. Demand is constrained mainly by cancer incidence, physician prescriptions, treatment capacity, and clinical protocols, so cheaper planning will not produce a proportional increase in radiation treatments. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount pressure and a replace outcome.
fable5_rationale: The core work — reviewing scans, calculating radiation doses, and designing treatment plans on a computer — is almost entirely digital and is already being transformed by AI-driven auto-planning and deep-learning dose optimization tools (e.g., knowledge-based planning, adaptive radiotherapy systems), placing it squarely in AI's path. Demand for radiation treatment planning is driven by cancer incidence, not by the cost or speed of planning; patients won't receive 10x more radiotherapy courses because plans become cheaper, though daily adaptive replanning offers some modest volume expansion. With only 4,800 workers and projected flat employment, productivity gains from AI planning tools will likely translate into fewer dosimetrists per clinic rather than expanded demand. High disruption combined with structurally inelastic demand makes this a replace scenario, with remaining roles shifting toward QA and plan review under physicist oversight.
grok45_rationale: Core work is almost entirely digital and computational—reviewing CT/MRI scans, optimizing radiation dose distributions, and designing delivery plans via specialized software—placing it squarely in AI’s path; existing auto-contouring, inverse-planning, and ML-based TPS tools already materially accelerate these tasks and will continue to do so. Demand for treatment plans is tightly coupled to the fixed incidence of radiotherapy-eligible cancers and the number of available linear accelerators, so a 10x productivity gain does not unlock proportional new volume. Regulatory oversight, liability, and the clinical bottleneck of patient throughput further limit expansion, producing headcount contraction rather than offsetting growth.

title: Medical equipment repairers
claude_rationale: Medical equipment repair is predominantly hands-on physical work requiring on-site presence, manual dexterity, and real-world troubleshooting of complex electromechanical systems. While AI may assist with diagnostic software and documentation, the core tasks of disassembling equipment, replacing parts, calibrating machines, and performing preventive maintenance remain fundamentally manual. Demand elasticity is low because medical facilities have fixed equipment needs based on patient capacity and regulatory requirements - making repairs 10x faster wouldn't lead hospitals to purchase dramatically more equipment or need proportionally more repair services. The moderate disruption score and low elasticity place this firmly in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical repair, installation, and calibration of medical equipment requiring dexterity, physical stamina, on-site presence, and mechanical troubleshooting—tasks AI cannot perform directly. AI may assist with diagnostics, predictive maintenance scheduling, technical manual lookup, and software/cybersecurity tasks, but these are peripheral to the physical work. Demand is moderately elastic, driven by growth in medical equipment volume from chronic disease prevalence and an aging population rather than by AI cost reductions. Since disruption is low (≤6), this occupation is resilient: AI augments diagnostics but does not reshape the physically grounded core work.
opus5_rationale: Core work is hands-on physical repair, calibration, and installation of equipment in clinical settings — requiring dexterity, physical strength, and on-site presence that AI cannot substitute. AI does touch peripheral and diagnostic layers: predictive maintenance analytics, AI-assisted troubleshooting from manuals and error logs, and documentation could make each technician more efficient, and the growing software/cybersecurity component of connected devices shifts skills somewhat. Demand is moderately elastic — aging equipment fleets, expanding imaging and monitoring installations, and more IoT-connected devices mean more maintenance work, though hospital budgets and equipment counts cap growth. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient; BLS already projects 13% growth.
openai_rationale: Medical equipment repairers perform a mix of physical and technical tasks, including installation, maintenance, and repair of complex medical devices. While AI can assist with diagnostics and predictive maintenance, the hands-on nature of the work and the need for physical presence limit AI's impact on core tasks, resulting in moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while increased efficiency could lead to some expansion in service capacity, the demand for repair services is primarily driven by the existing and growing stock of medical equipment rather than cost. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing the core work.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially help with diagnostic support, technical manuals, remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, recordkeeping, software updates, and troubleshooting workflows. However, the core job still requires on-site physical work: installing equipment, testing and calibrating devices, replacing parts, using tools, moving equipment, and ensuring safety in clinical environments. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper maintenance could enable more preventive service and support a growing installed base of medical devices, but total demand is still constrained by healthcare facilities, regulation, and the physical stock of equipment. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on installation, calibration, disassembly, parts replacement, and testing at healthcare sites, all of which require dexterity and physical presence. AI can improve fault diagnosis, retrieve technical guidance, predict maintenance needs, and automate records, but it cannot readily perform the physical repair or assume responsibility for safety-critical equipment. Demand is relatively inelastic because maintenance volume is tied to the installed equipment base, regulatory schedules, and actual failures rather than the price of technician time. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI mainly enhancing technician productivity rather than replacing the core role.
fable5_rationale: The core work — physically installing, disassembling, calibrating, and repairing electromechanical and hydraulic medical equipment on-site — requires hands-on presence, dexterity, and physical strength that AI cannot replace. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like fault diagnosis, pulling technical manual guidance, predictive maintenance scheduling, and record-keeping, but these are complements rather than substitutes for the manual repair itself. Demand is largely driven by the installed base of medical equipment and healthcare utilization rather than repair cost, so even faster diagnostics would only modestly expand total work. With low disruption to core tasks and strong projected employment growth from expanding healthcare demand, this occupation is resilient.
grok45_rationale: Core work centers on physical installation, hands-on diagnosis with tools, mechanical/electronic repairs, calibration, and on-site presence around patients and heavy equipment, so AI mainly assists peripheral tasks like predictive maintenance software, remote diagnostics, record-keeping, and software updates rather than displacing the manual core. Demand elasticity is moderate because healthcare volume and equipment proliferation (driven by aging populations and chronic disease) create some expansion if repairs become cheaper and faster, enabling broader deployment and better upkeep, yet structural limits from facility capacity and regulation prevent unlimited growth. With disruption only moderate, the occupation remains resilient as AI does not reshape the essential in-person technical work.

title: Medical records specialists
claude_rationale: Medical records specialists perform almost entirely digital tasks - reviewing records, coding diagnoses, data entry, and maintaining electronic health records - all of which are prime targets for AI automation. AI can already handle much of the pattern recognition, coding classification, and data processing that forms the core of this work. Demand elasticity is very low because healthcare organizations need a fixed amount of medical coding and record maintenance regardless of cost - patients don't generate more medical records just because processing becomes cheaper, and regulatory requirements for record-keeping remain constant. The BLS already acknowledges that AI-powered solutions are affecting demand for these workers.
opus_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital and cognitive — reviewing records, assigning standardized codes, data entry, and retrieval — all squarely in AI's path, and AI-powered coding tools are already being adopted as noted in the BLS outlook itself. Demand is structurally fixed: the volume of patient records to be coded is determined by healthcare utilization, not by the cost or speed of coding, so productivity gains translate directly into fewer workers per record rather than vastly more coding output. With high disruption (9) and inelastic demand (2), this fits the replace category; even modest population-driven volume growth is likely to be more than offset by per-worker productivity gains from AI.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital text processing: reading clinical documentation and assigning standardized codes, entering and retrieving data in EHR systems. Computer-assisted coding and NLP already automate much of this, and LLMs are rapidly closing the gap on the ambiguous cases that previously required human coders. Demand is structurally fixed — coding volume tracks the number of patient encounters and claims, not the cost of coding, so 10x cheaper coding produces no more encounters and only modest new demand for auditing, denial management, and compliance review. High disruption paired with inelastic demand means productivity gains convert to headcount reduction, with surviving roles concentrated in exception handling and AI output validation.
openai_rationale: Medical records specialists primarily engage in digital tasks such as data entry, coding, and maintaining electronic health records, which are highly susceptible to AI automation. AI tools are already capable of automating many of these tasks, such as coding and data retrieval, suggesting high disruption. However, the demand for medical records specialists is relatively inelastic; while efficiency gains are possible, the volume of medical records processed is not likely to increase significantly with reduced costs. Thus, productivity improvements are more likely to reduce headcount rather than expand demand, leading to a 'replace' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: Medical records specialists perform predominantly digital, rules-based, language-heavy work: extracting information from clinical notes, checking completeness, assigning billing and diagnosis codes, and entering data into EHR systems. AI systems are already well suited to clinical documentation review, automated coding suggestions, error detection, and record retrieval, with humans increasingly shifting toward exception handling, audits, and compliance oversight. Demand is relatively inelastic because the volume of medical records is tied mainly to healthcare encounters, regulation, and reimbursement workflows rather than the price of coding labor, although aging and chronic disease will add some baseline growth. Because disruption is very high and cheaper coding is unlikely to create enough new work to offset automation, the occupation fits the replace category.
gpt56sol_rationale: The occupation is almost entirely computer-based and centers on extracting, validating, classifying, and entering structured information—tasks increasingly handled by AI-enabled EHR, coding, and document-processing systems. Humans will remain important for ambiguous documentation, provider clarification, audits, privacy compliance, and exception handling, but automation can substantially reduce routine coding and recordkeeping labor. Demand is driven mainly by the number of healthcare encounters and regulatory requirements, so making records processing much cheaper will not generate proportionately more work, although population aging will increase baseline volume. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount pressure and a shift toward oversight and complex cases.
fable5_rationale: The core tasks — reviewing records, assigning standardized diagnosis and procedure codes, and entering data into EHR systems — are entirely digital, rule-based classification work that sits directly in AI's path, and autonomous coding tools are already deployed and improving rapidly. Demand for medical coding is driven by patient encounter volume and payer requirements, not by cost or speed of coding, so making the work 10x cheaper does not generate meaningfully more records to code. While healthcare volume grows modestly with an aging population, that growth cannot absorb the productivity gains from AI coding systems, so headcount contraction is likely despite BLS's current positive projection. High disruption combined with inelastic demand places this occupation squarely in the replace category.
grok45_rationale: Core work is almost entirely digital and cognitive—reviewing clinical documentation, assigning ICD/CPT codes, EHR data entry, and accuracy checks—all of which current NLP and AI coding tools already perform or assist at high accuracy, with rapid further gains expected. Demand for these services is tightly coupled to the fixed volume of patient encounters and billing events rather than to the cost or speed of coding itself; cheaper processing does not generate meaningfully more healthcare utilization or records. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to substantial headcount contraction as AI absorbs the bulk of the workload.

title: Medical scientists
claude_rationale: Medical scientists face high disruption as AI increasingly assists with data analysis, literature review, hypothesis generation, experimental design, and pattern recognition in biological data - core cognitive tasks that comprise much of their work. However, demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster research capabilities could dramatically expand medical research across underserved diseases, personalized medicine, and global health challenges where current research is limited by cost and complexity. The combination of high disruption with high elasticity suggests medical scientists will be augmented rather than replaced, with each scientist able to conduct far more research projects and investigations than currently possible.
opus_rationale: Disruption is high because much of medical research—hypothesis generation, data analysis, literature review, experimental design, grant and paper writing—is cognitive and increasingly accelerated by AI tools that can model proteins, predict drug interactions, and analyze trial data far faster than humans; however, the wet-lab experimentation, clinical trial supervision, and physical sample handling keep it below the very-high tier. Elasticity is high because demand for medical research is enormous and currently bottlenecked by cost and speed: cheaper, faster discovery would unlock vastly more research into diseases, drug candidates, and personalized therapies rather than satisfy a fixed quota of studies. With disruption >= 7 and elasticity >= 7, productivity gains are absorbed by expanded research output, so headcount stays stable or grows while each scientist becomes dramatically more productive, fitting the augment category.
opus5_rationale: Medical research is heavily knowledge- and data-intensive: literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, study design, statistical analysis, grant writing, and manuscript preparation are all directly in AI's path, and AI-driven protein structure prediction, target identification, and trial-data analysis are already reshaping workflows. Wet-lab experimentation, clinical trial oversight, and biosafety work still require human presence, which keeps disruption below maximum. Elasticity is high because the space of unanswered biomedical questions is effectively unbounded and currently rationed by cost, time, and funding — cheaper discovery expands the number of targets pursued, diseases studied, and trials run, and existing job growth projections already reflect strong latent demand. Because productivity gains are likely absorbed by more research output rather than fewer researchers, with the human role shifting toward directing AI-assisted programs and validating results in the lab, this is augmentation rather than replacement.
openai_rationale: Medical scientists engage in a mix of cognitive and experimental tasks, including designing studies, analyzing data, and writing grant proposals. AI can assist significantly in data analysis, hypothesis generation, and even in some aspects of experimental design, but the core work still requires human oversight and creativity. Thus, disruption is high but not maximal. Demand elasticity is high because advancements in AI could make research more efficient, potentially unlocking new areas of study and increasing the volume of research conducted. As healthcare needs grow, particularly with an aging population, the demand for medical research is likely to expand, absorbing productivity gains and potentially increasing headcount.
gpt55_rationale: Medical scientists do substantial cognitive and digital work—literature review, hypothesis generation, study design, statistical analysis, grant writing, publication, drug discovery, and interpretation of clinical or molecular data—that AI can already materially accelerate. Disruption is not higher because much of the occupation remains tied to wet-lab experimentation, clinical trials, biological uncertainty, safety procedures, regulatory requirements, and expert scientific judgment. Demand elasticity is high because biomedical research has enormous unmet demand in cancer, Alzheimer’s, chronic disease, antimicrobial resistance, rare diseases, and personalized medicine, so cheaper research would likely expand the number of questions, targets, and therapies pursued. The net effect is augment: AI will substantially change workflows and required skills, but expanded research output and persistent health needs should absorb much of the productivity gain rather than simply reduce headcount.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will substantially reshape literature review, hypothesis generation, experimental design, biomedical data analysis, drug discovery, grant writing, and publication, although laboratory experiments, clinical validation, safety oversight, and scientific judgment still require significant human involvement. Demand is highly elastic because cheaper and faster research would enable more disease targets, drug candidates, personalized therapies, and studies than current budgets and researcher capacity permit. Aging populations, chronic disease, and large unmet medical needs reinforce this latent demand, though laboratory and regulatory bottlenecks prevent an even higher score. Thus, medical scientists are likely to become far more productive and work differently, while expanding research activity supports stable or growing employment.
fable5_rationale: A large share of a medical scientist's core work — literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, experimental design, statistical analysis of trial data, and grant/manuscript writing — is directly in AI's path, and tools like protein-structure prediction and AI-driven drug discovery are already reshaping the field; hands-on wet lab work tempers the score but is often delegated to technicians. Demand elasticity is high because the appetite for cures and treatments is effectively unbounded — cheaper, faster research means more diseases investigated, more compounds screened, and more trials run, with an aging population and chronic disease burden fueling funding. Productivity gains are likely absorbed by dramatically expanded research output rather than headcount cuts, consistent with BLS's much-faster-than-average growth projection. High disruption paired with high elasticity makes this a clear augment case.
grok45_rationale: Medical scientists perform predominantly knowledge-work tasks—hypothesis generation, study design, data analysis from trials and samples, grant writing, and publication—where AI already accelerates literature synthesis, bioinformatics, experimental design, and even molecular discovery, with rapid further gains expected; physical lab handling, clinical oversight, and high-stakes judgment keep it from the highest tier. Demand elasticity is high because society has vast unmet needs for treatments of aging-related, chronic, and emerging diseases; 10x cheaper/faster research would unlock far more trials, drug candidates, and personalized studies rather than simply shrinking headcount. The combination therefore produces augmentation: each scientist becomes dramatically more productive while total research output and employment expand.

title: Medical transcriptionists
claude_rationale: Medical transcription is almost entirely digital work involving converting speech to text, which AI speech recognition and natural language processing can now do with high accuracy. The BLS already notes that speech recognition technology is reducing demand for transcriptionists and increasing productivity of remaining workers. Demand for medical transcription services is highly inelastic - healthcare providers need a fixed amount of documentation regardless of cost, and patients don't generate more medical encounters just because transcription becomes cheaper. The combination of very high AI disruption and very low demand elasticity makes this a clear replacement scenario.
opus_rationale: The work is entirely digital language processing—converting voice to text and editing—which is squarely in the direct path of speech recognition and NLP models that already produce high-quality drafts. The disruption score is very high because AI ambient documentation tools increasingly let physicians document encounters in real time, eliminating the transcription step entirely. Demand is highly inelastic: the volume of medical documentation is fixed by the number of patient encounters, so making transcription cheaper does not generate more reports—it simply requires fewer workers. With very high disruption and near-zero elasticity, headcount contracts, matching the BLS-projected decline.
opus5_rationale: The work is entirely digital audio-to-text conversion and editing — precisely what modern ASR and LLM-based ambient documentation tools already perform at or above human accuracy, and AI scribes are being adopted rapidly across physician offices and hospitals. Demand is strictly bounded by the number of patient encounters; cheaper documentation does not create more clinical notes, so productivity gains flow directly into fewer workers. With maximal disruption and near-zero elasticity, headcount contraction is the only outcome, consistent with the BLS decline projection, which likely understates the pace.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of medical transcriptionists are highly susceptible to disruption by AI, particularly through advancements in speech recognition and natural language processing. These technologies can automate much of the transcription process, reducing the need for human intervention. As a result, the disruption score is very high. On the elasticity dimension, demand for medical transcription is relatively inelastic; even if transcription becomes cheaper and faster, the volume of medical reports needed does not increase proportionally. Thus, productivity gains are unlikely to lead to a significant expansion in demand, resulting in a low elasticity score. Consequently, the net effect is 'replace' as AI absorbs core tasks without a compensatory increase in demand.
gpt55_rationale: Medical transcription is almost entirely digital, language-based work: listening to dictation, converting it into text, editing drafts, and entering documentation into EHR systems. Speech recognition, natural language processing, and ambient clinical documentation tools already perform much of the core task, with humans increasingly limited to exception handling, quality review, and compliance-sensitive edits. Demand is relatively inelastic because the volume of medical transcription is tied to patient encounters and required documentation, and cheaper transcription does not cause physicians or patients to consume vastly more reports. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity means productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount, so the net effect is replace.
gpt56sol_rationale: The occupation consists almost entirely of routine digital language processing—transcribing, formatting, checking, and entering dictated medical information—which speech recognition and generative AI increasingly perform directly. Human review remains valuable for ambiguous audio, clinical inconsistencies, legal compliance, and patient-safety risks, but improved models will reduce the amount of review required per document. Demand is highly inelastic because documentation volume is largely tied to the number of patient encounters, and cheaper transcription will not produce substantially more encounters or reports. Consequently, productivity gains will allow fewer transcriptionists to handle the existing workload, making replacement the most likely net effect.
fable5_rationale: Medical transcription is fully routine digital language processing — AI speech recognition and LLM-based ambient documentation tools already perform the core task (converting dictation to formatted medical reports) with high accuracy, and the residual editing/QA role is rapidly shrinking as models improve. Demand is inelastic: the volume of clinical documentation is driven by patient encounters, not by transcription cost, so a 10x cheaper transcription process does not generate 10x more dictation — it simply requires fewer humans. BLS already projects decline, and ambient AI scribes are accelerating this beyond the official forecast. With maximum disruption and near-zero demand elasticity, this is a textbook replace occupation.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—listening to medical dictation, converting speech to structured reports, editing speech-recognition drafts for accuracy, and applying medical terminology—are almost entirely digital, language-based, and cognitive, placing them squarely in the path of advancing AI speech-to-text and NLP systems that already produce usable drafts and are rapidly improving. Demand for transcription is inelastic because the volume of reports is fixed by the number of patient encounters and clinical documentation requirements; making the process 10x cheaper or faster does not generate more medical visits or more reports. Consequently, productivity gains translate directly into fewer workers needed, matching the BLS projection of employment decline and fitting the replace category.

title: Meeting, convention, and event planners
claude_rationale: Event planning involves significant knowledge work that AI can assist with - vendor research, scheduling optimization, budget tracking, communication drafting, and logistics coordination - but requires substantial human presence for client relationships, venue inspections, real-time problem solving, and on-site event management. The demand elasticity is high because cheaper, more efficient event planning could unlock significant latent demand from smaller businesses, individuals, and organizations that currently forgo professional planning due to cost, while existing clients might host more frequent or elaborate events. The combination of meaningful AI assistance with strong demand expansion suggests workers will become more productive rather than displaced.
opus_rationale: Disruption is moderate: significant portions of the work are cognitive and digital (researching venues, drafting communications, comparing bids, managing schedules, surveying attendees) where AI tools materially help, but the core work requires in-person relationship-building, on-site venue inspection, real-time problem-solving during live events, and physical presence that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster planning could unlock more events at the lower end (smaller weddings, corporate gatherings), but demand for professional planners is constrained by budgets, the inherently social and high-touch nature of events, and the fact that major events are discrete, infrequent purchases. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI augments the administrative and research tasks but does not reshape the relationship-driven, physically present core of the role.
opus5_rationale: A substantial slice of the job — vendor research, RFPs, budget spreadsheets, contract drafting, registration systems, attendee communications, post-event surveys and reporting — is digital and already being compressed by AI and event-tech platforms, which will meaningfully change how planners spend their days. But the core of the occupation remains in-person and relational: site inspections, live negotiation with venues and caterers, on-site crisis management, reading a client's or attendee's mood, and physically running the event, none of which AI performs. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper planning labor lets more mid-size organizations and individuals afford professional coordination, yet total event volume is capped by the hard costs of venues, food, travel, and calendar time, so the planner fee is not the binding constraint on demand. With disruption at 5, this fits 'resilient' — AI reshapes the back-office workflow and raises the number of events one planner can juggle, but the human, on-the-ground core keeps headcount roughly on its modest growth path.
openai_rationale: AI can significantly impact the planning and coordination aspects of event planning, such as venue selection, scheduling, and logistics management, which are increasingly supported by AI tools. However, the human element in client interaction and on-site management remains crucial, keeping disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is high because as AI reduces costs and increases efficiency, more individuals and organizations can afford to host events, thus expanding the market. The combination of high disruption and high elasticity suggests that while the nature of the work will change, the overall demand for event planners will grow, leading to an 'augment' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: AI can substantially assist the digital and cognitive parts of event planning, including drafting schedules, budgets, proposals, vendor comparisons, attendee communications, registration workflows, surveys, and contingency plans. However, the core job still depends heavily on client trust, negotiation, relationship management, venue inspection, vendor coordination, and real-time problem-solving at unpredictable in-person events. Demand has moderate elasticity: cheaper planning tools could let more small businesses, nonprofits, couples, and community groups use professional planning support, but the number and scale of events remain constrained by budgets, calendars, venues, and social need. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to displace the human-centered and on-site core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can substantially accelerate venue research, budgeting, scheduling, vendor comparisons, communications, contract review, registration, and attendee feedback analysis. However, client relationship management, venue inspection, negotiation, vendor coordination, and real-time handling of unpredictable event problems still require human judgment and physical presence. Lower planning costs could make professional services accessible for more small events, but demand is constrained by the number of events and by venue, catering, travel, and entertainment costs. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI improving productivity and reducing administrative workload without fully reshaping its presence-intensive core.
fable5_rationale: A substantial portion of the work — vendor research, soliciting bids, budgeting, scheduling, attendee communications, and post-event billing — is digital coordination work that AI tools can already accelerate significantly, but the core still requires physical site inspections, in-person negotiation, relationship management with venues and clients, and real-time on-site troubleshooting during live events. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper planning services could unlock some latent demand (smaller businesses and individuals hiring planners for events they'd otherwise self-organize), but the total number of weddings, conventions, and corporate gatherings is bounded by social and budgetary factors, not planning costs. With disruption at the 6 boundary — the human-presence and trust components anchoring the role — this occupation fits resilient: AI will streamline the back-office half of the job while the experiential, logistical, and interpersonal core remains human-driven.
grok45_rationale: Disruption is moderate-to-high because a large share of the work—client scoping, venue research and bidding, budgeting, vendor coordination, and post-event analysis—is cognitive, language-based, and already assisted by AI tools for proposals, optimization, and communications, yet core duties still require physical venue inspection, on-site real-time problem-solving, and interpersonal relationship management that AI cannot fully absorb. Elasticity is moderate because dramatically cheaper planning would unlock more professional help for personal events (weddings, reunions) and more frequent smaller corporate or hybrid gatherings, but overall demand remains constrained by venue capacity, attendee time, and the dominant non-planning costs of events themselves. With disruption at the upper edge of the moderate range, the occupation is resilient: AI will reshape tools and peripheral workflows without displacing the human-centric core of event orchestration.

title: Metal and plastic machine workers
claude_rationale: While AI and automation are advancing in manufacturing (CNC programming, predictive maintenance, quality control), the core work remains predominantly physical - operating heavy machinery, handling materials, and performing hands-on setup and maintenance tasks that require real-world presence and manual dexterity. The disruption is moderate as AI assists with programming and monitoring but doesn't replace the fundamental physical operations. Demand elasticity is low because manufacturing output is driven by broader economic demand for goods rather than the cost of machine operation; making machining 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically increase total demand for manufactured parts. The net effect is resilient as AI enhances but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core physical work.
opus_rationale: The core work is physical and hands-on: setting up machines, loading materials, swapping cutting tools, inspecting parts, and monitoring equipment on the factory floor. AI and automation (CNC, robotics) do reshape the industry, but the disruption here comes primarily from industrial machine automation rather than generative AI absorbing cognitive tasks; the manual setup, material handling, and inspection presence still requires human workers, keeping disruption low-to-moderate. Demand elasticity is low because output is driven by physical manufacturing orders that are capped by foreign competition and capital investment rather than unlocked by cheaper labor, so productivity gains translate into headcount reduction (BLS projects -7%). Because disruption is well below 7, this falls into the resilient category—AI touches the periphery and automation pressures employment, but it does not transform the fundamental physical nature of the core work.
opus5_rationale: Core work is physical machine setup, loading, tool changing, and inspection on the shop floor — AI language/vision models touch only the programming (CAM/CNC), quality-inspection, and process-optimization slices, and the CNC programmer subgroup is the one segment squarely in AI's path. The bigger threat here is conventional automation and robotics rather than AI per se, which is why BLS already projects a 7 percent decline driven by CNC adoption and offshoring, not by generative AI. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: demand for machined parts is derived from manufacturing output and constrained by global competition and capital investment, so cheaper programming does not multiply part volumes proportionally, though some reshoring and cheaper short-run/custom fabrication could unlock modest new demand. Net effect is 'resilient' in the classification sense — AI reshapes the periphery (programming, inspection, predictive maintenance) rather than the hands-on core — even though total headcount continues to erode from automation trends predating AI.
openai_rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while AI and automation, particularly CNC technology, are increasingly used in metal and plastic machine work, much of the work still requires human oversight, setup, and maintenance. The elasticity score is low because the demand for these roles is not highly elastic; improvements in efficiency do not significantly increase demand for machine-produced parts, as the market is constrained by existing manufacturing needs and competition. The net effect is 'resilient' because although AI and automation will change some aspects of the work, the core tasks still require human intervention, and demand is not expected to expand significantly to offset productivity gains.
gpt55_rationale: AI and adjacent automation will materially affect machine monitoring, CNC programming, toolpath generation, visual inspection, predictive maintenance, and the ability of one operator to oversee multiple machines. However, much of the occupation still requires physical setup, loading and unloading materials, changing tools, troubleshooting equipment, measuring parts, and maintaining safety around real machines, which keeps disruption below the high-disruption threshold. Demand for machined metal and plastic parts would expand somewhat if production became cheaper, especially through reshoring and more customization, but it is constrained by downstream product demand, materials costs, capital equipment, and global competition. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best categorized as resilient, even though employment may continue to decline from broader factory automation.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will improve CNC programming, machine setup, predictive maintenance, process optimization, and automated visual inspection, while enabling one operator to oversee more equipment. However, loading materials, changing tools, handling irregular parts, troubleshooting machinery, and working safely around physical production systems still require substantial on-site labor and mechanical skill. Demand is relatively inelastic because it is derived from demand for manufactured parts and finished goods, so lower production costs will increase output only modestly and may primarily reduce labor per unit. The occupation is therefore resilient under the specified taxonomy because disruption remains moderate, although conventional robotics and automation will continue to reduce operator headcount and shift jobs toward programming, setup, and maintenance.
fable5_rationale: The core work is physical — loading materials, tending machines, replacing tooling, and inspecting parts on a factory floor — which limits direct AI disruption, though AI-driven CNC programming, machine vision inspection, and predictive monitoring will erode the cognitive slices of the job (setup, quality checks, program generation). Elasticity is low: demand for machined parts is driven by downstream manufacturing output and foreign competition, not by the cost of operator labor, so productivity gains from automation translate into fewer operators per machine rather than more parts consumed. The occupation's decline (BLS projects -7%) stems mainly from robotics and CNC automation rather than AI reshaping knowledge work, and the hands-on setter/operator core remains outside AI's direct path over the next decade. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient to AI specifically, even as long-run automation pressure shrinks headcount.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks mix physical machine setup, material handling, tool changes, and on-floor monitoring with cognitive elements like blueprint interpretation, CNC programming, parameter adjustment, and inspection; AI already aids via computer vision QC, predictive maintenance, toolpath optimization, and code generation, but unpredictable real-world machine intervention and factory presence keep disruption moderate rather than high. Demand for the parts produced expands only modestly if costs fall, constrained by end-market saturation for goods, material costs, and global competition, so productivity gains historically and prospectively shrink headcount rather than unlock large latent volume. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation remains resilient overall even as automation continues the projected employment decline.

title: Microbiologists
claude_rationale: Microbiologists face moderate-to-high disruption as AI increasingly assists with data analysis, pattern recognition in microscopic images, genetic sequencing analysis, and research literature review, but core laboratory work like specimen collection, culture maintenance, and experimental design still requires human expertise and physical presence. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper and faster microbial analysis could dramatically expand applications in personalized medicine, environmental monitoring, food safety, and biotechnology development - areas currently limited by cost and throughput constraints. The combination of meaningful AI assistance with strong demand expansion potential places this in the augment category, where productivity gains drive market growth rather than job displacement.
