opus_rationale: Microbiology involves substantial hands-on lab work — culturing organisms, running experiments, collecting field samples, operating physical equipment — that AI cannot perform, anchoring disruption to the moderate range. However, AI materially accelerates the cognitive portions: experimental design, genomic/sequence analysis, literature synthesis, report writing, and pattern recognition in microbial data, so the knowledge-work component is meaningfully affected. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper, faster analysis could expand research output in drug discovery, biofuels, and public health, but headcount growth is constrained by physical lab requirements and grant funding limits. Since core work remains heavily lab-bound and disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
opus5_rationale: Microbiology blends substantial wet-lab bench work — culturing organisms, handling specimens, operating microscopes and incubators, field sampling — with knowledge work like experimental design, genomic/sequence analysis, literature review, grant writing, and reporting, where AI is already materially useful. The physical, hands-on, and biosafety-constrained portion of the job caps disruption at moderate-to-high rather than very high, though lab automation plus AI-driven analysis will reshape workflow significantly. Elasticity is high: drug discovery, antimicrobial resistance surveillance, environmental and food-safety testing, and biomanufacturing all have large latent demand currently gated by research cost and cycle time, so cheaper/faster analysis tends to expand the number of experiments and programs rather than shrink staff. Because core disruption stays at 6 given the irreducible bench and field component, the occupation lands in the resilient category, with AI acting as a productivity multiplier on the analytical side.
openai_rationale: Microbiologists engage in a mix of laboratory work, research, and analysis, which AI can assist but not fully replace due to the need for human judgment and creativity in experimental design and interpretation. AI tools can enhance data analysis and automate some routine tasks, but the core work remains hands-on and requires human oversight. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can accelerate research processes, the demand for microbiologists is not heavily suppressed by cost, and the growth in demand is driven by specific needs in pharmaceuticals and environmental research. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing core tasks.
gpt55_rationale: Microbiologists perform substantial cognitive and digital work—literature review, experimental design, bioinformatics, image analysis, technical writing, and grant/report preparation—that AI can materially accelerate. However, the core occupation still depends heavily on wet-lab work, culturing organisms, specimen handling, safety protocols, equipment use, and real-world experimental judgment, limiting full automation over the next decade. Demand could expand meaningfully in drug discovery, infectious disease surveillance, environmental monitoring, industrial biotech, and synthetic biology if research becomes cheaper, but it remains constrained by lab capacity, regulation, funding, and long development timelines. Because disruption is significant but not high enough to fully reshape the hands-on core of the job, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will substantially assist literature review, experimental design, genomic and imaging analysis, microorganism classification, and technical writing. However, core duties still involve physical sample handling, culturing organisms, operating laboratory equipment, enforcing biosafety procedures, and interpreting uncertain experimental results in real-world contexts. Cheaper and faster research could support more drug discovery, diagnostics, environmental monitoring, and industrial biotechnology, but funding, regulation, laboratory capacity, and biological testing cycles limit demand expansion. Because AI reshapes the analytical portions without replacing the hands-on experimental core, the occupation remains resilient.
fable5_rationale: Microbiologists' work is a mix of hands-on wet-lab tasks — culturing, isolating, and maintaining microorganisms, running physical experiments — and knowledge work like data analysis, report writing, and grant applications. AI substantially accelerates the analytical and writing portions (genomic analysis, literature review, experimental design hypotheses), but the core laboratory bench work requires physical presence and is only partially addressed by lab automation, yielding moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster microbial research would expand drug discovery, biofuels, and environmental applications, though funding cycles and lab infrastructure cap how quickly demand scales. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the desk-work half while the lab-work core remains human-driven.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks mix physical lab work (culturing, experiments, equipment use) with heavy cognitive components (experimental design, microbial identification/classification via imaging or sequencing data, statistical analysis, grant writing, and technical reporting); AI already materially accelerates the latter through image recognition, genomic ML models, literature synthesis, and protocol optimization, and will deepen this over 10 years even as wet-lab presence remains. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster microbial research and testing unlocks substantial latent applications in drug discovery, synthetic biology, industrial fermentation, biofuels, environmental remediation, and public-health surveillance that are currently constrained by cost and throughput. The combination produces an augment outcome: each microbiologist becomes dramatically more productive while total output and employment expand rather than contract.

title: Middle school teachers
claude_rationale: Middle school teaching involves substantial knowledge work - lesson planning, assessment, content delivery, and individualized instruction - that AI can meaningfully assist with through automated grading, personalized learning platforms, and curriculum generation. However, the core human elements of classroom management, emotional support, and real-time adaptation to student needs remain essential. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper, AI-enhanced education could unlock massive latent demand for personalized tutoring, smaller class sizes, and more individualized attention that is currently constrained by cost and teacher availability. The combination of moderate-to-high disruption with high elasticity suggests teachers will become more productive rather than replaced.
opus_rationale: The core work of middle school teaching is in-person classroom management, supervision of adolescents, emotional support, and real-time engagement—activities requiring sustained human presence that AI cannot replace. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like lesson planning, grading, generating materials, and personalized practice content, which raises disruption to a moderate level, but the central job remains physically and socially anchored. Demand elasticity is low because student enrollment is fixed by demographics, class sizes and staffing are constrained by budgets and regulation, and cheaper AI tools do not increase the number of children needing teachers (the BLS projects a slight decline). Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI augments teacher productivity at the margins but does not reshape the core supervisory and relational work.
opus5_rationale: Lesson planning, grading, assessment design, and parent communication are language-based tasks where AI tools are already materially useful, so the knowledge-work portion of the job is genuinely disrupted. But the core of middle school teaching is in-person supervision, behavior management, motivation, and social-emotional development of adolescents — custodial and relational work that requires physical presence and cannot be automated, which caps disruption at the upper edge of moderate. Elasticity is moderate at best: student enrollment is demographically fixed and publicly funded, so cheaper instruction does not produce more students, though it could deepen individualized support and tutoring within existing staffing. Because disruption stays at 6 and the core classroom role remains intact, the occupation is resilient — teachers' workflows shift toward AI-assisted planning and grading rather than the job disappearing.
openai_rationale: AI can assist middle school teachers by automating administrative tasks like grading and lesson planning, and by providing personalized learning tools for students. However, the core task of teaching, which involves direct interaction with students, remains largely human-centric. This results in a moderate disruption score. On the elasticity side, making education more efficient and personalized could significantly increase demand for educational services, as more students could benefit from tailored learning experiences. Thus, the elasticity is high, leading to an 'augment' net effect where AI enhances productivity and potentially increases demand for teachers.
gpt55_rationale: AI can substantially assist middle school teachers with lesson planning, differentiated materials, grading, feedback, parent communication, and individualized practice, so a meaningful share of the cognitive and administrative workload is exposed. However, the core job also involves in-person classroom management, motivation, supervision, adolescent development, relationship-building, and legal/custodial responsibilities that are difficult to automate. Demand elasticity is limited because the number of middle school students is largely fixed by demographics and public school staffing is constrained by budgets, class-size rules, and regulation, though cheaper AI-enabled instruction could modestly expand tutoring and personalization. Because disruption is meaningful but the core occupation still requires human presence and authority, the occupation is best classified as resilient rather than replaced.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will substantially assist with lesson planning, grading, assessment design, parent communications, and personalized instructional materials. However, classroom management, student supervision, motivation, social-emotional support, and real-time adaptation to adolescents still require a trusted human presence. Demand is constrained by student enrollment, class sizes, licensing rules, and public-school budgets, so greater productivity is unlikely to generate proportionally more teaching services. Because AI reshapes many supporting tasks without replacing the occupation's in-person core, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: AI already materially assists the knowledge-work portions of teaching—lesson planning, grading, differentiated materials, parent communication—but the core of middle school teaching is in-person: managing classrooms of adolescents, supervision, motivation, and social-emotional guidance, which keeps disruption at the boundary of moderate-high. Elasticity is low because demand is set by student demographics (projected to decline) and public budgets, not price; making teaching 10x more productive doesn't create more middle schoolers, though it may modestly reduce class sizes or teacher counts. The custodial and relational core of the job is not in AI's path, so despite substantial workflow changes, the occupation is best characterized as resilient with a shifting toolkit rather than restructured or replaced.
grok45_rationale: AI already materially alters core cognitive tasks such as lesson planning, content creation, grading, assessment design, and differentiation, so disruption is high even though real-time classroom management, adolescent social-emotional support, and physical supervision still require human presence. Demand elasticity is only moderate because the student population is demographically fixed and schooling is compulsory, yet cheaper/faster teaching can unlock latent demand for smaller classes, more specialized or enrichment offerings, and higher-quality individualized support within existing budgets. The combination produces restructuring: the occupation persists but the skill mix shifts heavily toward AI orchestration, facilitation, and relationship work, displacing those who do not adapt.

title: Military careers
claude_rationale: Military careers involve substantial physical presence, combat readiness, leadership in unpredictable environments, and human judgment in life-or-death situations that AI cannot replicate. While AI may assist with logistics, intelligence analysis, and administrative tasks, the core military functions of physical operations, command decisions under stress, and maintaining unit cohesion remain fundamentally human. Demand for military personnel is determined by geopolitical threats and national security needs rather than economic efficiency, making it highly inelastic to productivity improvements. The occupation remains resilient as AI touches only peripheral support functions while core military duties require irreplaceable human capabilities.
opus_rationale: Military careers span an enormous range of roles, but the core of the occupation centers on physical readiness, combat capability, security clearances, leadership under fire, and human presence in unpredictable real-world environments — tasks AI cannot replace. AI will materially change intelligence analysis, logistics, cyber, and administrative support roles, but the dominant mass of the force (combat, transportation, protective service, hands-on technical work) remains physical and human-dependent, yielding a moderate disruption score. Demand for military headcount is driven by geopolitical threat levels and policy/budget decisions rather than by productivity or cost efficiency, so it is highly inelastic to AI-driven gains. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the work core is fundamentally physical and policy-driven, the occupation is resilient overall, with AI augmenting peripheral knowledge-work specialties rather than reshaping the core mission.
opus5_rationale: Military careers span a vast range of specialties, but the bulk of personnel (combat arms, transportation, maintenance, logistics, protective service) perform physically embodied, presence-dependent work in unpredictable environments; AI will heavily reshape intelligence analysis, cyber, targeting, ISR processing, and administrative/logistics planning, and autonomous systems will change some crew and pilot roles, giving a moderate overall disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because force size is set by congressional appropriations, geopolitical threat assessment, and recruiting pools rather than by the cost or speed of producing military output — cheaper analysis does not cause the nation to buy 10x more soldiers. Headcount is politically determined and has been roughly stable for decades, so productivity gains show up as capability shifts and reallocation across specialties rather than large contraction or expansion. Because disruption remains at or below the moderate range for the aggregate occupation, the resilient category fits, though specific specialties (intelligence analyst, admin, imagery interpretation) will be restructured internally.
openai_rationale: Military careers involve a significant amount of physical and unpredictable real-world tasks, such as combat and field operations, which are not easily disrupted by AI. While AI can assist in areas like logistics, strategy, and data analysis, the core tasks require human presence and decision-making in dynamic environments. The demand elasticity is low because the size of the military is determined by strategic needs rather than cost or speed of operations. Thus, even if AI enhances productivity, it does not lead to a proportional increase in demand for military personnel. The occupation remains resilient as AI impacts peripheral tasks but does not fundamentally change the core nature of military work.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially change many military tasks, especially intelligence analysis, surveillance, targeting support, logistics, cyber operations, simulation-based training, maintenance, and administrative work. However, the occupation as a whole still requires physical readiness, deployment, command responsibility, teamwork, security presence, and human accountability in unpredictable and dangerous environments. Demand for military personnel is relatively inelastic because force size is driven by national security strategy, budgets, law, and geopolitical threats rather than the unit cost of producing military output. Because disruption is substantial but still low-to-moderate for the broad occupation, the net effect is resilient rather than replacement.
gpt56sol_rationale: Military careers span physical combat, field operations, maintenance, leadership, healthcare, logistics, and digital intelligence, so AI will substantially alter planning, surveillance, administration, and some technical specialties but cannot replace much of the required real-world presence and human command authority. Autonomous systems may reduce personnel needs in selected roles, while creating new work in cyber operations, robotics, electronic warfare, and AI oversight. Total personnel demand is relatively inelastic because it is set primarily by national-security strategy, force-readiness requirements, and congressional budgets rather than the market price of individual military services. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although disruption will vary sharply across specialties.
fable5_rationale: Military careers span combat, transportation, healthcare, and administration, but the core of most roles requires physical presence, deployment readiness, and operation in unpredictable, dangerous environments where AI assists rather than substitutes; AI and autonomous systems will meaningfully reshape some specialties (intelligence analysis, logistics, drone operations) but not the bulk of enlisted and officer work. Elasticity is unusual here because force size is set by policy, budget, and geopolitical strategy rather than market price — productivity gains from AI do not straightforwardly translate into either more 'consumption' of military service or headcount cuts, though pressure toward smaller, tech-heavy forces exists. With disruption at a moderate level and demand determined politically, the occupation as a whole is resilient, even as specific specialties shift toward AI-enabled systems operation.
grok45_rationale: Military careers span a wide mix of roles, from combat specialties and transportation that demand physical presence, fitness, and real-time judgment in unpredictable hostile environments, to technical, intelligence, logistics, and administrative work where AI already assists with analysis, simulation, predictive maintenance, and planning; overall this yields only moderate disruption as core missions still require human leadership, accountability, and boots-on-the-ground capability. Demand elasticity is low because force size is set by geopolitics, threat assessments, and congressional end-strength authorizations rather than market price or productivity; AI force-multipliers (autonomous systems, better ISR) are more likely to enable smaller or differently composed units than to expand total personnel demand. The combination of moderate disruption and inelastic demand places the occupation firmly in the resilient category.

title: Mining and geological engineers
claude_rationale: Mining and geological engineers face moderate disruption as AI can assist with data analysis, mine design optimization, and report generation, but core work requires physical site evaluation, safety oversight, and complex engineering judgment in unpredictable real-world environments. Demand elasticity is low because mining operations are driven by commodity needs and regulatory requirements rather than cost - making mining 10x cheaper wouldn't create 10x more demand for minerals, and mine locations are geologically constrained. The disruption score of 6 places this in the resilient category, where AI enhances but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core engineering and safety oversight responsibilities.
opus_rationale: A significant portion of mining engineering work is digital and cognitive — mine design, geological analysis, technical report writing, and production monitoring — all of which AI can meaningfully assist. However, core duties require on-site presence, supervising mine construction, inspecting safety conditions, and field work in remote locations, which keeps disruption moderate rather than high. Demand is constrained by the physical limits of mineral extraction, regulatory and environmental approvals, and commodity market cycles, so productivity gains tend to reduce headcount rather than expand the workforce (BLS projects flat employment with automation offsetting growth). Because disruption falls at or below 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes the analytical periphery but the physical, on-site, safety-critical core remains human-dependent.
opus5_rationale: A substantial part of the job — geological modeling, ore-body estimation, mine planning optimization, environmental/reclamation analysis, and technical report writing — is digital and squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven exploration analytics and autonomous mining systems are already reshaping these workflows. But the core role remains anchored in site-specific physical reality: supervising shaft and tunnel construction, inspecting walls and roofs, monitoring air quality, verifying equipment hazards, and signing off as a licensed PE in remote field conditions. Demand is inelastic because mine development is gated by commodity prices, capital intensity, permitting, and land access rather than by engineering cost or speed — cheaper analysis does not create more ore bodies or approved mines. With disruption at 6 and elasticity at 4, the occupation lands in resilient: AI reshapes the analytical toolkit of a small, licensure-protected workforce without displacing the field-based, accountability-bearing core.
openai_rationale: Mining and geological engineering involves a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, such as designing mines and ensuring safety, which are not fully automatable by AI. While AI can assist in data analysis and modeling, the need for human oversight in safety and environmental considerations remains critical. Demand elasticity is low because the need for mining engineers is closely tied to the demand for minerals, which is not highly sensitive to cost reductions. Thus, while AI may enhance productivity, it is unlikely to significantly alter headcount, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: AI can substantially assist the digital and analytical parts of mining and geological engineering, including geological modeling, mine-plan optimization, production monitoring, environmental analysis, safety documentation, and technical report drafting. However, the occupation still depends heavily on site-specific engineering judgment, field conditions, regulatory accountability, worker safety, construction oversight, and coordination with physical mining operations, so AI is unlikely to absorb the core role end-to-end. Demand elasticity is limited because the number of mines, mineral deposits, permits, capital projects, and commodity-driven extraction decisions will not expand dramatically just because engineering analysis is cheaper. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient rather than replaced or restructured.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially improve geological modeling, mine design optimization, production monitoring, hazard detection, and technical reporting. However, core responsibilities still require site-specific judgment, field inspections, coordination of physical operations, regulatory accountability, and safety-critical decisions in unpredictable environments. Demand is derived mainly from mineral production and the number of viable mining projects, so cheaper engineering may enable some additional exploration and optimization but will not generate proportionate growth in projects. With moderate disruption and limited demand elasticity, the occupation is resilient, although workflows and staffing within engineering teams will change.
fable5_rationale: Mining and geological engineers split their time between digital knowledge work (mine design, geological modeling, technical reports, production analysis) that AI tools can increasingly accelerate, and irreplaceable on-site work such as supervising shaft construction, inspecting mine walls and equipment, and ensuring regulatory safety compliance in unpredictable physical environments. The elasticity score is low-to-moderate because demand is driven by commodity markets, deposit availability, and permitting regimes rather than the cost of engineering labor — cheaper engineering analysis does not meaningfully expand the number of viable mines, though critical mineral demand for EVs and electronics provides some tailwind. With disruption at 5, the physical, safety-critical, and site-bound core of the work keeps this occupation resilient, even as AI reshapes the modeling and reporting portions of the job.
grok45_rationale: Core work mixes high-end knowledge tasks (mine design, geological modeling, optimization, technical reporting, production analysis) that AI already accelerates via simulation, generative design, and sensor analytics with irreducible on-site supervision, safety inspections, and physical construction oversight in remote environments, placing disruption in the high but not extreme range. Demand for mining engineering services is constrained by commodity prices, capital intensity of mines, environmental permitting, and geology rather than engineering cost or speed, so 10x productivity gains unlock only limited additional exploration or reclamation work. Because disruption sits at the upper edge of the moderate-to-high band, the occupation remains resilient: AI reshapes analytical tools and workflows but does not eliminate the need for human engineers on the ground.

title: Models
claude_rationale: AI disruption is high because core modeling tasks—posing for photos, displaying products, and creating visual content—are increasingly being replaced by AI-generated imagery, virtual models, and deepfake technology that can create realistic human likenesses without human models. Demand elasticity is low because the need for product promotion and advertising is relatively fixed; companies don't dramatically increase their marketing spend just because AI models are cheaper, and regulatory/brand authenticity concerns limit adoption. The combination of high disruption and low elasticity points to significant headcount contraction as AI-generated models become more sophisticated and widely accepted.
opus_rationale: Modeling is physical posing, but its core output—images for advertising—is now directly in AI's path; generative AI can create photorealistic synthetic models and reuse/alter existing model images without new shoots, undermining the core economic value of the human model. Demand is largely inelastic because advertising image needs are bounded by the number of products and campaigns, and cheaper synthetic imagery substitutes for rather than expands human modeling work. With disruption high and elasticity low, productivity gains accrue to brands and AI tools rather than expanding human headcount, consistent with the BLS-projected decline driven explicitly by AI image reuse. This fits 'replace' (disruption >= 7, elasticity <= 4).
opus5_rationale: Although modeling is a physically embodied job, its economic output is an image or video — precisely what generative AI now produces synthetically, and brands are already substituting AI-generated or AI-reused model imagery for paid shoots (BLS explicitly flags this). Segments that require literal physical presence (runway, fit modeling, trade shows, art-class and clinical/standardized-patient posing) are insulated, which caps disruption below the very-high range, but the large commercial print/e-commerce/catalog segment is squarely in AI's path. Elasticity is very low: cheaper imagery expands the volume of advertising content, yet that extra volume is fulfilled by synthetic models rather than more human bookings, so productivity gains accrue to brands and AI tools, not to model headcount. High disruption plus demand that does not flow back to human workers yields replacement, consistent with the already-projected employment decline.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of models involve physical presence and appearance, which are not easily replicated by AI. While AI can assist in digital marketing and virtual modeling, the need for human models in live events and photo shoots remains. Thus, disruption is moderate. Demand elasticity is low because the need for models is not significantly suppressed by cost; AI advancements may reduce demand slightly as digital alternatives become more prevalent. Overall, the occupation is resilient as AI impacts peripheral tasks but does not fundamentally alter the core work.
gpt55_rationale: A large share of modeling work for catalogs, online ads, product promotion, and portfolio-based casting is visual content production, which is directly affected by generative AI, virtual models, image editing, and reuse of existing likenesses. Human presence remains important for runway shows, live events, fit modeling, trade shows, and some brand campaigns, so disruption is high but not total. Demand for modeled imagery may expand as ads become cheaper to produce, but much of that expansion can be served by synthetic or reused images rather than additional human models. Because disruption is high and elasticity for human headcount is low, the occupation fits the replace category.
gpt56sol_rationale: Generative imagery, digital avatars, virtual try-on systems, and image-reuse tools can substitute for human models in much of the high-volume advertising, catalog, and online retail market. Runway shows, fitting work, live promotions, and artist sessions still require physical presence, preventing an even higher disruption score. Cheaper content will increase the number and variety of promotional images, but much of that expansion will use synthetic models rather than create additional human assignments, so demand for human-model headcount is relatively inelastic and the net effect is replacement.
fable5_rationale: Although modeling involves a physical human body, the actual product is a digital image or video — precisely what generative AI can now produce. AI-generated virtual models, image reuse licensing, and virtual try-on technology can substitute for many photo shoots, catalog work, and e-commerce imagery, putting the core output squarely in AI's path. Elasticity is low: even though cheap imagery means brands produce far more visual content, that expanded demand is largely satisfied by synthetic models rather than more human bookings, and premium demand for celebrity or runway models is fixed and concentrated. With high disruption and little demand absorption for human workers specifically, the occupation faces significant headcount contraction outside a small live-event and high-fashion niche.
grok45_rationale: Core commercial tasks such as posing for print/online ads, product catalogs, and digital campaigns are already being substantially displaced by generative AI image/video tools that create photorealistic virtual models, composites, and infinite variations without a human subject, while runway, fitting, and live event work remain physical but represent a smaller share. Demand elasticity is low because the need for actual human models is constrained by the finite number of physical fashion shows, trade events, and brand campaigns that specifically require real people; expanded digital content volume is absorbed by AI rather than more human bookings. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore produces net replacement and headcount contraction, matching the BLS outlook that AI image reuse and digital alternatives will limit employment.

title: Music directors and composers
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts composition work through tools that can generate melodies, harmonies, and arrangements, and assists with scoring and orchestration, but music direction requires real-time human leadership of live performers that AI cannot replicate. Demand elasticity is high because AI-assisted composition dramatically lowers barriers to music creation, enabling more content for films, games, commercials, and independent artists who previously couldn't afford custom compositions. While AI transforms the compositional toolkit, the expanded market for affordable, customized music should create more opportunities overall for music professionals who adapt to AI-augmented workflows.
opus_rationale: The composing portion of this work is highly disrupted—AI music generation tools can already produce arrangements, jingles, and background scores, directly threatening the commercial composition segment. However, the music director/conductor role is fundamentally a live, physical, interpersonal leadership task involving real-time human performance and ensemble coordination, which AI cannot replace, pulling the blended disruption score down to 6. On elasticity, cheaper music production could expand demand for low-cost commercial and background music, but the prestige live-performance segment (orchestras, opera, religious organizations comprising the majority of employment) is funding-constrained and culturally tied to human performers, limiting expansion to moderate. Because the core conducting and live-leadership work remains human-centric and disruption stays at 6, this occupation is resilient rather than facing wholesale restructuring.
opus5_rationale: The occupation is bifurcated: composers do largely digital, creative knowledge work that generative music models already touch directly (jingles, stock/production music, arranging, mockups, scoring drafts), while music directors — the majority of employment, concentrated in churches, schools, and performing arts companies — spend their days rehearsing, auditioning, conducting live ensembles, and building relationships with musicians and donors, tasks that require embodied presence and real-time human judgment. Blending the two yields moderate disruption: AI reshapes the composer workflow and erodes the low-end commercial music market, but leaves live direction essentially intact. Elasticity is moderate — cheap music unlocks far more scored content for video, games, and advertising, yet the concert/church/school ensembles that employ most of these workers are funding-constrained and their headcount is fixed by the number of ensembles, not by production cost. Because over half of the workforce sits in roles whose core work AI cannot perform, the occupation scores at the resilient boundary, though individual commercial composers will face genuine restructuring pressure.
openai_rationale: AI can assist music directors and composers in tasks such as arranging music, generating new compositions, and even conducting virtual orchestras. However, the core creative and interpretative aspects of music direction and composition still require human intuition and artistic vision, which limits AI's disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can make music creation more accessible and cheaper, the demand for live performances and unique compositions is not infinitely expandable due to cultural and funding constraints. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing the human elements of the work.
gpt55_rationale: AI music-generation and audio-production tools already affect composing, arranging, lyric drafting, demo creation, orchestration, and promotional materials, putting a large share of the composer side directly in AI’s path. Music directors and conductors are less automatable because rehearsals, live performance leadership, interpersonal coaching, auditions, and community presence still require human judgment and embodied authority. Demand could expand for inexpensive custom music in video, games, advertising, social media, churches, and small productions, but it is limited by attention scarcity, nonprofit and school funding constraints, and continued preference for human-led live performance. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is likely to restructure rather than broadly disappear or grow unchanged.
gpt56sol_rationale: Generative music systems can already produce drafts, arrangements, orchestrations, lyrics, and synthetic recordings, putting much of composers’ digital creative workflow directly in AI’s path. Music directors are less exposed because conducting rehearsals, interpreting performances, leading musicians, and maintaining community relationships require real-time human presence and trust. Lower production costs will expand demand for customized music across video, games, advertising, and online media, but audience attention, arts funding, and the number of live ensembles constrain how much additional employment results. The occupation therefore faces substantial skill and workflow changes, while only moderate demand expansion makes restructure the best fit.
fable5_rationale: This occupation splits into two halves: music directors, whose core work is leading live rehearsals and performances with human ensembles (largely in churches, schools, and performing arts companies employing ~70% of workers) and is minimally AI-exposed, and composers, whose work is directly in the path of generative music AI that can already produce jingles, background scores, and stock music. The blended disruption lands at moderate-high, pulled down by the in-person conducting majority but up sharply for commercial composition. Elasticity is limited: while cheaper music production expands content volume somewhat, AI-generated music tends to substitute for commissioned composition rather than expand paid composer demand, and live directing demand is capped by nonprofit and school funding constraints. Because the dominant employment base is hands-on, presence-required directing work, the occupation as a whole is resilient — though commercial composers specifically face significant displacement risk.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks blend highly AI-vulnerable cognitive work (composing, arranging, score interpretation and selection—already transformed by generative tools like Suno/AIVA and notation software) with human-presence leadership (live rehearsals, conducting, auditions, and interpersonal direction of ensembles). This yields high disruption as AI materially reshapes the creative pipeline even if live conducting remains human. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster composition unlocks more media, game, ad, and indie scores, yet live directing demand stays constrained by fixed institutional needs (churches, orchestras), arts funding, and audience capacity. The occupation therefore restructures around AI collaboration and distinctive human leadership rather than pure replacement or pure expansion.

title: Musicians and singers
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts music creation through composition tools, vocal synthesis, and production software, but live performance and human emotional connection remain central to the occupation. Demand elasticity is high because AI-powered tools dramatically lower barriers to music creation and distribution, enabling more independent artists to produce and share music while expanding opportunities for personalized content, background music, and niche genres. The combination of meaningful AI disruption in production workflows with strong demand expansion from reduced costs and democratized creation tools leads to an augment effect where musicians can produce more diverse content for expanded markets.
opus_rationale: While AI can generate music and synthetic vocals that may compete with recorded/session/background work, the core of this occupation—live performance, audience connection, stage presence, and the cultural authenticity of human artists—remains fundamentally physical and human, limiting disruption to a moderate level. Demand for live music has some room to expand with cheaper production tools that lower barriers for independent artists, but the live performance market is constrained by venue capacity, audience time, and the premium placed on human authenticity. Because disruption sits at or below 6, the occupation is classified as resilient: AI reshapes the recorded and production periphery (and may pressure session/background work) but does not transform the irreplaceable live-performance core.
opus5_rationale: The core of this occupation — live performance in concert halls, clubs, and houses of worship (nearly half self-employed, 35% in religious/civic organizations) — depends on embodied human presence, physical technique, and audience connection that generative AI cannot substitute for. AI does materially threaten specific adjacent segments: session work, background vocals, jingles, library/stock music, and demo recording, where synthetic audio is already commercially usable, and it changes promotion and production workflows, which lifts disruption to the middle of the range. Elasticity is low because live-music demand is capped by venue capacity, ticket spending, leisure time, and declining classical and church attendance; cheaper music production does not create more paid performance slots, and it may actually flood the recorded market and depress rates. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation lands in the resilient category — AI reshapes the recording-adjacent periphery and income mix, but not the live performance core.
openai_rationale: AI can assist musicians and singers in areas like music production, promotion, and distribution, but the core tasks of performing live and creating original music remain human-centric. AI tools can enhance the creative process but are unlikely to replace the unique human elements of performance and artistry. Demand elasticity is high as AI can lower production costs and broaden access to music, potentially increasing the consumption of music and live performances. However, the core creative and performance aspects of the occupation remain resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: AI music generation, voice synthesis, mixing tools, and promotional automation will materially affect recording, demo production, background vocals, session work, and self-marketing. However, much of the occupation is live, embodied performance where audience demand is tied to authenticity, stage presence, reputation, and social experience rather than just the sound output. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper production will create more music and content, but listener attention, venue capacity, church participation, and arts budgets limit how much additional demand translates into paid human musician jobs. Because disruption is significant but the core live-performance role remains only moderately reshaped, the occupation fits the resilient category.
gpt56sol_rationale: Generative AI can produce recordings, backing tracks, synthetic vocals, promotional content, and practice aids, materially changing studio work and career management. However, live performance, auditions, rehearsals, physical technique, and audience connection remain embodied activities in which the human performer is often the product. Lower production costs will generate substantially more music and personalized content, although limited listener attention and substitution by fully synthetic music constrain demand for paid human performers. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high across the occupation's core performance tasks, the occupation fits the resilient category.
fable5_rationale: AI music generation directly threatens studio-based segments — session work, backing tracks, jingles, and background/stock music — but the core of this occupation is live, embodied performance where audiences specifically value human presence and authenticity, which AI cannot substitute. Elasticity is modest: cheaper music production mostly benefits AI-generated output rather than expanding demand for human performers, and live performance demand is constrained by leisure time and venue economics, though the 'human-made' premium may strengthen as synthetic music floods the market. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient overall — recording-centric musicians face real displacement, but performers in churches, live venues, and touring acts will see AI touch only the periphery of their work.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on live performance, physical instrument playing or singing, rehearsals, and real-time audience interaction that require human presence, musical talent, and stamina; AI already assists composition, studio production, practice feedback, and social-media promotion but leaves the performative core intact, producing only moderate disruption. Elasticity is moderate because dramatically cheaper/faster output would expand use of music in media, advertising, games, and more frequent local/private events, yet overall demand remains constrained by finite audience attention, venue capacity, and time. With disruption only moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI tools augment peripheral and creative-support work without reshaping the fundamental human performance role.

title: Natural sciences managers
claude_rationale: Natural sciences managers have moderate disruption as AI can assist with data analysis, report generation, and project monitoring, but the core work requires human judgment for strategic planning, team leadership, stakeholder communication, and complex decision-making in research environments. Elasticity is low because demand for management positions is relatively fixed - organizations need a certain number of managers regardless of AI productivity gains, and regulatory/structural constraints limit expansion of management roles. The disruption score of 6 places this occupation in the resilient category, where AI enhances peripheral tasks but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core managerial and leadership responsibilities.
opus_rationale: Much of the work involves knowledge tasks—reviewing research, drafting reports, analyzing data, and communicating findings—which AI tools can materially assist, pushing disruption toward moderate-high. However, the core of the role is leadership, team supervision, strategic decision-making, and interpersonal coordination requiring human judgment and accountability, which keeps disruption at 6 rather than higher. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster research could expand R&D output and the number of projects requiring oversight, but management headcount is flexible and can be consolidated. Since disruption is at or below 6, the occupation falls into the resilient category: AI augments the analytical periphery but does not reshape the fundamentally human leadership core.
opus5_rationale: Much of the role's paperwork — drafting operational reports, reviewing research, writing proposals, budgeting, literature synthesis, and status communication — is language- and analysis-heavy and already materially aided by AI, and the scientific work being supervised is itself being reshaped by AI-driven discovery tools. However, the core of the job is accountable human leadership: hiring, evaluating, and motivating scientists, negotiating resources across units, ensuring lab safety and supply, and bearing responsibility for regulatory and scientific judgment — activities that require presence, authority, and trust rather than text generation. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster R&D should expand the volume of research projects and product development that organizations undertake, but management headcount is capped by span-of-control flexibility and by budget-constrained funders like the federal government and grant agencies. With disruption at 6, the periphery of the job changes considerably while the supervisory core persists, placing this occupation in the resilient category with a gradual skill shift toward AI-literate research portfolio management.
openai_rationale: Natural sciences managers primarily engage in supervisory, strategic planning, and coordination tasks, which are predominantly cognitive and involve complex decision-making. AI can assist in data analysis and project management, but the core tasks of leadership and interpersonal communication remain human-centric, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can enhance productivity, the demand for managerial oversight does not expand proportionally as it is tied to the number of scientists and projects rather than cost. Thus, the role is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing core functions.
gpt55_rationale: Natural sciences managers perform substantial cognitive and language-based work—setting research strategy, reviewing scientific work, drafting reports, budgeting, coordinating teams, and communicating with executives or clients—all areas where AI tools can materially improve speed and scope. However, the role also depends on human leadership, accountability, personnel management, lab safety, regulatory judgment, and coordination in physical research or production environments, so AI is unlikely to replace the full managerial function. Demand for scientific R&D and product development could expand as AI lowers the cost of experimentation and analysis, but it is constrained by funding, regulation, physical lab capacity, and organizations’ ability to widen managerial spans of control. The occupation is therefore likely to be substantially restructured, with fewer purely administrative managers and greater value placed on those who can use AI to oversee larger, more complex scientific programs.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially accelerate literature review, experimental analysis, reporting, budgeting, scheduling, and project monitoring. However, scientific judgment, regulatory accountability, laboratory oversight, strategic prioritization, and the hiring and leadership of specialized teams remain strongly human-centered. Cheaper and faster research should stimulate additional R&D and product development, but funding constraints, laboratory capacity, regulation, and flexible manager-to-staff ratios limit headcount expansion. Because AI substantially assists rather than overtakes the occupation's core leadership and real-world coordination functions, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: Much of this role's paperwork—drafting operational reports, budgeting, project monitoring, literature and research review—is squarely in AI's path, and AI research tools will change how scientific work is planned and evaluated. However, the core of the job is leadership: hiring, motivating, and evaluating scientists, coordinating across units, and overseeing physical labs, which remains human-centered and gives a disruption score at the top of the moderate band rather than high. Elasticity is moderate: AI-accelerated science could expand R&D activity and thus the teams needing oversight, but managers are flexible in span of control, and AI-driven flattening of hierarchies could offset that expansion. With disruption at 6, the occupation is resilient—AI streamlines the administrative periphery while the interpersonal and organizational core persists.
grok45_rationale: Core duties center on cognitive and language-based knowledge work—setting research strategies, budgeting, reviewing scientific output, drafting reports, and providing technical guidance—which AI already assists via analysis, summarization, project tools, and decision support, even as interpersonal leadership, hiring, and lab/field presence remain human. This places the role in the high-disruption band shared with other managers. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster management can unlock additional R&D projects and larger supervised teams in expanding fields like biotech, yet overall demand remains constrained by research funding, regulatory limits, and the flexibility of span-of-control, so productivity gains only partially expand headcount. The combination of high disruption and moderate elasticity therefore produces restructuring: the occupation persists but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI orchestration and higher-level scientific judgment.

title: Network and computer systems administrators
claude_rationale: Network and systems administration involves predominantly digital tasks like configuring software, managing servers, monitoring systems, and troubleshooting - all areas where AI automation tools are rapidly advancing and already being deployed. The BLS projects a 4% decline partly due to automation of routine tasks and outsourcing to managed services. Demand elasticity is low because organizations have relatively fixed infrastructure needs that don't expand significantly even if administration becomes cheaper - a company doesn't need 10x more network management just because it's more affordable. The combination of high AI disruption potential with constrained demand growth points to workforce contraction.
opus_rationale: The work is predominantly digital and cognitive — configuring systems, monitoring performance, automating tasks, diagnosing problems — all directly in AI's path, and much routine administration is already being automated and shifted to DevOps and Networks-as-a-Service models. Demand elasticity is low: organizations have a relatively fixed number of networks and systems to maintain, and cheaper administration does not cause businesses to consume dramatically more network infrastructure; productivity gains flow into headcount reduction rather than expanded output, consistent with the BLS-projected 4% decline. With disruption at 8 and elasticity at 4, this fits 'replace' — AI absorbs core routine work while demand fails to expand enough to preserve jobs.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely digital — configuration, monitoring, scripting, patching, log analysis, ticket triage, user provisioning — all directly in the path of AI agents, infrastructure-as-code, and AIOps tooling, though a residual hands-on component remains for physical hardware, cabling, and on-site incident response. Demand elasticity is low: organizations need a roughly fixed amount of network and server uptime, and cheaper administration does not lead firms to consume dramatically more 'administered infrastructure'; the same forces (cloud, Networks-as-a-Service, DevOps consolidation) actually pull the function out of the occupation entirely. BLS already projects a 4 percent decline before accounting for accelerating automation. High disruption combined with inelastic, structurally shrinking demand puts this squarely in the replace category, with surviving roles skewing toward senior automation/cloud engineering.
openai_rationale: Network and computer systems administrators face high disruption due to AI and automation, which are increasingly capable of handling routine tasks like monitoring, maintenance, and even some troubleshooting. The shift towards cloud services and Networks-as-a-Service further reduces the need for traditional in-house administrators. However, demand elasticity is low to moderate; while some demand may increase due to lower costs and new capabilities, it is constrained by the fixed nature of network infrastructure needs. Thus, the occupation will likely restructure, requiring administrators to adapt by focusing on more strategic, high-level tasks and integration with emerging technologies.
gpt55_rationale: Network and computer systems administration is heavily digital and rule-based: monitoring alerts, diagnosing incidents, configuring systems, scripting automation, managing permissions, patching, and documenting changes are all areas where AI and AIOps tools can materially improve productivity. Some work still requires human judgment, accountability, security oversight, vendor coordination, and occasional physical presence for hardware or network infrastructure, but the core workflow is increasingly automated, cloud-managed, and software-defined. Demand elasticity is limited because most organizations need a reliable baseline of administration rather than vastly more administration when it becomes cheaper; productivity gains are likely absorbed through fewer admins per server, network, or user, plus outsourcing to managed and cloud services. Given high disruption and relatively low demand expansion, the occupation fits the replace category, especially for routine systems and network administration roles.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most administration tasks are digital and increasingly automatable through AI-assisted troubleshooting, infrastructure-as-code, autonomous monitoring, cloud platforms, and managed network services. Physical installation, organization-specific integration, security accountability, and response to unusual outages still require skilled humans, but the role will shift from routine maintenance toward automation, architecture, governance, and incident management. Lower administration costs will support more infrastructure and stronger security, yet demand expansion is constrained because organizations need only a limited number of administrators and can consolidate work through cloud and service providers. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with fewer traditional administrators but continued demand for workers who master cloud, DevOps, security, and AI-enabled operations.
fable5_rationale: The core work — configuring systems, managing permissions, diagnosing issues, monitoring performance — is predominantly digital and cognitive, and AI-driven automation (AIOps, self-healing infrastructure, LLM-assisted troubleshooting and scripting) is already absorbing routine administration; only residual physical hardware tasks resist automation, and cloud migration is eliminating even those. Elasticity is low because an organization's need for network and system administration scales with its infrastructure footprint, not with the cost of administration — companies won't consume 10x more sysadmin work if it gets cheaper, and cloud consolidation plus Networks-as-a-Service further concentrate the remaining work with fewer providers. BLS already projects a 4% decline, consistent with productivity gains translating directly into headcount reduction. High disruption with inelastic demand puts this squarely in the replace category.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on digital configuration, monitoring, security, performance optimization, scripting, and remote troubleshooting of networks and systems—areas where AI tools (AIOps, automated remediation, log analysis, config generation) already materially accelerate work and will deepen further, even if occasional hardware installs remain. Demand is inelastic because organizations need a relatively fixed quantum of reliable infrastructure rather than 10x more administration; cheaper/faster delivery simply consolidates headcount via automation, DevOps absorption, and Networks-as-a-Service, consistent with the projected employment decline. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore produces net replacement of roles.

title: News analysts, reporters, and journalists
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts journalism's core tasks - research, writing, fact-checking, and content creation are all digital knowledge work that AI tools already assist with meaningfully, and the trajectory points toward AI handling much more of the information gathering, analysis, and writing process. However, demand elasticity is low because news consumption is relatively fixed - people don't consume dramatically more news just because it's cheaper to produce, and advertising revenue (the primary funding source) is already declining regardless of production costs. The combination of high disruption to core digital tasks and constrained demand growth due to structural industry challenges points to significant headcount contraction.
opus_rationale: Core tasks—researching, writing, editing, summarizing, and creating content across platforms—are predominantly language and cognitive work that AI tools already perform competently, driving a high disruption score, though in-person interviews, field reporting, and source relationships remain partly human. Demand elasticity is low because the industry's revenue base (advertising) is structurally declining and total appetite for original journalism is not strongly suppressed by production cost; cheaper content production tends to flood the market with low-value material rather than expand paid demand for professional reporters. With disruption >=7 and elasticity <=4, plus an already-declining BLS outlook, the occupation fits replace, as productivity gains and AI-generated content translate into headcount contraction rather than expanded output.
opus5_rationale: Journalism is predominantly language-based knowledge work — researching, drafting, editing, summarizing, and repurposing content across platforms — all directly in AI's path; automated wire copy, earnings and sports recaps, transcription, and multi-platform rewriting are already being generated by AI today. The residual human core (cultivating sources, on-scene reporting, on-air presence, investigative accountability work) keeps it from a 9-10. Elasticity is low: total news consumption is bounded by audience attention and, critically, by advertising and subscription revenue that does not grow when production gets cheaper — cheaper content production floods an already saturated market and further erodes the ad revenue base rather than expanding paid employment. With high task disruption, a structurally declining revenue model, and BLS already projecting -4%, productivity gains accrue as smaller newsrooms rather than more journalists, fitting 'replace,' though a premium tier of brand-name investigative and on-air talent will persist.
openai_rationale: AI is significantly impacting journalism by automating tasks such as data analysis, content generation, and even some aspects of reporting. Tools like AI-driven news writing and automated content curation are already in use, indicating high disruption. However, the demand for news content is somewhat elastic; while AI can produce content faster and cheaper, the overall demand is constrained by audience size and advertising revenue. The net effect is 'restructure' because while AI will change how journalists work, those who adapt to using AI tools can thrive in a transformed landscape.
gpt55_rationale: Journalism has substantial digital, cognitive, and language-based work: researching background material, drafting articles and scripts, summarizing updates, editing for style, creating headlines, and repurposing content across platforms are all directly affected by current AI tools. Human reporters remain important for source development, interviews, field presence, judgment, verification, and accountability, but many newsroom production tasks can be accelerated or partially automated. Demand elasticity is limited because news consumption is constrained by audience attention, trust, and weak advertising/subscription economics, though cheaper AI-enabled production may expand some niche and hyperlocal coverage. Given high disruption and relatively low elasticity, AI is likely to reduce headcount in routine reporting and content-production roles while leaving a smaller set of journalists focused on original reporting, verification, and distinctive analysis.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can materially accelerate research, transcription, drafting, editing, fact comparison, multimedia production, and adaptation of stories across platforms. However, source development, field reporting, original investigation, interviews, verification, and trusted public presence still require substantial human judgment and relationships. Cheaper production may support more niche and personalized coverage, but audience attention, advertising revenue, and willingness to pay limit how much additional journalism can be monetized. The occupation therefore faces restructuring toward verification, investigation, source cultivation, and AI-assisted multimedia work, with fewer roles centered mainly on routine content production.
fable5_rationale: Writing, summarizing, updating stories, and analyzing information are directly in AI's path, and routine coverage (earnings reports, sports recaps, weather, aggregation) is already being automated; only original reporting requiring source relationships and field presence resists, warranting a disruption of 7. Demand elasticity is low because news consumption is not cost-suppressed — the industry's constraint is collapsing advertising revenue and consolidation, not production capacity, so 10x cheaper content production does not translate into proportionally more paid journalist jobs. BLS already projects a 4% decline before accounting for accelerating AI-driven content generation. High disruption combined with structurally weak demand places this occupation in the replace category, with surviving roles concentrated in investigative, relationship-driven, and on-camera work.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks such as researching topics, writing and updating stories, analyzing information, scripting for broadcast, and reviewing for accuracy/style are predominantly cognitive and language-based knowledge work where AI tools already draft content, summarize sources, assist fact-checking, and speed multimedia production; human elements like in-person interviews, source relationships, and on-location reporting remain but are increasingly AI-augmented. Demand elasticity is low because news consumption is constrained by finite audience attention and existing free abundance rather than production cost or speed, so 10x cheaper output does not unlock dramatically more reading/viewing or new markets sufficient to offset productivity gains. Structural factors like ad-revenue decline and media consolidation further cap expansion. High disruption paired with low elasticity therefore implies AI absorbs substantial core work without compensatory demand growth, producing net headcount contraction.

title: Nuclear engineers
claude_rationale: Nuclear engineering involves significant knowledge work including design, analysis, and regulatory compliance that AI can assist with, but the core work requires deep domain expertise, safety-critical decision making, and physical oversight of nuclear facilities that AI cannot replace. The field has strict regulatory requirements and involves life-safety considerations that limit AI's direct application to core tasks. Demand elasticity is low because nuclear power deployment is constrained by regulatory approval processes, public acceptance, capital requirements, and policy decisions rather than engineering costs - making nuclear services 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically expand nuclear facility construction or operations. The disruption score of 6 places this in the resilient category despite some AI assistance potential.
opus_rationale: Nuclear engineering involves substantial computational design, simulation, modeling, and analysis work that AI can meaningfully accelerate, but core responsibilities also require physical presence at plants, regulatory oversight, hands-on safety monitoring, and accountability that AI cannot assume, holding disruption at moderate. Demand has some upside given renewed interest in nuclear power and small modular reactors, but is heavily constrained by regulation, capital intensity, long construction timelines, and public/political factors, yielding moderate elasticity. Because disruption sits at 6 — below the high-disruption threshold — the occupation qualifies as resilient: AI augments design and analysis tasks but does not reshape the safety-critical, regulated, physically-anchored core of the work.
opus5_rationale: A large share of nuclear engineering is computational — neutronics and thermal-hydraulic simulation, shielding and dose calculations, safety-case analysis, and voluminous regulatory documentation — all of which AI can meaningfully accelerate, so disruption is real and already visible in design and licensing workflows. However, the core work is anchored in physical plant oversight, onsite construction and maintenance monitoring, NRC-licensed accountability, and safety-critical judgment that must be signed by a credentialed human, capping disruption at the upper-moderate range. Elasticity is moderate: there is genuine latent demand from SMRs and data-center power needs, but the binding constraints are capital, siting, supply chains, and regulatory throughput rather than engineering labor cost, so cheaper analysis unlocks only some additional projects. Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the safety/regulatory core resists automation, the occupation is best classified as resilient, with the skill mix shifting toward AI-assisted modeling and verification.
openai_rationale: Nuclear engineering involves a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, including design, testing, and regulatory compliance, which are not fully automatable by AI. While AI can assist in simulations and data analysis, the core tasks require human oversight and decision-making, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is low because the need for nuclear engineers is driven by regulatory and safety requirements rather than cost or speed. The job outlook is declining due to a shift towards renewable energy, suggesting that productivity gains from AI will not significantly expand demand. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing core tasks.
gpt55_rationale: Nuclear engineering includes substantial digital and cognitive work—simulation, calculations, design documentation, regulatory analysis, and technical writing—so AI can materially improve productivity in modeling, code generation, optimization, and compliance drafting. However, the core work is safety-critical, highly regulated, tied to physical facilities and experiments, and requires accountable human engineering judgment, which limits full automation over the next decade. Demand elasticity is low because the number of nuclear projects is constrained more by regulation, capital costs, public policy, construction timelines, and federal or utility budgets than by the cost of engineering labor alone. Because disruption is meaningful but not above the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is best classified as resilient rather than replace or restructure.
gpt56sol_rationale: Much of nuclear engineering consists of computer-based modeling, simulation, design optimization, technical writing, data analysis, and regulatory review, all of which AI can materially accelerate. Physical inspections, experiments, facility-specific judgment, security requirements, and legally accountable safety decisions limit full automation, but the core workflow will still change substantially. Demand is constrained by the small number of nuclear facilities, long construction timelines, regulation, and capital costs, so cheaper engineering is unlikely to generate proportionate growth in projects. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to headcount pressure and consolidation of work among AI-enabled engineers.
fable5_rationale: Much of nuclear engineering is analytical knowledge work — dose calculations, reactor simulations, technical documentation, and compliance review — where AI tools will materially assist, but the core work is bound to physical facilities, safety-critical oversight, security clearances, and NRC licensing regimes that require accountable human judgment and on-site presence. Demand for nuclear engineers is governed less by engineering cost than by capital-intensive plant construction, regulatory approval timelines, and energy policy; even a 10x productivity gain would not unlock proportionally more reactors, though renewed interest in SMRs and data-center power provides some upside. With disruption at 5, the occupation's core is not reshaped by AI even as its computational and documentation tasks are augmented, making it resilient — consistent with BLS projections of roughly flat employment driven by industry structure rather than automation.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on cognitive work—reactor and shielding design, radiation transport simulations, safety analysis, procedure writing, and regulatory compliance review—which are already materially assisted by computational tools and will be further accelerated by AI generative design, optimization, and data analysis; physical plant presence and ultimate human accountability for safety-critical decisions prevent full automation. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster engineering can unlock more advanced-reactor concepts, medical-isotope work, and space applications in some segments, yet overall headcount growth remains capped by capital costs, licensing timelines, and policy constraints on nuclear deployment. High disruption paired with only moderate elasticity therefore implies the occupation persists but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI orchestration, systems judgment, and regulatory expertise.

title: Nuclear medicine technologists
claude_rationale: Nuclear medicine technologists have moderate disruption because while AI can assist with image analysis and record-keeping, the core work requires hands-on preparation and administration of radioactive drugs, direct patient interaction, and strict safety protocols that demand human oversight. The work is fundamentally physical and safety-critical, limiting AI's ability to replace core functions. Demand elasticity is low because nuclear medicine procedures are medically necessary rather than elective - patients don't get 10x more nuclear scans just because AI makes analysis faster or cheaper, and the procedures are already ordered based on clinical need rather than cost constraints. The combination of moderate disruption and low elasticity places this occupation in the resilient category, where AI may improve efficiency in peripheral tasks but won't fundamentally reshape the profession.
opus_rationale: The core work is physical and hands-on: preparing and administering radioactive drugs, positioning and reassuring patients, operating large imaging equipment, and following strict radiation safety protocols requiring physical presence. AI may assist with image processing, dosing calculations, and record-keeping, but the radiopharmaceutical handling and patient interaction cannot be automated, keeping disruption low. Demand is relatively inelastic since the number of nuclear imaging procedures is driven by clinical need, physician referrals, and regulation rather than cost or speed, so cheaper AI assistance would not dramatically expand procedure volume. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient — AI touches the periphery but does not reshape the core hands-on role.
opus5_rationale: Core work is hands-on and physical: preparing and handling radiopharmaceuticals, positioning and reassuring patients, operating and maintaining imaging hardware, and following radiation safety protocols — none of which AI can perform without robotics. AI touches only peripheral portions such as image reconstruction/denoising, dose optimization, scheduling, and documentation, which may modestly speed workflow per scan. Demand is driven by clinical need, physician referrals, reimbursement, and radiopharmaceutical supply rather than technologist productivity, so cheaper scan processing unlocks only limited additional volume (some growth from expanding theranostics and cancer imaging). With low disruption to the physical core, the occupation is resilient; AI becomes a tool within an unchanged job.
openai_rationale: Nuclear medicine technologists perform tasks that are a mix of physical and cognitive activities, such as preparing and administering radioactive drugs and operating imaging equipment. While AI can assist with imaging analysis and record-keeping, the core tasks require human presence and judgment, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is low because the need for nuclear medicine procedures is driven by medical necessity rather than cost, and regulatory and safety considerations limit expansion. Therefore, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing the core work.
gpt55_rationale: Nuclear medicine technologists perform some digital and cognitive tasks—dose calculations, equipment operation, imaging workflows, documentation, and quality control—that AI can assist through automation, image acquisition support, scheduling, and error checking. However, the core job remains hands-on and regulated: preparing and administering radioactive drugs, positioning and monitoring patients, following radiation-safety protocols, and responding to clinical situations in person. Demand would expand only modestly if workflows became cheaper or faster because use is constrained by medical necessity, radiation exposure, physician orders, reimbursement, equipment capacity, and licensing rules, though aging-related cancer care and theranostics create some growth. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment peripheral and technical tasks than replace the occupation, making the net effect resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core tasks require in-person patient care, physical preparation and administration of radiopharmaceuticals, equipment operation, and strict radiation-safety procedures that AI cannot readily perform autonomously. AI can improve scheduling, documentation, dose calculation, image acquisition, quality control, and protocol selection, but these are primarily assistive changes. Lower costs could modestly increase imaging and treatment volumes, especially as the population ages, but clinical indications, radiation exposure limits, regulation, equipment capacity, and radiopharmaceutical supply constrain demand. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI affects peripheral and technical workflow components without replacing its hands-on core.
fable5_rationale: The core work—preparing and administering radiopharmaceuticals, physically positioning patients, operating imaging equipment, and enforcing radiation safety—is hands-on and requires human presence with hazardous materials; AI assists mainly with peripheral tasks like image quality checks, protocol optimization, and record-keeping. Elasticity is low because nuclear imaging volume is driven by clinical indications, physician referrals, radiopharmaceutical supply, and reimbursement rather than technologist labor cost, so faster workflows would not unlock dramatically more scans.
