With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI may streamline scheduling, dosing calculations, and documentation, but the essential patient-facing, physical, and safety-critical duties remain human work.
grok45_rationale: Core work centers on physical patient handling, precise preparation and injection of radiopharmaceuticals, real-time operation of specialized scanners, and radiation safety protocols that require on-site presence and cannot be fully digitized; AI can assist with dosage calculations, image optimization, and records but leaves the majority of daily tasks intact. Demand for nuclear medicine procedures is driven by clinical necessity, aging demographics, and strict radiation-exposure limits rather than price or speed, so even large productivity gains would not unlock large volumes of additional scans. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation falls into the resilient category regardless of elasticity.

title: Nuclear technicians
claude_rationale: Nuclear technicians perform primarily hands-on monitoring, maintenance, and safety work in highly regulated physical environments that require human presence for safety and regulatory compliance. title: Optometrists

Demand elasticity is high because vision care is currently limited by cost and access - cheaper, faster diagnostic tools could enable more frequent screenings, expand care to underserved populations, and catch problems earlier when treatment is more effective. Since disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient—AI augments diagnostics and improves throughput but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, regulated, patient-facing core of the work.

But the core of the job remains a hands-on, in-person encounter: slit-lamp examination, refraction refinement with patient feedback, contact lens fitting, minor procedures, prescribing under state licensure, and counseling patients — none of which AI performs autonomously, and scope-of-practice regulation protects the role. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, faster screening could pull in currently under-served patients and raise exam frequency, but routine eye exams are habit- and insurance-bound rather than cost-suppressed, so expansion is real but bounded. With disruption at the middle of the range and the physical/regulated exam untouched, the occupation is resilient — AI compresses the interpretive workload and lets optometrists see more patients rather than displacing them.
openai_rationale: Optometrists perform a mix of tasks, including diagnostic tests, prescribing corrective lenses, and providing treatments, which require human interaction and decision-making skills. opus_rationale: The core work of photography requires physical presence to capture real subjects, scenes, and events — a portrait, wedding, news event, or product shoot demands a human behind the camera in the real world, which AI cannot replicate. However, the postproduction, editing, composition assistance, and notably generative image creation are squarely in AI's path, and AI-generated imagery plus stock photo services already pressure commercial and stock-oriented segments. On elasticity, demand for professional capture services is fairly fixed by social needs (weddings, portraits, news) and is being eroded rather than expanded by cheaper alternatives like smartphones and AI generation, so productivity gains do not unlock large latent demand. Because the disruption to the core physical capture work stays at or below 6 and AI mostly displaces peripheral or generative substitutes rather than reshaping the act of professional photography, the occupation is best classified as resilient with slow growth.
opus5_rationale: Photography mixes physical presence (weddings, events, portraits, photojournalism) with heavily digital workflows — editing, retouching, culling, cataloging — that AI already automates well; more importantly, generative image models directly substitute for large segments of commercial, product, stock, and advertising photography, which is where much of the paid work sits. Event, portrait, and news photography still require a human on location with a camera and client rapport, capping disruption below the very-high tier. Demand elasticity is limited: people don't want 10x more wedding albums or headshots, and cheaper imagery is increasingly satisfied by synthetic generation or smartphones rather than by hiring more photographers. The combination of significant substitution in commercial/stock work with essentially fixed demand for ceremonial and portrait shoots points to headcount contraction, especially at the lower-paid commercial end.
openai_rationale: AI impacts photographers by enhancing digital editing and potentially automating some aspects of photo composition and selection. However, the core tasks of capturing images, especially in dynamic or creative settings, still require human presence and artistic judgment. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can make photography more efficient, the demand for high-quality, personalized photography is not heavily suppressed by cost. Therefore, while AI tools will augment photographers' capabilities, the occupation remains resilient due to the continued need for human creativity and interaction.
gpt55_rationale: AI will substantially affect photographers’ digital workflow, especially culling, retouching, color correction, background replacement, portfolio management, marketing, and in some commercial uses the creation of synthetic images that substitute for shoots. However, much of the occupation still depends on being physically present at weddings, portraits, news events, schools, real estate sites, or commercial locations, plus directing subjects, managing lighting, and handling clients in real time. Demand elasticity is moderate: cheaper image production would increase visual content for ecommerce, advertising, social media, and small businesses, but demand for event and portrait photography is constrained by the number of real occasions and clients’ desire for authentic images. Because disruption is meaningful but not enough to fully reshape the physical, interpersonal core of the occupation, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Generative imagery, automated retouching, culling, tagging, marketing, and portfolio management will substantially change photographers’ workflows and displace some stock, product, and routine commercial photography. However, weddings, portraits, news events, and location-specific assignments still require physical presence, interpersonal skill, direction, and authentic documentation. Cheaper image production will expand visual-content demand, but much of that growth will be satisfied by synthetic images rather than additional photographers, yielding moderate elasticity and substantial restructuring rather than broad augmentation.
fable5_rationale: The core act of capturing real people, events, and moments — weddings, portraits, news, sports — requires physical presence and cannot be generated, but AI heavily disrupts post-production editing and directly threatens commercial, stock, and product photography where generative images substitute for shoots. Elasticity is low: demand for photos is already saturated by smartphones and cheap stock libraries, so making professional photography faster and cheaper does not unlock much latent demand — people won't hire 10x more wedding or portrait photographers. The occupation lands at moderate disruption because the majority of employment (event, portrait, journalism) is anchored in unpredictable real-world presence, making it resilient overall, though the commercial/stock segment specifically faces significant contraction as generative AI absorbs that work.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks mix physical on-location capture, client interaction, lighting/equipment handling, and real-world presence (weddings, portraits, news, commercial shoots) with digital post-processing and planning; AI already materially assists editing, enhancement, and composition suggestions but cannot replace the unpredictable real-world shooting that defines most work, keeping disruption moderate. Cheaper/faster output via AI tools would unlock meaningful latent demand in e-commerce product imagery, marketing content, and affordable personal/event photography, though event volume and smartphone/stock alternatives limit full expansion. Because disruption remains moderate, AI primarily augments tools and workflows without reshaping the occupation's physical-creative core, fitting the resilient category.

title: Physical therapist assistants and aides
claude_rationale: Physical therapist assistants and aides perform predominantly hands-on, physical work requiring direct patient contact, manual therapy techniques, and real-world presence for safety and care quality - areas where AI has minimal impact. While AI might assist with some administrative tasks like scheduling or documentation, the core work of helping patients with exercises, providing manual therapy, observing patient responses, and ensuring safety during movement requires human touch and judgment. Demand for physical therapy services is highly elastic due to an aging population, chronic disease management needs, and currently unmet demand constrained by cost, suggesting that any productivity gains would likely expand access rather than reduce headcount. However, since AI disruption to the core work is minimal, this occupation remains resilient to AI transformation.
opus_rationale: The core work is intensely physical and hands-on: manual therapy, guiding exercises, moving and lifting patients, and providing compassionate in-person care. AI can only touch peripheral tasks like scheduling, documentation, and insurance forms, leaving the vast majority of daily duties untouched. Demand is highly elastic given an aging population and chronic-disease prevalence, with physical therapy currently constrained by cost and provider availability, so cheaper administrative overhead could free up more direct care time. Because disruption is far below the threshold of 7, the occupation is resilient regardless of strong demand growth.
opus5_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical care: guiding exercises, manual therapy, gait training, moving patients, and setting up equipment — all requiring physical presence, dexterity, and human empathy that AI cannot substitute. AI touches only peripheral tasks like documentation, scheduling, insurance forms, and progress tracking, which may modestly reduce administrative burden (most relevant for aides' clerical duties). Demand elasticity is high because rehabilitation needs are large and currently rationed by cost and insurance reimbursement, and an aging population plus remote-monitoring tools could expand therapy volume. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes recordkeeping and possibly exercise adherence monitoring, not the treatment itself.
openai_rationale: Physical therapist assistants and aides perform tasks that are predominantly physical and hands-on, such as helping patients with exercises and setting up equipment, which limits the potential for AI disruption. While AI may assist with administrative tasks or patient monitoring, the core therapeutic activities require human interaction and empathy. Demand elasticity is moderate as the aging population and increased prevalence of chronic conditions drive demand for physical therapy services. However, insurance reimbursement constraints may limit expansion. Overall, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption due to its hands-on nature and steady demand growth.
gpt55_rationale: AI can affect documentation, scheduling, insurance forms, patient education, exercise reminders, and remote monitoring, but the core work involves hands-on patient assistance, manual therapy, gait and balance training, equipment setup, cleaning, and physically helping patients move. Over the next decade, AI-enabled rehab tools and computer vision may improve supervision and home exercise adherence, but they are unlikely to replace the in-person, licensed, compassionate, physically interactive role of physical therapist assistants and aides. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower-cost therapy could expand access for aging patients, chronic disease management, post-injury rehabilitation, and home-based care, though insurance reimbursement, clinical supervision rules, and the finite need for therapy sessions limit expansion. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and the core occupation is anchored in physical patient care, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core duties require in-person patient observation, hands-on therapy, physical assistance, equipment setup, and interpersonal support, limiting AI substitution. AI can streamline documentation, scheduling, insurance forms, progress tracking, and exercise guidance, but these are peripheral or supervisory aids rather than replacements for direct care. Lower costs could unlock meaningful unmet rehabilitation demand, especially among older adults and people with chronic conditions, although insurance rules and the finite need for treatment constrain expansion. Consequently, AI will improve workflows without fundamentally reshaping most of the occupation, making it resilient.
fable5_rationale: The core work is hands-on physical care — guiding exercises, manual therapy, transferring patients, and setting up equipment — which AI cannot perform; AI only touches peripheral tasks like documentation, scheduling, and progress notes. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population and chronic disease create substantial latent demand for rehabilitation, though insurance reimbursement rules constrain how much cheaper delivery translates into more consumption. With disruption at 2, the occupation is clearly resilient — BLS projects much-faster-than-average growth, and AI-driven documentation tools would if anything free assistants for more patient contact rather than displace them.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on hands-on patient interaction—guiding exercises, massage, stretching, gait training, lifting/moving patients, and equipment setup—which require physical presence, dexterity, and stamina that AI cannot replace in the next decade; AI only peripherally aids documentation, scheduling, or progress notes. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs would expand access for aging populations, chronic conditions, and underserved patients, unlocking more sessions and home-care utilization, yet insurance rules, patient physical limits, and finite clinical need cap unlimited growth. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient as AI touches only admin edges while human physical care stays essential.

title: Physical therapists
claude_rationale: Physical therapy involves substantial hands-on manual therapy, patient observation, physical demonstration, and real-time adaptation to patient responses - core activities that require human presence and tactile skills that AI cannot replicate. While AI could assist with treatment planning, progress tracking, and administrative tasks, the fundamental work remains physical and interpersonal. Demand elasticity is high because physical therapy is currently limited by cost and access - cheaper delivery through AI-assisted efficiency could expand services to underserved populations and enable more preventive care. However, with disruption at only moderate levels, this occupation falls into the resilient category despite high demand elasticity.
opus_rationale: The core work of physical therapy is hands-on, physical, and requires in-person presence — manual therapy, demonstrating exercises, physically assisting and moving patients — which AI cannot perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like documentation, progress tracking, treatment plan suggestions, and remote monitoring, leaving the central duties intact. Demand is meaningfully elastic given aging demographics, growing chronic conditions, and a shift toward nonopioid pain management, so cheaper administrative support would free therapists for more patient care. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: Physical therapy is fundamentally hands-on: manual therapy, guided exercise, gait observation, and in-person motivation of patients in pain. AI can assist with documentation, referral review, exercise-program generation, motion-capture analytics, and remote adherence monitoring, but these are peripheral supports rather than replacements for the core physical encounter. Elasticity is high because demand for rehabilitation is currently suppressed by cost, visit caps, and access — an aging population and nonopioid pain management create large latent demand — but this expansion is realized through human clinicians plus PT assistants, not AI substitution. Because disruption stays well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient, with AI mainly reducing administrative burden and extending reach via hybrid telehealth models.
openai_rationale: Physical therapy is predominantly a hands-on occupation requiring physical presence and direct patient interaction, which limits the potential for AI to disrupt core tasks significantly. While AI can assist with administrative tasks and potentially enhance diagnostic accuracy, the core therapeutic activities remain largely manual. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make certain aspects of therapy more efficient, the fundamental need for human interaction and the growing demand due to an aging population and chronic conditions suggest that demand will expand. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: Physical therapy includes substantial cognitive work—assessment, care-plan design, documentation, patient education, and progress monitoring—that AI can assist through automated notes, exercise-plan generation, computer-vision movement analysis, and remote coaching. However, the core of the occupation remains hands-on, licensed, relational, and physically present, especially for manual therapy, safe mobility training, and adapting treatment to pain, frailty, or complex conditions. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper, AI-supported therapy could expand access for chronic pain, aging-related mobility issues, post-surgical rehab, and preventive care, but use is still constrained by insurance coverage, referrals, patient time, and the need for in-person treatment. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment peripheral and monitoring tasks than replace the central clinical role, making the occupation resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can streamline documentation, review medical histories, suggest care plans, and use computer vision or wearables to monitor exercises and progress. However, diagnosis through physical observation, hands-on therapy, safe patient movement, real-time adaptation, and interpersonal motivation still require substantial human presence and dexterity. Demand is relatively elastic because lower costs and greater availability could unlock considerable unmet rehabilitation, preventive-care, chronic-pain, and aging-related needs, but AI does not fundamentally replace the occupation's physical core, making it resilient.
fable5_rationale: Physical therapy is fundamentally hands-on work — manual therapy, guiding exercises, observing movement, and physically assisting patients — that AI cannot perform; AI's role is limited to documentation, treatment plan suggestions, and motion-analysis tools that assist rather than replace the core work. Elasticity is moderate: an aging population, chronic disease prevalence, and nonopioid pain management create real latent demand, though insurance coverage and time-per-patient constraints limit unbounded expansion. With disruption low, productivity tools at most free up time for more patient contact rather than reducing headcount. This fits squarely in the resilient category — AI touches the administrative periphery while the physical, interpersonal core remains human.
grok45_rationale: Core PT work centers on real-time physical observation of movement, hands-on manual therapy, patient handling, and in-person exercise demonstration, all of which require human presence and dexterity; AI already assists secondary tasks such as chart review, gait analysis from video, plan drafting, and documentation but does not displace the physical core, placing disruption firmly in the moderate mixed range. Demand is currently constrained by cost, insurance session limits, and access shortages, so large productivity or price improvements would unlock substantially more utilization for aging populations, chronic conditions, preventive wellness, and underserved patients. Because disruption remains only moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI augments peripheral cognitive work while the hands-on service model and expanding need keep headcount stable or growing.

title: Physician assistants
claude_rationale: While AI can assist with diagnostic support, medical record analysis, and treatment recommendations, physician assistants' core work requires physical examination, hands-on procedures, patient interaction, and real-time clinical judgment that AI cannot fully replicate. The disruption score of 6 reflects moderate AI assistance in knowledge work portions while preserving essential human-centered care. Elasticity is high (8) because cheaper, faster healthcare delivery could dramatically expand access, especially in underserved areas where cost and provider shortages currently limit care. However, since disruption remains at 6, this falls into the resilient category where AI enhances rather than fundamentally reshapes the occupation.
opus_rationale: PAs combine substantial cognitive/diagnostic work (history-taking, interpreting tests, treatment planning) that AI can meaningfully assist with, alongside hands-on physical care like examinations, suturing, setting bones, and surgical assistance that requires human presence — placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand is highly elastic: aging populations, chronic disease growth, provider shortages, and underserved rural areas mean cheaper/faster care unlocks large latent demand, and PAs are specifically valued because they expand provider capacity. Despite high elasticity, the core work is only moderately disrupted (physical presence, licensure, and supervised clinical judgment dominate), so the occupation is resilient — AI augments documentation and decision support but does not reshape the hands-on, patient-facing core.
opus5_rationale: PA work blends substantial cognitive/diagnostic tasks that AI can meaningfully support (history review, differential diagnosis, test interpretation, documentation, prescribing decision support) with hands-on physical care — physical exams, suturing, setting bones, injections, surgical assistance — plus licensure and supervision requirements that anchor the role to a human clinician. AI will reshape documentation burden and diagnostic workflow but cannot perform the physical or legally accountable core, keeping disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is high: primary care access is severely supply-constrained, especially in rural and underserved areas, so any productivity gain gets absorbed by more patients seen rather than fewer PAs. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient — AI acts as a throughput multiplier on top of already strong demographic-driven demand growth.
openai_rationale: Physician assistants perform a mix of cognitive and physical tasks, including patient examination, diagnosis, and treatment, which require human interaction and empathy. While AI can assist with diagnostic tools and patient record management, the core tasks still require human presence and decision-making. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make certain tasks more efficient, the overall demand for healthcare services is driven by demographic trends and the increasing prevalence of chronic conditions. Thus, AI will augment rather than replace the role, maintaining headcount as demand for healthcare services grows.
gpt55_rationale: AI will substantially affect the cognitive and administrative parts of physician assistant work, including documentation, clinical decision support, test interpretation, differential diagnosis, patient education, and treatment planning. However, the core role still requires licensed clinical judgment, physical examination, procedures, prescribing responsibility, patient trust, and in-person care in unpredictable settings such as clinics, hospitals, emergency departments, and surgery. Demand elasticity is high because healthcare access is constrained by cost, provider shortages, aging demographics, chronic disease, and underserved communities, so productivity gains would likely be absorbed into more visits, monitoring, and preventive care. Because disruption is meaningful but not enough to displace the hands-on licensed clinical core, the occupation fits the resilient category.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially assist with documentation, history review, diagnostic interpretation, treatment planning, and patient education. However, physical examinations, procedures, emergency judgment, patient relationships, and licensed clinical accountability require human presence, keeping disruption moderate. Demand is relatively elastic because aging populations, chronic disease, clinician shortages, and underserved communities create substantial unmet need that lower-cost care could unlock. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI increasing PA capacity rather than replacing the hands-on clinical role.
fable5_rationale: PAs perform substantial hands-on clinical work — physical exams, suturing, setting bones, immunizations, surgical assistance — that requires in-person human presence and is beyond AI's reach; AI meaningfully assists the cognitive portions like diagnosis, test interpretation, documentation, and treatment research, yielding moderate disruption. Elasticity is high because healthcare demand is heavily suppressed by cost and provider shortages, especially in rural and underserved areas where PAs are already primary providers, and an aging, chronically ill population creates near-continuous latent demand. With disruption at 5, the core clinical work remains fundamentally human, making this occupation resilient — AI will augment charting and diagnostic support while headcount grows strongly, consistent with BLS's 20% projected growth.
grok45_rationale: Core PA work mixes cognitive tasks (history review, diagnosis, test interpretation, prescribing, patient education) that AI already assists via diagnostic tools, ambient documentation, and decision support with irreplaceable physical presence for exams, procedures like suturing or casting, and real-time patient interaction under variable clinical conditions, placing it firmly in the moderate range. Demand elasticity is high because healthcare access remains constrained by cost, wait times, and provider shortages—especially primary care, rural, and chronic-disease management—so large productivity gains would unlock substantially more visits and services rather than simply shrinking headcount. With disruption only moderate, AI reshapes peripheral workflows and augments decision-making without displacing the occupation’s essential human-in-the-loop role, yielding a resilient net effect consistent with BLS’s already strong projected growth.

title: Physicians and surgeons
claude_rationale: While AI is increasingly useful for diagnostic imaging analysis, clinical decision support, and administrative tasks, the core work of physicians requires complex human judgment, physical examination skills, patient interaction, and real-time adaptation to unpredictable medical situations that AI cannot fully replicate. The disruption is moderate because AI augments rather than replaces the fundamental physician-patient relationship and clinical reasoning. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster medical services could dramatically expand access to healthcare, especially in underserved areas, and enable more preventive care and early interventions. However, since disruption remains moderate at 5, this falls into the resilient category where AI enhances but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core medical practice.
opus_rationale: Physician work blends substantial cognitive/diagnostic tasks (history-taking, image interpretation, treatment planning, documentation) that AI already meaningfully assists with—and some specialties like radiology and pathology are heavily image/data-based—but the core of most physician work requires physical examination, hands-on procedures, surgery, real-time clinical judgment under liability, and human compassion, keeping disruption moderate rather than high. Demand elasticity is high because healthcare need is enormous and currently rationed by physician scarcity, cost, and access; cheaper, faster diagnostics and AI-augmented productivity would unlock large amounts of latent demand, especially with an aging population and chronic-disease burden. Because aggregate disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold (AI augments the knowledge portions but cannot replace the licensed, physical, judgment-laden core), the net effect is resilient—AI reshapes workflows and tools without contracting headcount.
opus5_rationale: Physician work blends heavily cognitive components AI already touches — differential diagnosis, chart review, documentation, image and lab interpretation, patient messaging — with irreducible physical and interpersonal work: physical exams, procedures, surgery, emergency stabilization, and legally accountable judgment. Aggregate disruption lands at 6 because image-centric specialties (radiology, pathology, dermatology) face far more exposure than surgeons, anesthesiologists, and generalists whose value is hands-on presence; ambient documentation and decision support mostly remove drudgery rather than replacing the core role. Elasticity is high: access to physician care is severely cost- and supply-constrained (shortages, long waits, underserved rural and safety-net populations), so cheaper, faster care throughput would be absorbed by more patients seen and more preventive and chronic-disease management delivered. Because disruption stays at or below 6 — licensure, malpractice liability, and the need for a physical, accountable clinician anchor the job — the occupation is resilient, with AI reshaping workflow and documentation rather than headcount.
openai_rationale: AI is increasingly capable of assisting with diagnostic tasks, data analysis, and even some surgical planning, but the core tasks of physicians and surgeons, such as patient interaction, physical examination, and complex decision-making, still require human expertise. Thus, disruption is moderate. Demand elasticity is low because healthcare services are largely driven by population health needs rather than cost; even if AI makes some processes faster, the overall demand for physicians and surgeons is not highly suppressed by current costs. Therefore, the occupation is resilient, as AI will augment but not replace the essential human elements of the role.
gpt55_rationale: AI will substantially affect physicians' cognitive and administrative work, including documentation, triage, diagnostic support, test interpretation, care-plan drafting, and patient communication. However, the occupation still depends heavily on licensed clinical judgment, physical examination, procedures, surgery, bedside interaction, liability-bearing decisions, and coordination in unpredictable real-world settings, so AI is more likely to reshape workflows than absorb the full role. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper physician input would unlock some latent demand in primary care, chronic disease management, mental health, and underserved areas, but utilization is constrained by insurance, regulation, facilities, patient capacity, and the fact that many services are medically rather than consumer-demand driven. Because disruption is significant but not above the high-disruption threshold for the broad occupation, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially accelerate documentation, triage, diagnostic interpretation, treatment planning, and patient communication, with especially large effects in image- and data-intensive specialties. However, physical examination, procedures, surgery, emergency judgment, patient trust, team leadership, and legal accountability continue to require licensed physicians, limiting occupation-wide disruption. Lower costs could unlock meaningful unmet demand, particularly in primary care, mental health, and underserved communities, but insurance, regulation, training capacity, and the finite need for medical care constrain expansion. Because disruption remains moderate across this diverse occupation, AI is more likely to increase physician capacity and shift task composition than to reshape or replace the profession wholesale.
fable5_rationale: AI is already meaningfully changing the cognitive portions of medicine — diagnostic reasoning, image interpretation, clinical documentation, and chart review — but the core of most physician work requires physical presence: exams, procedures, surgery, and high-stakes patient interaction under licensure requirements that mandate a human in the loop. Elasticity is high because healthcare demand is heavily suppressed by cost, physician shortages, and long wait times; cheaper and faster physician time would be readily absorbed by an aging population with rising chronic disease burden. Certain subspecialties like radiology and pathology face much higher disruption, but the aggregate occupation is anchored in embodied, regulated care. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI augments the knowledge work while the hands-on, patient-facing core remains human.
grok45_rationale: Core physician and surgeon work mixes cognitive tasks (diagnosis, test interpretation, treatment planning, documentation) that AI already assists via imaging tools, ambient scribes, and decision support with irreplaceable physical and presence-based tasks (exams, procedures, surgery, real-time patient counseling and crisis management), keeping disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is high because cost, wait times, and access barriers currently suppress large volumes of care; 10x productivity gains would unlock more preventive visits, chronic-disease management, elective procedures, mental-health services, and care in underserved markets. With disruption remaining at or below the moderate threshold, AI primarily augments peripheral and knowledge components without reshaping the occupation’s human-centered core, producing a resilient net effect.

title: Physicists and astronomers
claude_rationale: AI significantly disrupts core physics and astronomy tasks including data analysis, mathematical modeling, computational simulations, and even theory generation, with AI already transforming how physicists process large datasets and develop models. Demand elasticity is moderate - while AI-accelerated research could unlock new discoveries and applications (especially in materials science, drug discovery, and technology development), growth is constrained by limited research funding, long academic career pipelines, and the specialized nature of advanced physics research. The occupation will survive but require substantial skill adaptation toward AI-augmented research methodologies.
opus_rationale: Much of physics and astronomy work is heavily computational and cognitive—data analysis, modeling, simulation, software development, and writing papers and proposals—all of which AI tools can already materially accelerate, driving a high disruption score. However, core elements like designing physical experiments, operating particle accelerators and telescopes, and generating genuinely novel theoretical insight remain human-anchored, keeping disruption below the very-high tier. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster analysis could unlock more research output and broaden the range of problems tackled, but the field is structurally constrained by federal funding budgets that cap headcount growth regardless of productivity gains. With high disruption and moderate elasticity, the occupation fits restructure—skill sets shift toward AI-augmented modeling and analysis, and adaptable researchers thrive while routine computational roles compress.
opus5_rationale: Core work — deriving and testing theory, writing simulation and analysis code, mining large observational datasets, drafting papers and grant proposals — is almost entirely cognitive and digital, and AI systems are already materially useful for literature synthesis, code generation, numerical modeling, and pattern-finding in telescope and accelerator data, so disruption is very high; the main non-digital residue is instrument design, lab work, and observatory operations. Elasticity is only moderate because headcount is set almost entirely by federal research budgets, fixed telescope/accelerator capacity, tenure lines, and grant cycles rather than by unit cost of analysis — cheaper science mostly means more papers per physicist, not proportionally more physicists — though applied segments (medical physics, quantum information, semiconductors, materials) do have genuine latent commercial demand that could absorb some gains. With disruption >= 7 and elasticity in the 5-6 band, the occupation persists but reshapes: value shifts toward posing good questions, designing experiments and instruments, and validating AI-generated results, while routine computation, coding, and manuscript production skills lose differentiation.
openai_rationale: The work of physicists and astronomers involves a mix of theoretical and experimental tasks, many of which are cognitive and data-driven, such as developing models, conducting experiments, and analyzing data. AI can assist in data analysis and modeling, but the core tasks require human creativity and interpretation, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could speed up research processes, the demand for physicists and astronomers is primarily driven by research funding and scientific inquiry, which are not significantly suppressed by cost. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not replacing the core work.
gpt55_rationale: Physicists and astronomers do a large amount of digital and cognitive work—mathematical modeling, coding, simulation, literature review, data analysis, proposal writing, and scientific publishing—where AI tools can materially accelerate workflows. However, the occupation also depends on frontier scientific judgment, experimental design, specialized instruments, laboratory or observatory access, and peer validation, which limits full automation. Demand could expand in applied areas such as materials, quantum technologies, medical physics, fusion, and space science, but academic and federal research funding, facility bottlenecks, and grant structures constrain how much cheaper analysis translates into more headcount. The result is substantial restructuring of skills and workflows rather than straightforward replacement or broad employment expansion.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI directly affects core tasks such as literature review, mathematical modeling, simulation, software development, data analysis, proposal drafting, and scientific writing. Human scientists remain essential for selecting consequential questions, validating novel theories, designing and operating specialized experiments, and exercising judgment when evidence is ambiguous. Faster research could support more hypotheses, analyses, and technology development, but demand is constrained by public research budgets, scarce facilities, long experimental cycles, and limited academic positions. The occupation therefore is likely to be substantially restructured around AI-enabled research rather than broadly replaced or expanded enough to qualify as augment.
fable5_rationale: Much of physicists' and astronomers' daily work — mathematical modeling, writing analysis code, processing datasets, drafting papers and grant proposals — is exactly the digital, cognitive work AI is rapidly absorbing, and AI research assistants are already accelerating theory and simulation work; however, experimental design, hands-on instrument work, and lab operations keep disruption below the highest tier. Elasticity is moderate: while there is essentially unlimited scientific inquiry to pursue, headcount is tightly coupled to federal research budgets and grant funding rather than to the unit cost of analysis, so a 10x productivity gain likely means more science per scientist rather than proportionally more scientists. This combination fits restructure — the field persists but shifts toward researchers who direct AI-driven analysis, design experiments, and validate results, while those doing routine computation and data-processing work are displaced.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks such as theory and model development, mathematical analysis of data, software coding for simulations, equipment design via computation, proposal writing, and paper drafting are almost entirely cognitive and digital, placing them squarely in AI’s path; current tools already accelerate literature synthesis, hypothesis generation, and numerical work, with experimental and observational components increasingly AI-assisted even if physical apparatus remains. Demand is highly elastic because fundamental and applied physics research is bottlenecked by researcher time and cost; 10x productivity would unlock far more industrial R&D, materials discovery, quantum and fusion projects, medical-physics applications, and space science that are currently suppressed by limited grants and slow cycles. Consequently headcount is expected to hold or grow as total scientific output expands, fitting the augment category.

title: Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters
claude_rationale: This occupation scores low on disruption because the core work is predominantly physical and hands-on - installing pipes, welding, troubleshooting leaks, and working in tight spaces with heavy materials. While AI might help with peripheral tasks like cost estimation or reading digital blueprints, the fundamental work of physically manipulating pipes and fixtures in unpredictable real-world environments remains beyond AI's capabilities. Elasticity is low because demand for plumbing services is relatively inelastic - buildings need a fixed amount of plumbing infrastructure regardless of cost, and people don't suddenly need 10x more pipes if installation becomes cheaper. The resilient category fits because AI disruption remains minimal to the core physical work.
opus_rationale: The core work is physical and hands-on: installing pipes, fixing leaks, soldering, working in tight spaces, and troubleshooting systems in unpredictable real-world environments — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only peripheral tasks like cost estimation, blueprint/BIM design assistance, and scheduling. Demand is driven by physical infrastructure needs, building codes, and emergency repairs, which are not strongly suppressed by cost or speed, so productivity gains in admin tasks won't dramatically expand the work. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is firmly resilient regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: Core work is intensely physical and site-specific: crawling into tight spaces, soldering, cutting and fitting pipe, diagnosing leaks by feel and observation in unpredictable existing structures. AI touches only peripheral tasks — estimating and bidding, scheduling, dispatch, BIM-assisted layout, code lookup, and customer communication — which are a small share of the day for most workers. Demand is moderately elastic in that cheaper diagnostics and admin overhead could let small shops take more jobs and unlock some deferred maintenance, but the binding constraint is skilled labor hours and licensing, not information cost. With disruption well under 6, this is clearly resilient; AI is most likely a back-office productivity aid that slightly increases billable field time per plumber.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters are highly physical and hands-on, involving installation, maintenance, and repair of piping systems, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist with peripheral tasks like cost estimation and blueprint reading, the core work remains largely unaffected, resulting in a low disruption score. Demand elasticity is low because the need for these services is driven by construction and maintenance requirements, which are not significantly suppressed by cost. Even with increased productivity, the demand for physical installation and repair work does not expand dramatically, leading to a resilient net effect.
gpt55_rationale: The core work of plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters is hands-on installation, repair, inspection, troubleshooting, lifting, fitting, welding, and working in variable physical environments such as homes, factories, crawlspaces, and construction sites. AI can help with peripheral tasks such as estimating, scheduling, code lookup, blueprint/BIM review, diagnostics, customer communication, and inventory planning, but it is not close to replacing the manual dexterity and on-site judgment required for most jobs. Demand would expand somewhat if services became cheaper and faster, especially for deferred maintenance, renovations, and proactive inspections, but it is constrained by the stock of buildings, construction activity, codes, and the physical need for on-site labor. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and AI mainly augments administrative and planning tasks rather than reshaping the core trade, the occupation is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core work requires physical presence, dexterity, tool use, and troubleshooting in varied and often confined environments, putting it largely beyond near-term AI automation. AI can assist with estimates, scheduling, code lookup, blueprint interpretation, BIM planning, and diagnostics, but these are secondary to installation and repair. Lower costs could stimulate some additional maintenance, renovations, and system upgrades, although demand remains constrained by the building stock, construction activity, and the frequency of failures. The low disruption score therefore makes the occupation resilient despite modest opportunities for demand expansion.
fable5_rationale: The core work — installing pipes, soldering, troubleshooting leaks, maneuvering in crawl spaces — is physical, hands-on, and performed in unpredictable real-world environments far from AI's reach; AI helps only peripherally with estimates, scheduling, code lookup, and BIM planning. Demand for plumbing is driven by construction volume and physical system failures, not by the cost of the knowledge work AI could speed up, so productivity gains from AI tools would unlock only modest additional demand. This is a textbook resilient trade: low disruption means the occupation's core remains intact regardless of elasticity, and BLS projections confirm steady, average-paced growth.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on physical installation, repair, welding, and troubleshooting of pipes and fixtures in unpredictable real-world sites, requiring strength, dexterity, and on-site presence that AI cannot perform; AI only assists peripheral elements like cost estimates, BIM blueprint analysis, and code checks. Demand is only modestly elastic because plumbing needs are largely fixed by building stock, maintenance cycles, and construction volume rather than being heavily cost-suppressed, so cheaper/faster work unlocks limited extra renovations or upgrades but not massive new consumption. With disruption well below the high threshold, the occupation remains resilient as AI does not reshape the hands-on core work.

title: Podiatrists
claude_rationale: Podiatry involves substantial hands-on physical examination, manual procedures, and surgical interventions that require direct patient contact and tactile skills, limiting AI's ability to disrupt core tasks. While AI may assist with diagnostic imaging analysis, treatment planning, and administrative tasks, the fundamental work of physical examination, surgery, and patient care remains human-centered. Demand elasticity is low because foot and ankle problems occur at relatively fixed rates tied to aging, diabetes, and injury patterns - making podiatric care 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically increase the incidence of conditions requiring treatment. The moderate disruption and low elasticity place this firmly in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: Podiatry is fundamentally hands-on physical medicine—diagnosing, treating, and surgically operating on feet, ankles, and lower legs—requiring in-person examination and manual procedures that AI cannot perform. AI may assist with diagnostic imaging interpretation, documentation, and treatment-planning peripherally, but the core surgical and physical-treatment tasks remain firmly human. Demand is somewhat constrained by an aging population needing more care but capped by competition from other physicians and licensing/regulatory structure. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches administrative and diagnostic edges but does not reshape the physical, patient-facing core.
opus5_rationale: Podiatry is heavily hands-on: physical exams of feet, surgery, wound debridement, orthotic fitting, and in-person patient care dominate daily work. AI can meaningfully assist with imaging interpretation (x-rays, diabetic foot ulcer risk screening), documentation, coding, and triage, which reduces administrative burden but leaves the core procedural and diagnostic touch work intact. Demand has moderate elasticity — aging populations, diabetes, and obesity create latent need, and cheaper AI screening could funnel more undiagnosed patients into treatment, but reimbursement limits and competition from other physicians cap expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the paperwork and screening periphery, not the clinical core.
openai_rationale: Podiatrists perform a combination of diagnostic, treatment, and surgical tasks that require physical presence and direct patient interaction, which limits AI's ability to disrupt core tasks significantly. While AI can assist with diagnostics and administrative tasks, the hands-on nature of the work keeps disruption low. Demand elasticity is low because the need for podiatric services is not heavily suppressed by cost; it is driven by specific medical needs that do not scale with reduced costs. Therefore, the net effect is resilient, as AI will augment but not replace the core functions of podiatrists.
gpt55_rationale: Podiatrists do use cognitive medical judgment, imaging review, documentation, prescribing, and patient education, all of which AI can assist through decision support, charting, triage, and diagnostic aids. However, the core occupation remains heavily grounded in in-person physical exams, hands-on treatment, wound care, procedures, surgery, and licensed clinical responsibility, so AI is unlikely to absorb the central work over the next decade. Demand could expand moderately if AI-enabled tools make screening, orthotics, documentation, and follow-up cheaper, especially for diabetes, obesity, aging-related mobility problems, and underserved patients, but utilization is still limited by insurance, referrals, patient visits, and substitution by other clinicians. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can assist with imaging review, diagnostic support, documentation, treatment planning, and practice administration. However, physical examinations, procedures, surgery, orthotic fitting, and patient interaction require licensed clinicians with hands-on presence. Lower costs could unlock some preventive and diabetic foot care, but demand remains constrained by medical need, reimbursement, regulation, and substitution by other providers. Therefore, AI will improve podiatrists’ productivity without fundamentally replacing or reshaping the occupation’s core work.
fable5_rationale: Podiatrists' core work — physical exams, surgery, wound care, and hands-on treatment of feet and ankles — requires physical presence and manual dexterity that AI cannot replicate; AI assists only with peripheral tasks like imaging interpretation, documentation, and practice administration. Demand for foot care is driven by demographics (aging, diabetes, obesity) rather than price, so making the diagnostic or administrative portions cheaper would not meaningfully expand the number of surgeries or treatments consumed, especially since patients can already substitute other physicians. With low disruption to the hands-on core, this occupation is clearly resilient to AI over the next decade.
grok45_rationale: Podiatrists' core duties center on physical exams, hands-on nonsurgical treatments, and foot/ankle surgery that require real-world presence and manual skill; AI can assist with x-ray interpretation, diagnostic suggestions, charting, and research but leaves the majority of daily work largely unchanged, producing only moderate disruption. Demand is driven by medical necessity (diabetes, aging, injuries) rather than latent unmet desire for more procedures, so even large productivity gains would expand volume only modestly under regulatory and clinical constraints. With disruption at a moderate level, the occupation remains resilient: AI tools will improve efficiency at the margins without displacing or fundamentally restructuring the role.

title: Police and detectives
claude_rationale: Police work involves substantial physical presence, real-world interactions, and split-second decision-making in unpredictable situations that AI cannot handle. While AI assists with administrative tasks like report writing, database searches, and evidence analysis, the core duties of patrolling, responding to emergencies, making arrests, and community interaction remain fundamentally human-centered. Demand for police services is relatively inelastic - communities need a baseline level of public safety regardless of cost, and legal/regulatory frameworks limit how policing is structured. The moderate disruption from AI tools combined with low demand elasticity keeps this occupation in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: Core police work is physical and presence-based — patrolling, responding to emergencies, apprehending suspects, conducting interviews, and managing volatile real-world situations that AI cannot perform. AI does meaningfully assist peripheral knowledge tasks like report writing, database searches, evidence analysis, predictive policing, and surveillance, which raises disruption to moderate, but the irreplaceable physical and judgment-based duties keep it from going higher. Elasticity is low because demand for policing is driven by public safety needs and constrained by government budgets rather than the cost or speed of service, so productivity gains do not unlock dramatically more demand. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: AI augments documentation and investigation but does not reshape the fundamentally human, physical core of the work.
opus5_rationale: Core police work is physical, in-person, and unpredictable — patrol, traffic stops, arrests, crime scene response, and community interaction cannot be automated. AI meaningfully touches the paperwork and analytic periphery: report drafting from bodycam audio, evidence triage, license plate and facial recognition, predictive deployment, and digital forensics for detectives (the most exposed sub-group). Elasticity is moderate because public safety demand is real but headcount is capped by municipal budgets, civil-service structures, and political constraints rather than by cost of production, so productivity gains mostly free officers for more field time rather than expanding or shrinking rosters. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient: skill mix shifts toward tech-assisted investigation while headcount stays roughly flat.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of police and detectives involve a mix of physical presence, decision-making, and interaction with the public, which limits the extent to which AI can disrupt the occupation. While AI can assist with data analysis and administrative tasks, the unpredictable and human-centric nature of law enforcement keeps disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is low because the need for police services is driven by public safety requirements and budget constraints rather than cost or speed. Thus, even with increased efficiency, the headcount is unlikely to expand significantly, leading to a 'resilient' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: AI can materially assist with report writing, transcription, database searches, surveillance review, evidence triage, dispatch support, and investigative pattern analysis. However, the core of policing still requires unpredictable real-world presence, legal authority, physical intervention, de-escalation, judgment under uncertainty, arrests, testimony, and public accountability. Demand for police services is relatively inelastic because staffing is driven by public safety needs, law, politics, and government budgets rather than by the marginal cost of producing reports or investigations. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is likely to change tools and workflows more than replace the central human role.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially assist with report writing, records searches, evidence review, video analysis, dispatch, and investigative lead generation. However, patrol, emergency response, interviews, arrests, conflict management, evidence collection, and courtroom testimony require physical presence, legal authority, and accountable human judgment. Demand is constrained by crime incidence, public-sector budgets, staffing rules, and community preferences, so cheaper administrative and analytical work is unlikely to produce proportionally more policing. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although administrative workflows and some detective tasks will be substantially redesigned.
fable5_rationale: Core police work — patrolling, responding to emergencies, making arrests, de-escalating conflicts, testifying in court — requires physical presence in unpredictable real-world situations that AI cannot perform, though AI meaningfully assists report writing, records searches, evidence analysis, and investigative work (especially for detectives). Demand for policing is set by public budgets, crime levels, and political decisions rather than cost per unit of output, so productivity gains won't dramatically expand headcount, though modest latent demand exists for faster case clearance. With disruption at 4, the occupation is resilient: AI will speed up paperwork and investigations but the sworn-officer role remains fundamentally hands-on and human-facing.
grok45_rationale: Core duties such as patrolling, responding to calls, making arrests, securing crime scenes, and physical intervention require real-world presence, physical capability, and on-the-spot judgment that AI cannot replace, though AI already assists peripheral tasks like report writing, database searches, evidence analysis, and predictive tools. Demand is constrained by government budgets, political decisions, crime incidence rates, and social limits on policing intensity, so productivity gains are unlikely to unlock large latent expansion in headcount. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes support functions without displacing the human-centered core of the work.

title: Political scientists
claude_rationale: Political scientists' core work involves research, data analysis, policy evaluation, and forecasting—predominantly knowledge-based tasks that AI can increasingly handle through advanced data processing, pattern recognition, and predictive modeling. AI tools are already transforming how research is conducted and analyzed in social sciences. However, demand elasticity is low because political analysis needs are largely fixed by institutional requirements and government budgets, with limited expansion potential even if analysis becomes cheaper and faster. The combination of high AI disruption potential and constrained demand growth points to workforce contraction.
opus_rationale: The core work — researching political systems, analyzing public opinion data, testing theories, forecasting trends, and writing reports — is almost entirely cognitive, language-based, and data-driven, placing it squarely in AI's path; modern LLMs and analytics tools already perform literature synthesis, survey analysis, and trend forecasting effectively. Demand is structurally constrained: 67% of these jobs sit in the federal government and depend heavily on budget allocations rather than market price, so cheaper analysis does not unlock proportionally more consumption, and BLS already projects a 3% decline. The small, inelastic, government-dependent demand combined with high task automatability means productivity gains translate to fewer needed analysts rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category.
opus5_rationale: Political scientists' core work — literature review, survey and voting data analysis, policy evaluation, forecasting, and report/article writing — is almost entirely digital, language- and analysis-based, placing it squarely in AI's path; LLMs already draft policy memos and code statistical analyses competently. Demand is highly inelastic because employment is dominated by federal government (67%) and grant/institution-funded roles where headcount is set by budget appropriations and organizational structure, not by the marginal cost of analysis; cheaper policy research does not create dramatically more funded positions, and BLS already projects decline. Some latent demand exists among smaller advocacy groups and firms wanting policy analysis they previously couldn't afford, but regulatory and budgetary caps limit it. High disruption plus low elasticity in a small, budget-constrained occupation points to headcount contraction rather than expansion.
openai_rationale: Political scientists engage in tasks that are predominantly cognitive and analytical, such as researching political systems, analyzing data, and developing theories. AI can assist in data analysis and trend forecasting, but the nuanced understanding of political contexts and the development of new theories still require human insight. Thus, the disruption score is moderate. Demand elasticity is low because the need for political analysis is not significantly suppressed by cost; it is more constrained by the limited number of organizations requiring such expertise. Consequently, productivity gains from AI are unlikely to lead to a proportional increase in demand. The net effect is 'resilient' as AI will augment but not replace the core tasks of political scientists.
gpt55_rationale: Political scientists perform predominantly digital, cognitive, and language-heavy work: collecting and analyzing survey and policy data, monitoring events, forecasting trends, and writing reports or articles. Current AI tools can already accelerate literature review, document analysis, data coding, drafting, and scenario generation, though humans remain important for research design, credibility, institutional knowledge, and judgment in politically sensitive contexts. Demand elasticity is limited because most employment is in government or grant-funded settings where budgets, headcount, and the number of major policy decisions do not expand proportionally when analysis becomes cheaper. With high disruption and relatively low demand expansion, AI is likely to reduce the need for some analysts while leaving a smaller set of senior experts and client-facing researchers.
gpt56sol_rationale: Political scientists perform predominantly digital and language-intensive work, including literature review, data analysis, policy evaluation, forecasting, monitoring, and report writing, all of which AI can substantially accelerate. Human judgment remains important for causal inference, political context, research design, sensitive advice, and stakeholder credibility, so full automation is unlikely. Demand may expand somewhat as cheaper analysis enables more policy scenarios and monitoring, but federal funding, institutional budgets, and a limited need for formal political research constrain that expansion. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to significant productivity-driven headcount pressure and a replace classification.
fable5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — researching political topics, analyzing survey data, monitoring events, forecasting trends, and writing reports — are digital, language-based knowledge work squarely in AI's path, with current LLMs already capable of drafting policy analyses and synthesizing large document sets. Demand elasticity is low: two-thirds of these jobs sit in the federal government where headcount is budget-driven rather than price-driven, and while cheaper analysis could unlock some latent demand from advocacy groups and think tanks, the institutional appetite for political science research is structurally capped rather than cost-suppressed. BLS already projects a -3% decline before accounting for AI acceleration. High disruption combined with low elasticity points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—researching political systems, collecting and analyzing survey/historical/voter data, developing theories, evaluating policies, forecasting trends, and writing/publishing reports—are almost entirely cognitive, language-based, and digital, already materially assisted by LLMs for synthesis, modeling, and drafting, with rapid further trajectory. Demand is heavily constrained by federal budgets (67% of jobs), institutional funding, and limited positions in think tanks or consulting, so productivity gains do not unlock dramatic new consumption of political analysis the way cheaper software or content does. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore implies AI absorbs substantial core work without offsetting headcount growth, producing contraction.

title: Postal service workers
claude_rationale: Postal service work involves significant physical components (walking routes, lifting packages, door-to-door delivery) that AI cannot replace, though AI can assist with mail sorting and route optimization. The disruption is moderate because while sorting technology continues to advance, the core delivery function remains fundamentally physical. Demand elasticity is very low because mail volume is largely fixed by regulatory requirements and consumer behavior - faster or cheaper postal operations don't generate significantly more mail volume, especially as digital communication continues to replace physical mail. The moderate disruption combined with structural constraints keeps this occupation in the resilient category.
opus_rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical—carriers deliver mail on foot and by vehicle (64% of the workforce), and sorters load/unload trucks and operate machinery—tasks requiring real-world presence that AI cannot perform, though automated sorting (already long-established) does erode the processing roles. Demand is inelastic: physical mail volume is structurally declining due to digital communications, and cheaper/faster sorting does not create more letters to deliver; productivity gains let carriers absorb larger routes rather than expanding total demand. Because disruption sits well below the 7 threshold and is concentrated in peripheral automation rather than reshaping the physical delivery core, this occupation is resilient to AI even as it slowly contracts for unrelated structural reasons.
opus5_rationale: The bulk of this occupation (mail carriers, ~64%, plus handlers loading trucks) is physical last-mile delivery and parcel handling that AI software cannot perform; automation pressure here comes from mechanical sorting equipment and route consolidation rather than language-model AI, and that automation is already largely mature. Some disruption applies to sorters and clerks via OCR/automated sorting and self-service kiosks, but this is incremental rather than transformative. Demand elasticity is low: mail volume is structurally declining due to digital substitution and is not price- or speed-constrained, though parcel growth from e-commerce provides partial offset. Disruption is well below the threshold, so the occupation is classified resilient to AI specifically — even though headcount continues its slow secular decline for non-AI reasons.
openai_rationale: Postal service workers perform a mix of physical and administrative tasks, with a significant portion involving physical mail handling and delivery, which limits AI's impact. While AI and automation can assist with sorting and processing tasks, the core delivery work remains largely manual. Demand elasticity is low because the volume of mail is not highly sensitive to cost reductions; people won't send significantly more mail if it's cheaper. Despite some technological advancements, the overall demand for postal services is declining, leading to a 'resilient' classification due to low disruption and inelastic demand.
gpt55_rationale: Postal service work is heavily physical and place-based: carriers walk or drive routes, handle parcels, collect signatures, and interact with real-world addresses and customers. AI and automation can materially improve sorting, address recognition, routing, customer-service kiosks, and back-office processing, but the largest share of the occupation still requires physical delivery and local presence. Demand elasticity is low because total letter-mail volume is structurally declining and households or businesses are unlikely to send dramatically more mail just because processing is cheaper, although parcels may see some limited expansion. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation fits the resilient category even though employment may continue to decline from automation and digital substitution.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most postal work involves physical collection, handling, transport, and delivery in real-world environments, especially because mail carriers make up most employment. AI-enabled sorting, address recognition, route optimization, self-service, and customer-service tools will automate processing and allow larger delivery routes, but they will not eliminate the need for substantial physical labor within the next decade. Demand is highly inelastic because cheaper processing is unlikely to generate much more letter mail, although parcel delivery provides some support. The occupation is therefore resilient under the defined framework because disruption remains moderate, even though automation and declining mail volume will gradually reduce headcount.
fable5_rationale: The bulk of this workforce (mail carriers, 64%) does physical delivery work that AI cannot perform without autonomous vehicle/robotics maturity; however, sorters and clerks face real pressure from AI-powered OCR sorting machines and self-service kiosks, putting overall disruption at moderate. Elasticity is very low: mail volume is structurally declining due to digital communication, and making sorting or delivery cheaper does not induce people to send more letters — productivity gains translate directly into fewer workers, as BLS's -5% projection reflects. The net effect is 'resilient' because disruption stays below 7 — the core delivery work is physical and AI touches mainly the sorting/processing periphery — though headcount will still shrink gradually due to secular volume decline rather than AI displacement per se.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks for the majority of workers (mail carriers) remain physical—walking/driving routes, lifting parcels, and outdoor delivery in variable conditions—while AI mainly optimizes routing, enhances OCR/sorting machinery, and supports kiosks or chat for clerks; this is mixed assistance rather than replacement of hands-on work. Demand is inelastic because letter volume is already structurally declining due to digital substitution and package growth is constrained by competition and fixed logistics needs, so productivity gains simply enlarge routes or cut headcount rather than expand total mail volume. The occupation therefore fits resilient: AI touches peripherals and accelerates existing automation trends but does not reshape the physical core, consistent with BLS’s projected mild decline.

title: Postsecondary education administrators
claude_rationale: Postsecondary education administrators face moderate disruption as AI can assist with data analysis, record management, and some administrative tasks, but the core work requires human judgment for admissions decisions, student counseling, policy development, and relationship building with stakeholders. Demand elasticity is low because the number of administrative positions is largely fixed by institutional structure and student enrollment levels - making admissions or registration processes more efficient doesn't create demand for more administrators. The disruption score of 6 places this occupation in the resilient category, where AI enhances peripheral tasks but doesn't fundamentally reshape the human-centered leadership and interpersonal aspects of educational administration.
opus_rationale: The work mixes substantial administrative/data tasks (records management, application processing, scheduling, data analysis) that AI can automate or accelerate with deeply human leadership, interpersonal, advising, and policy functions (deans, provosts, student affairs) that resist automation. This places disruption at a moderate level since AI heavily affects registrar and admissions back-office work but not the relationship-driven and governance core. Elasticity is low because demand is structurally tied to student enrollment and institutional budgets, with deans/provost roles capped at a fixed number per institution—cheaper administration won't generate dramatically more administrators. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI streamlines tasks but does not reshape the fundamental human-centered nature of the role.
opus5_rationale: Much of this work is administrative knowledge work — reviewing applications, scheduling courses, maintaining records, producing enrollment data — which AI can substantially automate, and admissions/registrar functions are already being augmented by AI screening and scheduling tools. However, a large share of the role is interpersonal and institutional: advising students, managing staff, faculty tenure and budget decisions, campus events, governance, and accountability that institutions will not delegate to AI, which caps disruption at the upper edge of moderate. Elasticity is low because demand is tied to student enrollment and a fixed number of dean/provost slots — cheaper administration does not create more students or more institutions, so gains show up as leaner back offices rather than growth. Because the core relational and decision-authority work remains human while the routine processing thins out, the occupation is best classified as resilient with quiet contraction in the clerical-adjacent tiers.
openai_rationale: Postsecondary education administrators engage in a mix of tasks, including decision-making, interpersonal communication, and data analysis, which can be partially supported by AI tools. However, the core responsibilities, such as overseeing student services and faculty research, require human judgment and interaction, limiting AI's disruption to moderate levels. Demand elasticity is low because the number of administrative roles is largely determined by student enrollment and institutional budgets, which are not significantly influenced by productivity gains. Thus, while AI may enhance efficiency, it is unlikely to lead to a substantial increase in demand for these roles, making the occupation resilient to AI-driven changes.
gpt55_rationale: Much of this occupation consists of digital and language-heavy administrative work: application review, student communications, records management, scheduling, reporting, policy drafting, and data analysis are all directly affected by AI. Human judgment, campus presence, relationship management, crisis response, and institutional leadership remain important, but many registrar, admissions, and routine student-services workflows can be substantially automated or handled by AI-assisted systems. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of students, institutions, courses, and formal administrative decisions does not expand dramatically just because administration becomes cheaper. Given high disruption and limited demand expansion, AI is likely to reduce headcount in routine administrative roles while leaving a smaller set of higher-skill human administrators overseeing systems and handling complex cases.
gpt56sol_rationale: Much of the occupation consists of digital knowledge work—application review, records management, scheduling, compliance checks, data analysis, communications, and advising—that AI can automate or substantially accelerate. Leadership, sensitive student interactions, institutional accountability, recruitment travel, and crisis management still require human judgment and presence, preventing a higher disruption score. Demand is constrained by enrollment, institutional budgets, and a relatively fixed number of senior posts, so cheaper administration is unlikely to generate enough additional work to offset productivity gains, making headcount contraction likely, especially in admissions and registrar functions.
fable5_rationale: Much of this occupation's routine digital work — processing applications, maintaining records, scheduling courses, producing transcripts and enrollment data — is squarely in AI's path, and registrar and admissions-processing functions face substantial automation. However, the occupation also includes deans, provosts, and student affairs roles centered on institutional leadership, tenure and budget decisions, student advising, and in-person relationship-building, which keeps overall disruption at the moderate-high boundary rather than clearly high. Elasticity is low: demand is tied to student enrollment and constrained state budgets, and cheaper administration will not cause universities to consume dramatically more administrators — institutions have a fixed number of deanships and will pocket efficiency gains. The net effect is resilient overall, though the more clerical subfunctions (registrar, admissions processing) will likely see headcount pressure while leadership and student-facing roles persist.
