Because disruption stays at or below 6 (the hands-on therapeutic core is not reshaped), the occupation is resilient, with AI mostly relieving paperwork burden and letting each clinician serve more clients.
openai_rationale: Speech-language pathologists perform tasks that are highly personalized and require human empathy, critical thinking, and direct interaction with clients, which limits the extent to which AI can disrupt the core of their work. While AI can assist with diagnostic tools and tracking progress, the core therapeutic tasks remain human-centric. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make some aspects of therapy more efficient, the demand for personalized treatment is driven by demographic trends and increased awareness of speech disorders. Thus, AI will augment but not replace the need for human practitioners, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: AI can meaningfully assist speech-language pathologists with documentation, automated speech/language assessment, therapy exercise generation, progress tracking, telepractice, and augmentative communication tools. However, the core work still depends heavily on licensed clinical judgment, rapport with children and medically vulnerable patients, observing nuanced communication behavior, coordinating with families and care teams, and in swallowing cases hands-on clinical evaluation. Demand is fairly elastic because many schools, families, older adults, stroke patients, and underserved communities face unmet needs due to cost, access, and provider shortages, so cheaper AI-enabled services would likely expand screening and treatment intensity. Because disruption is substantial but still bounded by in-person clinical, interpersonal, and regulatory requirements, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can automate documentation, analyze speech patterns, support screening, generate treatment plans, and deliver adaptive practice exercises, materially changing the digital and language-based portions of the job. However, diagnosis and therapy still depend heavily on clinical judgment, patient rapport, family counseling, real-time behavioral observation, and hands-on swallowing assessment. Demand is relatively elastic because lower-cost teletherapy and AI-supported care could expand access amid provider shortages, although licensing, reimbursement, and school budgets limit expansion. Because AI substantially assists but does not fully reshape the human-centered clinical core, the occupation remains resilient.
fable5_rationale: SLP work is language-centered, so AI speech recognition, pronunciation analysis, and practice apps can meaningfully assist assessment, documentation, and at-home drilling — but core treatment requires in-person clinical judgment, hands-on swallowing therapy, real-time adaptation to clients with impaired communication, and counseling of families, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is high because demand is heavily suppressed by cost and therapist shortages (long school waitlists, underserved stroke and autism populations), so cheaper AI-assisted therapy delivery would expand total service consumption substantially. With disruption at 5, the occupation is resilient: AI augments practice sessions and paperwork while the licensed clinician remains central, consistent with BLS's 15% projected growth.
grok45_rationale: Core SLP work centers on in-person assessment, real-time interactive therapy (articulation modeling, swallowing exercises, fluency practice), and family counseling that require physical presence, clinical observation, and adaptive human interaction; AI already assists with speech-sample analysis, documentation, and home-practice apps but leaves the bulk of daily client-facing tasks largely unchanged, placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand is currently constrained by shortages, waitlists, school budgets, and cost, so cheaper/faster delivery via AI tools would unlock substantial latent need among children with developmental issues, autism, and an aging population with stroke/dementia-related disorders. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI augments peripheral and knowledge tasks without displacing the human-centered core, consistent with projected strong employment growth.

title: Stationary engineers and boiler operators
claude_rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while AI can assist with monitoring systems through advanced sensors and predictive maintenance analytics, the core work remains highly physical - operating valves, inspecting equipment, performing repairs, and responding to mechanical failures in real-world industrial environments. The elasticity score is low because demand for boiler and mechanical system operation is tied to fixed building infrastructure and industrial capacity - making systems 10x more efficient doesn't create demand for 10x more buildings or factories. Since disruption is moderate (4) rather than high (≥7), this occupation falls into the resilient category where AI touches peripheral monitoring tasks but doesn't reshape the fundamentally hands-on nature of the work.
opus_rationale: The core work is overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: operating, inspecting, repairing, and maintaining boilers and mechanical equipment on-site, crawling inside equipment, replacing valves and gaskets, and responding to real-time physical conditions. AI and computerized controls already assist with monitoring gauges and data logging, but the essential troubleshooting, manual repair, and licensed safety-critical presence cannot be automated. Demand is fixed by the number of physical buildings and industrial facilities requiring utilities, so cheaper monitoring software does not generate more boilers to tend. Because disruption is low and centered on peripheral monitoring tasks, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: Core work is hands-on physical operation, inspection, and repair of boilers, turbines, and HVAC equipment in dirty, confined, on-site environments — tasks AI cannot perform. AI and IoT sensor automation can improve monitoring, predictive maintenance, and logging, which trims some routine gauge-watching and record-keeping, but licensing requirements and safety regulations mandate a qualified human on premises. Elasticity is low because demand is determined by the fixed stock of buildings and industrial plants needing utilities, not by the cost of the labor. Low disruption places this firmly in the resilient category, consistent with BLS's modest 2 percent growth projection.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of stationary engineers and boiler operators are predominantly physical and hands-on, involving the operation and maintenance of mechanical equipment. While AI can assist with monitoring and data logging, the physical presence and manual skills required for repairs and inspections limit AI's impact. Thus, disruption is low. Demand elasticity is also low because the need for these services is driven by the operational requirements of facilities, which do not expand significantly with cost reductions. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: AI and advanced controls can improve monitoring, anomaly detection, energy optimization, logging, and predictive maintenance for boilers and building systems. However, the core job still requires licensed human oversight, physical inspection, manual adjustment, troubleshooting, repair, and safety response in hazardous real-world facilities. Demand is fairly inelastic because the number of hospitals, schools, hotels, plants, and large buildings needing steam or mechanical systems is not likely to expand much just because operation becomes cheaper. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate and much of the work requires on-site mechanical presence, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI-enabled controls, predictive maintenance, anomaly detection, and automated logging will materially improve monitoring, diagnostics, and operating efficiency. However, physical inspections, repairs, emergency response, safety accountability, and work in hazardous equipment spaces still require skilled on-site workers. Demand is tied to the fixed number of facilities and utility systems rather than the price of operator labor, so productivity gains will create little additional work; nevertheless, the occupation remains resilient because its hands-on core limits disruption.
fable5_rationale: The core of this occupation is hands-on mechanical work — repairing valves, replacing bearings, crawling inside boilers, lubricating parts — which AI cannot perform; only the monitoring, gauge-reading, and log-keeping portions are in AI's path, and much of that is already automated via computerized controls. Elasticity is low because demand for boiler and HVAC operation is fixed by the building stock and equipment installed base — cheaper monitoring does not lead facilities to consume more steam or hire more operators, and remote monitoring may slightly reduce headcount per facility. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient: AI-enhanced sensors and predictive maintenance tools will assist workers but the physical maintenance, safety inspection, and licensed-operator requirements keep humans central to the role.
grok45_rationale: Core duties center on physical operation, inspection, repair, and maintenance of boilers, valves, turbines, and HVAC equipment in real facilities, requiring on-site presence, mechanical dexterity, and handling of hazardous conditions that AI cannot perform; AI only peripherally aids sensor monitoring, predictive alerts, and log-keeping. Demand is tightly tied to the fixed stock of large buildings, hospitals, and plants that need utilities, with virtually no latent expansion if the work becomes cheaper or faster. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient regardless of modest efficiency gains.

title: Substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors
claude_rationale: While AI tools can assist with documentation, treatment planning, and some assessment tasks, the core work of counseling requires deep human connection, empathy, crisis intervention, and real-time emotional support that AI cannot replicate. The disruption score is moderate because AI may help with administrative tasks and provide decision support, but the fundamental therapeutic relationship remains human-centered. Demand elasticity is high because mental health and addiction services are severely undersupplied - cheaper and more accessible tools could help expand access to underserved populations and enable more preventive care. However, since disruption remains moderate, this occupation falls into the resilient category where AI enhances rather than transforms the core work.
opus_rationale: The core work depends on human empathy, trust-building, crisis intervention, and in-person therapeutic relationships that AI cannot replicate, though AI can assist with documentation, treatment plan drafting, screening, and triage—placing disruption at a moderate level. Demand is heavily suppressed by cost, stigma, and provider shortages, so cheaper access could unlock significant latent demand for mental health and addiction services, giving high elasticity. Despite the favorable elasticity, the disruption score remains at or below 6 because the human-centered, physically-present core tasks are largely insulated from AI, making 'resilient' the appropriate category.
opus5_rationale: The work is language-based, which puts intake assessment, treatment-plan drafting, documentation, and even some psychoeducation and between-session support squarely in AI's path — chatbot-based CBT tools already exist. But the therapeutic core depends on trust, empathy, crisis intervention, in-person and residential settings, court-mandated supervision, and licensure requirements, so AI mostly offloads paperwork and augments rather than replaces sessions, keeping disruption moderate. Elasticity is very high: mental health and addiction treatment demand is massively suppressed by cost, stigma, and provider shortages, so any productivity gain gets absorbed by unmet need rather than headcount cuts. Because disruption stays at or below 6, this is resilient — AI reshapes documentation and triage at the periphery while clinical headcount continues its strong projected growth.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of substance abuse, behavioral disorder, and mental health counselors involve significant interpersonal interaction, empathy, and nuanced understanding of human behavior, which are not easily replicable by AI. While AI can assist with administrative tasks and provide some diagnostic support, the core counseling work remains largely human-centric, leading to a moderate disruption score. However, the demand for mental health services is high and growing, driven by increased awareness and societal acceptance of mental health issues, suggesting high elasticity. Even if AI makes certain aspects of the work more efficient, the overall demand for these services is likely to expand, absorbing productivity gains and maintaining or increasing headcount.
gpt55_rationale: Counseling is heavily language-based and cognitive: assessment, psychoeducation, treatment planning, progress documentation, and between-session support are all areas where AI tools can materially assist or partially automate. However, the core therapeutic relationship, crisis intervention, mandated-care accountability, clinical judgment, and work with distressed or high-risk clients still require licensed human professionals, keeping disruption from being even higher. Demand elasticity is high because mental health and addiction treatment have large unmet need due to cost, access, stigma, and provider shortages; cheaper AI-enabled care would likely lead to more screening, coaching, follow-up, and lower-acuity support. Because disruption is high but latent demand is also high, AI is more likely to expand counselors’ reach and reshape workflows than simply reduce headcount.
gpt56sol_rationale: Counseling is predominantly language- and knowledge-based, so AI can materially assist with screening, documentation, treatment planning, routine coaching, progress monitoring, and between-session support. However, therapeutic trust, nuanced assessment, crisis intervention, accountability, and licensed clinical judgment will continue to require substantial human involvement. Demand is highly elastic because mental health and addiction services are severely capacity-constrained and often unaffordable, so lower costs and greater productivity would unlock extensive unmet demand. High disruption combined with very high elasticity therefore points to augmentation rather than broad counselor replacement.
fable5_rationale: Counseling is language-based work in principle, and AI chatbots and documentation tools will assist with treatment plans, progress notes, and between-session support — but the core value lies in human trust, empathy, crisis intervention, and therapeutic alliance, which clients and regulators largely will not accept from machines, especially for addiction and court-mandated treatment. Elasticity is very high: mental health and substance abuse care demand is massively suppressed by cost, provider shortages, and access barriers, so cheaper adjunct capacity would be absorbed by enormous unmet need (BLS already projects 17% growth). With disruption at a moderate 5, the occupation is resilient — AI reshapes documentation and peripheral tasks while the counselor-client relationship remains the irreducible core, and strong latent demand further protects headcount.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on building therapeutic alliances, crisis intervention, empathy-driven sessions, and in-person work with distressed clients in clinical or residential settings, so AI only assists peripheral elements like documentation, progress tracking, treatment-plan suggestions, and psychoeducation materials rather than replacing the relational core. Demand elasticity is high because mental health and addiction services face massive unmet need, long waitlists, and cost/access barriers; making counseling dramatically cheaper and more productive would unlock far more prevention, mild-case treatment, family support, and ongoing care. The moderate disruption score places the occupation in the resilient category, as AI tools will raise productivity at the margins without reshaping the essential human presence required.

title: Surgical assistants and technologists
claude_rationale: Surgical assistants and technologists perform primarily hands-on, physical tasks in sterile operating room environments that require real-time human presence, dexterity, and immediate response to surgeons' needs - AI cannot replace the physical manipulation of instruments, patient positioning, or sterile field maintenance. While AI may assist with some peripheral tasks like inventory management or scheduling, the core work remains fundamentally manual and requires human judgment in unpredictable surgical situations. Demand for surgical procedures is relatively inelastic as it's driven by medical necessity rather than cost considerations - even if AI made certain aspects more efficient, the number of surgeries needed is primarily determined by patient health conditions, not productivity gains.
opus_rationale: Disruption is very low because the core work is intensely physical and hands-on—sterilizing equipment, positioning patients, passing instruments, holding retractors, suturing, and maintaining a sterile field in real-time within an operating room. These tasks require manual dexterity, physical presence, and split-second responsiveness that AI cannot replicate; AI might assist peripherally with inventory tracking or robotic surgical equipment setup but does not touch the central duties. Elasticity is moderate because surgical demand is genuinely expanding with an aging population and the shift to outpatient surgery centers, so cheaper/faster adjacent processes could unlock more procedures. Because disruption is well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient—AI affects only the edges of this physically grounded role.
opus5_rationale: The work is almost entirely hands-on and physical: sterilizing instruments, draping and positioning patients, passing instruments, holding retractors, suturing and suctioning in a sterile operating field. AI touches only peripheral elements like inventory tracking, scheduling, instrument counting, and robotic surgery setup, and surgical robots still require human scrub personnel at the table. Demand is moderately elastic — an aging population and cheaper, faster outpatient surgery could unlock meaningful additional procedure volume — but surgery volume is capped by surgeon supply, OR capacity, and reimbursement. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI changes the surrounding technology stack, not the core role.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of surgical assistants and technologists are predominantly physical and hands-on, involving direct patient care and assistance during surgeries, which limits AI's ability to disrupt these roles significantly. While AI may assist with peripheral tasks like inventory management or scheduling, the essential duties require human presence and dexterity. Demand elasticity is low because the number of surgeries is driven by medical need rather than cost or speed. Even if AI improves efficiency, the demand for surgeries is unlikely to increase proportionally, leading to limited expansion in headcount. Thus, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption.
gpt55_rationale: The core work of surgical assistants and technologists is hands-on, sterile, real-time operating-room support: preparing rooms, handling instruments, positioning patients, maintaining sterility, suctioning, suturing, and responding physically during procedures. AI may improve peripheral tasks such as inventory tracking, instrument counting, scheduling, documentation, robotic-equipment setup, and surgical checklists, but it is unlikely to replace the need for trained human presence in the OR over the next decade. Demand elasticity is limited because the number of surgeries is constrained by patient need, surgeons, facilities, insurance coverage, and safety regulation, though cheaper support could modestly expand outpatient capacity. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the core occupation remains embodied and safety-critical, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core tasks are hands-on, time-critical, and performed in a sterile, unpredictable operating-room environment, including positioning patients, passing instruments, maintaining sterility, and directly assisting with incisions or closure. AI may improve equipment setup, inventory tracking, documentation, robotic-system support, and procedural guidance, but replacing the required dexterity and physical presence would require major advances in robotics. Demand is relatively inelastic because surgical volume is constrained by medical need, reimbursement, facility capacity, and the availability of surgeons, although lower costs could modestly expand elective and outpatient procedures. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will mainly enhance peripheral and coordination tasks rather than reshape its physical core.
fable5_rationale: The core work — sterilizing equipment, positioning patients, passing instruments, holding retractors, suturing — is entirely physical, hands-on, and performed in a sterile operating room where real-time dexterity and presence are essential; AI touches only peripheral tasks like scheduling, inventory tracking, and documentation. Surgical robotics may change workflows over time but still requires human technologists to set up and support equipment, and full automation of instrument handling is far beyond a 10-year horizon. Demand for surgery is driven by clinical need and an aging population rather than the cost of assistant labor, so productivity gains in this role would not dramatically expand surgical volume. With minimal disruption to core tasks and projected employment growth, this occupation is clearly resilient.
grok45_rationale: Core duties—sterilizing and arranging instruments, patient positioning and prepping, maintaining sterile fields, passing tools, counting supplies, and hands-on assisting (clamping, suctioning, suturing)—are almost entirely physical, manual, and require real-time presence in the unpredictable OR environment; AI can only touch peripheral tasks such as inventory tracking or robotic-system setup. Demand for surgical procedures is driven by medical necessity, demographics, and facility capacity rather than the marginal cost or speed of technologists, so even large productivity gains unlock only limited additional volume (mainly elective/outpatient cases). Because disruption remains low, the occupation stays resilient regardless of modest elasticity.

title: Survey researchers
claude_rationale: Survey research is highly digital and cognitive work involving survey design, statistical analysis, data interpretation, and report generation - all areas where AI tools are already making significant impact through automated survey platforms, advanced analytics, and natural language processing for data interpretation. Demand elasticity is low because organizations typically conduct surveys for specific research needs with relatively fixed budgets and timelines; making surveys 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically increase the total volume of surveys conducted, as demand is constrained by organizational decision-making cycles and regulatory requirements rather than cost. The combination of high AI disruption potential and inelastic demand suggests significant headcount contraction, which aligns with the BLS projection of -5% employment decline.
opus_rationale: Survey research is overwhelmingly digital and cognitive work—designing questionnaires, sampling, statistical analysis, and report writing—all squarely in AI's path, with LLMs and automated analytics tools already capable of generating survey instruments, cleaning data, and producing summaries. Demand is structurally constrained and already shrinking: the BLS projects a 5% decline as data mining, big-data methods, and social media scraping displace traditional survey collection, so cheaper/faster survey work does not unlock proportional new demand. The number of distinct surveys an organization needs is relatively fixed, and alternative data sources substitute for surveys entirely, capping any expansion. High disruption combined with low, declining elasticity points to headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.
opus5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — background research, questionnaire drafting and cognitive testing, sampling design, weighting/nonresponse adjustment, statistical analysis, and report/visualization writing — are digital and language- or code-based, and current LLM plus statistical tooling already handles much of it; AI can even simulate respondent panels and pretest wording, making disruption very high despite occasional in-person focus-group facilitation. Elasticity is low because demand for survey-based insight is capped by client research budgets and, more importantly, is being actively substituted away by passive big data, digital trace data, and social media analytics; cheaper surveys do not make organizations commission proportionally more of them, and respondent fatigue limits volume. BLS already projects a 5 percent decline in this small (8,800-job) occupation. High disruption combined with structurally shrinking, inelastic demand fits 'replace' — the surviving roles will concentrate in methodological oversight at a smaller headcount.
openai_rationale: Survey researchers are highly susceptible to AI disruption due to the digital and analytical nature of their work. AI can already assist in designing surveys, analyzing data, and even conducting some forms of data collection, such as online surveys. As AI tools become more sophisticated, they will further automate these tasks, reducing the need for human intervention. However, the demand elasticity is low because the need for survey data is not significantly suppressed by current costs or speeds. The decline in traditional survey methods, combined with the efficiency gains from AI, suggests that the headcount for survey researchers will likely shrink, leading to a 'replace' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: Survey researchers do predominantly cognitive, digital, and language/statistics-based work: drafting questionnaires, choosing methods, cleaning and analyzing data, visualizing results, and writing summaries. AI tools can already materially accelerate survey design, question testing, statistical coding, nonresponse analysis, dashboarding, and report generation, though human judgment remains important for sampling validity, interpretation, ethics, and client needs. Demand has some latent upside because cheaper surveys and analysis could let more organizations run frequent research, but it is constrained by respondent fatigue, sampling quality, privacy limits, and substitution from passive data, social media, and big-data methods. Because disruption is high and elasticity is limited, productivity gains are likely to reduce the need for specialized survey researcher headcount rather than fully expand demand.
gpt56sol_rationale: Survey research is predominantly digital and cognitive, and AI can already accelerate background research, questionnaire drafting, statistical coding, data analysis, visualization, and report writing. Human expertise remains important for sampling strategy, bias and nonresponse correction, instrument validity, fieldwork oversight, and defensible interpretation. Lower costs will enable more frequent and accessible research, but respondent availability, data quality, institutional budgets, and competition from behavioral and administrative data limit demand expansion. Thus, the occupation will persist with fewer routine tasks and a stronger emphasis on methodology, quality assurance, and strategic interpretation.
fable5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — designing questionnaires, testing question wording, correcting for nonresponse bias, running statistical analysis, and summarizing results in tables and reports — are digital, language-based, and squarely in the path of current AI tools, which can already draft surveys, code responses, and analyze data end to end. Elasticity is low because demand for traditional survey research is being actively substituted away by data mining, passive behavioral data, and social media analytics; making surveys 10x cheaper unlocks only modest latent demand (small organizations running more polls) and cannot offset the structural shift, as reflected in BLS's projected -5% decline even before aggressive AI adoption. With disruption of 8 and elasticity of 3, productivity gains translate into fewer researchers rather than more surveys, making 'replace' the fitting category.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—questionnaire design, statistical analysis, sampling adjustments, data summarization, and report writing—are almost entirely digital/cognitive and already partially automated by AI tools for question generation, response coding, and insight extraction, placing the occupation squarely in AI’s path. Elasticity is only moderate because cheaper, faster surveys would unlock more frequent market research and academic polling among cost-sensitive organizations, yet overall demand remains constrained by respondent fatigue, regulatory survey requirements, and substitution from big-data/social-media analytics. High disruption combined with moderate demand expansion therefore implies the role survives but requires substantial skill shifts toward AI oversight, complex methodology, and hybrid data sources.

title: Surveying and mapping technicians
claude_rationale: While AI and automation affect data processing aspects (GIS analysis, CAD work, image processing), the core work remains heavily physical - fieldwork in varied terrain, operating surveying instruments, setting markers, and ground-truthing data. Drones and advanced sensors change efficiency but still require human operators and interpretation. Demand shows moderate elasticity as cheaper/faster surveying could enable more frequent mapping updates, smaller project feasibility, and expanded infrastructure monitoring, but growth is constrained by the physical nature of development and regulatory requirements. The disruption score of 5 places this in resilient territory where AI augments rather than transforms the fundamental work.
opus_rationale: The work is split between physical fieldwork (visiting sites, placing markers, operating instruments, working in rugged terrain) and digital data processing (GIS, CAD, map editing, calculations). AI and automation (drones, automated data processing) materially affect the office/data portions, but the core field presence and judgment-based verification remain human-dependent, keeping disruption moderate. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper mapping unlocks more projects, but it is structurally tied to physical construction, infrastructure, and land development activity. Since disruption is at or below 6, the occupation is classified resilient—AI reshapes the periphery and improves efficiency without eliminating the irreplaceable field-based core.
opus5_rationale: The occupation splits between physical fieldwork — visiting sites, setting markers, operating instruments in rugged terrain — and digital processing of GIS/CAD data, where AI-assisted point-cloud classification, automated feature extraction, and drone/LiDAR photogrammetry pipelines already materially reduce manual labor. That mixed profile caps disruption around 6: the office-side mapping and data-processing tasks are squarely in AI's path, but the site-presence and equipment-handling core is not. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper, faster surveying does unlock more frequent as-built scans, digital twins, infrastructure monitoring and higher-resolution municipal GIS layers, though total demand is still tied to construction, land transaction, and utility project volumes and to licensed surveyor sign-off. Because the physical field component keeps disruption at or below 6, the occupation is best classified resilient, with the caveat that the purely desk-based mapping/GIS technician subset faces meaningfully more displacement risk than the field subset.
openai_rationale: Surveying and mapping technicians perform a mix of physical and digital tasks, with AI and automation already assisting in data processing and map creation. However, the need for fieldwork and human judgment in interpreting data and ensuring accuracy keeps disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is moderate as well; while AI can enhance productivity, the need for accurate and updated geographic data is growing, but not explosively so. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing the human role.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially affect the office and data-processing side of this occupation, including GIS database maintenance, image interpretation, CAD/GIS map updating, error checking, and integration of drone, satellite, and survey data. However, a substantial share of the job still requires real-world field presence: visiting sites, finding or setting markers, operating instruments, dealing with terrain and weather, and verifying conditions on the ground. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper mapping and surveying data will support more infrastructure planning, utilities management, environmental monitoring, construction, and digital-twin applications, but many land-survey tasks are tied to fixed construction, property, and regulatory needs. Because disruption is significant but remains capped by physical fieldwork and verification requirements, the occupation fits the resilient category rather than full restructuring or replacement.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI, computer vision, drones, and automated GIS tools will substantially accelerate image processing, feature extraction, calculations, database maintenance, and map production. However, much of the occupation still requires travel, instrument operation, marker placement, equipment troubleshooting, and judgment in unpredictable outdoor environments. Cheaper geospatial data will support additional mapping for infrastructure, utilities, development, and environmental monitoring, although demand remains partly constrained by the number of physical projects and legally required surveys. Because AI significantly improves the office-based portion without eliminating the field-based core, the occupation is resilient rather than highly disrupted.
fable5_rationale: The occupation splits between physical fieldwork (setting markers, operating instruments in rugged terrain, drone operation on site) and digital processing (GIS data assembly, map editing, CAD work). AI plus automated photogrammetry can heavily absorb the office-based mapping and data-processing tasks, but the on-site measurement, marker location, and equipment work require physical presence, capping disruption at moderate. Elasticity is moderate-to-high because cheaper geospatial data unlocks meaningful latent demand — utilities, construction, infrastructure, and autonomous systems all consume more mapping when it's faster and cheaper — but legal boundary surveys are tied to fixed real-estate transaction volumes. With disruption at 5, the core field-based work remains largely intact, making this occupation resilient, though technicians focused purely on desk-based GIS work will face more pressure than field crews.
grok45_rationale: Core work mixes substantial physical fieldwork (site visits, instrument operation, marker placement, rugged outdoor conditions) with digital tasks (GIS/CAD processing, image editing, data entry, map creation from drone/satellite sources), so AI already assists the knowledge portions via computer vision and automated analysis but cannot replace on-site presence or accuracy verification. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper/faster surveying unlocks more frequent updates, detailed GIS applications, and smaller projects, yet demand remains partly constrained by construction cycles, legal requirements, and infrastructure budgets rather than expanding without limit. With disruption only moderate, AI reshapes tools and efficiency at the periphery without eliminating the occupation's essential human elements, fitting the resilient category.

title: Surveyors
claude_rationale: Surveying involves substantial fieldwork requiring physical presence to take precise measurements in varied terrain and weather conditions, though modern surveyors do use GPS, GIS, and CAD technologies for data collection and processing. The disruption score reflects that while AI can assist with data analysis, mapping, and report generation, the core work of establishing legal property boundaries requires on-site measurement and verification that cannot be fully automated. Demand elasticity is low because surveying is primarily driven by regulatory requirements for property transactions, construction permits, and legal documentation - making surveys cheaper wouldn't significantly increase the number of property sales or construction projects. The net effect is resilient because the physical measurement requirements and regulatory nature of the work limit AI's ability to reshape the core occupation.
opus_rationale: Surveying combines significant physical fieldwork (traveling to sites, taking measurements in rugged terrain, marking property lines) with cognitive office tasks like data interpretation, GIS/CAD mapping, and legal record analysis. AI, drones, and automated total stations meaningfully boost the office/analysis and data-processing portions and are already increasing productivity, but the core requires licensed human presence in the field and legally binding certification, capping disruption at moderate. Demand is somewhat tied to construction, infrastructure, and resource extraction cycles and would expand modestly if cheaper, but is structurally constrained by regulation, licensing requirements, and the fixed amount of land/projects needing surveys. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the periphery and improves productivity without replacing the licensed, physically-present core work.
opus5_rationale: Surveying blends substantial fieldwork — traveling to sites, setting instruments, walking rugged terrain, physically marking boundaries — with digital tasks like records research, CAD/GIS processing, data reduction, and report preparation. AI plus drones/LiDAR automation meaningfully compresses the office and data-processing half of the job and speeds deed/title research, but licensed professional judgment, legal certification, court testimony, and on-site presence keep the core intact. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper surveys could unlock more frequent boundary verification, as-built and monitoring surveys tied to construction and infrastructure cycles, though it is ultimately capped by the volume of land transactions and building projects and by state licensure. With disruption at 5 the occupation falls in the resilient band — technology raises productivity per surveyor (as BLS notes) without reshaping the fundamental role.
openai_rationale: Surveyors' work involves a mix of fieldwork and office tasks, with significant reliance on technology like GPS, GIS, and CAD. While AI can enhance data processing and map creation, the physical presence required for field measurements and legal certification limits disruption to moderate. Demand elasticity is low because the need for precise property boundaries and legal documentation is relatively fixed, with limited expansion potential. Thus, while AI will augment surveyors' capabilities, it won't drastically alter headcount, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: Surveying has substantial digital and cognitive components—record searches, GIS/CAD mapping, data validation, report preparation, and legal documentation—that AI, drones, lidar, computer vision, and automated instruments can materially improve. However, the occupation still depends on field presence, site judgment, legal certification, client interaction, and reconciling physical conditions with official records, which limits full automation. Demand is only moderately elastic because surveying is tied to construction, real estate transactions, infrastructure, mining, and legal boundary needs; cheaper surveys may increase usage somewhat, but people will not need dramatically more boundary certifications absent more projects. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to replace the core licensed, field-based role, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can accelerate title research, data validation, point-cloud interpretation, mapping, CAD/GIS production, and report preparation, while drones and robotic instruments further automate data collection. However, substantial fieldwork, site-specific judgment, discrepancy resolution, legal certification, and licensed accountability remain difficult to automate fully. Demand is tied mainly to property transactions, construction, infrastructure, mining, and regulatory requirements, so lower costs may increase survey scope and frequency but are unlikely to produce a proportional surge in projects. The occupation is therefore resilient, although productivity gains may limit headcount growth and shift work toward oversight, interpretation, and certification.
fable5_rationale: Surveying blends office-based knowledge work (records research, GIS analysis, map and report preparation) that AI can substantially accelerate with essential fieldwork requiring physical presence on rugged terrain to set monuments and verify conditions — plus legal licensure requirements that mandate a human certify boundaries. Drones, robotic total stations, and AI-assisted data processing already boost productivity, but demand is largely tethered to construction activity and real estate transactions, which are driven by external economic factors rather than survey cost; cheaper surveys unlock only modest latent demand (e.g., more frequent monitoring, smaller projects getting surveyed). With disruption at 5, the core field-and-certification work remains human-anchored, making this occupation resilient despite meaningful AI assistance in the office portion.
grok45_rationale: Surveyors combine physical fieldwork (site measurements with GPS/total stations, terrain navigation) with cognitive/digital tasks (legal record searches, GIS/CAD mapping, data verification, report preparation). AI already assists the latter via automated feature extraction, point-cloud processing, and document analysis, but core on-site presence, equipment operation, legal certification, and court testimony keep disruption moderate. Demand is anchored to construction volume, property transactions, and infrastructure projects rather than surveying cost; cheaper/faster output may unlock some extra mapping or planning work but is constrained by real-world project pipelines and regulation, yielding low elasticity. AI therefore touches supporting tasks without reshaping the occupation’s core, producing a resilient net effect.

title: Tax examiners and collectors, and revenue agents
claude_rationale: Tax examination and collection work is predominantly digital and analytical, involving pattern recognition, document review, data analysis, and rule-based decision making - all areas where AI excels and is already being deployed. Modern AI can process tax returns, identify discrepancies, flag suspicious deductions, and even conduct initial assessments far more efficiently than humans. However, demand for tax enforcement is relatively fixed - governments need a certain level of compliance monitoring regardless of cost, and taxpayers don't voluntarily increase their audit frequency when it becomes cheaper. The productivity gains from AI will primarily translate to fewer workers needed rather than expanded tax enforcement activities.
opus_rationale: The core work—reviewing tax returns, verifying deductions, evaluating financial documents, matching records, and flagging discrepancies—is almost entirely digital, rule-based cognitive work directly in AI's path, with automated matching and anomaly detection already widely deployed in tax administration. Demand is highly inelastic because the volume of tax returns and collections is fixed by the number of taxpayers and statutory requirements, not by cost or speed; cheaper processing simply means fewer humans are needed rather than more auditing being demanded. Government budget constraints and the inherently capped workload reinforce headcount contraction, consistent with the BLS-projected decline. High disruption plus very low elasticity squarely fits the replace category.
opus5_rationale: The core work — reviewing returns, matching documentation, applying tax code rules, flagging questionable deductions, and computing penalties and interest — is almost entirely digital, rule-based document analysis that AI and automated matching systems already perform well; field collections and taxpayer negotiation are the main human-anchored residual. Demand is highly inelastic because it is set by the number of filers and by government budget appropriations rather than by the cost of examination; even if audits became 10x cheaper, political and statutory limits, plus fixed headcount budgets, cap expansion (some latent demand exists since audit coverage rates are low, which is why elasticity isn't a 1-2). With high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains flow into fewer positions, reinforcing the already-projected employment decline. Remaining roles will concentrate in complex corporate revenue-agent work and in-person collection enforcement.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of tax examiners, collectors, and revenue agents involve reviewing tax returns, conducting audits, and evaluating financial information, which are predominantly knowledge-based and increasingly subject to automation by AI. AI tools can already assist in identifying discrepancies and automating routine checks, suggesting high disruption potential. However, demand elasticity is low because the need for tax examination is largely driven by regulatory requirements rather than market demand. Even if AI makes these processes faster and cheaper, it does not significantly increase the volume of work, leading to a likely reduction in headcount.
gpt55_rationale: The work is heavily digital, document-based, and rules-driven: reviewing returns, checking deductions and credits against tax law, analyzing financial records, drafting notices, maintaining case files, and prioritizing questionable returns are all in AI’s direct path. Human judgment, legal authority, taxpayer negotiation, and some field audits remain important, especially for complex businesses and collections, but much of the routine examination and correspondence workflow can be automated or AI-assisted. Demand has some latent upside because governments could audit more returns and pursue more delinquent accounts if enforcement became cheaper, but it is capped by budgets, political constraints, due-process requirements, and the finite number of tax filings. Because disruption is high and demand expansion is limited, AI is likely to reduce headcount for routine examiner and collector roles while preserving fewer, more complex human enforcement positions.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most return review, document analysis, liability calculation, case prioritization, recordkeeping, and taxpayer correspondence are structured digital tasks that AI can substantially automate. Human judgment, legal accountability, sensitive negotiations, investigations, and field audits remain important, especially for complex or contested cases. Although cheaper enforcement could enable governments to examine more questionable returns, demand is constrained by the finite tax base, statutory processes, enforcement priorities, and public budgets, so productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount and concentrate remaining workers on complex cases.
fable5_rationale: The core work — reviewing tax returns, verifying deductions against tax law, cross-referencing financial records, and flagging discrepancies — is rule-based digital document analysis squarely in AI's current capability path, with only field audits and sensitive collection negotiations requiring human presence. Elasticity is low because demand is set by government budgets and legislative priorities rather than price: cheaper auditing does not mean society consumes 10x more tax enforcement, and while there is latent demand to close the tax gap, headcount is structurally capped by public funding and political constraints (BLS already projects a 2% decline). High disruption combined with budget-constrained inelastic demand means productivity gains will translate directly into fewer examiners needed, making 'replace' the appropriate category.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on reviewing digital tax returns, applying tax rules to credits/deductions, analyzing financial records, and flagging discrepancies—predominantly cognitive and language-based work already being automated by AI document analysis, anomaly detection, and tax-law models, with only secondary field audits and collections requiring human presence. Demand for enforcement is largely fixed by the volume of returns and government budgets/politics rather than price; while cheaper AI could enable somewhat more audits, latent expansion is capped and productivity gains will primarily shrink headcount rather than scale output proportionally. This combination of high disruption and low elasticity fits replace, as AI absorbs routine examination volume without enough new demand to offset workforce contraction.

title: Taxi drivers, shuttle drivers, and chauffeurs
claude_rationale: This occupation faces very high disruption as autonomous vehicles are already being tested and deployed in limited markets, with the core task of driving being directly in AI's path through self-driving technology. The elasticity is low because demand for transportation trips is relatively fixed - people don't take dramatically more rides just because they're cheaper, and regulatory constraints limit rapid expansion of transportation services. With high disruption and low elasticity, this occupation fits the replace category as AI-powered autonomous vehicles will likely absorb much of the driving work without proportional demand expansion to maintain employment levels.
opus_rationale: The core work is physically driving passengers in unpredictable real-world conditions, which AI can only partially address through navigation aids and dispatch optimization today; autonomous vehicles are an emerging long-term threat but face regulatory, technical, and geographic limits that keep disruption moderate over the next decade. Demand has some elasticity—cheaper rides via automation could expand usage, and aging populations and paratransit needs add structural growth—but social, regulatory, and capital constraints cap rapid expansion. Because disruption remains at or below 6 (the physical driving task is not yet reshaped at its core within the 10-year window), the occupation is classified as resilient, with BLS even projecting above-average headcount growth.
opus5_rationale: Although the work is physical rather than digital, driving is the single physical task AI is most directly and aggressively automating: robotaxi fleets are already commercially deployed and scaling in multiple US metros, and the core task set (navigate, pick up, transport, collect fare) is almost fully addressable by autonomous systems, with only luggage handling, wheelchair assistance, and concierge/executive-assistant duties resisting. This justifies a high disruption score even though the peripheral customer-service and paratransit segments remain human for the next decade. Elasticity is low from the worker's perspective: cheaper rides do unlock substantial latent trip demand, but that expansion is served by driverless vehicles rather than by each human driver completing 10x more trips — a driver's output is capped by hours in a car, so productivity gains accrue to the platform and vehicle, not to human headcount. High disruption plus structurally capped per-worker output points to replacement, with residual demand concentrated in assisted-transport, luxury chauffeur, and paratransit niches.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of taxi drivers, shuttle drivers, and chauffeurs are predominantly physical and require real-world presence, such as driving and interacting with passengers. While AI can assist with navigation and dispatching, it cannot replace the human element of driving and customer service, leading to a low disruption score. However, if AI were to make these services cheaper and more efficient, there could be moderate demand expansion, especially in urban areas and for specialized services like paratransit. The net effect is resilient because the core work remains largely unchanged by AI, and any productivity gains are likely to be absorbed by increased demand rather than a reduction in headcount.
gpt55_rationale: Although the job is physically situated in the real world, the core task of operating a vehicle is directly targeted by autonomous-driving AI, and dispatch, routing, pricing, and fleet management are already heavily algorithmic. Full automation will likely be uneven over the next decade because of regulation, weather, liability, passenger assistance, luggage, wheelchair needs, and complex urban edge cases, but robotaxis and autonomous shuttles can materially change the occupation in some markets. Demand would expand if rides became much cheaper, especially for ride-hailing, airport shuttles, older adults, and people without cars, but travel time, trip-purpose limits, and regulation prevent unlimited growth. The result is best classified as restructure: many traditional driving tasks are at risk, while remaining work shifts toward customer assistance, specialized transport, supervision, and operation in geographies or use cases not yet automated.
gpt56sol_rationale: Driving is physical and requires real-world judgment, but autonomous-vehicle AI directly targets the occupation’s core task and is already operating in limited, geofenced markets. Adoption over the next decade will remain constrained by weather, complex roads, regulation, liability, and passenger needs such as luggage or wheelchair assistance, so disruption will be substantial but uneven. Much cheaper rides would generate additional trips, especially among older adults, people with disabilities, and households without cars, but travel-time and congestion constraints limit demand expansion. The occupation therefore restructures toward assisted transportation, premium service, supervision, and difficult routes while routine urban trips increasingly become automated.
fable5_rationale: Unlike most physical occupations, driving is the direct target of embodied AI: robotaxis (Waymo, and expanding competitors) are already operating commercially in the same dense metro markets where taxi and ride-hail employment is concentrated, putting the core task squarely in AI's path over a 10-year horizon. Elasticity is low for the occupation itself—while cheaper rides would expand total ride volume substantially, autonomous vehicles capture that expanded demand without drivers, so productivity gains flow to fewer human workers rather than more driving jobs. Segments requiring human presence (paratransit assistance, wheelchair lifts, executive chauffeur duties, luggage handling) provide partial insulation, but they represent a minority of the workforce. High disruption combined with demand growth that bypasses human drivers points to significant headcount contraction, fitting the replace category.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on vehicle operation, real-time navigation, and passenger handling in unpredictable traffic and weather; AI already transforms matching/routing via apps and GPS while autonomous vehicles (already deployed in limited markets) are on a clear 10-year trajectory to absorb the driving itself, making disruption high. Demand for rides has some latent upside if costs fall, yet expansion is capped by road capacity, regulation, and the fact that any growth will be met by robotaxis rather than more human drivers. High disruption plus low-moderate elasticity therefore produces net replacement and headcount contraction for the occupation.

title: Teacher assistants
claude_rationale: Teacher assistants face moderate-to-high disruption as AI can increasingly handle administrative tasks like recordkeeping, grade calculations, and basic instructional reinforcement through personalized tutoring systems. However, the core human elements—supervising students, providing emotional support, managing behavior, and working with special needs students—remain essential. Demand elasticity is high because personalized educational support is currently constrained by cost and staffing limitations; AI-enhanced teacher assistants could dramatically expand access to individualized attention, especially in underserved schools and for special education needs. The combination of meaningful AI augmentation with strong latent demand for personalized educational support suggests the occupation will evolve rather than contract.
opus_rationale: The core work of teacher assistants is physical and interpersonal—supervising students, providing one-on-one attention, assisting special-needs students with feeding and hygiene, monitoring recess and buses, and managing classroom behavior. AI may help with peripheral tasks like recordkeeping, attendance, and generating learning materials, but the in-person supervision and physical caregiving cannot be automated. Demand is structurally constrained by school budgets, student-to-staff ratios, and the inherent need for human presence rather than by cost or speed of producing output, so productivity gains do not unlock large new demand. Because disruption is low and the work depends on irreplaceable physical and relational presence, this occupation is resilient to AI.
opus5_rationale: The core of this job is physical, in-person presence: supervising students at recess and lunch, managing behavior, lifting and assisting special-needs students with feeding and hygiene, and providing the human attention a lead teacher cannot. AI can absorb some peripheral tasks (attendance, grade calculation, preparing materials) and adaptive tutoring software may substitute for a portion of one-on-one lesson reinforcement, but these are a minority of daily duties and cannot replace custodial supervision or caregiving. Demand elasticity is moderate: there is genuine latent demand for more individualized student support, but headcount is set almost entirely by school district budgets and state aide-to-student ratios rather than by productivity or price, so cheaper AI tools would not translate into more aides being hired. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient — its trajectory will continue to be driven by school funding and enrollment rather than by AI.
openai_rationale: Teacher assistants perform a mix of tasks, including reinforcing lessons, supervising students, and helping with administrative duties. While AI can assist with some administrative tasks and potentially offer digital tutoring aids, the core responsibilities of providing personalized attention and supervision are less susceptible to automation. The demand for teacher assistants is relatively inelastic; even if AI makes some tasks more efficient, the need for human presence in educational settings, especially for special education, remains. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption, with limited impact on headcount.
gpt55_rationale: Teacher assistants have a mix of instructional, administrative, supervisory, and caregiving tasks, and AI can materially help with lesson reinforcement, practice exercises, translation, progress tracking, and recordkeeping. However, much of the job depends on in-person classroom presence, behavior management, student supervision, relationship-building, and in special education or childcare settings, hands-on physical assistance that AI cannot replace well over the next decade. Demand for individualized student support is substantial, but public school budgets, staffing models, enrollment levels, and safety requirements limit how much cheaper AI-enabled assistance translates into more teacher-assistant jobs. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient: AI will change tools and workflows, but not fully reshape or absorb the core role.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can materially assist with lesson reinforcement, personalized exercises, progress tracking, grading, and recordkeeping. However, much of the occupation requires in-person supervision, behavior management, relationship building, and hands-on support for young or disabled students. Demand for individualized instruction could expand, but enrollment, staffing budgets, and the need for physical coverage limit that expansion. Because AI changes the instructional and administrative portions without replacing the occupation’s presence-dependent core, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: The instructional-reinforcement portion of the job (reviewing lessons, drilling material) is squarely in AI tutoring's path, and admin tasks like grading and attendance are easily automated, but the core of the role — physical supervision, behavior management, and hands-on care for special education students including feeding and hygiene — requires human presence that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper individualized instruction via AI could shift some tutoring demand away from aides, but demand for adult supervision is tied to student headcount and school budgets, not instruction cost, with special-needs support providing a structural demand floor. Because most daily work is physical and interpersonal rather than digital, disruption stays at 4, making this occupation resilient even as its tutoring-adjacent tasks migrate to AI tools.
grok45_rationale: Teacher assistants spend substantial time on physical presence tasks—supervising recess/lunch/field trips, managing behavior, and providing hands-on support for special-needs students (hygiene, mobility)—so AI can only assist peripheral cognitive pieces such as recordkeeping, material prep, and some one-on-one lesson reinforcement via tutoring software. Demand is constrained by fixed student demographics, public-school budgets, and regulatory staffing ratios; even if AI made assistance far cheaper, schools would not expand headcount dramatically. Because disruption remains moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI augments admin and instructional support without displacing the core human-presence role.

title: Technical writers
claude_rationale: Technical writing is highly susceptible to AI disruption as it involves core tasks like writing, editing, content creation, and information synthesis that AI excels at - current tools can already draft technical documentation, create user guides, and convert complex information into accessible formats. Demand elasticity is moderate because while cheaper technical writing could unlock some latent demand (more products getting proper documentation, smaller companies creating user guides), growth is constrained by the fact that documentation needs are typically tied to specific products and regulatory requirements rather than being infinitely expandable. The net effect is restructure because technical writers will need to shift toward higher-level skills like user experience research, cross-functional collaboration, and strategic content planning while AI handles routine documentation tasks.
opus_rationale: Technical writing is almost entirely language-based digital work—drafting manuals, editing, standardizing content, generating FAQs—all squarely in the direct path of LLMs that already produce competent documentation from product specs. Demand elasticity is low because documentation needs are largely fixed by the number of products and features shipped; cheaper writing does not cause companies to produce dramatically more manuals, though some latent demand for richer, multi-format content exists. With disruption at 8 and elasticity at 4, productivity gains translate mostly into fewer writers needed per project rather than expanded output, consistent with BLS noting AI will suppress already-flat employment growth.
opus5_rationale: Technical writing is almost entirely digital language work — drafting manuals, editing, standardizing terminology, restructuring content for different audiences and formats — which is squarely in the path of current LLMs, and AI tools already draft and localize documentation from code, specs, and SME interviews. Demand has some latent expansion (more products documented, more languages, richer multimedia, always-current docs), but documentation is a cost center tied to the number of products shipped rather than a service consumers buy more of when cheaper, so volume growth is structurally capped. With very high disruption and only low elasticity, productivity gains mostly convert into smaller documentation teams where a few senior writers curate AI output and manage information architecture, matching BLS's own note that AI productivity will slow employment growth.
openai_rationale: Technical writing is highly susceptible to AI disruption due to its predominantly digital and language-based nature. AI tools can assist in drafting, editing, and even generating technical content, which aligns closely with the core tasks of technical writers. However, the demand elasticity is moderate. While AI can increase productivity, the demand for technical writing is not heavily suppressed by cost, and the need for human oversight and customization remains. Thus, while AI will significantly alter the skill set required, it will not eliminate the need for human technical writers entirely, leading to a 'restructure' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: Technical writing is predominantly digital, language-based knowledge work, and current AI systems can already draft, revise, summarize, translate, standardize, and adapt documentation from specifications, code, tickets, and product notes. Human workers will still be important for validating technical accuracy, interviewing subject-matter experts, understanding user needs, managing documentation architecture, and handling liability-sensitive or highly specialized material. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper documentation enables better internal knowledge bases, localization, personalized help, and more frequent updates, but it remains constrained by the number of products, regulatory requirements, and organizational willingness to maintain documentation. Because disruption is high but demand expansion is only moderate, the occupation is likely to restructure rather than disappear, with fewer purely drafting roles and more emphasis on technical judgment, information design, and AI-assisted documentation workflows.
gpt56sol_rationale: Technical writing is predominantly digital and language-based, and AI can already draft, revise, summarize, translate, standardize, and reformat documentation from source materials. Human expertise remains important for eliciting undocumented knowledge, validating technical accuracy, understanding user needs, conducting usability work, and managing legal or safety risks. Lower costs will support more frequent updates, broader product coverage, and better documentation for smaller organizations, but demand remains constrained by the number of products, compliance needs, and users' limited appetite for documentation. The occupation therefore will restructure around subject-matter judgment, verification, information architecture, and AI-enabled content operations, with fewer roles focused mainly on drafting.
fable5_rationale: Technical writing is almost entirely digital, language-based knowledge work — drafting manuals, FAQs, and how-to guides is squarely in the path of current LLMs, which can already generate first-draft documentation directly from code, specs, or engineer interviews. Demand for documentation is largely derivative of product output rather than price: companies will not consume 10x more manuals just because they are cheaper, and much documentation may be replaced by AI-generated, on-demand answers rather than static docs, capping elasticity at low levels despite some latent demand for better localization and coverage. With high disruption and low demand expansion, productivity gains translate into fewer writers needed, with remaining roles shifting toward content strategy, review, and prompt/knowledge-base curation. BLS's near-zero projected growth already hints at this contraction pressure.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks—researching products, drafting/editing manuals, FAQs, and multi-modal content, standardizing across platforms—are almost entirely digital, language-based, and cognitive, with current LLMs already generating usable first drafts from specs or code and accelerating revision cycles. Demand expands moderately because cheaper documentation unlocks more thorough coverage, multi-language versions, interactive media, and professional docs for smaller firms and open-source projects, yet overall volume remains tethered to the finite pace of product releases rather than exploding. High disruption plus only moderate elasticity means the occupation persists but shifts toward AI orchestration, domain expertise, usability research, and complex multi-stakeholder coordination; non-adapters face displacement while adapters produce far more output.

title: Telecommunications technicians
claude_rationale: Telecommunications technicians perform predominantly physical, hands-on work including climbing towers, installing cables, splicing fiber optics, and troubleshooting hardware in unpredictable real-world environments. While AI might assist with some diagnostic tasks or record-keeping, the core work of physical installation, repair, and maintenance of telecommunications infrastructure requires human presence and manual dexterity. Demand for telecommunications services is relatively inelastic - people and businesses need a fixed amount of connectivity regardless of installation costs, and productivity gains in installation speed don't translate to dramatically more infrastructure being built. The occupation remains resilient as AI cannot meaningfully change the fundamentally physical nature of the work.
opus_rationale: Disruption is low because the core work is physical: climbing towers, splicing fiber optic cables, installing equipment in homes, digging trenches, and working in cramped or elevated spaces. AI can assist with remote diagnostics, network monitoring, and troubleshooting (central office technicians already correct issues remotely), but the hands-on installation and repair tasks require unpredictable real-world presence and dexterity that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low-to-moderate because demand is driven by infrastructure buildout cycles (5G, broadband expansion) that are largely complete, and newer fiber technologies require less frequent maintenance—productivity gains don't unlock much new physical demand. Since disruption is well under 6, this occupation is resilient: AI touches the monitoring and diagnostic periphery but leaves the physical core intact.
opus5_rationale: Core work is hands-on physical installation and repair — climbing towers, splicing fiber, crawling in attics, working in customer premises — which AI cannot perform without robotics that is far from deployment. AI touches only peripheral elements: remote network monitoring, automated fault diagnostics and self-healing networks, scheduling optimization, and AR-assisted troubleshooting guides, which can modestly reduce truck rolls and diagnostic labor per job. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because telecom buildout is driven by capital investment cycles, spectrum policy, and broadband funding rather than technician labor cost, and newer fiber infrastructure inherently needs less maintenance. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient to AI even though BLS projects mild decline for structural (infrastructure cycle) reasons rather than AI substitution.
openai_rationale: Telecommunications technicians primarily perform physical tasks such as installing and repairing equipment and cables, which are not easily automated by AI. While AI can assist in diagnostics and remote monitoring, the core work remains hands-on. Thus, the disruption score is low. Demand elasticity is also low because the need for telecommunications infrastructure is relatively stable and not significantly suppressed by cost. Even with increased efficiency, the demand for technicians does not expand proportionately, as infrastructure projects are finite and maintenance needs are consistent. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI-driven changes.
gpt55_rationale: Telecommunications technicians do use digital diagnostics, network monitoring systems, records, and customer communication, so AI can improve troubleshooting, documentation, scheduling, predictive maintenance, and remote guidance. However, the core work is still hands-on installation, repair, cable splicing, equipment setup, climbing, lifting, and working in homes, businesses, central offices, poles, trenches, or towers, which limits direct AI substitution over the next decade. Demand elasticity is fairly low because the need for telecom installation and repair is driven by infrastructure cycles, subscriber locations, permitting, and maintenance requirements rather than simply the cost of technician labor, though cheaper work could modestly accelerate upgrades or small deployments. Because disruption is low-to-moderate and the physical field component remains central, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: Core tasks involve traveling to worksites, climbing, handling cables and equipment, splicing fiber, and performing repairs in varied physical environments, which AI alone cannot readily execute. AI-enabled monitoring, diagnostics, scheduling, documentation, and troubleshooting guidance will improve productivity and reduce some remote or routine maintenance work. Cheaper service could support additional network upgrades and broader connectivity, but demand is constrained by infrastructure buildout cycles, capital budgets, and the declining maintenance needs of newer equipment. Because disruption remains low and concentrated in peripheral cognitive tasks, the occupation is resilient despite some ongoing employment pressure.
fable5_rationale: The core work — climbing towers, splicing fiber, installing lines, and physically repairing equipment in homes, central offices, and outdoor sites — is hands-on and requires unpredictable real-world presence, keeping AI's impact limited to peripheral tasks like diagnostics, remote monitoring, scheduling, and documentation. Elasticity is modest: telecom infrastructure demand is driven by build-out cycles (5G, broadband expansion) and durable low-maintenance technologies like fiber, not by the cost of technician labor, so cheaper knowledge work won't unlock much additional installation demand. AI-enhanced remote diagnostics and self-healing networks may trim some truck rolls, but the physical installation and repair core remains intact. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is resilient — its projected decline stems from infrastructure maturity, not AI displacement.
grok45_rationale: Core work is predominantly physical and site-specific—climbing towers/poles, splicing fiber, installing routers and lines in homes/businesses, and hands-on repairs—making AI largely irrelevant beyond peripheral diagnostics, remote monitoring alerts, predictive maintenance software, and record-keeping. This matches low-disruption trades like electricians. Elasticity is limited because infrastructure demand is constrained by project completion cycles, saturation of connectivity needs, and reduced maintenance for modern fiber/5G systems; cheaper/faster work unlocks only modest expansion in underserved areas rather than transformative volume. Low disruption therefore keeps the occupation resilient overall.

title: Tellers
claude_rationale: Teller work is highly digital and routine - counting cash, processing transactions, verifying accounts, and recording data electronically - tasks that AI and automation can handle well, with enhanced ATMs and video kiosks already replacing many teller functions. Demand for teller services is highly inelastic because banking transaction volume is relatively fixed regardless of processing speed or cost, and customers increasingly prefer self-service digital options over human interaction for routine transactions. The combination of high AI disruption potential and inelastic demand creates a clear replacement scenario, which aligns with the BLS projection of 13% employment decline.
opus_rationale: Teller work is a mix of physical cash handling and digital transaction processing; while ATMs, mobile banking, and enhanced kiosks already automate much of the routine work, the in-person presence, identity verification, and customer-service interaction keep a human element, putting disruption at a moderate level rather than fully digital. Demand is highly inelastic—people do not perform dramatically more banking transactions just because they are cheaper or faster; the volume is structurally fixed and already shifting away from branches. Despite low elasticity, the disruption score falls at 6 (driven mainly by automation eliminating positions rather than AI reshaping the core human-facing role), so it lands in the resilient category by the threshold rule, though the occupation is clearly contracting due to broader automation and branch closures rather than generative AI specifically.
opus5_rationale: Teller work is routine transaction processing, identity verification, account Q&A, and light product referral — nearly all of which is already being absorbed by mobile banking, enhanced ATMs, video kiosks, and AI chat/voice agents; the only genuinely physical component is cash handling, which machines already do well. Demand elasticity is very low: cheaper transaction processing does not make people deposit checks or exchange currency 10x more often, and branch traffic is structurally declining as customers self-serve. Productivity gains therefore flow directly into fewer tellers per branch and fewer branches, consistent with the BLS -13% projection. High disruption plus near-fixed demand puts this squarely in the replace category, with surviving roles skewing toward complex problem resolution and sales referral.
openai_rationale: The role of tellers is highly susceptible to disruption by AI and automation, as many of their core tasks, such as processing transactions and handling customer inquiries, can be digitized or automated.
