Technologies like enhanced ATMs and online banking already reduce the need for in-person transactions. The demand elasticity is low because the need for tellers is not significantly suppressed by cost; rather, it is driven by the number of physical bank branches and customer preference for digital services. As AI makes these services more efficient, the headcount for tellers is expected to shrink, leading to a 'replace' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: Teller work is heavily composed of routine transaction processing, identity verification, balance checks, account questions, and electronic recordkeeping, all of which are directly exposed to ATMs, mobile banking, chatbots, remote video tellers, and AI-assisted customer service. Some physical cash handling and in-branch interpersonal service remain, but the core workflow is already being automated and centralized. Demand is highly inelastic because cheaper teller transactions do not cause customers to deposit checks, withdraw cash, or visit branches many times more often; in fact, branch traffic is structurally declining. With high disruption and very low demand expansion, AI and related automation are likely to reduce headcount substantially.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most teller transactions are routine, rules-based, and already being shifted to mobile banking, enhanced ATMs, video kiosks, and AI-enabled customer-service systems, although some cash handling and complex in-person interactions remain. Demand is highly inelastic because cheaper transaction processing will not cause customers to make substantially more deposits, withdrawals, or branch visits. High disruption combined with minimal demand expansion means banks can serve customers with fewer tellers, making replace the appropriate category.
fable5_rationale: Teller work is dominated by routine transaction processing, account queries, and record-keeping — tasks already heavily absorbed by mobile banking, enhanced ATMs, and AI-powered customer service, with the remaining physical cash handling also increasingly automated. Demand is highly inelastic: making transactions faster or cheaper does not cause people to visit bank branches more; in fact, consumers are actively migrating away from in-person banking regardless of cost. BLS already projects a 13% decline, and AI chatbots plus automated kiosks will accelerate the reduction of tellers per branch and branch counts overall. High disruption combined with fixed-to-shrinking demand places this squarely in the replace category.
grok45_rationale: Core teller tasks—verifying identities, processing deposits/checks, recording transactions electronically, balancing drawers, and answering routine account questions—are predominantly routine, cognitive, and digital, already being materially automated by online banking, mobile deposits, enhanced ATMs, video kiosks, and AI chatbots, with physical cash handling steadily declining. Demand elasticity is low because the total volume of banking transactions is essentially fixed (or shrinking for in-person channels) and not suppressed by teller cost; customers prefer free self-service digital options rather than consuming more human teller interactions even if they become cheaper. High disruption combined with inelastic demand therefore produces net replacement and headcount contraction, consistent with the already-projected 13% decline.

title: Top executives
claude_rationale: Top executives face moderate disruption as AI can assist with data analysis, financial reporting, and strategic planning tasks, but the core responsibilities of leadership, relationship building, high-stakes decision-making, and organizational governance require human judgment, emotional intelligence, and accountability that AI cannot replicate. Demand elasticity is low because executive positions are structurally limited by organizational hierarchy and governance needs - companies don't suddenly need 10x more CEOs just because AI makes some executive tasks more efficient. The disruption score of 6 places this occupation in the resilient category, where AI augments certain analytical and administrative aspects but doesn't fundamentally reshape the core leadership and strategic responsibilities.
opus_rationale: Top executive work involves substantial cognitive tasks like analyzing financial reports, identifying cost savings, and formulating strategy that AI tools can meaningfully augment, but the core of the job—leadership, accountability, negotiation, high-stakes judgment, stakeholder relationships, and bearing ultimate responsibility for organizational outcomes—is inherently human and not in AI's direct path. AI will reshape how executives gather information and model decisions but cannot assume the legal, fiduciary, and social authority the role requires. Demand for executives is structurally fixed by the number of organizations rather than the cost or speed of executive output, so productivity gains do not unlock proportionally more demand. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the analytical periphery while the decision-making and leadership core remains intact.
opus5_rationale: Much of the executive information-processing layer — analyzing financial statements, sales reports, drafting policies, preparing board materials, scheduling and coordinating operations — is squarely in AI's path, and general/operations managers will see reporting and planning workflows substantially automated. But the irreducible core is accountability, legal and fiduciary authority, negotiation, motivating and appointing people, and bearing responsibility for outcomes; organizations require a human decision-maker regardless of how cheap analysis becomes, and much of the role involves in-person presence and political/relational capital. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper management overhead could let more small ventures and units exist (and self-employed executives are 26% of chief executives), but headcount is fundamentally tied to the number of organizations and units rather than to output volume, so gains partly compress middle-layer management. With disruption at 6, the occupation is best classified as resilient — AI reshapes how executives get information and possibly thins the ranks of coordination-heavy operations managers, but does not displace the core authority function.
openai_rationale: Top executives engage in predominantly cognitive and strategic tasks, such as planning, decision-making, and leadership, which are less susceptible to direct AI replacement. AI can assist in data analysis and decision support, but the core tasks require human judgment and interpersonal skills. While AI could enhance productivity, the demand for top executives is not highly elastic due to the strategic nature of their roles and the limited number of executive positions available. Therefore, the net effect is 'resilient' as AI will augment but not fundamentally replace the role.
gpt55_rationale: Top executives perform highly cognitive work—strategy, budgeting, performance analysis, communications, and policy setting—so AI will materially improve decision support, reporting, scenario analysis, and drafting. However, the core of the role also depends on authority, accountability, leadership, negotiation, organizational legitimacy, and managing people in real institutional contexts, which limits full automation. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because the number of executive and general management roles is tied to the number and structure of organizations, not simply the cost of producing analysis or decisions. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to replace the human leadership and accountability function, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially automate executives’ analysis, reporting, planning, scheduling, drafting, and performance-monitoring tasks, although leadership, negotiation, accountability, and stakeholder trust remain human-intensive. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations generally will not employ many more executives simply because managerial analysis becomes cheaper; instead, executives may oversee broader spans of activity with fewer supporting management layers. With disruption reaching the high threshold and elasticity remaining low, the aggregate occupation—especially general and operations managers—is likely to experience headcount pressure even though human chief executives remain necessary.
fable5_rationale: Top executives do predominantly cognitive work — analyzing financials, drafting strategy, reviewing reports — where AI is already a powerful assistant, but the core of the role is accountability, negotiation, board relations, organizational leadership, and high-stakes judgment that stakeholders require a human to own; this keeps disruption at the boundary of moderate and high. Elasticity is low-to-moderate: organizations need roughly one CEO and a bounded layer of general managers regardless of how cheap analysis becomes, though AI-lowered barriers to starting and running small businesses could modestly expand the number of executive roles. With AI compressing the analytical staff work beneath executives more than the executive role itself, the occupation's core — deciding, leading, and being accountable — remains intact. Disruption at 6 places this in resilient, though executives who fail to leverage AI for decision support will be at a competitive disadvantage.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on knowledge work such as analyzing financials and performance data, formulating strategy and policies, and identifying cost or process improvements, all of which AI already assists materially via analytics, scenario modeling, and drafting; leadership, negotiation, and interpersonal accountability still require human presence, keeping disruption high rather than total. Demand elasticity is moderate because organizational hierarchies and the finite number of firms limit how many top roles can exist, yet cheaper/faster executive capacity can unlock better management in smaller firms and more ambitious scaling, producing some expansion without unlimited growth. High disruption paired with only moderate elasticity therefore fits restructure: the occupation persists but the skill mix shifts heavily toward AI orchestration and judgment, displacing those who fail to adapt.

title: Tour and travel guides
claude_rationale: Tour and travel guides have moderate disruption potential as AI can assist with research, route planning, and basic information delivery, but the core value lies in human presence, interpersonal engagement, storytelling, and real-time adaptation to group dynamics in physical spaces. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper tour services could expand access to guided experiences and enable more personalized or niche tours, but growth is constrained by the inherently location-based nature of tourism and physical capacity limits of attractions. Since disruption remains moderate (AI enhances but doesn't replace the human-centric experience), this occupation falls into the resilient category despite moderate demand elasticity.
opus_rationale: The core work is physical, in-person, and interpersonal — escorting groups, reading the room, adapting to weather and group needs, and providing live entertainment and human rapport. AI can assist with peripheral tasks like research, route planning, itinerary logistics, and language translation, but it cannot replace the embodied presence and personal engagement that define the role. Demand for guided experiences could expand somewhat as travel and leisure grow and AI lowers planning costs, but it's tied to physical tourism volume rather than unleashed by cheap digital output. With disruption well below 6, this occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.
opus5_rationale: The core of the job is in-person: physically leading groups, reading the room, managing logistics on the ground, and providing a human hospitality experience that tourists explicitly pay for. AI meaningfully helps with the peripheral knowledge work — researching site history, drafting scripts, planning routes, handling bookings and translation — and audio/AR self-guided apps offer some substitution at the low end, but they mostly compete with free/cheap alternatives rather than replace guided experiences. Demand is moderately elastic since cheaper trip planning and translation could expand tour offerings and niche/multilingual tours, but the service is inherently time-bound and labor-intensive, capping expansion. With disruption well below the threshold, the occupation is resilient; AI becomes a prep and marketing tool for guides rather than a substitute for their presence.
openai_rationale: Tour and travel guides perform tasks that are predominantly physical and interpersonal, such as leading tours, interacting with clients, and adapting to real-world conditions, which limits AI's ability to disrupt core tasks. While AI can assist with planning and information dissemination, the human element remains crucial. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can make planning more efficient, the unique human experience provided by guides is not easily scalable. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting peripheral tasks but not replacing the core human-centric work.
gpt55_rationale: AI can materially assist with research, itinerary planning, translation, ticketing, marketing, and even provide automated audio or AR-based narration, so a significant information-delivery portion of the job is exposed. However, the core work still involves in-person presence, group management, hospitality, adapting to weather and crowd conditions, safety, and creating a live social experience, which limits full automation. Demand could expand moderately because cheaper personalized tour content may encourage more visitors to use guided experiences, but travel time, site capacity, and the value of human interaction constrain that expansion. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the occupation’s core physical and interpersonal role, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can substantially assist with research, itinerary design, reservations, marketing, translation, and scripted narration, while apps and augmented-reality systems may substitute for basic informational tours. However, escorting groups, managing logistics and safety, adapting to real-world conditions, and providing engaging human interaction still require physical presence and interpersonal judgment. Lower-cost guidance may increase personalized and multilingual tour consumption somewhat, but demand is constrained by tourism volumes, site capacity, and travelers’ time, so the occupation remains resilient while its administrative and informational tasks become more automated.
fable5_rationale: The core work — physically escorting groups, reading the room, managing pacing, and providing engaging in-person interaction — requires human presence and social rapport that AI cannot replicate. AI meaningfully assists peripheral tasks like itinerary planning, research, marketing, and booking logistics, and AI audio guides may substitute for the lowest-value tours, but people who pay for guided experiences are largely buying human connection and entertainment. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper trip-planning could expand tourism volume somewhat, and the experience economy is growing, but demand is bounded by travel time and disposable income rather than guide cost. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient — BLS's projected 8% growth reflects that leisure demand outweighs any AI substitution at the margins.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on physical escorting of groups, real-time pacing adjustments, live interpersonal engagement, and handling unpredictable outdoor or site conditions, so AI only meaningfully assists peripheral knowledge work such as research, route planning, and script generation. Demand elasticity is moderate because AI-driven productivity that lowers the cost of high-quality guided experiences can unlock additional leisure travel and niche tours, yet expansion remains bounded by physical site capacity, seasonal constraints, and travelers’ limited free time. With disruption only in the moderate range, AI touches preparation and information delivery without reshaping the occupation’s essential human-presence requirements, placing it firmly in the resilient category.

title: Training and development managers
claude_rationale: Training and development managers face high disruption as AI can automate content creation, personalize learning paths, assess training needs through data analysis, and generate training materials - core knowledge work activities that comprise much of their role. However, demand elasticity is moderate because while cheaper AI-powered training tools will expand access to professional development, organizational training budgets and regulatory requirements for certain types of training create structural limits on demand expansion. The combination of high disruption and moderate elasticity places this occupation in the restructure category, where managers who adapt to leverage AI tools for content creation and data-driven insights will thrive, while those who don't will be displaced.
opus_rationale: The role involves substantial knowledge work—designing training content, selecting materials, evaluating program effectiveness—much of which AI tools (content generation, personalized learning platforms, analytics) can directly accelerate, pushing disruption toward the high end. However, core managerial duties like aligning training with business strategy, supervising staff, budgeting, and stakeholder collaboration require human judgment and presence, keeping disruption at a moderate 6. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper, AI-personalized training could expand reskilling efforts as workforces face continuous change, but headcount of managers (versus content output) is structurally capped. Since disruption is 6 (<=6), the occupation falls into resilient—AI reshapes how content and delivery work but the managerial core remains intact.
opus5_rationale: Core work — designing curricula, producing training content, assessing needs, evaluating program effectiveness — is predominantly digital and language-based, and generative AI already produces course materials, assessments, simulations, and personalized learning paths at a fraction of prior cost, so disruption is high; the leadership, budget, and stakeholder-alignment portions remain human. Elasticity is high because corporate learning is chronically underfunded and rationed by content-production cost, and AI-driven workforce change is itself creating enormous reskilling demand — cheaper, personalized training means far more of it gets delivered, not less. The likely path is each manager overseeing dramatically more content and more AI-assisted personalization rather than headcount shrinking, though the skill mix shifts toward learning-technology and AI-tool orchestration.
openai_rationale: Training and development managers are likely to experience moderate disruption due to AI, as their role involves a mix of digital and interpersonal tasks. AI can assist in creating and updating training materials, evaluating program effectiveness, and managing logistics, but human oversight and interpersonal skills remain crucial. The elasticity is high because as AI reduces costs and increases the efficiency of training programs, organizations are likely to expand their training efforts to enhance employee skills and adapt to new technologies. This expansion in demand for training services suggests that the occupation will be augmented rather than replaced by AI advancements.
gpt55_rationale: Training and development managers do substantial cognitive and digital work: assessing skill gaps, selecting or creating curricula, evaluating program effectiveness, managing learning platforms, and communicating training strategy. AI can materially automate or accelerate needs analysis, content generation, course personalization, vendor comparison, assessment design, and learning analytics, though stakeholder management, organizational judgment, budgeting, and leadership remain human-centered. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper customized training will unlock more reskilling, compliance, and employee-development activity, especially as AI changes other jobs, but the number of management roles is still constrained by organizational size and reporting structures. The occupation is therefore likely to be restructured rather than replaced, with managers shifting toward AI-enabled learning strategy, governance, and change management.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can substantially accelerate needs analysis, curriculum design, content creation, personalization, vendor evaluation, and measurement of training outcomes. However, stakeholder alignment, budget ownership, staff leadership, organizational judgment, and change management remain human-intensive. Lower costs and rapid workforce reskilling needs should expand training activity, but managerial demand is constrained by organizational budgets and spans of control. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-enabled learning strategy and oversight rather than experience wholesale replacement.
fable5_rationale: The core work — designing curricula, creating and selecting training content, assessing needs, and evaluating program effectiveness — is predominantly digital knowledge work where AI already generates instructional materials, personalizes learning paths, and analyzes training outcomes, though the managerial, budgeting, and stakeholder-alignment aspects retain human elements. Elasticity is moderate-to-good: AI-driven workplace transformation itself creates enormous continuous reskilling demand, and cheaper training production lets organizations train more people more often, but headcount growth is capped because AI simultaneously shrinks the specialist teams these managers oversee and consolidates content production. The role survives but shifts from managing instructional designers and course production toward orchestrating AI-powered learning platforms and strategic workforce capability planning, fitting the restructure category.
grok45_rationale: Core work is predominantly cognitive and digital—needs assessment, program design, content selection/creation, evaluation, and budget alignment—all of which AI already accelerates via generative content tools, adaptive learning platforms, and analytics, placing the role in the high-disruption band even though people leadership and organizational alignment remain human. Elasticity is high because organizations chronically under-invest in training due to cost and speed constraints; dramatically cheaper, faster, personalized programs unlock large latent demand for continuous reskilling, especially as AI itself reshapes jobs. Productivity gains are therefore absorbed by expanded training volume rather than pure headcount reduction, so the occupation is augmented: managers oversee far more sophisticated systems and larger portfolios of learning.

title: Training and development specialists
claude_rationale: Training and development work is highly disrupted by AI, as core tasks like creating training materials, designing curricula, assessing needs, and delivering content are predominantly knowledge-based and digital. AI tools already assist with content creation, personalized learning paths, and automated assessment. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster training development could unlock massive latent demand - organizations currently constrained by cost and time could provide more frequent upskilling, personalized learning, and compliance training. As technology accelerates and skills become obsolete faster, the need for continuous workforce development will expand dramatically when AI makes it more accessible and affordable.
opus_rationale: Disruption is high because core tasks—designing training materials, creating online learning modules, developing course content, and assessing needs through surveys—are largely digital and language-based, areas where generative AI already excels at content creation, instructional design, and personalization. However, the in-person delivery, facilitation, and interpersonal collaboration portions retain a human element, keeping it from the very-high tier. Elasticity is high because cheaper, faster training content production unlocks substantial latent demand: continuous upskilling driven by rapid technological change, regulatory compliance training, and personalized learning that was previously too costly to develop at scale. With AI dramatically lowering content production costs, organizations will produce far more tailored training, expanding total demand enough to absorb productivity gains and supporting the BLS-projected 11% growth.
opus5_rationale: Core tasks — needs assessment surveys, writing training manuals, building e-learning modules, quizzes and evaluation reports — are language- and content-generation work squarely in AI's path; authoring tools with generative AI already compress instructional design cycles from weeks to hours. The counterweight is live facilitation, stakeholder consultation, and organization-specific credibility, which keeps a human presence requirement and holds disruption at the lower end of 'high.' Elasticity is high because corporate training is chronically under-supplied and cost-rationed: personalized, role-specific, continuously updated curricula were previously unaffordable, and the AI transition itself is generating enormous new upskilling and compliance-training demand. Cheaper content production therefore expands the volume and granularity of training rather than shrinking headcount, though the skill mix shifts toward AI-assisted design, curation, quality control, and facilitation.
openai_rationale: Training and development specialists are likely to experience high disruption due to AI's ability to automate and enhance tasks like assessing training needs, designing materials, and delivering training through digital platforms. However, the core tasks still require human interaction and creativity, keeping disruption moderate. Demand elasticity is high because as AI makes training more efficient and personalized, more organizations will invest in continuous learning and upskilling, expanding the market for training services. Thus, the net effect is 'augment' as AI enhances productivity but demand grows to absorb these gains.
gpt55_rationale: Training and development specialists perform many language- and knowledge-based tasks that AI can materially accelerate, including drafting learning modules, quizzes, manuals, simulations, surveys, and evaluation reports. However, the occupation also depends on stakeholder consultation, organizational diagnosis, live facilitation, coaching, and change management, which limits full automation. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper training unlocks more frequent upskilling, personalized learning, compliance refreshers, and AI-related workforce retraining that many employers currently underprovide due to cost and time. Because disruption is high but expanded demand for training is likely to absorb much of the productivity gain, the net effect is best characterized as augment.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can already accelerate needs analysis, course design, content generation, assessment creation, program evaluation, and training administration, placing most of the occupation’s digital and cognitive tasks in its direct path. Human facilitation, organizational judgment, stakeholder coordination, and adaptation to workplace dynamics remain important, preventing near-total automation. Lower costs will support more customized and continuous training, especially as AI itself creates widespread reskilling needs, but employee time, compliance requirements, and corporate budgets limit how much training organizations will consume. The occupation therefore is likely to persist with substantially changed skills and higher output per specialist, fitting restructure.
fable5_rationale: A large share of core tasks — designing training manuals, creating e-learning modules, drafting course materials, and building assessments — is digital knowledge work squarely in AI's path, with generative tools already producing instructional content and even AI-driven adaptive learning; live facilitation and needs assessment retain human elements, keeping disruption at 7 rather than higher. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper training production and the accelerating need to reskill workers (ironically driven by AI itself) unlock meaningful latent demand for more frequent, personalized upskilling, but AI tutors and self-serve learning platforms can absorb much of that expanded volume without proportional headcount growth. The occupation persists but shifts from content authoring toward curating AI-generated materials, learning strategy, and change management. High disruption with moderate elasticity fits the restructure category — specialists who master AI-augmented instructional design will thrive while traditional content developers face displacement.
grok45_rationale: Core work is predominantly knowledge-based—needs assessment, instructional design, content creation for manuals/modules, and program evaluation—all of which AI already accelerates via generative tools, adaptive learning platforms, and analytics, even if live facilitation and interpersonal delivery still require humans. Demand elasticity is high because training has long been under-provided due to cost and time; dramatically cheaper, faster, personalized programs unlock substantial latent corporate demand for continuous upskilling, compliance, and technology-driven reskilling. The combination produces an augment outcome: specialists who leverage AI will each design and deliver far more training while overall headcount grows with expanded organizational investment.

title: Transportation, storage, and distribution managers
claude_rationale: Transportation, storage, and distribution managers face moderate disruption as AI tools can assist with route optimization, inventory tracking, demand forecasting, and data analysis, but the core work remains heavily focused on human leadership, staff management, client relationships, and real-world operational oversight that requires physical presence and interpersonal skills. Demand elasticity is low because logistics needs are largely tied to existing economic activity - making supply chains 10x more efficient doesn't create 10x more goods to move, and regulatory constraints limit how much operational efficiency translates to expanded demand. The disruption score of 6 places this in the resilient category, where AI enhances capabilities but doesn't fundamentally reshape the occupation's core human-centered management responsibilities.
opus_rationale: Disruption is moderate because while AI strongly enhances the analytical and planning portions of the job—route optimization, demand forecasting, inventory tracking, and supply chain coordination—the core role centers on supervising staff, physical facility oversight, resolving real-time disruptions, and leadership functions that require human presence and judgment. Elasticity is moderate as cheaper, faster logistics analysis enables more sophisticated supply chain operations and e-commerce growth, but headcount is tied to the physical footprint of warehouses, fleets, and facilities that must be managed regardless of AI efficiency gains. Because disruption stays at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the data-driven planning tools these managers use but does not displace the supervisory, interpersonal, and on-site problem-solving that defines the role.
opus5_rationale: A substantial share of this role — route and network optimization, demand and inventory forecasting, load planning, compliance log review, budgeting and reporting — is exactly the kind of data-heavy analytic work AI and optimization software are already absorbing, which pushes disruption toward the high end. But the core of the job remains physically situated supervision of warehouse and driver workforces, on-the-ground crisis response to disruptions, facility safety, and negotiation with carriers, suppliers, and clients, which caps disruption at moderate-high. Elasticity is moderate: goods volume is bounded by real physical throughput and facility count, so cheaper planning does not create proportionally more freight, though smaller firms could afford more sophisticated logistics management and e-commerce keeps expanding node counts. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands as resilient — AI reshapes the analytical toolkit and raises expectations for data fluency, but the supervisory and physical-coordination core endures.
openai_rationale: Transportation, storage, and distribution managers are increasingly reliant on digital tools and AI for tasks like logistics planning, inventory management, and compliance monitoring. AI can optimize routes, predict demand, and automate routine decision-making, which significantly changes how these managers operate. However, the core tasks still require human oversight and decision-making, especially in problem-solving and leadership roles. The elasticity is high because the growth of e-commerce and the need for efficient supply chains drive demand for these managers. As AI makes logistics more efficient, the volume of goods managed can increase, expanding the need for skilled managers to oversee these operations.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially change the planning, routing, inventory monitoring, compliance review, procurement analysis, budgeting, and disruption-response parts of transportation, storage, and distribution management. However, the job still requires human leadership, accountability, on-site operational judgment, safety oversight, labor management, and coordination in physical facilities and transportation networks. Demand can expand as cheaper logistics management supports more e-commerce, faster delivery expectations, and more complex supply chains, but it is still constrained by physical goods volumes, facilities, fleets, and labor. Because disruption is high while demand elasticity is moderate, the occupation is best categorized as restructure: fewer managers may oversee more operations using AI, and the skill mix will shift toward systems supervision, exception handling, and cross-functional coordination.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially automate routing, inventory planning, scheduling, compliance review, forecasting, reporting, and operational monitoring. However, managers will remain necessary for leadership, labor relations, safety accountability, facility oversight, cross-functional negotiation, and resolving unpredictable physical-world disruptions. Cheaper management and optimization can support growing e-commerce volumes and more complex supply chains, but demand is constrained by the underlying flow of goods and AI may let each manager oversee larger operations. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-assisted decision-making and exception management rather than experience either wholesale replacement or proportional job growth.
fable5_rationale: A substantial share of this job — route planning, inventory tracking, scheduling, compliance monitoring, and supply chain optimization — is analytical and already being transformed by AI-driven logistics software, warehouse management systems, and predictive analytics. However, the core still requires physical presence in warehouses and yards, direct supervision of frontline workers, hiring, safety enforcement, and real-time crisis resolution in the physical world, keeping disruption at the high end of moderate. Elasticity is moderate: e-commerce growth and more complex supply chains create some expanded need for coordination, but each manager overseeing an AI-optimized operation can span a larger scope, so headcount doesn't scale with output. With disruption at 6, the occupation lands as resilient — AI reshapes the planning tools but not the fundamentally on-site, people-management core.
grok45_rationale: Disruption is high because core duties—planning networks, budgeting, inventory/procurement oversight, performance evaluation, compliance monitoring, and disruption response—are predominantly cognitive, data-driven, and language-based; AI tools already deliver material gains in forecasting, route/inventory optimization, automated reporting, and anomaly detection, with further trajectory toward autonomous decision support. Elasticity is moderate: e-commerce and supply-chain complexity create some latent demand for more sophisticated management, and cheaper tools could extend advanced logistics to smaller firms, yet overall volume of goods movement and physical infrastructure constraints limit expansion, so productivity gains will not fully offset headcount pressure. The combination produces restructure—roles persist but shift heavily toward AI orchestration, exception handling, and strategic oversight, displacing managers who cannot adapt while rewarding those who can.

title: Travel agents
claude_rationale: Travel agents face very high disruption as their core tasks—researching destinations, comparing prices, booking reservations, and providing travel information—are predominantly digital and knowledge-based activities that AI can increasingly handle. Online booking platforms and AI-powered travel assistants already perform much of this work, with AI becoming more sophisticated at understanding preferences and making personalized recommendations. Demand elasticity is low because travel frequency is largely constrained by personal budgets, vacation time, and life circumstances rather than the cost of booking services—making travel planning 10x cheaper wouldn't cause people to take 10x more trips. The combination of high AI disruption of core tasks and limited demand expansion creates a classic replacement scenario where productivity gains translate directly to fewer workers needed.
opus_rationale: The core work — searching fares, building itineraries, comparing options, booking reservations, and advising on documents — is almost entirely digital, language-based, and information-retrieval work that AI and online booking platforms already perform directly; this has been eroding the occupation for two decades and AI accelerates it further. Demand elasticity is low because total travel volume is constrained by household budgets and time, not by the cost of booking; cheaper agent services do not dramatically increase how many trips people take, and self-service tools already absorb much of the latent demand. With disruption very high and elasticity weak, productivity gains translate into fewer agents rather than expanded output, fitting the replace category, though a residual niche for complex, high-touch, or luxury planning persists.
opus5_rationale: Nearly all core tasks — searching fares and schedules, comparing options, building itineraries, calculating costs, booking reservations, and answering destination questions — are digital information-retrieval and language tasks squarely in AI's path, and this occupation was already hollowed out by online booking platforms. Consumer-facing AI travel planners disintermediate the agent directly rather than making agents more productive, so productivity gains accrue to travelers and platforms, not to agent headcount. Latent demand for trip planning does exist (people would plan more elaborate trips if expert advice were free), but that demand will be captured by AI tools and OTAs; total travel spending is capped by household budgets and time off, not by planning cost. A residual high-touch niche (luxury, complex group, corporate duty-of-care, crisis rebooking, first-hand destination knowledge) will persist, but overall the combination of very high disruption and inelastic, disintermediated demand points to headcount contraction.
openai_rationale: Travel agents' work involves a significant amount of digital and cognitive tasks, such as booking travel and providing personalized advice, which AI can increasingly assist with. AI tools can automate itinerary planning, fare comparison, and booking processes, leading to high disruption. However, the demand elasticity is low because the core service of travel agents—personalized travel planning—is not significantly suppressed by cost. While AI can enhance efficiency, it does not substantially increase the overall demand for travel agents, as many consumers already use online platforms for travel arrangements. Thus, the occupation will likely restructure, with agents needing to adapt to more advisory and niche roles.
gpt55_rationale: Travel agents perform highly digital, language- and information-processing tasks: eliciting preferences, comparing fares and schedules, building itineraries, explaining rules, and making reservations. Generative AI and travel platforms can already automate much of trip research, itinerary construction, customer Q&A, and rebooking support, although humans retain value for complex, luxury, group, and emergency travel situations. Demand elasticity is limited because the main constraint on travel is travelers’ time and trip budgets, not the cost of planning itself, though cheaper personalized planning may expand use somewhat. Because disruption is high and elasticity is low, AI is likely to reduce headcount among generalist agents while preserving more specialized advisory roles.
gpt56sol_rationale: Nearly all core tasks—researching options, comparing fares, designing itineraries, explaining requirements, booking reservations, and handling changes—are digital and increasingly executable by AI connected to reservation systems. Human agents retain advantages in sales, accountability, complex disruptions, group travel, and luxury or specialized trips, but these represent a narrower share of the market. Cheaper planning may increase itinerary customization and make advisory services accessible to more travelers, yet travel demand remains constrained by consumers’ money and time, so it will not rise proportionally with productivity. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount contraction and concentration in complex, high-touch niches.
fable5_rationale: Travel agents' core tasks — researching options, comparing fares, building itineraries, booking reservations, and advising on destinations — are almost entirely digital, language-based information work squarely in AI's current capability path; AI trip-planning tools and booking agents already perform much of this today. Elasticity is low because travel demand is driven by disposable income and leisure time, not by the cost of agent services, and the occupation already lost most of its market to self-service online booking; making agent-style planning 10x cheaper mostly means consumers use AI directly rather than hiring more agents. A niche will persist for high-touch luxury, group, and complex corporate travel, but this is a small share of current headcount. High disruption combined with inelastic demand points clearly to replacement and continued contraction.
grok45_rationale: Travel agents' core tasks—researching fares and options, building itineraries, booking reservations, calculating costs, and advising on destinations/documents—are almost entirely digital, cognitive, and language-based, with AI already generating personalized plans, searching inventories, and handling changes far faster than humans. Physical elements like destination visits are peripheral, so disruption is very high. Elasticity is low because total travel volume is constrained by travelers' time, money, and desire rather than planning friction; cheaper/faster service mainly shifts simple and mid-market bookings to AI tools and platforms instead of expanding overall demand enough to preserve headcount. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore fits 'replace,' expecting significant contraction as AI absorbs the bulk of the work.

title: Tutors
claude_rationale: Tutoring faces high disruption as AI can already provide personalized instruction, generate practice problems, explain concepts, and track student progress - core tutoring functions that are predominantly cognitive and language-based. However, demand elasticity is very high because personalized education has been historically limited by cost and access, with vast latent demand from students who cannot afford private tutoring. AI-powered tutoring tools can dramatically reduce costs and increase availability, potentially expanding the market from hundreds of thousands to millions of students globally. While AI will reshape how tutoring is delivered, the massive expansion in accessible personalized education will likely create more opportunities for human tutors who can provide emotional support, motivation, and complex problem-solving that complements AI tools.
opus_rationale: Tutoring is predominantly cognitive, language-based instruction that AI can directly perform—explaining concepts, generating practice problems, providing feedback, and adapting to student level are all squarely in AI's path, driving a high disruption score. However, demand for personalized education is heavily suppressed by cost and access, so dramatically cheaper, scalable AI-assisted tutoring unlocks enormous latent demand across underserved students and subjects. While pure commodity homework-help may shift to software, human tutors who leverage AI for personalized, high-touch, motivational, and special-needs instruction can serve far more students, keeping headcount stable or growing. The combination of high disruption and high elasticity fits the augment category, even though BLS projects flat near-term growth.
opus5_rationale: Tutoring is almost entirely language- and cognition-based work — explaining concepts, generating practice problems, giving feedback, drilling vocabulary — which sits directly in generative AI's core competence, and BLS itself notes AI software can already perform many routine tutoring activities. Elasticity is very high because personalized one-on-one instruction has historically been rationed by cost: most students who need academic support never get it, and cheap adaptive instruction unlocks enormous latent demand across K-12 remediation, ESL, test prep, and adult reskilling. The likely equilibrium is that AI handles content delivery and drilling while human tutors shift toward motivation, accountability, diagnosis, special-needs support, and supervising AI-driven learning plans — a large expansion of the total tutoring market that keeps human headcount roughly stable to growing even as productivity per tutor rises. The main downside risk is that much of the expanded demand is captured by software vendors rather than human tutors, which would push this toward restructure; but the sheer scale of unmet demand and the irreplaceable relational/engagement component support augment.
openai_rationale: AI has the potential to significantly disrupt the tutoring occupation by automating many of the tasks involved, such as providing feedback, preparing session materials, and monitoring student progress. AI-driven platforms can offer personalized learning experiences and practice questions, reducing the need for human tutors in some areas. However, the demand elasticity for tutoring is very high. If AI makes tutoring more affordable and accessible, it could unlock significant latent demand, especially in underserved markets or for subjects where personalized attention was previously too costly. This combination of high disruption and very high elasticity suggests that while the nature of tutoring work will change, the overall demand for tutoring services will expand, leading to an 'augment' net effect.
gpt55_rationale: Tutoring is highly exposed because many core tasks—explaining concepts, generating practice questions, giving feedback, adapting pacing, tracking progress, and preparing for tests—are language- and knowledge-based tasks that AI systems can already perform meaningfully. Human tutors still add value through motivation, trust, behavioral management, special-needs support, and relationships with parents or teachers, so the occupation is not fully automatable. Demand elasticity is very high because individualized academic help has historically been constrained by cost, scheduling, and access, and cheaper AI-enabled tutoring could greatly expand how many students receive support and how often. The net effect is augment: routine tutoring tasks will be heavily automated, but expanded access and AI-assisted human coaching should absorb much of the productivity gain while substantially changing how tutors work.
gpt56sol_rationale: Tutoring is predominantly cognitive and language-based, and current AI systems can already explain concepts, generate practice materials, provide feedback, and track progress. Human tutors retain advantages in motivation, trust, behavioral management, and adapting to subtle emotional or special-education needs, so disruption is very high rather than complete. Demand is highly elastic because personalized instruction has historically been constrained by cost and access, and cheaper tutoring could greatly increase its use across subjects, ages, and income groups. The result is augmentation: tutors who combine AI-generated instruction with human coaching can serve many more students, although routine homework help and test practice will face substantial automation.
fable5_rationale: Tutoring is almost entirely language-based cognitive work — explaining concepts, generating practice problems, giving feedback — all squarely in the path of current generative AI, which can already deliver personalized instruction at near-zero marginal cost. However, demand for personalized education has been massively suppressed by cost: at $40-60/hour, most families and students cannot afford regular tutoring, so a 10x cost reduction unlocks enormous latent demand across K-12 support, test prep, adult learning, and language instruction. Human tutors who leverage AI for lesson prep, drills, and progress tracking can serve more students, and demand for accountability, motivation, and human connection (especially for younger and special-needs students) keeps humans in the loop even as pure content delivery shifts to software. The combination of high disruption and very high demand elasticity fits 'augment' — the role transforms into an AI-supervised coaching model, with the expanded market absorbing productivity gains, though tutors offering only rote content review face displacement.
grok45_rationale: Core tutoring tasks—explaining concepts, generating practice problems, providing feedback, and adapting instruction—are predominantly cognitive and language-based, with AI tools already delivering personalized explanations and drills at scale, placing the occupation in the high-disruption range similar to teachers. Demand elasticity is very high because personalized one-on-one instruction has long been cost-prohibitive for most families and lifelong learners; dramatic reductions in price and speed unlock near-unlimited latent demand across K-12, test prep, adult upskilling, and special-needs support. The combination of high disruption with very high elasticity means productivity gains expand total tutoring output rather than shrink headcount, fitting the augment category as AI multiplies the reach of human tutors who focus on motivation, complex adaptation, and relationship-building.

title: Umpires, referees, and other sports officials
claude_rationale: Sports officiating requires real-time physical presence, split-second judgment calls based on visual observation of live action, and human authority to manage disputes - core functions that AI cannot replicate. While AI might assist with some rule interpretation or replay analysis, the fundamental work remains anchored in human perception and decision-making during live sporting events. Demand for officiating is largely fixed by the number of games played, which is constrained by league structures, school schedules, and facility availability rather than cost, so productivity gains wouldn't meaningfully expand total demand. The low disruption and inelastic demand make this occupation resilient to AI transformation.
opus_rationale: The core work is physical and presence-based: positioning oneself on the field, making split-second visual judgments, running/squatting for extended periods, and managing human disputes with coaches and players. AI-assisted technologies (video replay, automated ball-strike systems, goal-line tech) augment certain calls but do not replace the human official who manages the game, enforces rules, and provides the social authority that participants accept. Demand is tied to the number of games played, which expands with growing sports participation but is structurally bounded by the number of contests rather than by cost of officiating. Because disruption stays low and the work remains fundamentally physical and in-person, the occupation is resilient.
opus5_rationale: The core work is physical presence at live events, positioning, split-second judgment, and managing human disputes with players and coaches — almost none of which AI can replace. Automated ball-strike systems, goal-line technology, and video review do encroach on specific calls at elite levels, but these affect a tiny fraction of the 19,300 jobs (the vast majority officiate youth, high school, and recreational sports where cameras and tracking systems are cost-prohibitive), and even in pro leagues humans remain on the field to administer the game. Elasticity is moderate: demand is driven by the number of games played and youth sports participation, not by officiating cost, though officiating shortages suggest some latent unmet demand. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient — AI becomes a decision-support tool at the top of the pyramid rather than a substitute for the workforce.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of umpires, referees, and other sports officials are predominantly physical and require real-time decision-making and presence at sporting events, which limits AI's ability to disrupt the occupation significantly. While AI and video replay technology can assist in reviewing decisions, the human element remains crucial. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could enhance the speed and accuracy of officiating, the demand for sports officials is not heavily suppressed by cost or speed, as the role is integral to the structure of sports events. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption, with technology augmenting rather than replacing human officials.
gpt55_rationale: AI and computer vision can meaningfully assist with specific officiating tasks such as line calls, strike zones, timing, replay review, and detection of some rule violations, especially in professional and televised sports. However, the core job still requires real-time physical presence, positioning, judgment under ambiguous conditions, player safety oversight, communication, and dispute management in unpredictable live environments, particularly at youth, school, and recreational levels where most events lack advanced infrastructure. Demand for officiating is mostly tied to the number of games, teams, facilities, and sports participation, so making calls cheaper or faster would not create dramatically more sporting events. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient despite some task-level automation.
gpt56sol_rationale: Computer vision, sensor systems, and automated replay will increasingly assist or replace specific calls such as line judgments, scoring, and ball tracking. However, the core role still requires real-world presence, dynamic positioning, safety oversight, contextual judgment, communication, and dispute management, especially in youth and amateur sports where advanced technology is less economical. Demand is tied mainly to the number of organized competitions, so cheaper officiating could support some additional events but is constrained by participation, facilities, schedules, and league funding. Because AI will significantly alter selected decisions without broadly eliminating the human-centered officiating role, the occupation is resilient overall.
fable5_rationale: While AI-assisted officiating technology (automated ball-strike systems, Hawk-Eye line calling) is advancing at elite professional levels, the vast majority of officials work youth, high school, and recreational games where installing camera and sensor infrastructure is cost-prohibitive, and the core job requires physical presence, game management, safety oversight, and de-escalating disputes with players and coaches. Demand elasticity is low because the number of officials needed is fixed by the number of games played — cheaper officiating technology doesn't cause society to play meaningfully more games. With disruption well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient: AI may assist calls at the margins in televised sports, but on-field human authority remains central.
grok45_rationale: Core work requires physical presence on the field or court, real-time positioning, stamina, split-second human judgment under pressure, and direct interaction with players/coaches, so AI tools (video replay, automated line calls) assist only peripheral decision support rather than reshaping daily tasks. Demand for officials is driven by the fixed volume of games and sports participation rather than the cost or speed of officiating; even if AI made the role dramatically cheaper, the number of events would expand only modestly at amateur levels and not enough to offset productivity gains. Because disruption remains low, the occupation is resilient overall.

title: Urban and regional planners
claude_rationale: Urban and regional planners work primarily with digital tools (GIS software, data analysis, visualization tools) and knowledge-based tasks like analyzing data, creating reports, and developing plans - areas where AI is already making significant inroads. AI can increasingly handle data analysis, pattern recognition in urban development, and even generate planning recommendations based on multiple variables. However, demand elasticity is low because planning needs are largely driven by population growth and regulatory requirements rather than cost - communities don't suddenly need 10x more planning when it becomes cheaper, and government budgets constrain expansion regardless of efficiency gains.
opus_rationale: Much of planning involves cognitive, data-driven work — GIS analysis, data gathering, feasibility assessment, and report writing — which AI tools can materially accelerate, pushing disruption to the moderate-high boundary. However, the core work also involves stakeholder negotiation, public meetings, political judgment, site inspection, and discretionary decisions on plan approval that require human presence and accountability, capping disruption at 6. Demand is structurally constrained by government budgets, regulatory processes, and the fixed number of jurisdictions, so cheaper analysis would not dramatically expand headcount. Since disruption stays at the moderate level (<=6), the occupation is best classified as resilient: AI augments the analytical periphery without reshaping the human-centric core.
opus5_rationale: Planning work is predominantly knowledge work — data gathering and analysis, GIS mapping, scenario modeling, drafting comprehensive plans, reviewing site plans against zoning codes, and writing reports — all directly in AI's path, and generative AI plus automated GIS/zoning-compliance tools already materially accelerate these tasks. However, the occupation retains substantial non-automatable components: public hearings, stakeholder negotiation, political judgment, site visits, and legally accountable recommendations, which caps disruption below the very-high tier. Elasticity is moderate: cheaper analysis could unlock more frequent plan updates, faster permitting review, and planning capacity for small and rural jurisdictions that currently go without, but headcount is fundamentally gated by government budgets, fixed numbers of jurisdictions, and statutory processes rather than by analytical throughput. High disruption with moderate, budget-constrained demand expansion means the role persists but shifts toward facilitation, political navigation, and oversight of AI-generated analysis — a restructuring of the skill set rather than wholesale replacement.
openai_rationale: Urban and regional planners engage in a mix of tasks, including data analysis, stakeholder meetings, and site inspections. AI can assist with data analysis and GIS tasks, but the core work involves significant human judgment and interpersonal skills, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make planning more efficient, the demand for urban planning is constrained by government budgets and regulatory processes. Thus, while AI will augment planners' capabilities, it is unlikely to drastically change headcount, making the occupation resilient.
gpt55_rationale: Urban and regional planners do substantial digital and cognitive work—GIS analysis, demographic and environmental data synthesis, zoning research, report writing, scenario modeling, and presentation preparation—that AI can materially accelerate. However, the core occupation also depends heavily on stakeholder meetings, public process, local political judgment, site-specific context, regulatory accountability, and recommendations that must be defended to officials and communities. Demand could expand moderately if planning analysis becomes cheaper, especially for smaller jurisdictions and more frequent scenario testing, but public budgets, permitting timelines, and statutory processes limit how much additional planning work is consumed. Because AI reshapes many analytical tasks but does not replace the human-facing and governance-centered core, the occupation is best classified as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can materially accelerate GIS analysis, regulatory research, scenario modeling, site-plan review, report drafting, and public-presentation preparation, affecting a large share of planners’ knowledge work. However, field observation, stakeholder negotiation, public meetings, political judgment, and accountable approval recommendations remain human-centered. Lower costs could enable more frequent plan updates, deeper scenario analysis, and planning services for smaller jurisdictions, but government budgets, statutory processes, and finite development activity limit demand expansion. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-enabled analysis and stronger facilitation and judgment skills rather than disappear or expand proportionally with productivity.
fable5_rationale: Much of planners' analytical work — data gathering, GIS analysis, feasibility studies, report writing, zoning code research — is squarely in AI's path and will be heavily automated. However, the core of the job is political and interpersonal: negotiating with elected officials, developers, and residents, running public hearings, and building consensus around contested land-use decisions, which keeps disruption at the top of the moderate band rather than high. Elasticity is low because 84% of planners work in government where headcount is set by budgets and political processes, not by the marginal cost of planning analysis; cheaper analysis does not mean cities approve 10x more plans. The net effect is resilient — AI transforms the analytical toolkit but the stakeholder-facing, judgment-and-legitimacy core of the occupation remains human, though planners who don't adopt AI-driven GIS and analysis tools will lose ground.
grok45_rationale: Core work is predominantly knowledge-based—data analysis from censuses and studies, GIS modeling, feasibility assessments, report writing, and scenario planning—all of which AI already accelerates via automated mapping, predictive simulations, generative design, and document drafting, even as stakeholder meetings, public hearings, and site inspections retain human requirements. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster planning unlocks more detailed climate/housing/transportation studies and better coverage for smaller jurisdictions or private consulting, yet total volume remains constrained by fixed numbers of local governments, political processes, and public budgets rather than expanding unboundedly. This produces a restructure outcome: the occupation persists with substantially shifted skills toward AI orchestration and community facilitation, displacing those who do not adapt while elevating those who do.

title: Veterinarians
claude_rationale: Veterinary work involves substantial hands-on physical examination, surgery, and direct animal interaction that AI cannot replicate, though AI can assist with diagnostics, imaging analysis, and record-keeping. The disruption score of 5 reflects this mixed nature - significant knowledge work components but core tasks requiring physical presence and manual dexterity. Elasticity is high (7) because cheaper diagnostic tools and AI-assisted care could expand access to veterinary services, particularly in underserved areas, and enable more preventive care as costs decrease. However, since disruption remains moderate at 5, this falls into the resilient category where AI enhances rather than reshapes the core occupation.
opus_rationale: The core work of veterinarians is heavily physical and hands-on—examining animals, performing surgery, dressing wounds, vaccinating, and traveling to farms—which AI cannot replace, though AI does assist with diagnosis, imaging interpretation, and treatment recommendations, placing disruption in the moderate range. Demand elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster diagnostics could unlock latent demand (more pet owners pursuing advanced care, more underserved livestock coverage), but physical capacity and the need for in-person animal handling cap expansion. Because disruption remains at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments diagnostic and administrative tasks but does not reshape the fundamentally physical, compassion-driven core of veterinary practice.
opus5_rationale: Veterinary work is fundamentally hands-on: physical examination, surgery, dressing wounds, restraining frightened animals, and traveling to farms cannot be delegated to AI. AI meaningfully assists the diagnostic, imaging-interpretation, recordkeeping, and client-communication portions of the job, so disruption is moderate but not core-reshaping. Elasticity is high because veterinary care is heavily cost-suppressed — many owners forgo diagnostics and advanced procedures on price, and cheaper workups would unlock substantial latent demand, alongside chronic vet shortages especially in rural and food-animal practice. With disruption at 5, the occupation falls into the resilient category: AI improves throughput and diagnostic quality at the periphery while the physical, licensed core remains human.
openai_rationale: Veterinarians perform a mix of physical and cognitive tasks, such as diagnosing and treating animals, performing surgeries, and advising pet owners. While AI can assist with diagnostics and administrative tasks, the hands-on nature of surgeries and treatments limits disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI could make diagnostics faster and cheaper, the need for physical presence in treatment and surgery constrains dramatic demand expansion. Thus, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting but not fundamentally altering the core work.
gpt55_rationale: Veterinary work is a mixed occupation: AI can assist with diagnostic decision support, imaging interpretation, lab result review, records, client communication, and triage, but much of the core work involves hands-on exams, animal handling, surgery, wound care, vaccination, euthanasia, and emotionally sensitive owner interactions. Licensing, liability, and the need to work with unpredictable animals in clinics, farms, and other real-world settings limit full automation over the next decade. Demand has moderate elasticity because high costs currently suppress some pet care, diagnostics, preventive services, and advanced treatments, but total demand is constrained by pet populations, owner budgets, and the physical nature of care delivery. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, AI is more likely to augment veterinarians and clinic workflows than reshape or replace the occupation.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will materially assist with diagnostic reasoning, image interpretation, medical records, treatment planning, and owner communication. However, physical examinations, surgery, procedures, animal handling, emergency care, and emotionally sensitive interactions still require licensed veterinarians on site. Lower costs and faster service could unlock meaningful demand from budget-constrained pet owners and expand preventive care, although animal populations, owner willingness to pay, and clinic capacity limit that expansion. Because AI changes the cognitive portions of the job without replacing its hands-on core, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: Veterinary work is fundamentally hands-on — physical exams, surgery, dental work, euthanasia, and handling unpredictable animals cannot be done by AI, though diagnostic support, imaging interpretation, record-keeping, and client communication will be meaningfully assisted by AI tools (this is the prompt's own benchmark example for moderate disruption). Elasticity is moderate-to-high: pet healthcare demand is clearly cost-suppressed, and cheaper diagnostics and admin efficiency would let more owners pursue advanced care, but the physical clinical bottleneck limits how much throughput AI alone can unlock. Because the core work requires human presence and manual dexterity, the occupation is resilient — AI augments the diagnostic and administrative periphery while the vet's hands-on role remains intact, consistent with BLS's strong projected growth.
grok45_rationale: Core veterinary work centers on physical examination, wound treatment, surgery, vaccination, and handling unpredictable animals, all of which require real-world presence and manual dexterity; AI already assists with imaging analysis, differential diagnosis suggestions, and client communication but leaves the hands-on majority of tasks intact, placing disruption firmly in the moderate range. Demand elasticity is moderate because lower costs and faster throughput would unlock additional preventive visits, advanced procedures for cost-sensitive owners, and expanded livestock/wildlife coverage, yet overall volume remains constrained by the finite pet and farm-animal population and the time still required for physical procedures. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI augments peripheral knowledge work without reshaping the essential in-person clinical role.

claude_rationale: The disruption score is moderate because while AI could assist with some administrative tasks like record-keeping and scheduling, the core work involves direct physical animal care - feeding, bathing, restraining animals, cleaning facilities, and assisting with hands-on medical procedures that require human presence and manual dexterity. opus5_rationale: Core tasks are overwhelmingly physical and hands-on: feeding, bathing, restraining animals, cleaning cages, sterilizing instruments, and post-surgical monitoring. openai_rationale: The core tasks of veterinary assistants and laboratory animal caretakers are predominantly physical and hands-on, such as feeding, bathing, and restraining animals, which limits the impact of AI on these roles. gpt55_rationale: The core work is hands-on animal care: feeding, cleaning cages, restraining animals, moving patients, assisting during procedures, administering medications, and monitoring recovery in unpredictable physical environments. gpt56sol_rationale: Core tasks involve hands-on animal handling, cleaning, restraint, medication, sample collection, and perioperative care in unpredictable physical settings, placing most work beyond near-term AI capabilities. Lower costs could moderately increase veterinary utilization and research capacity, although demand remains constrained by veterinarian availability, facility capacity, and research requirements. fable5_rationale: The core work — feeding, bathing, restraining animals, cleaning kennels, sterilizing instruments, and providing hands-on post-surgical care — is almost entirely physical and requires unpredictable real-world presence with living animals, placing AI's impact at the periphery (perhaps scheduling or record-keeping). opus_rationale: The core work is physical and interpersonal—carrying trays, serving food, reading customers, and providing in-person hospitality—none of which AI can perform; AI touches only peripheral systems like ordering kiosks and point-of-sale technology, which marginally reduce headcount but don't reshape the job. Demand elasticity is low because dining-out volume is constrained by population, disposable income, and the value of human service in restaurants rather than by the cost of order-taking.
