Because disruption stays at or below 6 and the human relationship core remains central, the occupation is resilient—AI reshapes peripheral and administrative tasks but does not transform the fundamental work of consultative selling.
opus5_rationale: Much of the work — prospecting, lead qualification, cold outreach, product Q&A, quote and contract preparation, CRM logging, sales reporting, and follow-up — is language and data work squarely in AI's path, and AI-driven lead scoring, automated outreach and e-commerce ordering already reshape B2B selling; the residual core is relationship-building, in-person negotiation, and trade-show presence, which keeps disruption below the very high band. Elasticity is moderate: total B2B transaction volume is bounded by underlying goods demand rather than by sales-rep cost, so cheaper selling mostly means fewer reps per dollar of revenue, though longer-tail accounts and smaller customers that were previously uneconomic to cover can be served, and reps can carry larger territories. The result is an occupation that persists at roughly flat headcount but with a substantially shifted skill mix — transactional order-taking and inside-sales cold-calling erode toward automation while consultative, technical, and negotiation-heavy roles gain weight. That combination of high task disruption with only partial demand expansion fits restructure.
openai_rationale: The role of wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives involves a mix of digital and interpersonal tasks. AI can assist with customer relationship management, data analysis, and administrative tasks, but the core work of building relationships and negotiating deals remains human-centric, leading to moderate disruption. Demand elasticity is moderate; while AI can enhance productivity, the nature of B2B sales limits how much demand can expand purely due to cost reductions. As such, the occupation is resilient, with AI augmenting rather than replacing human roles.
gpt55_rationale: AI can materially automate or accelerate many core sales-rep tasks: prospect identification, lead scoring, personalized outreach, product explanations, quote generation, CRM updates, follow-ups, and routine order processing. Human reps remain important for complex B2B relationships, technical demonstrations, negotiation, trade shows, and trust-building, but inside sales and lower-complexity product categories are directly exposed to chatbots, self-service portals, and AI sales assistants. Demand elasticity is limited because the underlying demand for wholesale and manufactured goods is not created mainly by the cost of sales labor, and buyers have finite attention for outreach, though AI may expand coverage of small accounts. With high disruption and relatively low demand expansion, productivity gains are likely to reduce the need for many routine sales roles while preserving fewer, more consultative account-management positions.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can automate prospect identification, personalized outreach, product recommendations, quotations, order processing, CRM updates, reporting, and routine customer support, materially reducing the labor required per account. Complex negotiations, technical consultations, trade shows, site visits, and relationship building remain human-intensive, preventing an even higher disruption score. Demand for sales coverage may expand among smaller accounts, but it is constrained by the underlying volume of goods sold and customers’ limited appetite for additional sales contact. Consequently, productivity gains are likely to reduce representative headcount, especially in inside sales and standardized product categories, while preserving more technical and relationship-driven roles.
fable5_rationale: Much of this work — prospecting via directories, cold outreach, answering product questions, preparing quotes and contracts, order processing, sales reporting, and follow-up communication — is digital and language-based, squarely in the path of AI sales agents, chatbots, and B2B e-commerce self-service portals; only the relationship-building field visits for complex or technical products resist automation. Elasticity is low because demand for sales reps is derived from the volume of physical goods traded: making selling 10x cheaper does not make businesses buy meaningfully more industrial equipment, food, or office supplies, so productivity gains flow to fewer reps covering more accounts. The large transactional segment (routine reorders, nontechnical products, inside sales) faces direct headcount contraction as buyers shift to AI-assisted self-service. Relationship-intensive technical sales will persist, but the occupation overall fits 'replace' — high disruption with demand that cannot expand to absorb the productivity gains.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on prospecting, product explanation, negotiation, contract prep, and sales analysis—predominantly cognitive and language-based work where AI tools (lead scoring, generative pitches, CRM automation, chatbots) already deliver material productivity gains, even as outside sales retains some travel and relationship elements. Elasticity is moderate because lower sales costs unlock more outreach and market penetration for manufacturers and wholesalers, yet overall goods demand, online self-service channels, and competitive saturation prevent unlimited expansion. This produces a restructure outcome: the occupation persists but shifts heavily toward AI-augmented complex-deal and relationship skills, displacing those who cannot adapt.

title: Wind turbine technicians
claude_rationale: Wind turbine technicians perform predominantly physical work requiring climbing towers, manual repairs, and hands-on maintenance in challenging outdoor environments that AI cannot replicate. While AI might assist with diagnostic monitoring and data analysis, the core work of physically inspecting, climbing, repairing, and maintaining turbines at heights remains fundamentally human-dependent. The elasticity is high due to rapid expansion of wind energy infrastructure driven by climate goals and energy transition needs - cheaper maintenance could accelerate wind farm deployment. However, with disruption remaining low-to-moderate, this occupation falls into the resilient category where AI enhances peripheral tasks but doesn't reshape the core physical work.
opus_rationale: The core work is intensely physical: climbing 200-foot towers, rappelling to repair blades, lifting heavy parts, and hands-on mechanical/electrical repair in confined spaces—tasks AI cannot perform and only minimally assists via diagnostic monitoring. Elasticity is high because wind energy buildout is driven by surging electricity demand and clean energy policy, so cheaper/faster maintenance would enable more turbines to be deployed and serviced, with BLS projecting 50% employment growth. Despite strong demand growth, the disruption score is low because AI touches only the peripheral diagnostic and recordkeeping portions, leaving the physical core untouched, which places this firmly in the resilient category.
opus5_rationale: The core work is intensely physical — climbing 200+ foot towers, rappelling down blades, working in confined nacelles with hand and power tools — none of which AI can perform. AI touches only the periphery: predictive maintenance analytics from SCADA and sensor data may reorder maintenance schedules and improve diagnostics, plus drone-based inspection reduces some manual inspection time, but the repair itself still requires a human on site. Elasticity is high because demand is driven by electricity demand growth and the installed turbine fleet, not by technician cost; better diagnostics that raise turbine uptime increase the value of maintenance rather than eliminating it, and BLS projects 50% growth. With disruption well under 6, the occupation is resilient regardless of elasticity.
openai_rationale: Wind turbine technicians perform tasks that are predominantly physical and hands-on, such as climbing towers and performing maintenance and repairs on mechanical and electrical systems. AI and automation have limited impact on these core tasks, leading to a low disruption score. However, the demand for wind turbine technicians is expected to grow significantly due to the increasing adoption of wind energy, which is driven by the need for sustainable energy solutions. This results in high demand elasticity, as more wind turbines will require more technicians for maintenance and repair. Therefore, the occupation is resilient to AI disruption, with job growth driven by expanding demand for wind energy.
gpt55_rationale: Wind turbine technicians perform heavily physical, safety-critical work at height, including climbing towers, inspecting equipment, replacing components, and repairing mechanical, electrical, and hydraulic systems. AI can improve remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, fault diagnosis, documentation, scheduling, and drone-based visual inspection, but it does not replace the core hands-on repair and field presence required. Demand is moderately elastic because cheaper maintenance can lower wind power operating costs and support more turbine deployment, but the number of jobs is still constrained by installed turbine capacity, permitting, grid buildout, and physical maintenance needs. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate despite useful AI tools, the occupation is best categorized as resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI can improve remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, fault diagnosis, scheduling, and service documentation. However, the occupation’s core tasks require technicians to travel to turbines, climb towers, inspect equipment, and physically repair complex electrical, mechanical, and hydraulic systems in hazardous environments. Demand can expand as lower maintenance costs support additional wind deployment, although it remains constrained by the number of installed turbines and their service needs. Because AI primarily assists diagnosis and administration rather than replacing hands-on fieldwork, the occupation is resilient.
fable5_rationale: The core work is intensely physical — climbing 200-foot towers, rappelling to blades, replacing heavy components in confined nacelles at remote or offshore sites — which AI cannot perform. AI's role is peripheral: predictive maintenance analytics, remote diagnostics, and drone-based inspections may improve fault detection and reduce unnecessary trips, but a human must still travel to the site to make repairs. Elasticity is moderate-to-high since electricity demand growth and wind buildout (BLS projects 50% employment growth) mean any efficiency gains are readily absorbed by an expanding turbine fleet. With disruption well below 7, this occupation is clearly resilient, and structural demand tailwinds reinforce that.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks center on physical presence—climbing 200+ ft towers, confined-space mechanical/electrical/hydraulic repairs, blade work, and heavy-tool handling in outdoor/offshore conditions—so AI remains peripheral (predictive diagnostics, remote monitoring, data analysis, drone inspections). These tools already assist but do not displace the hands-on work, keeping disruption low. Elasticity is moderate because cheaper, faster maintenance lowers wind LCOE and can accelerate turbine deployment amid energy-transition demand, yet growth is still gated by capital construction, siting, and policy rather than unlimited latent service demand. Net effect is therefore resilient: AI augments efficiency at the margin without reshaping the occupation’s physical core.

title: Woodworkers
claude_rationale: Woodworking remains predominantly physical and hands-on work requiring manual dexterity, physical strength, and real-world problem-solving with materials that vary in grain, density, and characteristics. While CNC machines and computer-controlled equipment assist with precision cutting and shaping, the core tasks still involve physical manipulation of heavy materials, hand-tool work, assembly, finishing, and quality assessment that requires human judgment and tactile feedback. Demand elasticity is constrained by the fact that furniture and cabinet needs are relatively fixed - people don't suddenly buy 10x more cabinets if they become cheaper, and much of the market is driven by replacement cycles and home construction/renovation patterns rather than pure cost sensitivity. The low disruption score keeps this occupation in the resilient category despite moderate demand constraints.
opus_rationale: Woodworking is predominantly physical and hands-on—cutting, shaping, sanding, assembling, finishing wood and handling heavy materials—with AI relevant only to peripheral tasks like blueprint interpretation or CNC programming. The disruption is driven by ongoing CNC automation rather than AI specifically, and core tasks still require human presence, dexterity, and judgment, so the disruption score stays low. Demand for wood products is structurally constrained by raw material costs, physical production limits, and consumer markets, with limited latent demand to unlock if production gets cheaper. Because disruption is well below the threshold, this occupation is resilient—AI touches the periphery but does not reshape the core manual work.
opus5_rationale: Woodworking is predominantly physical: lifting bulky lumber, setting up and tending machines, hand assembly, sanding, staining, and finishing. AI touches only peripheral elements — CAD/design generation, CNC toolpath optimization, nesting/yield software, and quality inspection — while the ongoing automation pressure comes from CNC machinery rather than AI per se. Demand elasticity is low-to-moderate because furniture and cabinetry demand is tied to housing, renovation cycles, and material costs, not to the cost of design or programming labor; cheaper custom design could unlock some latent demand for bespoke cabinetry, but material and installation costs dominate. With disruption well under 7, the occupation is resilient in AI terms, though it continues its slow secular decline from conventional automation and import competition.
openai_rationale: Woodworking involves a significant amount of physical and manual tasks, such as operating machinery and assembling products, which limits the extent to which AI can disrupt core tasks. While CNC machines introduce some automation, the work remains largely hands-on. Demand elasticity is low because the market for wood products is not significantly suppressed by cost; automation primarily reduces labor needs rather than expanding demand. Thus, AI's impact will be peripheral, making the occupation resilient to major AI-driven changes.
gpt55_rationale: Woodworking includes some digital and technical tasks, such as reading drawings, programming or setting up CNC machines, optimizing cuts, and checking specifications, where AI-enabled design, toolpath generation, vision inspection, and maintenance systems can help. However, the core work still involves physical materials, machine tending, lifting, assembly, finishing, safety judgment, and hands-on adjustment to wood variability, so AI changes the periphery more than the center of the occupation. Demand could expand somewhat for cheaper customized cabinets, furniture, renovation products, and small-batch wood goods, but it is constrained by housing activity, durable-goods replacement cycles, material costs, and physical production capacity. Because disruption is moderate rather than high, the occupation is best classified as resilient, even though automation will continue to reduce some routine machine-operator roles.
gpt56sol_rationale: Most core tasks involve physically handling materials, setting up and monitoring machinery, assembling products, finishing surfaces, and making real-world quality and safety judgments. AI can improve design interpretation, CNC programming, inspection, maintenance, and production planning, but broader displacement would require capable robotics and greater factory automation rather than software AI alone. Cheaper production could increase demand for customized furniture, cabinetry, and renovation products, although durable-goods demand and construction activity impose limits, so the occupation remains resilient despite gradual automation.
fable5_rationale: Woodworking is fundamentally physical work — cutting, sanding, assembling, finishing, and handling heavy materials — where AI's direct impact is limited to peripheral tasks like generating CNC programs, interpreting drawings, and design assistance. The larger displacement pressure comes from traditional automation (CNC machines and robotics), not AI language or cognitive tools, which is why disruption scores low. Elasticity is modest: demand for furniture and cabinets is tied to housing and consumer spending, with some latent demand for custom work if design-to-fabrication costs drop, but it won't expand dramatically. With disruption well below 7, the occupation is resilient to AI specifically, though slow structural decline from automation continues.
grok45_rationale: Core woodworking tasks—lifting materials, operating saws/mills/sanders, hand-tool assembly, finishing, and machine maintenance—are predominantly physical and require real-world presence, so AI only peripherally assists via design optimization, CNC programming, or vision-based inspection. Demand for furniture, cabinets, and wood products is constrained by housing stock, renovation cycles, and space rather than pure cost, so even large productivity gains produce limited volume expansion and tend to shrink headcount, consistent with existing automation trends. Because disruption remains low-to-moderate, the occupation is resilient: AI does not reshape the essential hands-on work.

title: Writers and authors
claude_rationale: Writers and authors face very high disruption as their core work—creating written content, developing narratives, and crafting language—is directly in AI's capability path, with AI tools already materially changing how writing is done across all formats from blogs to screenplays. Demand elasticity is high because cheaper, faster content creation unlocks significant latent demand across digital media, marketing, entertainment, and personalized content where cost barriers previously limited production volume. While AI can generate much of the raw content, the combination of high disruption with high elasticity suggests the occupation will be augmented rather than replaced, as expanded content demand absorbs productivity gains.
opus_rationale: Writing is almost entirely a digital, language-based task that sits squarely in the path of generative AI, which already produces drafts, copy, and content at scale — driving a very high disruption score. Demand is moderately elastic: cheaper content unlocks more marketing copy, blogs, and niche material, but prestige work (novels, screenplays, branded voice, original creative vision) and the sheer glut of low-value AI content cap how much human authorship total demand can absorb. Because disruption is very high (>=7) and elasticity is moderate (5), the occupation survives but shifts substantially toward editing, prompting, curation, and high-trust creative/voice work, displacing those who only produce commoditized prose.
opus5_rationale: Writing is the single most directly automatable knowledge task by current LLMs — drafting copy, blog posts, content marketing, summaries, and even fiction outlines are already produced at near-zero marginal cost, so disruption is very high. Elasticity is mixed: total content volume expands enormously and cheap generation unlocks more marketing, localization, and self-publishing, but human attention is a hard cap, commodity content pay collapses, and demand for prestige human-authored work (novels, screenplays, speeches, brand voice) is bounded by audience time and gatekeeping. The result is a bifurcated occupation: high-volume commodity copywriting contracts sharply while roles shift toward prompting, editing, curating, fact-checking, and supplying distinctive voice and credibility. That skill-set migration with only moderate demand absorption fits 'restructure' rather than outright replacement or headcount growth.
openai_rationale: The core tasks of writers and authors, such as content creation, research, and editing, are highly susceptible to AI disruption. AI tools are already capable of generating text, conducting research, and assisting with editing, which significantly impacts the writing process. However, the demand for written content is highly elastic. As AI makes content creation faster and cheaper, the demand for personalized, niche, and high-volume content is likely to expand significantly, especially in digital and self-publishing markets. This combination of high disruption and high elasticity suggests that the occupation will be augmented by AI, with demand expanding to absorb productivity gains.
gpt55_rationale: Writing and authorship are almost entirely language-based, digital, and cognitive tasks, and current AI systems can already draft, revise, summarize research, generate ideas, adapt tone, and produce marketing or informational copy at scale. Human writers remain important for original reporting, lived experience, distinctive voice, client relationships, taste, accountability, and high-end creative work, but the workflow and required skills will change substantially. Demand for written content will expand as cheaper production enables more blogs, newsletters, ads, scripts, self-publishing, localization, and personalized content, but audience attention, brand trust, editorial standards, and fixed media budgets limit how much this expansion translates into more writer headcount. The result is restructuring: many routine writing tasks are automated or compressed, while successful writers increasingly act as editors, creative directors, subject-matter experts, prompt users, and curators of AI-assisted output.
gpt56sol_rationale: Writing is almost entirely digital and language-based, and generative AI already materially accelerates research, ideation, drafting, rewriting, and adaptation across formats. Lower production costs will unlock substantially more personalized marketing, online publishing, self-publishing, and multimedia content, although finite audience attention and demand for trusted human voices limit elasticity. Because output demand should expand significantly while human judgment, originality, source development, and reputational accountability remain valuable, the occupation is likely to be augmented and substantially reshaped rather than broadly eliminated.
fable5_rationale: Writing is almost entirely digital, language-based work that sits directly in the path of large language models — drafting copy, blog posts, marketing content, and even fiction are tasks AI already performs at commercially usable quality, driving a disruption score of 9. While total demand for written content will expand as production costs collapse, much of that expanded output can be generated by AI directly or by non-writers using AI tools, meaning the marginal demand does not flow back to professional human writers; commodity segments like content writing and copywriting face outright substitution, keeping elasticity low at 3. Some premium demand persists for distinctive voice, brand-name authors, and high-stakes creative work (screenwriting, speechwriting), but this is too small a share to offset contraction in the bulk of the occupation. High disruption combined with low effective elasticity for human labor places this occupation in the replace category.
grok45_rationale: Core tasks of writers and authors—researching, drafting, revising, and producing language-based content for books, ads, scripts, blogs, and more—are almost entirely digital and cognitive, placing them squarely in AI's path; generative models already produce usable drafts and outlines that materially change daily workflows. Demand elasticity is high because content production has long been constrained by cost and time: dramatically cheaper writing unlocks far more marketing copy, self-published books, personalized content, scripts, and online material that businesses and individuals previously forwent. Productivity gains are therefore absorbed by expanded total output rather than pure headcount reduction, allowing adaptable writers who leverage AI to produce substantially more. This combination of high disruption and high elasticity fits the augment category.

title: Zoologists and wildlife biologists
claude_rationale: Disruption is moderate because while AI can assist with data analysis, modeling, and report writing, the core work requires extensive fieldwork, direct animal observation, specimen collection, and hands-on research in natural environments that AI cannot replace. Elasticity is low because demand for wildlife research is primarily driven by conservation needs and government funding rather than cost considerations - making research 10x cheaper wouldn't dramatically expand the number of species studied or conservation projects undertaken due to regulatory and budgetary constraints. The net effect is resilient since AI touches peripheral tasks but doesn't reshape the fundamentally field-based, observational nature of the work.
opus_rationale: The work splits between cognitive tasks (data analysis, GIS modeling, writing papers, population forecasting) where AI offers meaningful assistance, and irreducible physical fieldwork (collecting specimens, handling wildlife, observing animals in remote habitats) that requires human presence. AI accelerates the analytical and reporting portions but the core research still demands on-site data collection and expert judgment, placing disruption at a moderate 5. Demand is highly inelastic because employment is constrained by government and grant budgets rather than cost or speed of output—cheaper analysis won't dramatically expand the number of funded conservation positions. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI touches the periphery and analytical tools without reshaping the fundamentally field-based, judgment-driven core.
opus5_rationale: A substantial share of the work is fieldwork — capturing, handling, and observing animals in remote terrain, collecting specimens, and running lab tests — which AI cannot perform, though AI-assisted camera-trap/bioacoustic identification, GIS modeling, population estimation, and literature/report writing already materially speed the analytical and documentation half of the job. That mix puts disruption in the moderate range: the core scientific judgment and field presence remain human, but data processing is being transformed. Elasticity is low because roughly 69% of employment is government-funded and demand is capped by appropriations and conservation budgets rather than by the cost of analysis; cheaper monitoring yields more data per biologist, not many more biologist positions. With disruption at or below 6, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes tools and workflows at the periphery while headcount stays roughly flat, as BLS projections suggest.
openai_rationale: Zoologists and wildlife biologists perform a mix of fieldwork and data analysis, with AI potentially aiding in data collection and analysis tasks. However, the core tasks of observing and interacting with wildlife in natural settings remain largely unaffected by AI. Thus, disruption is moderate. Demand elasticity is low because the work is often constrained by funding and regulatory factors, limiting the potential for demand expansion even if productivity increases. Therefore, the occupation is resilient, as AI will augment some tasks but not fundamentally change the nature of the work.
gpt55_rationale: AI will materially affect the analytical and documentation-heavy parts of this occupation, including GIS modeling, population estimation, literature review, statistical analysis, image/acoustic species identification, and report writing. However, a large share of core work still involves field observation, specimen collection, animal handling, ecological context, remote travel, and coordination with agencies and conservation stakeholders, which limits full automation. Demand could expand somewhat because cheaper monitoring and modeling would make more habitats and species feasible to study, but employment is heavily constrained by government and nonprofit budgets, permitting, and policy priorities. Because disruption is meaningful but not high enough to reshape the entire occupation, the net effect is resilient.
gpt56sol_rationale: AI will substantially accelerate species identification, camera and acoustic monitoring, GIS analysis, population modeling, literature review, and report writing. However, field observation, specimen collection, animal handling, experimental design, and context-sensitive conservation decisions still require substantial human presence and expertise. Cheaper analysis and monitoring could expand ecological research across more species and habitats, but government funding constraints and limited conservation budgets cap that expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although its analytical workflows will become significantly more AI-enabled.
fable5_rationale: The occupation is a genuine mix: data analysis, population modeling, GIS work, and report writing are squarely in AI's path (and AI-powered camera traps, acoustic monitoring, and image classification are already transforming wildlife data collection), but core fieldwork — handling animals, traveling to remote habitats, conducting physical sampling — requires human presence in unpredictable outdoor environments. Elasticity is low because ~69% of employment is government-funded, and demand is set by agency budgets and conservation policy rather than by cost or speed of the science; cheaper analysis will not translate into proportionally more funded positions. With moderate disruption and budget-capped demand, the occupation is resilient: AI reshapes the analytical portion of the work but does not displace the field-based core, and headcount will remain roughly flat as BLS projects.
grok45_rationale: Core duties center on fieldwork, specimen collection, animal handling, and on-site observation in remote or unpredictable habitats, which remain physical and presence-dependent; AI already aids modeling, GIS analysis, population estimation, and report writing but does not displace these foundational tasks, yielding only moderate disruption. Demand is largely government- and grant-funded with structural budget ceilings, so productivity gains from cheaper analysis or monitoring expand output only modestly rather than unlocking large latent markets. Because disruption stays at or below the moderate threshold, the occupation is resilient: AI touches analytical edges without reshaping the essential human role in wildlife study and conservation.
